arguments.markdown:
Tesla's reported segments describe a vehicle business earning an 18.1% gross margin that does not cover group research and development and selling costs, a storage business and a services business that together earn the group's operating profit, and a third quarter of 2026 in which both of those profit pools were helped by tariff refunds and warranty true-ups — so the return is earned on storage and on the cash pile, not on the car.

### Three segments, three different ways of getting paid

The automotive segment took 73.3% of third-quarter 2026 revenue ($20,560M of $28,046M), services and other 16.4% ($4,605M) and energy generation and storage 10.3% ($2,881M). The buyer differs in each. A retail or fleet customer pays cash or finances a car when control transfers; an energy customer — a utility, developer or data-centre operator — pays on project milestones and takes delivery across quarters; a service customer pays per transaction for collision repair, maintenance or a Supercharging session; and another automaker pays for regulatory credits at transfer of title, against negligible incremental cost. The mix has moved: energy was 6.2% of FY2023 revenue ($6,035M) and 13.5% in FY2025 ($12,771M), while automotive revenue fell from $82,419M to $69,526M. The only recurring software charge is FSD (Supervised) at $99 a month, with 1.74 million active subscriptions on 2026-09-30 against 1.04 million a year earlier [S8, S1, S121].

### The vehicle does not pay for the research budget

::: unit_economics
| Per vehicle delivered, Q3 2026 | USD | Note | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive revenue | 42,259 | $20,560M ÷ 486,532 deliveries | S9 |
| Cost of automotive revenue | (34,436) | materials, labour, overhead, warranty, tariffs | S8 |
| Automotive gross profit | 7,823 | 18.5% margin | S8 |
| Regulatory credits inside that profit | 232 | $113M ÷ 486,532; no matching cost | S8 |
| Automotive gross profit excluding credits | 7,590 | 18.1% of $20,447M ex-credit revenue | S8 |
| Group R&D and SG&A per vehicle | (9,817) | $4,776M ÷ 486,532, all charged to the car here | S9 |
| Automotive-only operating contribution | (1,994) | a loss before energy and services | derived |
| Energy and services gross profit per vehicle | 3,470 | $1,688M ÷ 486,532 | S8 |
| Group operating profit per vehicle | 1,476 | $718M ÷ 486,532 | S9 |
| Interest income per vehicle | 915 | $445M ÷ 486,532 | S8 |
| Pre-tax profit per vehicle | 1,965 | $956M ÷ 486,532 | S8 |
:::

The waterfall is the section's central fact: a delivered car carried $42,259 of automotive revenue and $34,436 of automotive cost, leaving $7,823 of gross profit, or $7,590 once regulatory credits are removed; spreading $4,776M of group research and development and selling cost over 486,532 deliveries costs $9,817 a vehicle, so the automotive line alone runs at roughly -$1,994 a vehicle. Energy and services add $3,470 a vehicle and turn that into $1,476 of group operating profit and, with $445M of interest income, $1,965 of pre-tax profit per vehicle. Cost per vehicle was $33,666 in Q4 2025, $35,786 in Q1 2026 and $34,436 in Q3 2026, so unit cost is not falling; the improvement in ex-credit automotive margin from 15.4% to 18.1% year on year arrived with a richer Asia-Pacific delivery mix in Q3 2026 rather than from the factory [S9, S8].

::: evidence
**Regulatory credits have stopped being the automotive margin, and nothing else has replaced them at the same price.**

Quarterly credit revenue fell from $542M in Q4 2025 to $380M in Q1 2026, $146M in Q2 2026 and $113M in Q3 2026, an 87% fall in three quarters, after $1,993M in FY2025 and $2,763M in FY2024 [S8, S83, S1]. Because credits cost almost nothing to produce, they were 45.8% of FY2025 operating income and 15.7% of the Q3 2026 figure; the line is now too small to swing a twelve-month forecast, which is why the question has moved from what happens when credits fall to what the car earns without them. Toyota and Stellantis left Tesla's European CO2 pool for the 2026 compliance year, with Subaru also reported out, and UBS put the pool at more than €1 billion of annual revenue [S123]. Tesla names no credit buyer in its filings and records no material deferred revenue against credits, so the remaining contracted volume cannot be verified.
:::

### Storage earns the best margin and the least predictable one

Energy generation and storage produced $954M of gross profit on $2,881M of revenue in Q3 2026 (33.1%), after 20.4% in Q2 2026 and 39.5% in Q1 2026. Revenue per GWh deployed fell from $274 per kWh in Q1 2026 to $210 per kWh in Q3 2026, and gross profit per kWh went from $108 to $47 to $70 across the three quarters. The segment is priced per project and per kWh, so margin moves with Megapack pricing, cell cost, tariff recoveries and warranty true-ups, and deployments land unevenly ($2,408M of revenue on 8.8 GWh in Q1 2026 against $2,881M on 13.7 GWh in Q3 2026). Services and other grew revenue 33% year on year to $4,605M and lifted gross profit to $734M, a 15.9% margin against 10.5% in Q3 2025 and an all-time high. The lines behind it are used-vehicle sales, collision and non-warranty maintenance, paid Supercharging across 8,904 stations and 84,465 connectors, and Tesla's insurance book — a mix of parts-and-labour businesses whose costs are largely variable over a charging network whose costs are largely fixed, so utilisation lifts the marginal margin. Rivian's software and services segment earned 42% on $605M of revenue in the same quarter, so Tesla's margin is well below the best comparable but on 7.6 times the revenue. Services now supplies 13.4% of group gross profit from 16.4% of revenue [S9, S120].

### What breaks even, and what cannot be measured

At Q3 2026 unit economics and constant group cost, the automotive line covers its share of the group only at about 611,000 deliveries a quarter, 26% above the 486,532 actually delivered. Tesla discloses no customer-acquisition cost — there is no marketing line in the statements, a sign of demand generated through FSD and owner referral rather than purchased — so SG&A at 7.2% of revenue is the nearest proxy and a CAC payback or LTV:CAC ratio cannot be computed from the filings; that limit matters, because the claim that Tesla acquires buyers more cheaply than Ford or GM is untested. The one disclosed software metric that would change this — an FSD attach rate above 75% of new North American deliveries — comes with no revenue figure, so the software margin remains an assertion rather than a measured unit economic [S115, S116, S119, S117].

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's strategy is no longer self-funded, and the filings now say so. With 2026 capital expenditure guided above $20 billion against $15.0 billion of trailing Adjusted EBITDA (Q4 2025 to Q3 2026), Tesla signed three credit agreements totalling $30 billion in September 2026 and states that heightened capital spending "will necessitate additional funding beyond our operating cash flow" [S8]. That sentence, not the robotaxi narrative, is the strategy disclosure that matters for the next twelve months: the autonomy, energy and robotics options are now financed partly with balance-sheet capacity.

### The plan has three pillars and one new capital sink

The stated plan, carried in the 10-K and in the 2025 CEO Performance Award, is to convert a hardware business into an autonomy and robotics business: FSD (Supervised) and Robotaxi, energy storage, and Optimus, funded by a vehicle business that delivered 1.32 million units in the first nine months of 2026 [S10]. What is new is the depth of vertical integration behind it — 225+ MW of training compute, an in-house inference chip, a Samsung foundry collaboration and a company semiconductor fab commissioning equipment in 2027 — which turns a software roadmap into a fixed-cost programme closer to a foundry than to an automaker.

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Robotaxi at commercial scale (1 million in operation, per the 2025 award) | No public date | 300+ Cybercabs claimed in Austin; 349 Texas registrations at 2026-10-15 | Whether autonomy has revenue at scale | S10, S9, S101 |
| Cybercab start of production | 1H 2026 (stated 2026-01) | Rides began 2026-09-03; 125,000+ capacity listed | Execution on the purpose-built robotaxi | S60, S9 |
| Tesla Semi volume production | 1H 2026 | Volume production began Q3 2026 | Heavy-truck adjacency | S60, S9 |
| Optimus Gen 3 start of production | Before end-2026 (stated 2026-01) | Production began at Fremont in Q3 2026 | Robotics credibility | S60, S9 |
| Megapack 3 and Megablock at Megafactory Houston | 2026 | Texas Megafactory began production Q3 2026 at 50 GWh planned; product-level start not disclosed | Energy as a genuine second engine | S60, S9 |
| Fully dry-electrode 4680 cells | Disclosed as achieved 2026-01 | Both electrodes made in Austin; 40+ GWh Texas capacity | Battery cost advantage | S60 |
| 400 MW of AI training compute | End-2026 | 225+ MW installed at Q3 2026 | Compute self-sufficiency | S9 |
| California driverless deployment permit | No public target | Not held at 2026-10-23; testing permit with driver only | Geographic expansion beyond Texas | S89 |

### The track record is mixed, and the split is informative

Energy and manufacturing promises have largely been kept: Megafactory Texas started production in Q3 2026, Optimus production began in Fremont ahead of the January 2026 target to start before the end of 2026, and 36.0 GWh of storage was deployed in nine months against 46.7 GWh for all of 2025. Autonomy promises have not: the 2025 award still lists "1 million Robotaxis in commercial operation" and "10 million active FSD subscriptions" as unmet operational milestones, against 300+ claimed Cybercabs and 1.74 million subscriptions, and none of the 423.7 million shares has been earned because the first tranche also needs $2.0 trillion of market capitalisation plus one operational milestone [S9, S10]. The pattern is that Tesla ships physical products within a quarter or two of plan and ships software-defined promises years late — which is why the robotaxi timeline should be discounted but the Megapack and Semi timelines should not.

### Resources fit the plan only at the low end

Nine-month capex of $13.01 billion against guidance of "in excess of $20 billion" leaves $7.0 billion for the fourth quarter, after a Q2 spike of $5.79 billion; the guidance was cut from "more than $25 billion" in the 10-Q rather than in the shareholder letter. Free cash flow of $1.53 billion in Q3 2026 depended on $2.59 billion of working-capital inflow, and $3.67 billion of equipment and construction spend sat unpaid in liabilities. Against that, $45.45 billion of cash and $30 billion of undrawn facilities mean the plan is affordable — just not self-funded. The mechanism matters: borrowing to fund a call option on autonomy converts equity risk into refinancing risk, and the return on that borrowing depends on Robotaxi revenue the company does not yet disclose, so the cost of the strategy now appears in interest and covenants rather than in a share count.

| Partner or counterparty | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Samsung | US manufacturing of semiconductors for AI inference and training | 2025 | In progress; Austin fab equipment commissioning 2027 | S1, S9 |
| SpaceX (related party) | Megapack purchases; $626m of energy revenue in 9M 2026 | Ongoing | $588m of the $729m receivable for undelivered Megapacks | S8 |
| xAI | Grok in-cabin assistant deployed in Cybercab | 2026 | Live; Tesla holds under 1% of SpaceX after a $2.0bn March 2026 investment | S9, S8 |
| Cell suppliers | Purchased lithium-ion cells for vehicles and storage | Not disclosed | Battery availability remains the limiting factor on vehicle output | S9 |

The related-party lines deserve emphasis. SpaceX bought $626 million of Megapacks in the first nine months of 2026, 7.4% of $8.43 billion of energy revenue, and $588 million of the receivable was billed for units not yet delivered — revenue quality a third-party backlog would not show. Tesla also invested $2.0 billion in SpaceX common stock in March 2026 and holds under 1% of the company [S8]. That is capital allocation and customer concentration inside the second engine, and it means the energy story is more dependent on one related buyer than the order-rate language implies.

### What the second curves are actually worth

Energy is the one adjacency already at scale and profitable: 13.7 GWh deployed in Q3 2026 alone, 50 GWh of new Texas capacity and record order rates, which is why it deserves to be valued as a business with a discount for the related-party share. Robotaxi is an option whose value is capped by permits and by the federal safety file rather than by manufacturing capacity — 300+ claimed Cybercabs is a pilot, and neither trips nor revenue are disclosed inside $4.605 billion of services revenue. Optimus is further still, with zero external sales and no published throughput, and the semiconductor fab adds a foundry's fixed-cost risk to a company already guiding more than $20 billion of capex. Margins carry the bill: Q3 2026 operating income was $718 million on $28.05 billion of revenue, a 2.6% operating margin, while regulatory credits, the highest-margin revenue line, fell from $2.76 billion in 2024 to $1.99 billion in 2025 [S1, S9]. For an investor this is the crux — the plan's returns sit in businesses with no disclosed revenue, while its costs land on a 2.6%-margin income statement.

### What must be true in twelve months

Three things must hold for the strategy to stay credible without new equity: Robotaxi revenue must be disclosed as its own line with paid trips growing outside Texas; capex must land at or below the guided floor with free cash flow positive before working-capital swings; and energy must keep compounding with third-party demand large enough to absorb the new capacity. The signposts are a California driverless deployment permit, a quarterly Robotaxi revenue disclosure, the close or escalation of NHTSA's EA26002, and whether the credit facilities are drawn at all. If all four move positively, the strategy is self-sustaining on debt and the option value is real; if none does, the company is borrowing against a low-margin auto business to fund revenue it cannot yet show, and the right posture is to wait for the Robotaxi line rather than pay for it in advance.

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's strategy is no longer self-funded, and the filings now say so. With 2026 capital expenditure guided above $20 billion against $15.0 billion of trailing Adjusted EBITDA (Q4 2025 to Q3 2026), Tesla signed three credit agreements totalling $30 billion in September 2026 and states that heightened capital spending "will necessitate additional funding beyond our operating cash flow" [S8]. That sentence, not the robotaxi narrative, is the strategy disclosure that matters for the next twelve months: the autonomy, energy and robotics options are now financed partly with balance-sheet capacity.

### The plan has three pillars and one new capital sink

The stated plan, carried in the 10-K and in the 2025 CEO Performance Award, is to convert a hardware business into an autonomy and robotics business: FSD (Supervised) and Robotaxi, energy storage, and Optimus, funded by a vehicle business that delivered 1.32 million units in the first nine months of 2026 [S10]. What is new is the depth of vertical integration behind it — 225+ MW of training compute, an in-house inference chip, a Samsung foundry collaboration and a company semiconductor fab commissioning equipment in 2027 — which turns a software roadmap into a fixed-cost programme closer to a foundry than to an automaker.

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Robotaxi at commercial scale (1 million in operation, per the 2025 award) | No public date | 300+ Cybercabs claimed in Austin; 349 Texas registrations at 2026-10-15 | Whether autonomy has revenue at scale | S10, S9, S101 |
| Cybercab start of production | 1H 2026 (stated 2026-01) | Rides began 2026-09-03; 125,000+ capacity listed | Execution on the purpose-built robotaxi | S60, S9 |
| Tesla Semi volume production | 1H 2026 | Volume production began Q3 2026 | Heavy-truck adjacency | S60, S9 |
| Optimus Gen 3 start of production | Before end-2026 (stated 2026-01) | Production began at Fremont in Q3 2026 | Robotics credibility | S60, S9 |
| Megapack 3 and Megablock at Megafactory Houston | 2026 | Texas Megafactory began production Q3 2026 at 50 GWh planned; product-level start not disclosed | Energy as a genuine second engine | S60, S9 |
| Fully dry-electrode 4680 cells | Disclosed as achieved 2026-01 | Both electrodes made in Austin; 40+ GWh Texas capacity | Battery cost advantage | S60 |
| 400 MW of AI training compute | End-2026 | 225+ MW installed at Q3 2026 | Compute self-sufficiency | S9 |
| California driverless deployment permit | No public target | Not held at 2026-10-23; testing permit with driver only | Geographic expansion beyond Texas | S89 |

### The track record is mixed, and the split is informative

Energy and manufacturing promises have largely been kept: Megafactory Texas started production in Q3 2026, Optimus production began in Fremont ahead of the January 2026 target to start before the end of 2026, and 36.0 GWh of storage was deployed in nine months against 46.7 GWh for all of 2025. Autonomy promises have not: the 2025 award still lists "1 million Robotaxis in commercial operation" and "10 million active FSD subscriptions" as unmet operational milestones, against 300+ claimed Cybercabs and 1.74 million subscriptions, and none of the 423.7 million shares has been earned because the first tranche also needs $2.0 trillion of market capitalisation plus one operational milestone [S9, S10]. The pattern is that Tesla ships physical products within a quarter or two of plan and ships software-defined promises years late — which is why the robotaxi timeline should be discounted but the Megapack and Semi timelines should not.

### Resources fit the plan only at the low end

Nine-month capex of $13.01 billion against guidance of "in excess of $20 billion" leaves $7.0 billion for the fourth quarter, after a Q2 spike of $5.79 billion; the guidance was cut from "more than $25 billion" in the 10-Q rather than in the shareholder letter. Free cash flow of $1.53 billion in Q3 2026 depended on $2.59 billion of working-capital inflow, and $3.67 billion of equipment and construction spend sat unpaid in liabilities. Against that, $45.45 billion of cash and $30 billion of undrawn facilities mean the plan is affordable — just not self-funded [S8, S102]. The mechanism matters: borrowing to fund a call option on autonomy converts equity risk into refinancing risk, and the return on that borrowing depends on Robotaxi revenue the company does not yet disclose, so the cost of the strategy now appears in interest and covenants rather than in a share count.

| Partner or counterparty | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Samsung | US manufacturing of semiconductors for AI inference and training | 2025 | In progress; Austin fab equipment commissioning 2027 | S1, S9 |
| SpaceX (related party) | Megapack purchases; $626m of energy revenue in 9M 2026 | Ongoing | $588m of the $729m receivable for undelivered Megapacks | S8 |
| xAI | Grok in-cabin assistant deployed in Cybercab | 2026 | Live; Tesla holds under 1% of SpaceX after a $2.0bn March 2026 investment | S9, S8 |
| Cell suppliers | Purchased lithium-ion cells for vehicles and storage | Not disclosed | Battery availability remains the limiting factor on vehicle output | S9 |

The related-party lines deserve emphasis. SpaceX bought $626 million of Megapacks in the first nine months of 2026, 7.4% of $8.43 billion of energy revenue, and $588 million of the receivable was billed for units not yet delivered — revenue quality a third-party backlog would not show. Tesla also invested $2.0 billion in SpaceX common stock in March 2026 and holds under 1% of the company [S8]. That is capital allocation and customer concentration inside the second engine, and it means the energy story is more dependent on one related buyer than the order-rate language implies.

### What the second curves are actually worth

Energy is the one adjacency already at scale and profitable: 13.7 GWh deployed in Q3 2026 alone, 50 GWh of new Texas capacity and record order rates, which is why it deserves to be valued as a business with a discount for the related-party share. Robotaxi is an option whose value is capped by permits and by the federal safety file rather than by manufacturing capacity — 300+ claimed Cybercabs is a pilot, and neither trips nor revenue are disclosed inside $4.605 billion of services revenue. Optimus is further still, with zero external sales and no published throughput, and the semiconductor fab adds a foundry's fixed-cost risk to a company already guiding more than $20 billion of capex. Margins carry the bill: Q3 2026 operating income was $718 million on $28.05 billion of revenue, a 2.6% operating margin, while regulatory credits, the highest-margin revenue line, fell from $2.76 billion in 2024 to $1.99 billion in 2025 [S1, S9]. For an investor this is the crux — the plan's returns sit in businesses with no disclosed revenue, while its costs land on a 2.6%-margin income statement.

### What must be true in twelve months

Three things must hold for the strategy to stay credible without new equity: Robotaxi revenue must be disclosed as its own line with paid trips growing outside Texas; capex must land at or below the guided floor with free cash flow positive before working-capital swings; and energy must keep compounding with third-party demand large enough to absorb the new capacity. The signposts are a California driverless deployment permit, a quarterly Robotaxi revenue disclosure, the close or escalation of NHTSA's EA26002, and whether the credit facilities are drawn at all. If all four move positively, the strategy is self-sustaining on debt and the option value is real; if none does, the company is borrowing against a low-margin auto business to fund revenue it cannot yet show, and the right posture is to wait for the Robotaxi line rather than pay for it in advance.

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's board is majority independent on paper, but the three decisions that mattered in 2024-2026 — a $2.0bn investment in the CEO's own AI company after shareholders rejected the measure, a pay award that can reach 423.7m shares, and the retention of a classified board — all went against the minority's expressed preference, so key-person and capital-allocation risk are real, formally disclosed, and only partly offset by the award's extreme vesting gates [S10].

### Independence is not the same as accountability

Nine directors sit on the board, seven of them independent under Nasdaq rules, with Robyn Denholm as independent chair since November 2018 and all four committees composed solely of independents. The structure that matters is elsewhere: three staggered classes with three-year terms, supermajority voting requirements that a 2025 management proposal failed to remove with 39.4% of shares outstanding in favour, and two family directors — Elon and Kimbal Musk — in the room. Compensation Committee chair Ira Ehrenpreis has also served on SpaceX's board since February 2026, the counterparty to Tesla's $2.0bn investment and $143.3m of 2025 revenue, a relationship the proxy deems immaterial without quantifying it [S10, S114].

### Pay is gated on market value, not on operating return

The 2025 CEO Performance Award is 423,743,904 shares in 12 equal tranches. Each tranche needs a market-capitalisation milestone first — from $2 trillion, 26.6% above the 2026-10-30 value, through nine $500bn and two $1tn steps to $8.5 trillion — and one of 12 operational milestones: four strategic-product goals (10m active FSD subscriptions, 1m bots delivered, 1m Robotaxis in commercial operation among them) or eight Adjusted EBITDA goals. Each earned share carries a $334.09 offset and a five-year hold, and tranches 11 and 12 also require a board-approved CEO succession framework, the only formal succession mechanism disclosed. Against that, General Motors paid Mary Barra $48.2m of realized compensation in 2025, and Musk has taken no salary since 2019 and has no employment agreement or severance; reported 2025 total compensation of $158.36bn was an accounting value, with realized pay at $0 [S10, S107, S109].

### The xAI vote is the test the board failed

At the 2025-11-06 meeting shareholders approved the pay award with 1,892,235,822 votes for, 564,940,908 against and 12,227,846 abstentions, 76.6% of votes cast, with 302,456,274 broker non-votes. A separate non-binding measure authorising funding for xAI drew 1.06bn votes for and 916.3m against but was recorded as rejected because Tesla's bylaws count abstentions as votes against; on 2026-01-16 the company nonetheless agreed to invest $2.0bn in xAI, completing on 2026-03-12 as SpaceX Class A stock after the SpaceX-xAI merger. The Audit Committee reviews related-person transactions above $120,000 under a written policy, but the sequence shows the review is procedural: a holder should assume future flows to Musk-controlled companies are a board decision, not a shareholder one [S59, S104, S105].

### One person carries the strategy; the bench is uneven

The 10-K says Musk "does not devote his full time and attention to Tesla" and lists management roles at SpaceX, xAI, Neuralink and The Boring Company, while the proxy records that xAI became a SpaceX subsidiary in February 2026 and that Musk is SpaceX's CEO, CTO and chairman. The operating bench is strongest in manufacturing and finance: Tom Zhu, SVP APAC and global vehicle manufacturing since June 2025, joined in 2014 and built Gigafactory Shanghai; Vaibhav Taneja has been CFO since August 2023 and inside Tesla's finance function since 2017. Demand execution is the weak spot: Omead Afshar left in June 2025, Troy Jones was dismissed as head of North American sales in July 2025, the North American service head left in August 2025 and Raj Jegannathan departed in February 2026 after 13 years. Headcount was 134,785 at 2025-12-31, so the departures are senior-level attrition, not a shrinking company [S1, S111, S124].

### What the record confirms, and what diligence must settle

Public records confirm the founder-market fit: Musk co-founded Zip2 (sold to Compaq in 1999) and PayPal (sold to eBay in 2002), has run Tesla since October 2008, and still owns 19.8% with 207,498,721 shares pledged. They also confirm the concentration: no chief operating officer, no permanent North American sales leader, a board with no automotive-OEM operating director, and a CEO whose other companies are now suppliers, investees and counterparties. The gaps a diligence team should close are the succession plan behind tranches 11-12, the terms and lenders behind the pledge, the fairness opinion, if any, for the $2.0bn xAI/SpaceX purchase, and references on Zhu and Taneja from SolarCity and Shanghai. The evidence supports a governance discount rather than a veto: incentives are aligned with the share price, but the holder is paying $1.58 trillion for a company whose key decisions are made by one person and ratified by a board the holder cannot replace [S10, S2].

::: evidence
**The strongest proof of execution is a manufacturing ramp the founder did not personally run; the strongest doubt is a board that proceeded with a related-party investment after shareholders rejected it.**

Tom Zhu built Gigafactory Shanghai, the largest plant in the system at more than 950,000 units, and Berlin set a quarterly production record in Q3 2026; Tesla passed 10.2m cumulative vehicles. The counterweight is procedural: an xAI funding measure lost on a 1.06bn-to-916.3m vote, yet $2.0bn was committed five weeks later, and the Compensation Committee chair sits on SpaceX's board [S9, S104, S10].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's technology position in 2026 is two facts usually merged in the narrative: the largest supervised-driving data pool and one of the cheapest large-scale EV manufacturing bases in the industry, and almost no verified driverless revenue. Active FSD subscriptions reached 1.74 million at 30 September 2026 against 10.2 million vehicles delivered to date — 17.1% of the lifetime fleet, up from 12.4% at 31 December 2025 — while cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles were "nearly two million", 1.2% of the 170 million-plus rider-only miles Waymo reports [S9]. That gap, not the subscription count, is what twelve months must close.

### What Tesla actually sells

| Product | Stage | Revenue or share | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FSD (Supervised) | Commercial, 9 EU countries | 1.74m subscriptions; revenue not disclosed | Unsupervised release | S9, S1 |
| Robotaxi / Cybercab | Commercial in Texas metros | Not disclosed inside $4.605bn services | Paid-trip disclosure | S9 |
| Model 3 / Model Y | Mature | 478,237 units, Q3 2026; 19.6% group gross margin | Next-gen platform | S9 |
| Cybertruck, Semi, Roadster | Ramp / design | 8,295 other-model units, Q3 2026 | Semi ramp; Roadster launch | S9 |
| Megapack, Powerwall | Scaling | $2.881bn in Q3 2026; 13.7 GWh | 50 GWh Texas ramp | S9, S60 |
| Optimus | Internal production | Zero external revenue | External pilot sale | S9, S99 |

### Mechanism: end-to-end vision and a one-sided flywheel

Tesla removed radar and now maps camera pixels directly to driving commands with an end-to-end neural network, trained on clips harvested from the fleet and run on in-house inference silicon. Training sits on Cortex 1 at more than 105 MW and Cortex 2 at more than 120 MW, with a 400 MW target by end-2026 and a company fab commissioning equipment in 2027 [S60]. The flywheel is real but overwhelmingly *supervised*: the Q3 2026 update charts cumulative FSD miles on a 0-16 billion axis, against 2.0 million unsupervised miles. Supervised miles teach perception; they do not certify that the network can be left alone, which is why the federal safety file matters more than the mileage chart.

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active FSD subscriptions | 1.74m (2026-09-30) | Company count | S9 |
| FSD penetration of fleet | 17.1% | 1.74m / 10.2m deliveries | S9 |
| Cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles | 2.0m, 8x QoQ | Company count | S9 |
| Installed AI training compute | 225+ MW | Company nameplate | S9 |
| 4680 capacity, Texas | 40+ GWh/yr, dry electrode both sides | Company nameplate | S60 |
| Storage deployed | 13.7 GWh Q3; 36.0 GWh 9M | Company deliveries | S9 |
| Optimus units in service | 1,000-1,200 | Independent estimate | S99 |

### The safety file is the binding constraint

NHTSA's Office of Defects Investigation opened Engineering Analysis EA26002 on 18 March 2026 into whether FSD detects degraded visibility — glare, fog, dust — and warns the driver in time, covering an estimated 3,203,754 vehicles from model years 2016-2026, after nine confirmed incidents including one pedestrian fatality; two further FSD probes remain open, one on traffic-law violations across 2,882,566 vehicles with 80 incidents [S87]. Tesla's own analysis reportedly found its degradation-detection update "may have affected" only 3 of 9 incidents, which points to an architectural limit of camera-only sensing rather than a tuning defect. An engineering analysis is the last step before a recall; a recall would narrow the operating domain or force hardware across millions of cars, at a company that self-insures product liability.

::: evidence
**The camera-only bet is being tested by the regulator, not the market.** EA26002 covers 3.2 million FSD-equipped vehicles and Tesla's fix reportedly addresses a third of the reviewed incidents [S87, S88, S100]. The filings confirm the investigation but give no remedy or timetable, which is the largest un-priced technical risk in the autonomy option.
:::

### Comparison: three different autonomy businesses

| Dimension | Tesla | Waymo | Chinese L3 OEMs | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sensing | Camera-only, in-house chip | Lidar + radar + camera | Camera + lidar, Nvidia compute | S9, S101 |
| Verified driverless scale | 2.0m cumulative miles | 170m+ rider-only miles; 500,000 paid rides/week | L3 conditional approvals since 2025-12 | S101, S103 |
| Regulatory position | Paid driverless in Texas under SB 2807 and TxDMV authorisation (required from 2026-05-28); California paid rides on a limousine permit, no autonomous-service authorisation | California deployment authorised | MIIT eight-department L3 pilot | S89, S90, S91 |
| Cost model | Owned fleet, self-insured | Owned fleet, partner-owned vehicles | Consumer cars, driver liable | S89, S103 |

### Moat: accumulation, not exclusion

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Supervised fleet data | 8 | 10.2m cars; FSD miles charted to 16bn | 4-6 years | S9 |
| Driverless operating experience | 5 | 2.0m unsupervised miles only | 2-3 years | S9 |
| Dry-electrode cell process | 7 | Battery Day 2020 to Austin output in 2026 | 3-4 years | S60 |
| Manufacturing and integration | 8 | 134,785 employees; cells, cathode, refining in-house | 5+ years | S1 |
| Training compute | 6 | 225+ MW against more than $20bn of 2026 capex | 2-3 years | S9, S8 |
| State permits | 6 | Bilateral and political; not purchasable | 1-3 years | S89, S91 |
| Composite | 6.5/10 | Minimum 3-year lead on a geofenced service | — | S9, S60 |

The replication test is unflattering to a patent story: 50 funded engineers with every published Tesla patent could build a geofenced driverless service in two to three years — Waymo needed eleven years from its 2009 start — but could not reproduce the fleet data or the factories. Tesla's 10-K concedes the point by design, pledging irrevocably not to sue any party acting in good faith for infringing its electric-vehicle patents. California is the harder gate: on 23 October 2026 the DMV lists Tesla Robotaxi LLC only as a testing-permit holder requiring a safety driver, and the state's regulator confirmed in March 2026 that Tesla is not operating an autonomous vehicle service, its paid rides running on a limousine permit [S1, S89, S90].

| IP instrument | Covers | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Patent non-assertion pledge | EV and related-equipment patents | Irrevocable for good-faith users | Removes patents as a barrier | S1 |
| Trade secrets, NDAs | Cell process, manufacturing know-how | In force | Protects dry-electrode yield | S1 |
| In-house inference silicon; Samsung US foundry deal | AI4/AI5 design and fabrication | Austin fab commissioning 2027 | Cost and performance control | S1, S9 |
| Patent portfolio (AI, batteries, robotics) | Not enumerated in filings | Counts not publicly disclosed | Cannot be assessed publicly | — |

Tesla publishes no patent count or list, so a patent-number-level table cannot be built from its disclosures; a USPTO assignee search is the source that would settle portfolio size and freedom-to-operate risk, and it has been requested.

### Optimus is a research programme with a production line

Tesla began Optimus production in Fremont in Q3 2026 and calls the process "suitable for a commercial product", but discloses no units, cycle times, error rates or customers; independent estimates put 1,000-1,200 units across Fremont and Giga Texas with zero external sales, and the CEO described early units as "primarily for learning and data collection" [S99]. Figure AI has logged 1,250+ hours at BMW and Agility Robotics 65,000+ hours across nine sites, both with paying customers — smaller companies with weaker balance sheets but better evidence. Optimus should carry no revenue in a 12-month model.

Tesla's manufacturing and supervised-data advantages are real and hard to buy, but the priced asset is unsupervised autonomy, which in 2026 has a fatality-linked engineering analysis, a single authorising state, a pilot fleet and no disclosed revenue. Confidence is high on filings and regulator records, medium on driverless scale, low on Optimus and robotaxi unit economics, where disclosure is absent rather than adverse. Three questions would move this: Robotaxi revenue, paid trips and cost per trip disclosed quarterly; a California driverless deployment permit; and 4680 cell cost per kWh against the purchased-cell benchmark. If the first and third come good while EA26002 closes without a hardware remedy, the option is worth materially more than a pilot; if the analysis converts to a recall that restricts the operating domain, the revenue bridge loses its main support.

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's board is majority independent on paper, but the three decisions that mattered in 2024-2026 — a $2.0bn investment in the CEO's own AI company after shareholders rejected the measure, a pay award that can reach 423.7m shares, and the retention of a classified board — all went against the minority's expressed preference, so key-person and capital-allocation risk are real, formally disclosed, and only partly offset by the award's extreme vesting gates [S10].

### Independence is not the same as accountability

Nine directors sit on the board, seven of them independent under Nasdaq rules, with Robyn Denholm as independent chair since November 2018 and all four committees composed solely of independents. The structure that matters is elsewhere: three staggered classes with three-year terms, supermajority voting requirements that a 2025 management proposal failed to remove with 39.4% of shares outstanding in favour, and two family directors — Elon and Kimbal Musk — in the room. Compensation Committee chair Ira Ehrenpreis has also served on SpaceX's board since February 2026, the counterparty to Tesla's $2.0bn investment and $143.3m of 2025 revenue, a relationship the proxy calls immaterial [S10].

### Pay is gated on market value, not on operating return

The 2025 CEO Performance Award is 423,743,904 shares in 12 equal tranches. Each tranche needs a market-capitalisation milestone first — from $2 trillion, 26.6% above the 2026-10-30 value, through nine $500bn and two $1tn steps to $8.5 trillion — and one of 12 operational milestones: four strategic-product goals (10m active FSD subscriptions, 1m bots delivered, 1m Robotaxis in commercial operation among them) or eight Adjusted EBITDA goals. Each earned share carries a $334.09 offset and a five-year hold, and tranches 11 and 12 also require a board-approved CEO succession framework, the only formal succession mechanism disclosed. Against that, General Motors paid Mary Barra $48.2m of realized compensation in 2025, and Musk has taken no salary since 2019 and has no employment agreement or severance; reported 2025 total compensation of $158.36bn was an accounting value, with realized pay at $0 [S10, S107, S109].

### The xAI vote is the test the board failed

At the 2025-11-06 meeting shareholders approved the pay award with 1,892,235,822 votes for, 564,940,908 against and 12,227,846 abstentions, 76.6% of votes cast, with 302,456,274 broker non-votes. A separate non-binding measure authorising funding for xAI drew 1.06bn votes for and 916.3m against but was recorded as rejected because Tesla's bylaws count abstentions as votes against; on 2026-01-16 the company nonetheless agreed to invest $2.0bn in xAI, completing on 2026-03-12 as SpaceX Class A stock after the SpaceX-xAI merger. The Audit Committee reviews related-person transactions above $120,000 under a written policy, but the sequence shows the review is procedural: a holder should assume future flows to Musk-controlled companies are a board decision, not a shareholder one [S59, S104, S105].

### One person carries the strategy; the bench is uneven

The 10-K says Musk "does not devote his full time and attention to Tesla" and lists management roles at SpaceX, xAI, Neuralink and The Boring Company, while the proxy records that xAI became a SpaceX subsidiary in February 2026 and that Musk is SpaceX's CEO, CTO and chairman. The operating bench is strongest in manufacturing and finance: Tom Zhu, SVP APAC and global vehicle manufacturing since June 2025, joined in 2014 and built Gigafactory Shanghai; Vaibhav Taneja has been CFO since August 2023 and inside Tesla's finance function since 2017. Demand execution is the weak spot: Omead Afshar left in June 2025, Troy Jones was dismissed as head of North American sales in July 2025, the North American service head left in August 2025 and Raj Jegannathan departed in February 2026 after 13 years. Headcount was 134,785 at 2025-12-31, so the departures are senior-level attrition, not a shrinking company [S1, S111, S124].

### What the record confirms, and what diligence must settle

Public records confirm the founder-market fit: Musk co-founded Zip2 (sold to Compaq in 1999) and PayPal (sold to eBay in 2002), has run Tesla since October 2008, and still owns 19.8% with 207,498,721 shares pledged. They also confirm the concentration: no chief operating officer, no permanent North American sales leader, a board with no automotive-OEM operating director, and a CEO whose other companies are now suppliers, investees and counterparties. The gaps a diligence team should close are the succession plan behind tranches 11-12, the terms and lenders behind the pledge, the fairness opinion, if any, for the $2.0bn xAI/SpaceX purchase, and references on Zhu and Taneja from SolarCity and Shanghai. For a 12-month holder the concentration is not a separately observable discount in the share price: it argues for a smaller position and for demanding evidence that Zhu and Taneja can run the operating business while Musk is elsewhere [S10, S2].

::: evidence
**The strongest proof of execution is a manufacturing ramp the founder did not personally run; the strongest doubt is a board that proceeded with a related-party investment after shareholders rejected it.**

Tom Zhu built Gigafactory Shanghai, the largest plant in the system at more than 950,000 units, and Berlin set a quarterly production record in Q3 2026; Tesla passed 10.2m cumulative vehicles. The counterweight is procedural: an xAI funding measure lost on a 1.06bn-to-916.3m vote, yet $2.0bn was committed five weeks later, and the Compensation Committee chair sits on SpaceX's board [S9, S104, S10].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's reported segments describe a vehicle business whose gross margin does not cover group research and development and selling costs, a storage business and a services business that together earn the group's operating profit, and a third quarter of 2026 in which both of those profit pools were helped by tariff refunds and warranty true-ups — the return is earned on storage and on the cash pile, not on the car.

### Three segments, three ways of getting paid

The automotive segment took 73.3% of third-quarter 2026 revenue ($20,560M of $28,046M), services and other 16.4% ($4,605M) and energy generation and storage 10.3% ($2,881M). The buyer differs in each. A retail or fleet customer pays cash or finances a car when control transfers; an energy customer — a utility, developer or data-centre operator — pays on project milestones across quarters; a service customer pays per transaction for collision repair, maintenance or a Supercharging session; another automaker pays for regulatory credits at transfer of title. The mix has moved: energy was 6.2% of FY2023 revenue ($6,035M) and 13.5% in FY2025 ($12,771M), while automotive revenue fell from $82,419M to $69,526M. The only recurring software charge is FSD (Supervised) at $99 a month, with 1.74 million active subscriptions on 2026-09-30 against 1.04 million a year earlier, and deliveries are increasingly financed rather than paid in cash, which shifts credit risk and cash timing into leasing and financing partners [S8, S1, S121].

### The vehicle does not pay for the research budget

::: unit_economics
| Per unit (one vehicle delivered), Q3 2026 | USD per unit | Note | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive revenue | 42,259 | $20,560M ÷ 486,532 deliveries | S9 |
| Cost of automotive revenue | (34,436) | materials, labour, overhead, warranty, tariffs | S8 |
| Automotive gross profit | 7,823 | 18.5% margin | S8 |
| Regulatory credits inside that profit | 232 | $113M ÷ 486,532; no matching cost | S8 |
| Automotive gross profit excluding credits | 7,590 | 18.1% of $20,447M ex-credit revenue | S8 |
| Group R&D and SG&A per unit | (9,817) | $4,776M ÷ 486,532, all charged to the car | S9 |
| Automotive-only operating contribution | (1,994) | a loss before energy and services | derived |
| Energy and services gross profit per unit | 3,470 | $1,688M ÷ 486,532 | S8 |
| Group operating profit per unit | 1,476 | $718M ÷ 486,532 | S9 |
| Interest income per unit | 915 | $445M ÷ 486,532 | S8 |
| Pre-tax profit per unit | 1,965 | $956M ÷ 486,532 | S8 |
:::

A delivered car carried $42,259 of automotive revenue and $34,436 of cost, leaving $7,823 of gross profit, or $7,590 once regulatory credits are removed; spreading $4,776M of group research and development and selling cost over 486,532 deliveries costs $9,817 a vehicle, so the automotive line alone runs at roughly -$1,994 a vehicle. Energy and services add $3,470 a vehicle and turn that into $1,476 of operating profit and, with $445M of interest income, $1,965 of pre-tax profit. Cost per vehicle was $33,666 in Q4 2025, $35,786 in Q1 2026 and $34,436 in Q3 2026, so unit cost is not falling; the rise in ex-credit automotive margin from 15.4% to 18.1% year on year arrived with a richer Asia-Pacific delivery mix in Q3 2026, not from the factory [S9, S8].

::: evidence
**The reported credit collapse is a clawback of past revenue, not yet a collapse in current demand — but the contracted backlog now says it is coming.**

Reported credit revenue fell from $542M in Q4 2025 to $380M in Q1 2026, $146M in Q2 2026 and $113M in Q3 2026, after $1,993M in FY2025 and $2,763M in FY2024 [S8, S83, S1]. The Q3 2026 figure is net of a $475M reversal of previously recognised credit revenue for contractual return of already-delivered credits, so gross credit sales in the quarter were about $588M — higher than Q4 2025 — and the reported line overstates the speed of the decline. The forward indicator is worse than the reported one: contracted credit obligations with original terms over one year fell to $384M at 2026-09-30 from $841M at 2025-12-31, only $201M of it due within twelve months, against $1,993M earned in FY2025. Toyota and Stellantis left Tesla's European CO2 pool for 2026, with Subaru also reported out, and UBS put the pool at more than €1 billion of annual revenue [S123]. Tesla names no credit buyer in its filings.
:::

### Storage earns the best margin and the least predictable one

Energy generation and storage produced $954M of gross profit on $2,881M of revenue in Q3 2026 (33.1%), after 20.4% in Q2 2026 and 39.5% in Q1 2026. Revenue per GWh deployed fell from $274 per kWh in Q1 2026 to $210 per kWh in Q3 2026, and gross profit per kWh went $108, $47, $70 across the three quarters, so the segment is priced per project and per kWh and its margin moves with Megapack pricing, cell cost, tariff recoveries and warranty true-ups. Demand evidence is strong: $10.73 billion of unsatisfied energy obligations at 2026-09-30 with $4.80 billion due within twelve months, and a Megapack book management described as nearly sold out through 2027. The counter-evidence is that part of that growth is a related party: SpaceX bought $626M of Megapacks in the first nine months of 2026 ($221M in Q3), left $729M of receivables at 2026-09-30 — $588M of it for units not yet delivered — and $648M of deferred revenue, so energy's fastest-growing account is the chief executive's other company [S8, S1, S117].

::: pricing
| Line of business | Pricing metric | Price per unit | Period | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vehicles | per vehicle delivered, blended across models | $42,259 revenue, $34,436 cost | Q3 2026 | S9 |
| Regulatory credits | per credit sold to another automaker | not disclosed; $113M net of a $475M reversal | Q3 2026 | S8 |
| Energy storage | per kWh deployed, Megapack and Powerwall blended | $210/kWh revenue, $70/kWh gross profit | Q3 2026 | S9 |
| FSD (Supervised) | per vehicle per month | $99 | 2026-10 | S121 |
| Megapack to SpaceX | per project, milestone billed | not disclosed; $626M of revenue | 9M 2026 | S8 |
| Vehicle leasing | per vehicle per month | not disclosed; $353M leasing revenue | Q3 2026 | S8 |
| Supercharging | per session or per kWh | not disclosed | Q3 2026 | S8 |
| Robotaxi and Cybercab | per ride | not disclosed | Q3 2026 | S9 |
:::

### Services is the quiet second engine

Services and other grew revenue 33% year on year to $4,605M and lifted gross profit to $734M, a 15.9% margin against 10.5% in Q3 2025 and an all-time high. The lines behind it are used-vehicle sales, collision and non-warranty maintenance, paid Supercharging across 8,904 stations and 84,465 connectors, and an insurance book — parts-and-labour businesses with largely variable costs riding on a charging network with largely fixed ones, so utilisation lifts the marginal margin. Rivian's software and services segment earned 42% on $605M of revenue in the same quarter, so Tesla's margin is well below the best comparable but on 7.6 times the revenue, and services now supplies 13.4% of group gross profit from 16.4% of revenue. The risk sits in the used-car and collision lines, which depend on the resale values that also underpin Tesla's lease residuals and insurance claims [S9, S120].

### What breaks even, and what cannot be measured

At Q3 2026 unit economics and constant group cost, the automotive line covers its share of the group only at about 611,000 deliveries a quarter, 26% above the 486,532 delivered. Tesla discloses no customer-acquisition cost — there is no marketing line in the statements — so SG&A at 7.2% of revenue is the nearest proxy and a CAC payback or LTV:CAC ratio cannot be computed from the filings; that limit matters, because the claim that Tesla acquires buyers more cheaply than Ford or GM is untested. Judged on operating margin, Tesla's 2.6% sits below GM's 8.2% EBIT-adjusted and Ford's 5.5%, while its 18.1% ex-credit gross margin is level with BYD's 18%: the difference is the operating cost line, not the car. For an investor underwriting the shares at the current quote, the implication is that the next twelve months pay for a storage margin that has printed anywhere between 20% and 40% and a software attach that carries no disclosed revenue — the diligence question is what FSD subscription revenue and Megapack-only margin actually are, because those two numbers decide whether the group earns more than its cost of capital [S115, S116, S119].

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's technology position in 2026 is two facts usually merged in the narrative: the largest supervised-driving data pool and one of the cheapest large-scale EV manufacturing bases in the industry, and almost no verified driverless revenue. Active FSD subscriptions reached 1.74 million at 30 September 2026 against 10.2 million vehicles delivered to date — 17.1% of the lifetime fleet, up from 12.4% at 31 December 2025 — while cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles were "nearly two million", 1.2% of the 170 million-plus rider-only miles Waymo reports [S9]. That gap, not the subscription count, is what twelve months must close.

### What Tesla actually sells

| Product | Stage | Revenue or share | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FSD (Supervised) | Commercial, 9 EU countries | 1.74m subscriptions; revenue not disclosed | Unsupervised release | S9, S1 |
| Robotaxi / Cybercab | Commercial in Texas metros | Not disclosed inside $4.605bn services | Paid-trip disclosure | S9 |
| Model 3 / Model Y | Mature | 478,237 units, Q3 2026; 19.6% group gross margin | Next-gen platform | S9 |
| Cybertruck, Semi, Roadster | Ramp / design | 8,295 other-model units, Q3 2026 | Semi ramp; Roadster launch | S9 |
| Megapack, Powerwall | Scaling | $2.881bn in Q3 2026; 13.7 GWh | 50 GWh Texas ramp | S9, S60 |
| Optimus | Internal production | Zero external revenue | External pilot sale | S9, S99 |

### Mechanism: end-to-end vision and a one-sided flywheel

Tesla removed radar and now maps camera pixels directly to driving commands with an end-to-end neural network, trained on clips harvested from the fleet and run on in-house inference silicon. Training runs on two in-house clusters at Gigafactory Texas, with a company-built fab for inference and training silicon under construction. The flywheel is real but overwhelmingly *supervised*: the Q3 2026 update charts cumulative FSD miles on a 0-16 billion axis, against 2.0 million unsupervised miles [S60]. Supervised miles teach perception; they do not certify that the network can be left alone, which is why the federal safety file matters more than the mileage chart.

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active FSD subscriptions | 1.74m (2026-09-30) | Company count | S9 |
| FSD penetration of fleet | 17.1% | 1.74m / 10.2m deliveries | S9 |
| Cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles | 2.0m, 8x QoQ | Company count | S9 |
| Installed AI training compute | 225+ MW | Company nameplate | S9 |
| 4680 capacity, Texas | 40+ GWh/yr, dry electrode both sides | Company nameplate | S60 |
| Storage deployed | 13.7 GWh Q3; 36.0 GWh 9M | Company deliveries | S9 |
| Optimus units in service | 1,000-1,200 | Independent estimate | S99 |

### The safety file is the binding constraint

NHTSA's Office of Defects Investigation opened Engineering Analysis EA26002 on 18 March 2026 into whether FSD detects degraded visibility — glare, fog, dust — and warns the driver in time, covering an estimated 3,203,754 vehicles from model years 2016-2026, after nine confirmed incidents including one pedestrian fatality; two further FSD probes remain open, one on traffic-law violations across 2,882,566 vehicles with 80 incidents [S87]. Tesla's own analysis reportedly found its degradation-detection update "may have affected" only 3 of 9 incidents, which points to an architectural limit of camera-only sensing rather than a tuning defect. An engineering analysis is the last step before a recall; a recall would narrow the operating domain or force hardware across millions of cars, at a company that self-insures product liability.

::: evidence
**The camera-only bet is being tested by the regulator, not the market.** EA26002 covers 3.2 million FSD-equipped vehicles and Tesla's fix reportedly addresses a third of the reviewed incidents [S87, S88, S100]. The filings confirm the investigation but give no remedy or timetable, which is the largest un-priced technical risk in the autonomy option.
:::

### Comparison: three different autonomy businesses

| Dimension | Tesla | Waymo | Chinese L3 OEMs | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sensing | Camera-only, in-house chip | Lidar + radar + camera | Camera + lidar, Nvidia compute | S9, S101 |
| Verified driverless scale | 2.0m cumulative miles | 170m+ rider-only miles; 500,000 paid rides/week | L3 conditional approvals since 2025-12 | S101, S103 |
| Regulatory position | Paid driverless in Texas under SB 2807 and TxDMV authorisation (required from 2026-05-28); California paid rides on a limousine permit, no autonomous-service authorisation | California deployment authorised | MIIT eight-department L3 pilot | S89, S90, S91 |
| Cost model | Owned fleet, self-insured | Owned fleet, partner-owned vehicles | Consumer cars, driver liable | S89, S103 |

### Moat: accumulation, not exclusion

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Supervised fleet data | 8 | 10.2m cars; FSD miles charted to 16bn | 4-6 years | S9 |
| Driverless operating experience | 5 | 2.0m unsupervised miles only | 2-3 years | S9 |
| Dry-electrode cell process | 7 | Battery Day 2020 to Austin output in 2026 | 3-4 years | S60 |
| Manufacturing and integration | 8 | 134,785 employees; cells, cathode, refining in-house | 5+ years | S1 |
| Training compute | 6 | 225+ MW against more than $20bn of 2026 capex | 2-3 years | S9, S8 |
| State permits | 6 | Bilateral and political; not purchasable | 1-3 years | S89, S91 |

The replication test is unflattering to a patent story: 50 funded engineers with every published Tesla patent could build a geofenced driverless service in two to three years — Waymo needed eleven years from its 2009 start — but could not reproduce the fleet data or the factories. arguments.markdown:
Tesla's board is majority independent on paper, but the three decisions that mattered in 2024-2026 — a $2.0bn investment in the CEO's own AI company after shareholders rejected the measure, a pay award that can reach 423.7m shares, and the retention of a classified board — all went against the minority's expressed preference, so key-person and capital-allocation risk are real, formally disclosed, and only partly offset by the award's extreme vesting gates [S10].

### Independence is not the same as accountability

Nine directors sit on the board, seven of them independent under Nasdaq rules, with Robyn Denholm as independent chair since November 2018 and all four committees composed solely of independents. The structure that matters is elsewhere: three staggered classes with three-year terms, supermajority voting requirements that a 2025 management proposal failed to remove with 39.4% of shares outstanding in favour, and two family directors — Elon and Kimbal Musk — in the room. Compensation Committee chair Ira Ehrenpreis has also served on SpaceX's board since February 2026, the counterparty to Tesla's $2.0bn investment and $143.3m of 2025 revenue, a relationship the proxy calls immaterial [S10].

### Pay is gated on market value, not on operating return

The 2025 CEO Performance Award is 423,743,904 shares in 12 equal tranches. Each tranche needs a market-capitalisation milestone first — from $2 trillion, 26.6% above the 2026-10-30 value, through nine $500bn and two $1tn steps to $8.5 trillion — and one of 12 operational milestones: four strategic-product goals (10m active FSD subscriptions, 1m bots delivered, 1m Robotaxis in commercial operation among them) or eight Adjusted EBITDA goals. Each earned share carries a $334.09 offset and a five-year hold, and tranches 11 and 12 also require a board-approved CEO succession framework, the only formal succession mechanism disclosed. Against that, General Motors paid Mary Barra $48.2m of realized compensation in 2025, and Musk has taken no salary since 2019 and has no employment agreement or severance; reported 2025 total compensation of $158.36bn was an accounting value, with realized pay at $0 [S10, S107, S109].

### The xAI vote is the test the board failed

At the 2025-11-06 meeting shareholders approved the pay award with 1,892,235,822 votes for, 564,940,908 against and 12,227,846 abstentions, 76.6% of votes cast, with 302,456,274 broker non-votes. A separate non-binding measure authorising funding for xAI drew 1.06bn votes for and 916.3m against but was recorded as rejected because Tesla's bylaws count abstentions as votes against; on 2026-01-16 the company nonetheless agreed to invest $2.0bn in xAI, completing on 2026-03-12 as SpaceX Class A stock after the SpaceX-xAI merger. The Audit Committee reviews related-person transactions above $120,000 under a written policy, but the sequence shows the review is procedural: a holder should assume future flows to Musk-controlled companies are a board decision, not a shareholder one [S59, S104, S105].

### One person carries the strategy; the bench is uneven

The 10-K says Musk "does not devote his full time and attention to Tesla" and lists management roles at SpaceX, xAI, Neuralink and The Boring Company, while the proxy records that xAI became a SpaceX subsidiary in February 2026 and that Musk is SpaceX's CEO, CTO and chairman. The operating bench is strongest in manufacturing and finance: Tom Zhu, SVP APAC and global vehicle manufacturing since June 2025, joined in 2014 and built Gigafactory Shanghai; Vaibhav Taneja has been CFO since August 2023 and inside Tesla's finance function since 2017. Demand execution is the weak spot: Omead Afshar left in June 2025, Troy Jones was dismissed as head of North American sales in July 2025, the North American service head left in August 2025 and Raj Jegannathan departed in February 2026 after 13 years. Headcount was 134,785 at 2025-12-31, so the departures are senior-level attrition, not a shrinking company [S1, S111, S124].

### What the record confirms, and what diligence must settle

Public records confirm the founder-market fit: Musk co-founded Zip2 (sold to Compaq in 1999) and PayPal (sold to eBay in 2002), has run Tesla since October 2008, and still owns 19.8% with 207,498,721 shares pledged. They also confirm the concentration: no chief operating officer, no permanent North American sales leader, a board with no automotive-OEM operating director, and a CEO whose other companies are now suppliers, investees and counterparties. The gaps a diligence team should close are the succession plan behind tranches 11-12, the terms and lenders behind the pledge, the fairness opinion, if any, for the $2.0bn xAI/SpaceX purchase, and references on Zhu and Taneja from SolarCity and Shanghai. For a 12-month holder the concentration is not a separately observable discount in the share price: it argues for a smaller position and for demanding evidence that Zhu and Taneja can run the operating business while Musk is elsewhere [S10, S2].

::: evidence
**The strongest proof of execution is a manufacturing ramp the founder did not personally run; the strongest doubt is a board that proceeded with a related-party investment after shareholders rejected it.**

Tom Zhu built Gigafactory Shanghai, the largest plant in the system at more than 950,000 units, and Berlin set a quarterly production record in Q3 2026; Tesla passed 10.2m cumulative vehicles. The counterweight is procedural: an xAI funding measure lost on a 1.06bn-to-916.3m vote, yet $2.0bn was committed five weeks later, and the Compensation Committee chair sits on SpaceX's board (sources S9, S104, S10).
:::

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's reported segments describe a vehicle business whose gross margin does not cover group research and development and selling costs, a storage business and a services business that together earn the group's operating profit, and a third quarter of 2026 in which both of those profit pools were helped by tariff refunds and warranty true-ups — the return is earned on storage and on the cash pile, not on the car.

### Three segments, three ways of getting paid

The automotive segment took 73.3% of third-quarter 2026 revenue ($20,560M of $28,046M), services and other 16.4% ($4,605M) and energy generation and storage 10.3% ($2,881M). The buyer differs in each: a retail or fleet customer pays cash or finances a car when control transfers; an energy customer — a utility, developer or data-centre operator — pays on project milestones across quarters; a service customer pays per transaction for collision repair, maintenance or a Supercharging session; another automaker pays for regulatory credits at transfer of title. The mix has moved: energy was 6.2% of FY2023 revenue ($6,035M) and 13.5% in FY2025 ($12,771M), while automotive revenue fell from $82,419M to $69,526M. The only recurring software charge is FSD (Supervised) at $99 a month, with 1.74 million active subscriptions on 2026-09-30 against 1.04 million a year earlier [S8, S1, S121].

### The vehicle does not pay for the research budget

|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive revenue | 42,259 | $20,560M ÷ 486,532 deliveries | S9 |
| Cost of automotive revenue | (34,436) | materials, labour, overhead, warranty, tariffs | S8 |
| Automotive gross profit | 7,823 | 18.5% margin | S8 |
| Regulatory credits inside that profit | 232 | $113M ÷ 486,532; no matching cost | S8 |
| Automotive gross profit excluding credits | 7,590 | 18.1% of $20,447M ex-credit revenue | S8 |
| Group R&D and SG&A per unit | (9,817) | $4,776M ÷ 486,532, all charged to the car | S9 |
| Automotive-only operating contribution | (1,994) | a loss before energy and services | derived |
| Energy and services gross profit per unit | 3,470 | $1,688M ÷ 486,532 | S8 |
| Group operating profit per unit | 1,476 | $718M ÷ 486,532 | S9 |
| Interest income per unit | 915 | $445M ÷ 486,532 | S8 |
| Pre-tax profit per unit | 1,965 | $956M ÷ 486,532 | S8 |

A delivered car carried $42,259 of automotive revenue and $34,436 of cost, leaving $7,823 of gross profit, or $7,590 once regulatory credits are removed; spreading $4,776M of group research and development and selling cost over 486,532 deliveries costs $9,817 a vehicle, so the automotive line alone runs at roughly -$1,994 a vehicle. Energy and services add $3,470 a vehicle and turn that into $1,476 of operating profit and, with $445M of interest income, $1,965 of pre-tax profit. Cost per vehicle was $33,666 in Q4 2025, $35,786 in Q1 2026 and $34,436 in Q3 2026, so unit cost is not falling; the rise in ex-credit automotive margin from 15.4% to 18.1% year on year arrived with a richer Asia-Pacific delivery mix in Q3 2026, not from the factory [S9, S8].

::: evidence
**The reported credit collapse is a clawback of past revenue, not yet a collapse in current demand — but the contracted backlog says it is coming.**

Reported credit revenue fell from $542M in Q4 2025 to $380M in Q1 2026, $146M in Q2 2026 and $113M in Q3 2026, after $1,993M in FY2025 and $2,763M in FY2024 [S8, S83, S1]. The Q3 2026 figure is net of a $475M reversal of previously recognised credit revenue for contractual return of already-delivered credits, so gross credit sales in the quarter were about $588M — higher than Q4 2025 — and the reported line overstates the speed of the decline. The forward indicator is worse: contracted credit obligations with original terms over one year fell to $384M at 2026-09-30 from $841M at 2025-12-31, only $201M of it due within twelve months, against $1,993M earned in FY2025. Toyota and Stellantis left Tesla's European CO2 pool for 2026, with Subaru also reported out, and UBS put the pool at more than €1 billion of annual revenue [S123]. Tesla names no credit buyer in its filings.
:::

### Storage earns the best margin and the least predictable one

Energy generation and storage produced $954M of gross profit on $2,881M of revenue in Q3 2026 (33.1%), after 20.4% in Q2 2026 and 39.5% in Q1 2026. Revenue per GWh deployed fell from $274 per kWh in Q1 2026 to $210 per kWh in Q3 2026, and gross profit per kWh went $108, $47, $70 across the three quarters, so the segment's margin moves with Megapack pricing, cell cost, tariff recoveries and warranty true-ups. Demand evidence is strong: $10.73 billion of unsatisfied energy obligations at 2026-09-30 with $4.80 billion due within twelve months, and a Megapack book management described as nearly sold out through 2027. The counter-evidence is that part of that growth is a related party: SpaceX bought $626M of Megapacks in the first nine months of 2026 ($221M in Q3), left $729M of receivables at 2026-09-30 — $588M of it for units not yet delivered — and $648M of deferred revenue, so energy's fastest-growing account is the chief executive's other company [S8, S1, S117].

### Services is the quiet second engine

Services and other grew revenue 33% year on year to $4,605M and lifted gross profit to $734M, a 15.9% margin against 10.5% in Q3 2025 and an all-time high. Behind it are used-vehicle sales, collision and non-warranty maintenance, paid Supercharging across 8,904 stations and 84,465 connectors, and an insurance book — parts-and-labour businesses with largely variable costs riding on a charging network with largely fixed ones, so utilisation lifts the marginal margin. Rivian's software and services segment earned 42% on $605M of revenue in the same quarter, so Tesla's margin is well below the best comparable but on 7.6 times the revenue, and services now supplies 13.4% of group gross profit from 16.4% of revenue. The risk sits in the used-car and collision lines, which depend on the resale values that also underpin Tesla's lease residuals and insurance claims [S9, S120].

### What breaks even, and what cannot be measured

At Q3 2026 unit economics and constant group cost, the automotive line covers its share of the group only at about 611,000 deliveries a quarter, 26% above the 486,532 delivered. Tesla discloses no customer-acquisition cost — there is no marketing line in the statements — so SG&A at 7.2% of revenue is the nearest proxy and a CAC payback or LTV:CAC ratio cannot be computed from the filings; that limit matters, because the claim that Tesla acquires buyers more cheaply than Ford or GM is untested. Judged on operating margin, Tesla's 2.6% sits below GM's 8.2% EBIT-adjusted and Ford's 5.5%, while its 18.1% ex-credit gross margin is level with BYD's 18%: the difference is the operating cost line, not the car. For an investor underwriting the shares at the current quote, the implication is that the next twelve months pay for a storage margin that has printed anywhere between 20% and 40% and a software attach that carries no disclosed revenue — the diligence question is what FSD subscription revenue and Megapack-only margin actually are, because those two numbers decide whether the group earns more than its cost of capital [S115, S116, S119].

Tesla's legal and ownership structure is unusually plain for a founder-led company — one class of stock, a Texas parent with no VIE or dual-class layer, and a CEO who owns 19.8% — so what constrains a 12-month equity return is not the charter but a 10.7% contingent dilution struck at market capitalisations from $2 trillion upward, no dividend or buyback, and a classified board that minority holders cannot replace. Tesla, Inc. trades on Nasdaq under TSLA; 3,952,648,559 shares were outstanding at 2026-09-30 and market capitalisation was $1.58 trillion at the $399.81 close on 2026-10-30 [S10, S112].

### One operating group, no holding-company layer

The registrant was incorporated in Delaware on 2003-07-01 and converted to a Texas corporation on 2024-06-13. The structure is flat: country operating companies, single-purpose solar and lease vehicles and insurance captives, with no contractual-control or variable-interest layer separating legal from economic ownership. The filings disclose no separate intellectual-property holding company; the listed parent files the group's consolidated accounts, while the operating subsidiaries hold the plants, local licences and financing books [S1, S58].

### The dilution path runs through a $2 trillion gate

Musk holds 699,580,882 shares, or 19.8%, including 286,428,773 restricted shares from the 2018 award, and 207,498,721 of his shares are pledged against personal borrowings. The 2018 award was exercised in full on 2026-06-16 for 303,960,630 shares, which is why the count rose 202m, or 5.4%, in the nine months to 2026-09-30. Forward dilution is the 2025 CEO Performance Award: 423,743,904 shares, 10.7% of the current count, in 12 equal tranches, none earned as of 2026-10-19. Each earned share carries a $334.09 offset payable in cash or shares, a five-year holding requirement, and every tranche needs a market-cap milestone before any operating milestone counts, starting at $2 trillion — 26.6% above the 2026-10-30 value — then nine $500bn and two $1tn increments to $8.5 trillion. The economics sit closer to a premium-struck option than a free grant: at $399.81 the gross spread is $65.72 a share, and at the plan's top the transfer is $769.6bn net of offsets, 9.1% of an $8.5 trillion capitalisation [S10, S107].

### What the customer actually buys

The business is three P&Ls sold to different budget owners. Automotive ($69.53bn of FY2025 revenue, 73% of the total) sells vehicles to consumers, leasing companies and fleets, and monetises the installed base through Supercharging, service, parts, used cars and insurance; the software layer is FSD (Supervised), with 1.74m active subscriptions at 2026-09-30. Energy ($12.77bn, 14% of revenue, 29.8% gross margin) sells Megapack and Powerwall to utilities, developers, industrial sites and, increasingly, data-centre operators whose budget is a power-availability capex line rather than a transport one. Services ($12.53bn, +19% in FY2025) is largely a captive aftermarket on Tesla's own parc. Growth has shifted from unit volume — Q3 2026 deliveries were 486,532, down 2% year on year — to storage deployment (13.7 GWh in Q3 2026), software attach and the Robotaxi and Optimus optionality the pay award is designed to reward [S1, S9].

### Capacity is built; volume is the question

Tesla runs eight primary plants: Fremont (Model 3/Y, more than 550,000 units), Shanghai (more than 950,000), Berlin (more than 375,000), Texas (Model Y more than 375,000, Cybertruck and Cybercab more than 125,000 each) and Nevada (Semi 25,000), plus Megapack plants in California (40 GWh), Shanghai (20 GWh) and Texas (50 GWh). Headcount was 134,785 at 2025-12-31. Nameplate vehicle capacity of 2.53m units against an annualised Q3 2026 run rate of 1.95m leaves a fifth of the system idle, while Semi, Cybercab and Optimus lines add depreciation before revenue; that is the mechanism by which a flat revenue year becomes either margin expansion or further compression [S9, S1].

### No payout, and a board that cannot be replaced

Tesla has never paid a dividend, has no repurchase authorisation and made no purchases in FY2025, while holding $45.45bn of cash and short-term investments; with no distribution, a holder's 12-month total return is the share price alone. Governance reinforces retention: the board has three classes, a 2025 management proposal to remove supermajority voting requirements won 39.4% of shares outstanding and failed, and the 2026-12-03 meeting asks holders only to elect three Class I directors, cast a say-on-pay vote and ratify the auditor. The counter-evidence is real — one share class is more minority-proportional than Rivian's ten-vote Class B, seven of nine directors are independent, the CEO takes no salary, and unearned award shares carry no independent votes because an irrevocable proxy votes them with the rest of the stock — but none of it returns cash or lets a majority change the charter. For a holder at $399.81 the structure therefore offers no cash yield, caps the upside above $2 trillion by 9.1%, and gives no route to force a change of capital-return policy: that argues for sizing the position as a price-only bet, not for rejecting the equity. The open question is whether a $1.58 trillion price for $94.83bn of revenue and a 16.2% automotive gross margin leaves anything after that gate is crossed [S1, S10, S114].
