{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 5 by Product Analyst, 8,734 characters)
Tesla's technology position in 2026 is two facts usually merged in the narrative: the largest supervised-driving data pool and one of the cheapest large-scale EV manufacturing bases in the industry, and almost no verified driverless revenue. Active FSD subscriptions reached 1.74 million at 30 September 2026 against 10.2 million vehicles delivered to date — 17.1% of the lifetime fleet, up from 12.4% at 31 December 2025 — while cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles were "nearly two million", 1.2% of the 170 million-plus rider-only miles Waymo reports [S9]. That gap, not the subscription count, is what twelve months must close.

### What Tesla actually sells

| Product | Stage | Revenue or share | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FSD (Supervised) | Commercial, 9 EU countries | 1.74m subscriptions; revenue not disclosed | Unsupervised release | S9, S1 |
| Robotaxi / Cybercab | Commercial in Texas metros | Not disclosed inside $4.605bn services | Paid-trip disclosure | S9 |
| Model 3 / Model Y | Mature | 478,237 units, Q3 2026; 19.6% group gross margin | Next-gen platform | S9 |
| Cybertruck, Semi, Roadster | Ramp / design | 8,295 other-model units, Q3 2026 | Semi ramp; Roadster launch | S9 |
| Megapack, Powerwall | Scaling | $2.881bn in Q3 2026; 13.7 GWh | 50 GWh Texas ramp | S9, S60 |
| Optimus | Internal production | Zero external revenue | External pilot sale | S9, S99 |

### Mechanism: end-to-end vision and a one-sided flywheel

Tesla removed radar and now maps camera pixels directly to driving commands with an end-to-end neural network, trained on clips harvested from the fleet and run on in-house inference silicon. Training runs on two in-house clusters at Gigafactory Texas, with a company-built fab for inference and training silicon under construction. The flywheel is real but overwhelmingly *supervised*: the Q3 2026 update charts cumulative FSD miles on a 0-16 billion axis, against 2.0 million unsupervised miles [S60]. Supervised miles teach perception; they do not certify that the network can be left alone, which is why the federal safety file matters more than the mileage chart.

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active FSD subscriptions | 1.74m (2026-09-30) | Company count | S9 |
| FSD penetration of fleet | 17.1% | 1.74m / 10.2m deliveries | S9 |
| Cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles | 2.0m, 8x QoQ | Company count | S9 |
| Installed AI training compute | 225+ MW | Company nameplate | S9 |
| 4680 capacity, Texas | 40+ GWh/yr, dry electrode both sides | Company nameplate | S60 |
| Storage deployed | 13.7 GWh Q3; 36.0 GWh 9M | Company deliveries | S9 |
| Optimus units in service | 1,000-1,200 | Independent estimate | S99 |

### The safety file is the binding constraint

NHTSA's Office of Defects Investigation opened Engineering Analysis EA26002 on 18 March 2026 into whether FSD detects degraded visibility — glare, fog, dust — and warns the driver in time, covering an estimated 3,203,754 vehicles from model years 2016-2026, after nine confirmed incidents including one pedestrian fatality; two further FSD probes remain open, one on traffic-law violations across 2,882,566 vehicles with 80 incidents [S87]. Tesla's own analysis reportedly found its degradation-detection update "may have affected" only 3 of 9 incidents, which points to an architectural limit of camera-only sensing rather than a tuning defect. An engineering analysis is the last step before a recall; a recall would narrow the operating domain or force hardware across millions of cars, at a company that self-insures product liability.

::: evidence
**The camera-only bet is being tested by the regulator, not the market.** EA26002 covers 3.2 million FSD-equipped vehicles and Tesla's fix reportedly addresses a third of the reviewed incidents [S87, S88, S100]. The filings confirm the investigation but give no remedy or timetable, which is the largest un-priced technical risk in the autonomy option.
:::

### Comparison: three different autonomy businesses

| Dimension | Tesla | Waymo | Chinese L3 OEMs | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sensing | Camera-only, in-house chip | Lidar + radar + camera | Camera + lidar, Nvidia compute | S9, S101 |
| Verified driverless scale | 2.0m cumulative miles | 170m+ rider-only miles; 500,000 paid rides/week | L3 conditional approvals since 2025-12 | S101, S103 |
| Regulatory position | Paid driverless in Texas under SB 2807 and TxDMV authorisation (required from 2026-05-28); California paid rides on a limousine permit, no autonomous-service authorisation | California deployment authorised | MIIT eight-department L3 pilot | S89, S90, S91 |
| Cost model | Owned fleet, self-insured | Owned fleet, partner-owned vehicles | Consumer cars, driver liable | S89, S103 |

### Moat: accumulation, not exclusion

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Supervised fleet data | 8 | 10.2m cars; FSD miles charted to 16bn | 4-6 years | S9 |
| Driverless operating experience | 5 | 2.0m unsupervised miles only | 2-3 years | S9 |
| Dry-electrode cell process | 7 | Battery Day 2020 to Austin output in 2026 | 3-4 years | S60 |
| Manufacturing and integration | 8 | 134,785 employees; cells, cathode, refining in-house | 5+ years | S1 |
| Training compute | 6 | 225+ MW against more than $20bn of 2026 capex | 2-3 years | S9, S8 |
| State permits | 6 | Bilateral and political; not purchasable | 1-3 years | S89, S91 |
| Composite | 6.5/10 | Minimum 3-year lead on a geofenced service | — | S9, S60 |

The replication test is unflattering to a patent story: 50 funded engineers with every published Tesla patent could build a geofenced driverless service in two to three years — Waymo needed eleven years from its 2009 start — but could not reproduce the fleet data or the factories. Tesla's 10-K concedes the point by design, pledging irrevocably not to sue any party acting in good faith for infringing its electric-vehicle patents. California is the harder gate: on 23 October 2026 the DMV lists Tesla Robotaxi LLC only as a testing-permit holder requiring a safety driver, and the state's regulator confirmed in March 2026 that Tesla is not operating an autonomous vehicle service, its paid rides running on a limousine permit [S1, S89, S90].

| IP instrument | Covers | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Patent non-assertion pledge | EV and related-equipment patents | Irrevocable for good-faith users | Removes patents as a barrier | S1 |
| Trade secrets, NDAs | Cell process, manufacturing know-how | In force | Protects dry-electrode yield | S1 |
| In-house inference silicon; Samsung US foundry deal | AI4/AI5 design and fabrication | Austin fab commissioning 2027 | Cost and performance control | S1, S9 |
| Patent portfolio (AI, batteries, robotics) | Not enumerated in filings | Counts not publicly disclosed | Cannot be assessed publicly | — |

Tesla publishes no patent count or list, so a patent-number-level table cannot be built from its disclosures; a USPTO assignee search is the source that would settle portfolio size and freedom-to-operate risk, and it has been requested.

### Optimus is a research programme with a production line

Tesla began Optimus production in Fremont in Q3 2026 and calls the process "suitable for a commercial product", but discloses no units, cycle times, error rates or customers; independent estimates put 1,000-1,200 units across Fremont and Giga Texas with zero external sales, and the CEO described early units as "primarily for learning and data collection" [S99]. Figure AI has logged 1,250+ hours at BMW and Agility Robotics 65,000+ hours across nine sites, both with paying customers — smaller companies with weaker balance sheets but better evidence. Optimus should carry no revenue in a 12-month model.

Tesla's manufacturing and supervised-data advantages are real and hard to buy, but the priced asset is unsupervised autonomy, which in 2026 has a fatality-linked engineering analysis, a single authorising state, a pilot fleet and no disclosed revenue. Confidence is high on filings and regulator records, medium on driverless scale, low on Optimus and robotaxi unit economics, where disclosure is absent rather than adverse. Three questions would move this: Robotaxi revenue, paid trips and cost per trip disclosed quarterly; a California driverless deployment permit; and 4680 cell cost per kWh against the purchased-cell benchmark. If the first and third come good while EA26002 closes without a hardware remedy, the option is worth materially more than a pilot; if the analysis converts to a recall that restricts the operating domain, the revenue bridge loses its main support [S9, S89]."}],"isError":false}

arguments.markdown:
Tesla sells for $399.81 on NasdaqGS at the 2026-10-30 close, a $1,580.4bn market capitalisation and $1,544.2bn of enterprise value, and on the businesses its filings describe — cars, storage, services — it is worth roughly $139-160bn, or $35-40 a share. That leaves $1.42-1.44tn, about 90% of the equity, resting on robotaxi, FSD and Optimus revenue the quarterly report does not yet book, and the buyer pays 103x trailing adjusted EBITDA for it. The judgement is that the reported businesses cannot carry the price, that the residual is an option requiring 17-34 years of installed Cybercab capacity, and that the shares are a claim on a multiple rather than on earnings [S8, S9].

| Metric | Value | Signal |
|---|---|---|
| Last price | $399.81, 2026-10-30 20:00 UTC, NasdaqGS, USD | — |
| Market capitalisation | $1,580.4bn on 3,952.6m shares | 5.4% more shares than at 2025-12-31 |
| Enterprise value | $1,544.2bn after $36.2bn net cash | Cash is 2.3% of the equity |
| 52-week range | $297.38-$498.83 | 51% of the way up the range |
| Returns | 1M +12.7%, 3M +28.5%, 12M -12.4% | 12M trails the S&P 500 by 23.2 points |
| Moving averages | 50-day $369.60 (+8.2%), 200-day $385.30 (+3.8%) | Extended after a 28.5% quarter |
| Liquidity | $13.8bn traded a day (20-day average) | No exit constraint on size |
| Trailing P/E | 439.4x against a peer median of 19.1x | Earnings, not price, did the falling |
| EV/adjusted EBITDA | 103.0x on $14,995m trailing | 144x before the $4,300m stock-compensation add-back |
| Insider activity, 6 months | No purchases; 19 sales of $13.3m, 17 under 10b5-1 plans | No management buying at these levels |
| Source | | S8, S11, S2 |

### The price pays for a multiple, not for earnings

Trailing revenue is $103.6bn, adjusted EBITDA $15.0bn, operating income $3.47bn and free cash flow $3.3bn, the last after $15.4bn of capital expenditure in twelve months [S9]. On those numbers Tesla trades at 445x EV/operating income, a 0.2% free-cash-flow yield and 14.9x sales, against 17.3x EV/EBITDA for BYD and 19.1x earnings for General Motors [S131, S15]. The EBITDA figure the company prefers is itself generous: it adds back $4.3bn of stock compensation, up from $2.8bn in FY2025, so the 103x becomes 144x on EBITDA before that add-back. One turn of EV/adjusted EBITDA is worth about $15bn, three years of net income: the price is a rating, and a delay in autonomy compresses the rating rather than the earnings.

### What the reported businesses are worth

| Method | Inputs | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive and regulatory credits | $75.0bn trailing revenue at 0.6-0.8x EV/sales (GM about 0.4x, Ford about 0.25x, BYD about 1.0x) | $45-60bn | S9, S15, S17, S132 |
| Energy generation and storage | $12.3bn trailing revenue, 30.2% nine-month gross margin, at 2.5-3.0x sales; cross-check CATL at 19.8x earnings | $31-37bn | S9, S133 |
| Services and other | $16.3bn trailing revenue, +32% year on year, at 1.5x sales | $24bn | S9 |
| Net cash at 2026-09-30 | $45.4bn cash and short-term investments less $9.3bn debt | $36.2bn | S8 |
| SpaceX equity stake | $2.0bn bought in Q1 2026 plus $863m unrealised gain | about $2.9bn | S9 |
| Total, reported businesses | | $139-160bn, $35-40 a share | |
| Residual in the share price | $1,580.4bn less the total | $1,420-1,441bn, 90-91% | |

The split matters more than the point estimate. Energy, the segment with the best margin at 33.1% gross in Q3 2026, is 12% of trailing revenue and shrank 16% year on year as Megapack average selling prices fell; services grew 32% and reached a record $734m of gross profit in the quarter. Neither can be stretched to a trillion dollars without abandoning the multiples their peers earn. Even a generous automotive recovery — a 10% operating margin on $75bn at 25x earnings — lifts the whole total only to about $285bn, $72 a share, and still leaves 82% of the price unexplained.

### What the price requires by 2030

| Multiple applied to enterprise value | Enterprise value | Required adjusted EBITDA | Versus $15.0bn trailing | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 17.3x (BYD's multiple) | $1,544.2bn | $89.3bn | 6.0x | S131 |
| 25x | $1,544.2bn | $61.8bn | 4.1x | |
| 40x | $1,544.2bn | $38.6bn | 2.6x | |
| 80x (the multiple management's own $4.0tn tranche implies on $50bn) | $1,544.2bn | $19.3bn | 1.3x | S127 |

Inverting the price gives the same answer. If the residual $1,441bn is discounted at 10% and valued at 20x 2030 operating income, it requires $105bn of 2030 operating income; at 40x, $53bn. At a 25% robotaxi margin and $100,000 of revenue per vehicle-year, that is 2.1-4.2m vehicles in commercial service by 2030. The Texas registry showed 1,051 authorised robotaxis on 2026-10-27, and installed Cybercab capacity in Texas is 125,000 units a year [S125, S9]. The market is therefore discounting 17-34 years of current factory output and two to four times management's own one-million-robotaxi milestone, which the board paired with a $3.5tn market capitalisation [S127]. The multiple also matters: at the $4.0tn tranche management's plan implies 80x adjusted EBITDA, below the 103x the shares carry today, so the price is already ahead of the pay design built to reward the outcome it assumes.

| Company | P/E (TTM) | EV/sales | EV/EBITDA (XBRL basis) | FCF yield | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tesla | 439.4x | 14.9x | 169.0x | 0.2% | S8, S11 |
| General Motors | 19.1x | n/m | n/m | 19.5% | S15, S16 |
| Ford | n/m | n/m | n/m | 11.3% | S17, S18 |
| Rivian | n/m | 2.6x | n/m | -23.8% | S19 |
| BYD | 21.2x | n/d | 17.3x | n/d | S132, S131 |
| CATL | 19.8x | n/d | n/d | n/d | S133 |
| Fluence Energy | n/m | n/m | n/m | -14.6% | S61, S62 |

Tesla's own history says the same thing as the peer table. The P/E was 34.0x at the end of 2022, 57.8x in 2023, 204.6x in 2024 and 420.8x in 2025 as diluted EPS fell from $4.90 to $1.08, and stands at 439.4x now [S11, S12, S1]. EV/sales is the more stable measure and is at 14.9x, inside its 14.7-16.5x band of the past three years, because revenue doubled while the shares went nowhere: the five-year return to 2026-10-30 is -0.8%. The regime this multiple is priced in makes that harder to hold: the 10-year Treasury yields 4.93%, up 0.84 points in twelve months, the VIX is 19.42, in its 77th percentile, and high-yield spreads have widened from 276 to 326 basis points [S22, S21, S46].

### Consensus, guidance and the dates that reset the multiple

Sell-side consensus is Hold — 24 buy, 1 strong buy, 20 hold and 3 sell across 48 firms — with an average target of $408.61, 2.2% above the close; a wider 83-analyst sample puts it at $442.13, 10.6% above [S128]. Individual targets run from Jefferies at $400 to RBC at $480, and Q3 2026 was a beat on adjusted earnings, $0.48 against $0.45. Tesla publishes no numeric revenue or EPS guidance; its outlook commits only to maximum capacity utilisation, a strong balance sheet and "hardware-related profits accompanied by an acceleration of SI, software and fleet-based profits", and the capital-expenditure outlook was cut from more than $25bn to about $20bn after the quarter. The dates that can move the multiple inside twelve months are the fourth-quarter 2026 results, expected in the last week of January 2027 on the pattern of the FY2025 10-K filed 2026-01-29, the first Cybercab deployment outside Austin as Dallas is prepared, further FSD approvals beyond the nine live European markets, and progress in the SpaceX combination study. The first 2025 award tranche crystallises at a $2,000bn market capitalisation, $506.05 a share and 26.6% above spot [S127].

The strongest counter-argument is that the premium is a fair price for an option that is visibly maturing: active FSD subscriptions reached 1.74m, up 67% year on year, the paid take rate in North America is above 75% of deliveries, unsupervised Robotaxi miles reached nearly 2m and the authorised fleet grew from 739 to 1,051 vehicles in eighteen days. If robotaxi unit economics are proven in 2027, 103x EBITDA on today's numbers is a discount to what the business would then earn. The arithmetic does not support the weaker version of that argument — energy alone caps out at $37bn — and no company in the comparison set earns Tesla's combination of a 30% energy gross margin and 32% services growth while trading above 30x earnings. Confidence in the valuation arithmetic is high; confidence in the durability of the multiple is low, because it rests on evidence the company has not disclosed. Three questions would settle it: revenue per robotaxi per week in Austin, the operating margin the energy segment earns at 130 GWh of installed capacity, and whether a buyback or dividend ever enters a capital-allocation policy that has never returned cash. Options-implied volatility and short interest were not retrieved.

Revenue fell for two years before the 2026 rebound while operating income fell throughout, from $8,891M in FY2023 to $3,466M trailing, because research and development rose from $3,969M to $8,861M and selling and administrative cost from $4,800M to $7,485M against gross profit that stayed between $17.1B and $20.0B. The Q3 2026 operating margin of 2.6% came on revenue flat year on year with deliveries down 2% to 486,532 from 497,099, so price, mix and a weaker dollar carried the top line. Reported against adjusted: Q3 2026 GAAP net income of $787M against non-GAAP of $1,697M, and diluted EPS of $0.22 against $0.48. The quarter also absorbed a $475M reversal of previously recognised regulatory credit revenue for returned credits, so the 2.6% operating margin understates the underlying figure by 1.7 points [S12, S13, S1, S8].

### Free cash flow is a payables loan and a capex pause

Nine-month operating cash flow of $14,897M exceeded the $13,014M of capital expenditure to leave $1,883M of free cash flow, against $6,220M for FY2025. Two facts weaken the conversion. Management attributes $3.51 billion of the $3.96 billion year-on-year operating-cash-flow increase to working capital, and in Q3 2026 alone free cash flow of $1,531M rested on a $2,590M working-capital inflow, of which accounts payable supplied $1,920M and accrued liabilities $1,950M; stripping it out, quarterly free cash flow was -$1,059M, and $3,670M of capex sat in liabilities at 2026-09-30. Across the nine months, payables rose $3,868M from 2025-12-31 to $17,239M and the cash conversion cycle fell to 2.6 days from 13.0, so without the payables build nine-month free cash flow would have been -$1,985M. Capital expenditure nearly doubled from $6,134M a year earlier, and the 2026 plan was restated between filings — "in excess of $25 billion" in the July 2026 report, "in excess of $20 billion" in the October 2026 one, and $20 billion on the Q3 2026 call — leaving full-year 2026 free cash flow between -$1,290M and +$1,160M depending on whether Q4 operating cash flow matches Q4 2025's $3,813M or Q3 2026's $6,263M [S8, S9, S83, S102].

### The balance sheet carries the plan; the off-balance items carry the risk

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| Interest coverage | 56.99x | 20.22x | 12.88x | 9.96x | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Stock-based compensation / revenue | 1.9% | 2.0% | 3.0% | 4.2% | S12, S13, S1, S8 |

Cash of $17,853M and short-term investments of $27,594M against $9,267M of debt gave $36,180M of net cash at 2026-09-30, and three credit agreements signed in September 2026 lifted unused committed facilities to $30.00B from $6.43B at 2025-12-31, so the $20B capex year is funded several times over without equity. The obligations outside the debt line matter more: $7,955M of minimum lease payments at 2025-12-31, of which $1,320M falls due within twelve months; an accrued warranty reserve of $7,414M that grew 20.9% in nine months against 10% delivery growth; and $7,055M of deferred revenue. Goodwill and intangibles of $381M are 0.2% of assets, so there is no acquisition accounting to discount, and interest coverage of 9.96x is ample but has fallen from 56.99x in FY2023 as operating income shrank [S8, S1].

### The capital is not earning its keep

Returns have fallen faster than margins. Return on invested capital went from 28.3% in FY2023 to 13.7%, 7.0% and 5.5% trailing, and return on equity from 27.9% to 3.8%; the 5.5% compares with a 4.93% ten-year Treasury yield on 2026-10-30, leaving 57 basis points for equity risk in a business whose operating margin has halved twice in three years. The capex record explains it: $41,778M spent in FY2023, FY2024, FY2025 and the first nine months of 2026 against a $5,425M fall in operating income over the same span — from FY2022's peak of $13,656M the fall is $10,190M — an incremental return that is negative at group level. Nothing has been returned to shareholders: no dividend and no repurchase from FY2021 to Q3 2026, while $2,000M of cash went into the xAI investment agreed in January 2026, converted into SpaceX Class A stock on 2026-03-12, and media reported the investment went ahead against a shareholder vote. GM authorised a $20B repurchase in the same quarter [S1, S8, S10, S115, S104].

### What flatters the number, and what would change it

Four items soften the reported result. Interest income of $1,301M was 42.9% of nine-month pre-tax income, and $445M was 46.5% of the Q3 2026 figure, against 17.5% in FY2024. Stock-based compensation of $3,346M in nine months is 4.3% of revenue and the main reason non-GAAP profit more than doubles GAAP profit; EPS is struck on 3,240M basic and 3,541M diluted weighted-average shares against 3,952,648,559 shares outstanding at 2026-09-30, and the 713M difference is the 423.7M unvested shares of the 2025 CEO award plus 286.4M restricted shares from the 2018 award, both excluded until earned — so dividing earnings by the diluted count understates the share base by 12%, and the award, if earned, lifts the count by a further 12%. An effective tax rate of 20% against 27% was helped by a smaller valuation-allowance release in Q2 2026, and cost of automotive sales benefited from what management calls warranty adjustments while the warranty reserve rose 20.9%. Sensitivity: a percentage point of ex-credit automotive margin is worth $800M a year on $80,000M of automotive revenue, 6.4 times a point of energy margin at $12,500M, and each $1B of capex is $1B of free cash flow. Base case FY2027 free cash flow of $2,000M assumes operating cash flow of $22,000M less capex of $20,000M with energy at 30% and automotive at 18%; energy back at Q2 2026's 20.4% and automotive at 15.4% removes $3,360M and turns it into -$1,360M; energy held at 33.1% adds $390M. The variable that moves the outcome most is capex, a management decision worth $5B in a single restatement between July and October 2026 — more than six points of automotive margin. The diligence question is what the 2027 capex number is and whether the payables build reflects renegotiated terms or deferred payments [S8, S83, S1, S117, S102].

::: info danger
The most serious red flag is the composition of free cash flow rather than its level: nine-month free cash flow is smaller than the rise in payables that produced it, capital expenditure was re-scoped in the same quarter that new credit lines were arranged, and the cash balance generating almost half of pre-tax profit is the only reason reported earnings look positive at the operating level. Reported free cash flow is a ceiling, not a run-rate.
:::

arguments.markdown:
Tesla closes at $399.81 on NasdaqGS on 2026-10-30, a $1,580.4bn market capitalisation and $1,544.2bn enterprise value; on the businesses its filings describe — cars, storage, services — it is worth $139-160bn, or $35-40 a share. The other $1,420-1,441bn, 90-91% of the equity, rests on robotaxi, FSD and Optimus revenue the quarterly report does not yet book, and the buyer pays 103x trailing adjusted EBITDA for the whole. The reported businesses cannot carry the price: the residual is an option requiring 17-34 years of installed Cybercab capacity, and the shares are a claim on a multiple rather than on earnings [S8, S9].

### The price pays for a multiple, not for earnings

Trailing revenue is $103.6bn, adjusted EBITDA $15.0bn, operating income $3.47bn and free cash flow $3.3bn after $15.4bn of capital expenditure [S9]. That is 445x EV/operating income, a 0.2% free-cash-flow yield and 14.9x sales, against 17.3x EV/EBITDA for BYD and 19.1x earnings for General Motors below. The EBITDA the company prefers adds back $4.3bn of stock compensation, up from $2.8bn in FY2025, so 103x becomes 144x before that add-back. One turn is worth $15.0bn, three years of net income: the price is a rating, and a delay in autonomy compresses the rating, not the earnings.

### The capital structure has already added supply

| Event | Date | Amount | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shares outstanding | 2025-12-31 to 2026-09-30 | +202m shares | 3,751m to 3,953m, +5.4% | S8 |

| 2025 CEO Performance Award | vote 2025-11-06 | 423,743,904 shares | contingent; every tranche gated from a $2,000bn market capitalisation | S10 |
| Dividends and buybacks | since 2010 | none | no dividend ever declared, no repurchase programme | S1 |

The 5.4% increase in nine months is the quiet dilution: 202m shares at $399.81 is $80.8bn of new equity, and the Form 4 record shows no insider buying against it. The award is the larger overhang, 10.7% of the current count, but it is conditional on a market capitalisation 26.6% above spot, so it is a cost of the bull case rather than of today's price.

### What the reported businesses are worth

| Method | Inputs | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive and regulatory credits | $75.0bn trailing revenue at 0.6-0.8x EV/sales, above GM and Ford's multiples | $45-60bn | S9, S15, S17 |
| Energy generation and storage | $12.3bn trailing revenue, 30.2% nine-month gross margin, at 2.5-3.0x sales; CATL earns 19.8x | $31-37bn | S9, S133 |
| Services and other | $16.3bn trailing revenue, +32% year on year, at 1.5x sales | $24bn | S9 |
| Net cash at 2026-09-30 | $45,447m cash and short-term investments less $9,267m debt | $36,180m | S8 |
| SpaceX equity stake | $2,002m bought in Q1 2026 plus $863m unrealised gain | $2,865m | S9 |
| Total, reported businesses | | $139-160bn, $35-40 a share | |
| Residual in the price | $1,580.4bn less the total | $1,420-1,441bn, 90-91% | |

The split matters more than the point estimate. Energy, the best-margin segment at 33.1% gross in Q3 2026, is 12% of trailing revenue and fell 16% year on year as Megapack prices fell; services grew 32% and set a record $734m of gross profit. Neither stretches to a trillion dollars at peer multiples. A generous automotive recovery — 10% operating margin on $75bn at 25x — lifts the total to $288bn, $73 a share, and still leaves 82% of the price unexplained.

### What the price requires by 2030

| Multiple applied to enterprise value | Required adjusted EBITDA | Versus $15.0bn trailing | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 17.3x, BYD's multiple | $89.3bn | 6.0x | S131 |
| 25x | $61.8bn | 4.1x | |
| 40x | $38.6bn | 2.6x | |
| 80x, the multiple management's own $4.0tn tranche implies on $50bn | $19.3bn | 1.3x | S127 |

Inverting the price gives the same answer. The residual $1,441bn, discounted at 10% and valued at 20x 2030 operating income, needs $105bn of 2030 operating income; at 40x, $53bn. At a 25% robotaxi margin and $100,000 of revenue per vehicle-year, that is 2.1-4.2m vehicles by 2030, against 1,051 authorised robotaxis in Texas on 2026-10-27 and 125,000 units of installed Cybercab capacity a year: 17-34 years of factory output and two to four times the one-million-robotaxi milestone the board paired with a $3.5tn market capitalisation [S125, S127]. Management's own ladder is also less demanding than the price: the $4.0tn tranche implies 80x adjusted EBITDA, below the 103x the shares carry.

| Company | P/E (TTM) | EV/sales | EV/EBITDA (XBRL basis) | FCF yield | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tesla | 439.4x | 14.9x | 169.0x | 0.2% | S8, S11 |
| General Motors | 19.1x | n/m | n/m | 19.5% | S15, S16 |
| Ford | n/m | n/m | n/m | 11.3% | S17, S18 |
| Rivian | n/m | 2.6x | n/m | -23.8% | S19 |
| BYD | 21.2x | n/d | 17.3x | n/d | S132, S131 |
| CATL | 19.8x | n/d | n/d | n/d | S133 |
| Fluence Energy | n/m | n/m | n/m | -14.6% | S61, S62 |

Tesla's own history agrees with the peer table. The P/E was 34.0x at the end of 2022, 57.8x in 2023, 204.6x in 2024 and 420.8x in 2025 as diluted EPS fell from $4.90 to $1.08, and is 439.4x now; EV/sales, the steadier measure, is 14.9x inside a 14.7-16.5x band, because revenue doubled while the shares returned -0.8% over five years. A 4.93% ten-year Treasury yield, a VIX at its 77th percentile and a 326bp high-yield spread make a 439x earnings multiple harder to hold than it was in 2021 [S11, S12, S22].

### Consensus, guidance and the dates that reset the multiple

Consensus is Hold — 24 buy, 1 strong buy, 20 hold and 3 sell across 48 firms — with an average target of $408.61, 2.2% above the close; an 83-analyst sample gives $442.13, 10.6% above [S128]. Targets run from Jefferies at $400 to RBC at $480, and Q3 2026 adjusted EPS was $0.48 against $0.45 expected. Tesla gives no numeric revenue or EPS guidance, commits only to maximum capacity utilisation and to "hardware-related profits accompanied by an acceleration of SI, software and fleet-based profits", and cut capital expenditure to approximately $20bn from more than $25bn. The dates that reset the multiple are the fourth-quarter 2026 results in the last week of January 2027, on the pattern of the FY2025 10-K filed 2026-01-29, the first Cybercab deployment outside Austin, and the SpaceX committee process.

The strongest counter-argument is that the premium buys an option that is maturing: 1.74m active FSD subscriptions, a paid take rate above 75% of North American deliveries, nearly 2m unsupervised Robotaxi miles, and a fleet that grew from 739 to 1,051 vehicles in eighteen days. If robotaxi unit economics are proven in 2027, 103x on today's EBITDA is a discount to what the business would then earn. The weak version fails — energy caps at $37bn — and no company in the peer table pairs a 30% energy gross margin with 32% services growth above 30x earnings. Confidence in the arithmetic is high and in the multiple's durability low, because the durability rests on evidence the company has not disclosed. Three questions would settle it: revenue per robotaxi-week in Austin, the energy segment's operating margin at 130 GWh of installed capacity, and whether a capital-return policy ever replaces permanent dilution.

rows.confidence: high on Tesla figures (filed statements) and on BNEF GW; medium on the GWh conversion.
rows.follow_up: How much of Tesla's storage backlog is priced at 2026 levels, and what is the contracted price per MWh?

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's problem is not that its markets are small; it is that the two that made it are now contracting while the two that grow are priced per unit, not per promise. Global electric-car sales are expected to reach 23.0 million units in 2026, 28% of all car sales, with the IEA projecting about half of global sales by 2035 on existing policies [S9, S137]. Dividing 23.0 million by 28% implies a global light-vehicle market of roughly 82 million units, so the electric pool is the whole investment case: Tesla delivered 1,324,681 vehicles in the first nine months of 2026 (358,023; 480,126; 486,532 by quarter) — a run-rate of about 1.77 million, or 7.7% of the 2026 electric pool and 2.2% of all cars. The category grows roughly 12% in units in 2026 while Tesla's third quarter fell 2% year on year. That is a share problem inside a growing market, and it changes what an investor is buying: not category growth, but the price Tesla can hold for a differentiated slice of it.

::: market-size
| Layer | Definition | 2026 size | How derived | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM — vehicles | Global light vehicles | ~82m units | 23.0m electric ÷ 28% share | S137 |
| SAM — vehicles | Global electric cars (BEV+PHEV) | 23.0m units | IEA forecast, 28% of sales | S137 |
| SOM — Tesla today | Tesla deliveries | 1.32m in 9M 2026; ~1.77m run-rate (7.7% of SAM) | Company quarterly delivery table | S9 |
| TAM — storage | Global storage deployments | 158 GW / 459 GWh | BloombergNEF 2026 forecast | S141 |
| SOM — Tesla storage | Tesla deployments | 36.0 GWh in 9M 2026 (≈7.8% of 2026E) | Company 10-Q plus deployment table | S8, S9 |
| TAM — paid robotaxi | Paid robotaxi revenue | $0.3-0.5bn fare-based, against $3.5-5.5bn third-party | ~500k rides/week × 52 × $12-18 assumed fare | S142, S144 |
:::

### The United States became a smaller market by policy, not by demand
Removing the $7,500 federal credit on 2025-09-30 cut the US electric pool by roughly a third: sales fell 36% year on year in Q4 2025 and 27% in Q1 2026 to 216,399 units, and were still 30.3% below the prior year through September 2026 even after a 7.7% sequential rebound to 266,630 in Q3 [S139, S145]. Two numbers matter more than the totals. Electric cars were 6.4% of all US new-vehicle sales in Q3 2026 and 5.7% in August, against roughly 8-9% while the credit was live; and Tesla's US volume fell 14.4% in the same nine months. The US market is therefore stabilising at a lower share, with Tesla holding 52.9% of it. A buyer of Tesla equity is effectively underwriting a 6-7% electric share of the US market for 2027, not a return to 2025 volumes; every incremental US unit has to be taken from a hybrid or a legacy BEV rather than from a subsidy-driven first-time buyer.

### China's reset is a price event, and the volume moved offshore
China's new-energy retail sales fell 16.7% year on year to 1.084 million in September 2026, the ninth consecutive monthly decline, with the first nine months down 12.8% to 7.758 million — while penetration reached a record 67.0% of retail because total passenger-car retail fell 28.0% [S138]. The composition is the signal: battery-electric retail fell 7.4%, plug-in hybrid retail fell 35.6% and range-extended electric fell 19.3%, while battery-electric wholesale rose 18.3% and NEV exports rose 163.5% to 558,000. Tightening the purchase-tax preference and withdrawing local subsidies raised the cash price of the cheapest cars first, and production went abroad instead of into domestic showrooms. For Tesla, which was the fourth-largest NEV brand by retail in September at 64,837 units, China is now a capped, price-deflationary volume market; the growth it can capture there is export-led, and exports carry tariffs and logistics that domestic sales do not.

### Europe is the only vehicle market growing fast enough to matter
EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,931,465 in January-September 2026, a 22.7% share against 16.1% a year earlier, and September alone ran at 290,117 units and a 29.9% share, up 72.9% year on year on a total market up 5.7% [S140, S147]. On those shares the electric pool grew roughly 49% in units, which is the only large market where Tesla can add volume without cutting price. The catch is that EU demand is regulation-created: the 2025-2027 CO2 step forces fleet averages down, and the Commission's proposal of 2025-12-16 to replace the 100% 2035 target with a 90% cut has moved the long-dated backstop into Parliament and Council, where environment ministers remain split. Two conclusions follow. Europe carries Tesla's 2026 volume growth (Berlin posted record production in Q3 2026), and the value of that growth is capped by a policy that is being renegotiated while it is being relied upon.

### Storage compounds in volume and deflates in price
Global storage installations reached 112 GW in 2025 and are forecast at 158 GW and 459 GWh in 2026, with India up 26-fold and Australia nearly doubling, and BloombergNEF sees 3.1 TW cumulative by 2036 [S141, S8]. Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in the first nine months of 2026 and about 7.8% of the forecast 2026 pool, but its storage revenue per GWh fell to roughly $210 million from $273 million a year earlier — a 23% decline — because Q3 energy revenue fell 16% while deployments rose 9.6%. The market is real, large and increasingly structural: Tesla reported its highest-ever order rate and backlog, and management ties demand to data-centre load growth rather than to subsidies. But an investor should model the segment on revenue per GWh falling faster than volume rises. At 2026 unit prices the 459 GWh pool is worth roughly $69-107 billion depending on whether Chinese or Tesla-level pricing is assumed; the difference between those two numbers is the entire margin question in the segment.

### Paid robotaxi is a Waymo-sized business, not a market yet
The only scaled paid autonomous service is Waymo's: about 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities as of 2026-03-27, roughly 26 million a year, which at an assumed $12-18 average fare is a $0.3-0.5 billion business [S142, S144]. Third-party research puts the 2026 robotaxi market at $3.5-5.5 billion and 2030 at anywhere from $27 billion to $204 billion; the estimates are more than 7x apart at 2030, which is the mark of a market sized from addressable ride-hailing spend rather than from observed fares. Tesla began Cybercab rides in Austin on 2026-09-03, reported cumulative unsupervised miles up eightfold quarter on quarter, and discloses no ride count, fare or robotaxi revenue. The credible serviceable market by 2028 is therefore set by permits and per-mile safety evidence, not by TAM studies: on today's record Tesla is roughly 12-24 months behind Waymo on verified paid scale, and a $50 billion 2028 robotaxi revenue line would require it to overtake the incumbent and multiply the entire 2026 paid market more than twenty-fold.

| Region | Market size (2026) | Growth | Tesla's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States | 266,630 EVs in Q3 2026; 6.4% of new-vehicle sales | −30.3% year to date; +7.7% QoQ in Q3 | Entered, 52.9% of the EV pool; US volume −14.4% | Credit repealed 2025-09-30; tariff and content rules under OBBBA | Ford, GM, Hyundai-Kia, Rivian, Toyota hybrids | S139, S145 |
| China | 7.758m NEV retail in 9M 2026; 67.0% penetration in September | −12.8% in 9M; BEV retail −7.4%, PHEV −35.6% | Entered; fourth-largest NEV brand at 64,837 in September | Purchase-tax preference tightened; local-brand cost advantage; export tariffs | BYD, Geely, Leapmotor, Xiaomi, Changan | S138 |
| European Union | 1,931,465 BEVs in 9M 2026; 22.7% share (29.9% in September) | ≈+49% BEV units in 9M; total market +5.7% | Entered; recovering off a weak 2025, Berlin at record output | CO2 2035 target under renegotiation; country-level incentives | Volkswagen, Renault, Stellantis, Hyundai-Kia, BYD | S140, S147 |
| Rest of world | Not disclosed by Tesla; Chinese NEV exports 3.887m in 9M 2026 (+138.8%) | Chinese NEV exports +163.5% in September | Entered; record quarterly deliveries in Canada, Australia, Japan and Taiwan | Tariffs on Chinese-built cars; charging build-out | BYD, Geely, Leapmotor, Toyota | S138, S9 |
| Storage (global) | 158 GW / 459 GWh in 2026E | +41% in GW after +48% in 2025 | Entered; 36.0 GWh in 9M 2026, ≈7.8% of 2026E | Cell supply, tariffs on Chinese cells, grid interconnection queues | CATL, Sungrow, Fluence, BYD | S141, S8 |
:::

::: evidence
**The demand Tesla is priced for grows everywhere except where it sells most.**

The IEA's 23 million-unit 2026 forecast is a global figure carried by Europe (about +20%) and by Chinese exports (+163.5% in September), while the two markets that supplied most of Tesla's 2024-2025 revenue — the United States and China — are down 30.3% and 12.8% year to date [S137, S138, S145]. Tesla's own disclosure that battery availability, not orders, limited Q3 2026 volume, together with its largest backlog in four years, is the counterweight: the constraint on the next two quarters may be supply rather than demand.
:::

The investor implication is allocation, not enthusiasm: weight the case toward storage (a 33.1% gross-margin business selling into a market growing 41% in gigawatts) and toward Europe, treat US vehicle revenue as a share-defence exercise at a lower market level, and value paid autonomy at zero until rides and fares are disclosed. The open questions that would move this assessment are Tesla's regional unit split for 2026 (it discloses only annual revenue by geography), the contracted price per MWh in its storage backlog, and its paid Robotaxi ride count and average fare in Austin.

Waymo is the only recent large mark for a robotaxi business, and it was struck at $126bn in February 2026 for a company with years of driverless operation, while the autonomy value Tesla's price embeds is 11.3-11.4x that. That is not proof the market is wrong — Tesla's version bundles the vehicle, the fleet and the software — but it is the best available base rate, and a 12-month holder has no precedent transaction to point to that would justify a higher mark. The alternative exit, a re-rating to the $2,000bn first tranche, is a 26.6% gain that depends on the market, not on the company, and the tranche itself requires an operational milestone in addition to the capitalisation [S130].

### The drawdown history is the risk that matters

The shares fell from $356.78 at the 2021 year end to $123.18 at the 2022 year end, a 65.5% loss, and from a 52-week high of $498.83 to a 52-week low of $297.38, a 40.4% fall, with the band now 50.4% as wide as the price. Over five years to 2026-10-30 the return is -0.8% while revenue rose from $53.8bn to $103.6bn, and over twelve months the stock is -12.4% against the S&P 500's +10.8%. A buyer at $399.81 is buying after a 28.5% three-month run and 8.2% above the 50-day average, at a VIX in its 77th percentile and a 4.93% ten-year Treasury yield — the entry point, not the company, is the risk [S11, S12].

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's problem is not that its markets are small; it is that the two that made it are contracting while the two that grow are priced per unit, not per promise. Global electric-car sales are expected to reach 23.0 million units in 2026, 28% of all car sales, with the IEA projecting about half of global sales by 2035 on existing policies [S9, S137]. Dividing 23.0 million by 28% implies a global light-vehicle market of roughly 82 million units, so the electric pool is the whole case: Tesla delivered 1,324,681 vehicles in the first nine months of 2026 (358,023; 480,126; 486,532 by quarter) — a run-rate of about 1.77 million, or 7.7% of the 2026 electric pool and 2.2% of all cars. The category grows roughly 12% in units in 2026 while Tesla's third quarter fell 2% year on year. That is a share problem inside a growing market, and it changes what an investor is buying: not category growth, but the price Tesla can hold for a differentiated slice of it.

**Market size, top-down and bottom-up**

| Layer | Definition | 2026 size | How derived | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM — vehicles | Global light vehicles | ~82m units | 23.0m electric ÷ 28% share | S137 |
| SAM — vehicles | Global electric cars (BEV+PHEV) | 23.0m units | IEA forecast, 28% of sales | S137 |
| SOM — Tesla today | Tesla deliveries | 1.32m in 9M 2026; ~1.77m run-rate (7.7% of SAM) | Company quarterly delivery table | S9 |
| TAM — storage | Global storage deployments | 158 GW / 459 GWh | BloombergNEF 2026 forecast | S141 |
| SOM — Tesla storage | Tesla deployments | 36.0 GWh in 9M 2026 (≈7.8% of 2026E) | 10-Q plus deployment table | S8, S9 |
| TAM — paid robotaxi | Paid robotaxi revenue | $0.3-0.5bn fare-based, against $3.5-5.5bn third-party | ~500k rides/week × 52 × $12-18 assumed fare | S142, S144 |

### The United States became a smaller market by policy, not by demand

Removing the $7,500 federal credit on 2025-09-30 cut the US electric pool by roughly a third: sales fell 36% year on year in Q4 2025 and 27% in Q1 2026 to 216,399 units, and were still 30.3% below the prior year through September 2026 even after a 7.7% sequential rebound to 266,630 in Q3 [S139, S145]. Two numbers matter more than the totals. Electric cars were 6.4% of all US new-vehicle sales in Q3 2026 and 5.7% in August, against roughly 8-9% while the credit was live; and Tesla's US volume fell 14.4% in the same nine months. The US market is stabilising at a lower share with Tesla holding 52.9% of it. A buyer of Tesla equity is underwriting a 6-7% electric share of the US market for 2027, not a return to 2025 volumes: every incremental US unit must be taken from a hybrid or a legacy BEV rather than a subsidy-driven first-time buyer.

### China's reset is a price event, and the volume moved offshore

China's new-energy retail sales fell 16.7% year on year to 1.084 million in September 2026, the ninth consecutive monthly decline, with the first nine months down 12.8% to 7.758 million — while penetration reached a record 67.0% of retail because total passenger-car retail fell 28.0% [S138]. The composition is the signal: battery-electric retail fell 7.4%, plug-in hybrid retail fell 35.6% and range-extended electric fell 19.3%, while battery-electric wholesale rose 18.3% and NEV exports rose 163.5% to 558,000. Tightening the purchase-tax preference and withdrawing local subsidies raised the cash price of the cheapest cars first, and production went abroad instead of into domestic showrooms. For Tesla, the fourth-largest NEV brand by retail in September at 64,837 units, China is now a capped, price-deflationary market; the growth it can capture there is export-led, and exports carry tariffs that domestic sales do not.

### Europe is the only vehicle market growing fast enough to matter

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,931,465 in January-September 2026, a 22.7% share against 16.1% a year earlier, and September alone ran at 290,117 units and a 29.9% share, up 72.9% year on year on a total market up 5.7% [S140, S147]. On those shares the electric pool grew roughly 49% in units, the only large market where Tesla can add volume without cutting price. The catch is that EU demand is regulation-created: the 2025-2027 CO2 step forces fleet averages down, and the Commission's proposal of 2025-12-16 to replace the 100% 2035 target with a 90% cut has moved the long-dated backstop into Parliament and Council, where environment ministers remain split. Europe therefore carries Tesla's 2026 volume growth (Berlin posted record production in Q3 2026), and the value of that growth is capped by a policy being renegotiated while it is being relied upon.

### Storage compounds in volume and deflates in price

Global storage installations reached 112 GW in 2025 and are forecast at 158 GW and 459 GWh in 2026, with India up 26-fold and Australia nearly doubling, and BloombergNEF sees 3.1 TW cumulative by 2036 [S141, S8]. Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in the first nine months of 2026, about 7.8% of the forecast 2026 pool, but its storage revenue per GWh fell to roughly $210 million from $273 million a year earlier — a 23% decline — because Q3 energy revenue fell 16% while deployments rose 9.6%. The market is large and increasingly structural: Tesla reported its highest-ever order rate and backlog, and management ties demand to data-centre load growth rather than subsidies. But model the segment on revenue per GWh falling faster than volume rises. At 2026 unit prices the 459 GWh pool is worth roughly $69-107 billion depending on whether Chinese or Tesla-level pricing is assumed; the gap between those two numbers is the whole margin question in the segment.

### Paid robotaxi is a Waymo-sized business, not a market yet

The only scaled paid autonomous service is Waymo's: about 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities as of 2026-03-27, roughly 26 million a year, which at an assumed $12-18 average fare is a $0.3-0.5 billion business [S142, S144]. Third-party research puts the 2026 robotaxi market at $3.5-5.5 billion and 2030 at anywhere from $27 billion to $204 billion; the estimates are more than 7x apart at 2030, the mark of a market sized from addressable ride-hailing spend rather than observed fares. Tesla began Cybercab rides in Austin on 2026-09-03, reported cumulative unsupervised miles up eightfold quarter on quarter, and discloses no ride count, fare or robotaxi revenue. The credible serviceable market by 2028 is set by permits and per-mile safety evidence, not TAM studies: on today's record Tesla is 12-24 months behind Waymo on verified paid scale, and a $50 billion 2028 robotaxi revenue line would require it to overtake the incumbent and multiply the entire 2026 paid market more than twenty-fold.

**Where the growth is, and where Tesla stands**

| Region | Market size (2026) | Growth | Tesla's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States | 266,630 EVs in Q3 2026; 6.4% of new-vehicle sales | −30.3% year to date; +7.7% QoQ in Q3 | Entered, 52.9% of the EV pool; US volume −14.4% | Credit repealed 2025-09-30; tariff and content rules under OBBBA | Ford, GM, Hyundai-Kia, Rivian, Toyota hybrids | S139, S145 |
| China | 7.758m NEV retail in 9M 2026; 67.0% penetration in September | −12.8% in 9M; BEV retail −7.4%, PHEV −35.6% | Entered; fourth-largest NEV brand at 64,837 in September | Purchase-tax preference tightened; local-brand cost advantage; export tariffs | BYD, Geely, Leapmotor, Xiaomi, Changan | S138 |
| European Union | 1,931,465 BEVs in 9M 2026; 22.7% share (29.9% in September) | ≈+49% BEV units in 9M; total market +5.7% | Entered; recovering off a weak 2025, Berlin at record output | CO2 2035 target under renegotiation; country-level incentives | Volkswagen, Renault, Stellantis, Hyundai-Kia, BYD | S140, S147 |
| Rest of world | Not disclosed by Tesla; Chinese NEV exports 3.887m in 9M 2026 (+138.8%) | Chinese NEV exports +163.5% in September | Entered; record quarterly deliveries in Canada, Australia, Japan and Taiwan | Tariffs on Chinese-built cars; charging build-out | BYD, Geely, Leapmotor, Toyota | S138, S9 |
| Storage (global) | 158 GW / 459 GWh in 2026E | +41% in GW after +48% in 2025 | Entered; 36.0 GWh in 9M 2026, ≈7.8% of 2026E | Cell supply, tariffs on Chinese cells, interconnection queues | CATL, Sungrow, Fluence, BYD | S141, S8 |

::: evidence
**The demand Tesla is priced for grows everywhere except where it sells most.**

The IEA's 23 million-unit 2026 forecast is carried by Europe (about +20%) and by Chinese exports (+163.5% in September), while the United States and China — the sources of most of Tesla's 2024-2025 revenue — are down 30.3% and 12.8% year to date [S137, S138, S145]. The counterweight is Tesla's own disclosure that battery availability, not orders, limited Q3 2026 volume, alongside its largest backlog in four years: the constraint on the next two quarters may be supply rather than demand.
:::

The investor implication is allocation, not enthusiasm: weight the case toward storage (a 33.1% gross-margin business selling into a market growing 41% in gigawatts) and toward Europe, treat US vehicle revenue as share defence at a lower market level, and value paid autonomy at zero until rides and fares are disclosed. The open questions that would move this assessment are Tesla's regional unit split for 2026, the contracted price per MWh in its storage backlog, and its paid Robotaxi ride count and average fare in Austin.

### The United States became a smaller market by policy, not by demand

Removing the $7,500 federal credit on 2025-09-30 cut the US electric pool by roughly a third: sales fell 36% year on year in Q4 2025 and 27% in Q1 2026 to 216,399 units, and were still 30.3% below the prior year through September 2026 even after a 7.7% sequential rebound to 266,630 in Q3 [S139, S145]. Two numbers matter more than the totals. Electric cars were 6.4% of all US new-vehicle sales in Q3 2026 and 5.7% in August, and Tesla's US volume fell 14.4% in the same nine months. The US market is stabilising at a lower share with Tesla holding 52.9% of it. Tesla equity is therefore a bet on a 6-7% electric share of the US market in 2027, not a return to 2025 volumes: every incremental US unit must be taken from a hybrid or a legacy BEV.

### China's reset is a price event, and the volume moved offshore

China's new-energy retail sales fell 16.7% year on year to 1.084 million in September 2026, the ninth consecutive monthly decline, with the first nine months down 12.8% to 7.758 million — while penetration reached a record 67.0% of retail because total passenger-car retail fell 28.0% [S138]. Tightening the purchase-tax preference and withdrawing local subsidies raised the cash price of the cheapest cars first, and production went abroad instead of into domestic showrooms. For Tesla, the fourth-largest NEV brand by retail in September at 64,837 units, China is a capped, price-deflationary market; the growth it can capture there is export-led and carries tariffs domestic sales do not.

### Europe is the only vehicle market growing fast enough to matter

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,931,465 in January-September 2026, a 22.7% share against 16.1% a year earlier, and September alone ran at 290,117 units and a 29.9% share, up 72.9% year on year on a total market up 5.7% [S140, S147]. On those shares the electric pool grew roughly 49% in units, the only large market where Tesla can add volume without cutting price. Europe carries Tesla's 2026 volume growth (Berlin posted record production in Q3 2026), and that growth is capped by a policy being renegotiated while it is relied upon.

### Storage compounds in volume and deflates in price

Global storage installations reached 112 GW in 2025 and are forecast at 158 GW and 459 GWh in 2026, with India up 26-fold and Australia nearly doubling; BloombergNEF sees 3.1 TW cumulative by 2036 [S141, S8]. Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in the first nine months of 2026, about 7.8% of the forecast 2026 pool, but its storage revenue per GWh fell to roughly $210 million from $273 million a year earlier — a 23% decline — because Q3 energy revenue fell 16% while deployments rose 9.6%. The market is large and increasingly structural: Tesla reported its highest-ever order rate and backlog and ties demand to data-centre load growth rather than subsidies. But model the segment on revenue per GWh falling faster than volume rises. At 2026 unit prices the 459 GWh pool is worth roughly $69-107 billion depending on whether Chinese or Tesla-level pricing is assumed — and that gap is the segment's whole margin question.

### Paid robotaxi is a Waymo-sized business, not a market yet

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's problem is not that its markets are small; it is that the two that made it are contracting while the two that grow are priced per unit, not per promise. Global electric-car sales are expected to reach 23.0 million units in 2026, 28% of all car sales, from more than 20 million in 2025, and the IEA projects half of global sales by 2035 [S9, S137]. Dividing 23.0 million by 28% implies 82 million light vehicles, so the electric pool is the whole case: Tesla delivered 1,324,681 vehicles in the first nine months of 2026 (358,023; 480,126; 486,532) — a run-rate of 1.77 million, or 7.7% of the 2026 electric pool and 2.2% of all cars. Unit growth of 15% in 2026 slows to a 7.7% CAGR to 2035 on the IEA's own 50%-share projection, while Tesla's third quarter fell 2% year on year. That is a share problem inside a decelerating market: what an investor buys is not category growth but the price Tesla can hold for a differentiated slice of it.

**Market size, top-down and bottom-up**

| Layer | 2026 size | How derived | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAM — global light vehicles | 82m units | 23.0m electric ÷ 28% share | S137 |
| SAM — global electric cars (BEV+PHEV) | 23.0m units | IEA forecast, 28% of sales | S137 |
| SOM — Tesla deliveries | 1.32m in 9M 2026; 1.77m run-rate (7.7% of SAM) | Quarterly delivery table | S9 |
| TAM — global storage deployments | 158 GW / 459 GWh | BloombergNEF 2026 forecast | S141 |
| SOM — Tesla storage | 36.0 GWh in 9M 2026 (7.8% of 2026E) | 10-Q plus deployment table | S8, S9 |
| TAM — paid robotaxi revenue | $0.3-0.5bn fare-based, against $3.5-5.5bn third-party | 500k rides/week × 52 × $12-18 assumed fare | S142, S144 |

### The two largest pools shrank by policy, not by demand

Removing the $7,500 federal credit on 2025-09-30 cut the US electric pool by 30.3% year to date: sales fell 36% year on year in Q4 2025 and 27% in Q1 2026 to 216,399 units, and were still 30.3% below the prior year through September 2026 even after a 7.7% sequential rebound to 266,630 in Q3, when electric cars were 6.4% of US new-vehicle sales and Tesla's own US volume fell 14.4% [S139, S145]. China's new-energy retail fell 16.7% year on year to 1.084 million in September 2026, the ninth consecutive decline, and 12.8% to 7.758 million in nine months, while penetration hit a record 67.0% only because total passenger-car retail fell 28.0%; battery-electric retail fell 7.4%, plug-in hybrid retail 35.6% and range-extended electric 19.3%, while battery-electric wholesale rose 18.3% and NEV exports 163.5% to 558,000 [S138]. Tightening China's purchase-tax preference and withdrawing local subsidies raised the cash price of the cheapest cars first and pushed production abroad. Tesla held 52.9% of the smaller US pool and was China's fourth-largest NEV brand by retail at 64,837 units: US equity value is now a bet on a 6-7% electric share of the US market in 2027, and China is a capped, price-deflationary market whose growth reaches Tesla through exports that carry tariffs.

### Europe is the only vehicle market growing fast enough to matter

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,931,465 in January-September 2026, a 22.7% share against 16.1% a year earlier, and September alone ran at 290,117 units and a 29.9% share, up 72.9% year on year on a total market up 5.7% [S140, S147]. On those two shares the electric pool grew 49% in units, the only large market where Tesla can add volume without cutting price. EU demand is regulation-created: the 2025-2027 CO2 step forces fleet averages down, and the Commission's 2025-12-16 proposal to replace the 100% 2035 target with a 90% cut has moved the long-dated backstop into Parliament and Council, where ministers remain split. Europe carries Tesla's 2026 volume growth (Berlin posted record production in Q3 2026), and that growth is capped by a policy being renegotiated while it is relied upon.

### Storage compounds in volume and deflates in price

Global storage installations reached 112 GW in 2025 and are forecast at 158 GW and 459 GWh in 2026, a 41% annual increase, with BloombergNEF seeing 3.1 TW cumulative by 2036 [S141, S8]. Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in the first nine months of 2026, 7.8% of the forecast 2026 pool, but its storage revenue per GWh fell to $210 million from $273 million a year earlier — a 23% decline — because Q3 energy revenue fell 16% while deployments rose 9.6%. The market is increasingly structural: Tesla reported its highest-ever order rate and backlog and ties demand to data-centre load growth, not subsidies. But model the segment on revenue per GWh falling faster than volume rises. At 2026 unit prices the 459 GWh pool is worth $69-107 billion depending on whether Chinese or Tesla-level pricing is assumed, and that gap is the segment's whole margin question.

### Paid robotaxi is a Waymo-sized business, not a market yet

The only scaled paid autonomous service is Waymo's: 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities as of 2026-03-27, which is 26 million a year and, at an assumed $12-18 average fare, a $0.3-0.5 billion business [S142, S144, S125]. Third-party research puts the 2026 robotaxi market at $3.5-5.5 billion and 2030 estimates span $27-204 billion, a 7.3x spread that marks sizes built from ride-hailing spend rather than observed fares. Tesla is scaling from a smaller base: Texas regulators listed 1,051 authorised Robotaxi vehicles on 2026-10-27 (544 Cybercab, 507 Model Y), up from 739 on 2026-10-09, against roughly 3,000 Waymo vehicles, and Tesla reports about 2 million cumulative unsupervised miles against Waymo's 170 million-plus. Tesla discloses no ride count, fare or robotaxi revenue. The serviceable market by 2028 is therefore set by permits and per-mile safety evidence, not TAM studies: a $50 billion 2028 robotaxi line would require Tesla to overtake the incumbent and multiply the 2026 paid market more than twenty-fold.

**Where the growth is, and where Tesla stands**

| Region | Market size (2026) | Growth | Tesla's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States | 266,630 EVs in Q3 2026; 6.4% of new-vehicle sales | −30.3% year to date; +7.7% QoQ in Q3 | Entered, 52.9% of the EV pool; US volume −14.4% | Credit repealed 2025-09-30; tariff and content rules under OBBBA | Ford, GM, Hyundai-Kia, Rivian, Toyota hybrids | S139, S145 |
| China | 7.758m NEV retail in 9M 2026; 67.0% penetration in September | −12.8% in 9M; BEV retail −7.4%, PHEV −35.6% | Entered; fourth-largest NEV brand at 64,837 in September | Purchase-tax preference tightened; local-brand cost advantage; export tariffs | BYD, Geely, Leapmotor, Xiaomi, Changan | S138 |
| European Union | 1,931,465 BEVs in 9M 2026; 22.7% share (29.9% in September) | 49% BEV unit growth in 9M; total market +5.7% | Entered; recovering off a weak 2025, Berlin at record output | CO2 2035 target under renegotiation; country-level incentives | Volkswagen, Renault, Stellantis, Hyundai-Kia, BYD | S140, S147 |
| Rest of world | Not disclosed by Tesla; Chinese NEV exports 3.887m in 9M 2026 (+138.8%) | Chinese NEV exports +163.5% in September | Entered; record quarterly deliveries in Canada, Australia, Japan and Taiwan | Tariffs on Chinese-built cars; charging build-out | BYD, Geely, Leapmotor, Toyota | S138, S9 |
| Storage (global) | 158 GW / 459 GWh in 2026E | +41% in GW after +48% in 2025 | Entered; 36.0 GWh in 9M 2026, 7.8% of 2026E | Cell supply, tariffs on Chinese cells, interconnection queues | CATL, Sungrow, Fluence, BYD | S141, S8 |

::: evidence
**The demand Tesla is priced for grows everywhere except where it sells most.**

The IEA's 23 million-unit 2026 forecast is carried by Europe (20% growth) and by Chinese exports (163.5% in September), while the United States and China — the sources of most of Tesla's 2024-2025 revenue — are down 30.3% and 12.8% year to date [S137, S138, S145]. The counterweight is Tesla's own disclosure that battery availability, not orders, limited Q3 2026 volume, alongside its largest backlog in four years: the next two quarters may be supply-constrained rather than demand-constrained.
:::

The implication is allocation, not enthusiasm: weight the case toward storage, Tesla's highest-margin segment and its fastest-growing pool, and toward Europe; treat US vehicle revenue as share defence at a lower market level; and value paid autonomy at zero until rides and fares are disclosed. What would move this assessment: Tesla's 2026 regional unit split, the contracted price per MWh in its storage backlog, and its Austin Robotaxi ride count and average fare.

arguments.markdown:
Tesla is winning the market that is shrinking and losing the one that is growing. It held 52.9% of US electric-vehicle sales in the first nine months of 2026 while that market fell 30.3%, and it was only China's fourth-largest new-energy brand in September at 64,837 retail units, 6.0% of new-energy retail and about 8.5% of battery-electric retail [S139, S145]. Its European volume recovered from a collapsed 2025 base, but the EU electric pool grew 49% in the same period, so recovery is not share gain. What Tesla actually owns is narrower than the narrative: the charging standard every major automaker has now licensed, 1.74 million active FSD subscriptions, and a storage gross margin of 33.1% against Fluence's 5.1%.

### In the United States, Tesla sets the price because it holds the pool
Tesla sold 144,094 US electric vehicles in Q3 2026 for 54% of the market, and 386,194 in nine months for 52.9%, while its own US volume fell 14.4% against a market down 30.3%. Share gains inside a contracting pool flatter the position: the absolute US revenue base is smaller than in 2025 despite record share. The mechanism is distribution. When a $7,500 credit disappears, the brand with the densest charging network and the deepest service footprint keeps the remaining buyers, and smaller entrants lose the sale faster than the leader does. The competitive question for the next twelve months is therefore not who takes US share from Tesla but whether Tesla can hold price: its automotive gross margin rose to 18.5% in Q3 2026 from 17.0% a year earlier even as regulatory-credit revenue fell 73% to $113 million, which is margin discipline, not a price war [S8, S9]. Rivian, the nearest US pure-play, earned an 8.2% gross margin in the same quarter, so Tesla's cost position in US BEVs is intact.

### China is where Tesla is the price taker
BYD sold 456,713 passenger cars in September 2026, of which 273,143 were battery-electric, and 3,078,490 in nine months — 2.3 times Tesla's 1,324,681 — while exporting 180,700 vehicles in the month [S138, S146, S149]. Around the fourth-placed Tesla sat Geely at 119,682 retail units, Leapmotor at 78,202 and Xiaomi at 40,015, with Xiaomi reaching 269,000 units in nine months against a 550,000 target in its second full year of carmaking. The price evidence is in the margins: BYD earned 19.46% gross margin overseas against 16.66% at home in 2025, which is a revealed domestic price ceiling that Tesla cannot price above without losing volume. Tesla's counter is cost and software rather than price — but its China retail of 64,837 in September was 3.8x smaller than BYD's, and Chinese battery-electric wholesale still grew 18.3% that month, so the pool was there and Tesla did not take it.

### Europe: growth in units, no evidence of share
EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,931,465 in January-September 2026 at a 22.7% share, and September ran at 29.9%, so the pool expanded 49% while Tesla's European deliveries recovered from a 2025 slump and Giga Berlin set a production record [S140, S147, S150]. A recovery off a collapsed base inside a pool growing at that rate is not proof of share gain, and Tesla discloses no EU unit count: ACEA's manufacturer table is the record that would settle it. The competitive structure also differs from the US. In Europe the buyer is choosing between compliance-driven models from Volkswagen, Renault, Stellantis and Hyundai-Kia, and imported Chinese BEVs that carry a tariff but still undercut on price. Tesla's advantage is software and charging density; its disadvantage is a two-model line-up against a much broader compliant field, with Model 3/Y accounting for 478,237 of 486,532 deliveries in Q3 2026.

### Storage is the one position Tesla clearly owns
Tesla's energy segment earned a 33.1% gross margin in Q3 2026 on 13.7 GWh, against Fluence's 5.1% in the June 2026 quarter and 13.1% for its 2025 fiscal year, while Tesla's storage revenue per GWh fell to $210 million from $273 million [S8, S9, S61]. That margin gap — six times the nearest listed integrator — is the clearest evidence of an unrivaled cost position anywhere in the case: in-house cells, one-piece factory assembly and Autobidder dispatch software compress installed cost, and the integrator without cell ownership absorbs the price decline instead. Two cautions keep it honest. Q3 2026 energy margin was flattered by $526 million of IEEPA tariff refunds booked against energy cost of revenue, so the underlying gap is narrower than 28 points; and CATL and Sungrow, the cell and inverter suppliers behind much of the global fleet, compete on the input Tesla must buy, which caps how long the integration premium survives at $210 per kWh.

### In paid autonomy, Tesla is the challenger with the permits to prove it
Waymo ran 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities by March 2026 with about 3,000 vehicles and more than 170 million rider-only miles, and raised $16 billion in February 2026 at a $126 billion post-money valuation [S89, S101, S142, S130]. Tesla began Cybercab rides in Austin on 2026-09-03, held 1,051 Texas-authorised Robotaxi vehicles on 2026-10-27 (544 Cybercab, 507 Model Y) up from 739 on 2026-10-09, and reports about 2.0 million cumulative unsupervised miles [S125, S9]. It is absent from California's driverless-testing and deployment permit lists, where Waymo holds deployment authorisation, and it discloses no robotaxi ride count or fare. The most dangerous competitor in the whole case is therefore not BYD but Waymo: BYD competes for the same buyer on price that Tesla can match with cost, while Waymo competes for the same regulatory permission to operate and has a two-order-of-magnitude lead in paid miles, a larger fleet and a war chest raised at a valuation that lets it absorb years of losses.

::: evidence
**Tesla's defensible positions are the charging standard, FSD subscriptions and storage margin — not vehicle share.**

Its 18.5% automotive gross margin and 33.1% energy gross margin were earned while regulatory credits fell 73% and Chinese battery-electric wholesale grew 18.3%, which says Tesla can hold price in the US and in storage while losing volume in China [S8, S9, S138]. The counter-evidence runs the other way in autonomy: Tesla's 2.0 million unsupervised miles against Waymo's 170 million-plus, and its absence from California's deployment permits, mean the option that carries most of the equity premium is the one where Tesla is furthest behind.
:::

:::

The competitive verdict is that Tesla is a high-margin incumbent in a shrinking US pool, a sub-scale participant in the world's largest BEV market, and a credible but trailing challenger in paid autonomy. Its wedge — vertical integration, the charging standard and storage cost — protects margin, not volume, which argues for underwriting unit growth below the market's and watching three numbers: Tesla's China retail share, its storage revenue per GWh, and Texas Robotaxi vehicle authorisations as a proxy for rides.

arguments.markdown:
Tesla is winning the market that is shrinking and losing the one that is growing. It held 52.9% of US electric-vehicle sales in the first nine months of 2026 while that market fell 30.3%, and it was only China's fourth-largest new-energy brand in September at 64,837 retail units, 6.0% of new-energy retail and about 8.5% of battery-electric retail [S139, S145]. Its European volume recovered from a collapsed 2025 base, but the EU electric pool grew 49% over the same period, so recovery is not share gain. What Tesla owns is narrower than the narrative: the charging standard every major automaker has licensed, 1.74 million active FSD subscriptions, and a storage gross margin of 33.1% against Fluence's 5.1%.

### In the United States, Tesla sets the price because it holds the pool
Tesla sold 144,094 US electric vehicles in Q3 2026 for 54% of the market, and 386,194 in nine months for 52.9%, with its own US volume down 14.4% against a market down 30.3%. Share gains inside a contracting pool flatter the position: the absolute US revenue base is smaller than in 2025 despite record share. The mechanism is distribution: when a $7,500 credit disappears, the brand with the densest charging footprint keeps the remaining buyers and smaller entrants lose the sale faster. The competitive question for the next twelve months is not who takes US share from Tesla but whether Tesla can hold price, and it has — automotive gross margin rose to 18.5% in Q3 2026 from 17.0% a year earlier while regulatory-credit revenue fell 73% to $113 million [S8, S9]. Rivian earned 8.2% in the same quarter: Tesla's US cost position is intact, not eroding.

### China is where Tesla is the price taker
BYD sold 456,713 passenger cars in September 2026, 273,143 of them battery-electric, and 3,078,490 in nine months — 2.3 times Tesla's 1,324,681 [S138, S146, S149]. Around Tesla sat Geely at 119,682 retail units, Leapmotor at 78,202 and Xiaomi at 40,015, the last reaching 269,000 units in nine months against a 550,000 target in year two. The price evidence is in the margins: BYD earned 19.46% gross margin overseas against 16.66% at home in 2025, a revealed domestic ceiling Tesla cannot price above without losing volume. Tesla's China retail was 3.8 times smaller than BYD's in September while Chinese battery-electric wholesale still grew 18.3%: the pool was there and Tesla did not take it.

### Europe: growth in units, no evidence of share
EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,931,465 in January-September 2026 at a 22.7% share, with September at 29.9%, so the pool expanded 49% while Tesla's European deliveries recovered from a 2025 slump and Giga Berlin set a production record [S140, S147, S150]. A recovery off a collapsed base inside a pool growing that fast is not proof of share gain, and Tesla discloses no EU unit count; ACEA's manufacturer table is the record that would settle it. There the buyer chooses between compliance-driven models from Volkswagen, Renault, Stellantis and Hyundai-Kia and imported Chinese BEVs that carry a tariff but still undercut on price. Tesla's advantage is software and charging density; its handicap is a two-model line-up against a broader compliant field, with Model 3/Y accounting for 478,237 of 486,532 deliveries in Q3 2026.

### Storage is the one position Tesla clearly owns
Tesla's energy segment earned 33.1% gross margin in Q3 2026 on 13.7 GWh, against Fluence's 5.1% in the June 2026 quarter and 13.1% for its 2025 fiscal year, while Tesla's storage revenue per GWh fell to $210 million from $273 million [S8, S9, S61]. That sixfold gap is the clearest unrivaled cost position in the case: in-house cells, one-piece assembly and Autobidder dispatch compress installed cost, while the integrator without cells absorbs the price decline. Two cautions. Q3 2026 energy margin was flattered by $526 million of IEEPA tariff refunds booked against energy cost of revenue, so the underlying gap is narrower than 28 points; and CATL and Sungrow supply the cells and inverters Tesla must buy, which caps how long the integration premium survives as system prices fall.

### In paid autonomy, Tesla is the challenger with the permits to prove it
Waymo ran 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities by March 2026 with about 3,000 vehicles and more than 170 million rider-only miles, and raised $16 billion in February 2026 at a $126 billion post-money valuation [S89, S101, S142, S130]. Tesla began Cybercab rides in Austin on 2026-09-03, held 1,051 Texas-authorised Robotaxi vehicles on 2026-10-27 (544 Cybercab, 507 Model Y) against 739 on 2026-10-09, and reports about 2.0 million cumulative unsupervised miles; it is absent from California's driverless deployment permits, where Waymo is authorised, and discloses no ride count or fare [S125, S9]. The most dangerous competitor in the case is therefore Waymo, not BYD: BYD competes for the same buyer at a price Tesla can match with cost, while Waymo competes for the same regulatory permission and holds a lead of nearly two orders of magnitude in paid miles and a larger fleet.
