Quick Answer

Waymo completed more than 20 million lifetime autonomous rides through December 2025 — tripling its annual volume in a single year — while logging 220.6 million rider-only miles by March 2026 across six U.S. cities. A $16 billion funding round in February 2026 valued the company at $126 billion, the largest capital raise in autonomous vehicle history.

According to Axis Intelligence Research’s analysis of Waymo’s official filings and CPUC-mandated reports: Waymo was delivering approximately 500,000 fully autonomous rides per week as of May 2026, up from 250,000 in April 2025. The fleet stood at roughly 3,700 Jaguar I-PACE vehicles, with a sixth-generation system now beginning deployment on the new Ojai platform. Annualized revenue reached $355 million as of February 2026.

Key Findings

Waymo completed 14 million fully autonomous trips in 2025 alone — more than triple the prior year — and surpassed 20 million lifetime rides by end of December 2025, according to Axis Intelligence Research’s analysis of Waymo’s official year-in-review disclosures.

The Waymo Driver logged 220.6 million rider-only miles through March 2026, achieving 90% fewer serious-injury-or-worse crashes than human drivers over the same distance in its operating cities, per Waymo’s NHTSA SGO-based Safety Impact Data Hub.

Waymo’s deadheading rate — the share of miles driven without a passenger — improved from 51.5% in January 2024 to 44.3% by September 2025, according to Axis Intelligence Research’s review of California CPUC quarterly filings; only 54% of total California miles were driven with a passenger aboard across the 14-month study period.

Waymo’s $126 billion post-money valuation in February 2026 implies a revenue multiple of approximately 355x on its $355 million annualized run rate, a ratio Axis Intelligence Research calculates by cross-referencing Alphabet’s SEC 8-K disclosures and Waymo’s publicly stated funding terms — a figure neither source states explicitly.

The average Waymo ride cost $19.69 in the San Francisco Bay Area during Q4 2025–Q1 2026, compared with $17.47 for Uber and $15.47 for Lyft — a 12.7% premium over Uber that collapsed from the 30–40% premium recorded just six months earlier, according to Obi’s 94,000-ride dataset.

Waymo Rides and Trip Volume Statistics

Waymo’s trip growth is the clearest measure of whether autonomous ride-hailing has moved from demonstration to operation. The answer, at this point, is unambiguous: it has.

From January to December 2025, Waymo’s year-in-review shows the company served more than 14 million autonomous trips — a figure that more than tripled its 2024 annual total. Riders spent over 3.8 million hours inside the vehicles. By December 2025, lifetime rides crossed 20 million.

The trajectory into 2026 continued the acceleration. Weekly paid rides hit 450,000 by December 2025, then crossed 500,000 by late Q1 2026, according to data referenced at the time of Alphabet’s Q1 2026 earnings.

This is the data that separates Waymo from every other entity in the autonomous vehicle space. It is also the data most likely to be misread — so the methodology matters as much as the number.

Waymo reports crash rates under NHTSA’s Standing General Order (SGO), which requires disclosure of any incident involving property damage or injury. Tesla’s “Active FSD Subscriptions” metric includes customers who paid upfront and customers who pay monthly. It leaves out free trials. Multiply 1.74 million by the $99 monthly U.S. price and you get roughly $2.07 billion a year, about double what management cited. That gap is what investors should study, and it extends the attach-rate debate we covered in Musk Says FSD Is the Product.

This analysis walks through what Tesla reported, how the Tesla Full Self-Driving count is built, why the run-rate math lands where it does, and what the hardware fleet underneath the software means for the next few quarters. Every figure comes from Tesla’s own disclosures or named outlets, and where Tesla has stayed silent, we say so.

 What Tesla Reported on October 21

Tesla, Inc. posted third-quarter revenue of about $28 billion. One report puts the exact figure at $28.05 billion, against $28.10 billion a year earlier. Vehicle sales fell 3% year over year, and deliveries came in at 486,532, down 2%. The core car business shrank slightly while the software line grew by two thirds.

The table below collects the numbers that matter for the FSD story, with the context Tesla or its reporters supplied.

MetricQ3 2026 figureContextRevenueAbout $28 billion ($28.05B in one report)Versus $28.10B a year earlierVehicle salesDown 3%Year over yearDeliveries486,532Down 2% year over yearActive FSD Subscriptions1.74 millionUp 67% year over yearU.S. FSD price$99 per monthFull Self-Driving (Supervised)FSD share of new North American deliveriesMore than 75%Tesla’s attach-rate figureFSD annual run rateApproaching $1 billionManagement statement, not audited revenuePaid FSD customers (CFO)Over 1.7 million50% on subscriptions for the first time

Read together, the rows tell a split story. Cars sold fell. Software attached to those cars rose sharply. TT News framed the quarter as a profit beat with cash flow that stayed positive, which fits a company leaning on mix and software rather than unit growth to hold the line.

How Tesla Counts Active FSD Subscriptions

The label says “subscriptions,” but the definition is broader. Tesla’s Active FSD Subscriptions figure includes upfront purchases and monthly subscriptions. It excludes free trials. A buyer who paid for Full Self-Driving outright when ordering a car counts the same as someone paying $99 each month.

That distinction changes how investors should read the number. A monthly subscriber generates a charge every 30 days until they cancel. An upfront buyer generates cash once, and that cash does not renew. Both belong in a measure of how many people use the product. Only one of them belongs in a measure of recurring revenue.

Tesla has not claimed the 1.74 million figure is all monthly subscribers, and any reading that treats it that way is unconfirmed. Chief financial officer Vaibhav Taneja was more careful on the call. He described over 1.7 million paid customers globally and said that, for the first time, half of them are on subscriptions. That sentence is the best clue outsiders have to the mix.

The growth rate deserves the same scrutiny. A 67% rise implies a base of roughly 1.04 million a year ago (our arithmetic, not a Tesla figure). Adding about 700,000 to that base in twelve months is real momentum. But the figure counts a stock of customers, and the stock includes people who bought years ago and never leave the tally.

The $99 Math: From 1.74 Million to a $2.07 Billion Ceiling

The simplest calculation is also the most misleading. At $99 a month, one subscriber pays $1,188 a year. Multiply by 1.74 million and the product is about $2.07 billion. Management did not say that. It said the subscription business approaches $1 billion. The difference is not a rounding error.

Why the arithmetic lands near $1 billion

Apply Taneja’s 50% subscription share to the 1.74 million total and you get about 870,000 monthly payers. At $1,188 a year each, that produces roughly $1.03 billion at list price. The result sits close to management’s “approaching $1 billion” phrasing. It is our illustration, not a disclosure, but it shows how the two statements can both be true at once.

Where discounts and free months enter

List price is a ceiling. Regional pricing, promotional months, and cancellations all pull real collections below it. Tesla does not publish the effect of any of them. The table shows how sensitive the run rate is to the subscription share alone, holding the price at $99 and the base at 1.74 million.

Every row is arithmetic on public inputs. None of them is a Tesla revenue number. The point is the spread. A ten-point swing in the mix moves the answer by roughly $200 million, which is why the split between upfront and monthly customers is the single most useful metric Tesla could add.

Why a Run Rate Is Not Revenue

A run rate takes a recent snapshot and annualizes it. It says what the business would earn over twelve months if today’s conditions held. It does not say what Tesla booked. Tesla has not published a standalone Full Self-Driving revenue figure, so the only public anchor is management’s “approaching $1 billion” statement.

Outside estimates already differ. BaseNor ran a headline putting the figure at a $1.1 billion annual run rate, a touch above management’s wording. Under Tesla’s own conservative phrasing, the safer reading is a little under $1 billion. When sources conflict, the lower figure is the one to carry.

Scale helps here. A $1 billion annual run rate equals about $250 million a quarter. Against roughly $28 billion of quarterly revenue, that is under 1% of the top line (again our arithmetic). FSD is not yet large enough to offset a 3% drop in vehicle sales. Its importance lies in margin potential and in the trend, not in today’s dollar contribution.

The 75% Attach Rate and What It Does to the Mix

Full Self-Driving was included in more than 75% of new North American deliveries in the quarter. That is the number behind the growth in the installed base. Opening (thesis sentence from plan): "The strongest case against a Sell at $399.81 is not that Tesla's businesses are worth more than $139-160bn; it is that the price can be re-rated by events the SOTP cannot see — a listed SpaceX counterparty, a California permit or a robotaxi revenue line — and the recommendation does not yet price that upside tail. On the evidence available, the Sell survives, but as a de-rating call with a capped short, not as a solvency or liquidation call." That's a judgement.

Paragraph 1: What would break the thesis — the upside risk. SpaceX merger: $2.01tn listed counterparty, committees, 20-35% premium expectations, 42-50% ownership, 50% vote hurdle, no merger vote 2026-12-03. Impact: +20-35% ($480-540), above bull $506. A short is run over. Probability medium-low but not 20% bull... The scenario set omits this branch. This is the most damaging possible error in the thesis: treating the exit as absent when a listed buyer exists. "No buyer can pay $1,580.4bn" is arithmetically true of GM/Ford/Rivian ($137bn combined) but false of SpaceX at $2.01tn.

Paragraph 2: SOTP arithmetic — where it overstates downside. Energy 2.5-3.0x sales may be low for 30% gross margin + 41% market growth; services 1.5x for 32% growth/15.9% margin may be low; FSD run-rate ~$1bn valued at zero is ~$20bn at 20x = $5/share; SpaceX stake $2.87bn may be marked at cost + gain but under 1% of a $2.01tn company. Total understatement maybe $15-35bn, $4-9/share. But the bigger problem: the SOTP implies $35-40 (-90%), while the bear case is $161 (-60%) and base $292 (-27%). The 12-month tradable downside is the multiple, not the SOTP; the SOTP overstates the *near-term* downside by ~$120/share because Tesla has never traded on SOTP. Conversely, the base case's 70x EBITDA embeds ~$1.0tn of autonomy value, so the recommendation's base is internally generous. Net: the SOTP is a fair floor and a poor 12-month target; use $161-292 as the trading range.

Paragraph 3: Probabilities. 20% bull may be slightly low on fundamentals? FSD 1.74m is inflated (half upfront), 2.0m miles is 0.9% of Waymo's 220.6m, Texas 1,051 vs Waymo ~3,700, Megapack "almost sold out" coexists with energy revenue -16% and revenue per GWh -23%. So the fundamental bull is not underweighted at 20%; if anything the four conditions (CA permit, robotaxi revenue line, energy margin >30%, capex ≤$20bn) are conjunctive. But the merger branch means the probability of a >+20% 12-month outcome is higher than 20% — maybe 30-35% when merger is included. Reallocate: Bull 20% fundamental + 12% merger = 32% upside branch; Base 40%; Bear 28%. Expected return: 0.32×+27 + 0.40×-27 + 0.28×-60 = 8.64 -10.8 -16.8 = -18.96%, still negative but less than -28%. So Sell survives with smaller edge. Could the base be too bearish because energy/services compound? Energy revenue fell 16% in Q3 despite deployments +9.6%; 33.1% margin flattered by tariff refunds; services record gross profit $734m but only 15.9% margin. Base at 70x is not bearish. So no.

Paragraph 4: Earnings quality double count. $475m credit reversal is an income-statement item (Q3 revenue/gross profit); payables build $3,868m is a cash-flow item (9M). Different statements, different periods, no double count. arguments.markdown:
The Sell at $399.81 survives the red-team pass, but not in the form the scenario table states it. It is defensible as a de-rating call on a 103x multiple. It is not defensible as a liquidation call, because the reported businesses are a floor near $40-50 a share rather than a target, and it is not defensible as a claim that no buyer exists: SpaceX traded at $147.79 for a $2.01tn market value against Tesla's $373.71 and $1.48tn on 2026-10-20, and both boards have formed independent committees to study a combination [S154]. That is the fact that most damages the thesis. The exit arithmetic is right about General Motors, Ford and Rivian — $137.0bn between them cannot buy a $1.58tn company — and wrong about the buyer set: RBC and JPMorgan expect a 20-35% premium for Tesla holders, holders would own about 42% of a combined company at market parity and 47-50% with that premium, and approval needs 50% of all shares outstanding, a hurdle the CEO called high, with no merger vote at the 2026-12-03 annual meeting [S154]. At $399.81 a 20-35% premium is $480-540 a share, above the $506.05 first award gate and above the bull case. The process can fail: no exchange ratio is agreed, the CEO sits on both sides, and the vote counts abstentions against. But a short that treats the exit as absent is short a stock with a dated, public, premium-bearing catalyst, and the expression should be a capped short with a stop at $506.05, not a naked one.

### The SOTP is a floor, not a twelve-month target

Where the SOTP overstates the downside is at the edges. Energy at 2.5-3.0x $12.3bn of sales ignores a 41% growth pool and a 30% gross margin; at 3.5-4.0x it is worth $12bn more. Services at 1.5x $16.3bn ignores 32% growth and a record $734m of gross profit; at 2.0x it is worth $8bn more. FSD's roughly $1bn run rate is carried at zero and is worth about $20bn at 20x, though part of it already sits inside services [S152, S8]. Those adjustments take the SOTP to $40-50 a share, not $35-40, and still leave 88-90% of the price unexplained. The larger problem is the framework: the SOTP implies -90%, the bear case -60% and the base case -27%, because the base applies 70x to $16.0bn of EBITDA and therefore embeds about $1.0tn of autonomy value. Tesla has never traded on SOTP, so $161-292 is the tradable range and $35-40 is what a liquidation would find; a reader who takes $35-40 as the twelve-month target is being handed a downside the recommendation does not forecast.

### Probabilities: right on the business, low on the event

The 20% bull weight is not too low on fundamentals. The 1.74m FSD count is company-reported and includes upfront buyers as well as monthly subscribers, only half the base is on subscriptions by the CFO's account, and management's run rate is about $1bn, under 1% of revenue [S152]; the 2.0m unsupervised miles are company-reported and equal 0.9% of Waymo's 220.6m rider-only miles at March 2026, not the 1.2% a 170m comparison implies [S151, S9]; Texas has 1,051 authorised vehicles against roughly 3,700 Waymo vehicles; and "almost sold out" for 2027 is a call statement, company-only, in a quarter when energy revenue fell 16% and revenue per GWh fell 23%. Four conjunctive conditions — a California permit, a robotaxi revenue line, energy above 30% and capex at $20bn — are not a 20% event. The event branch is where the weight is too low: a 10-12% merger weight at +27% lifts the upside to 30-32%, and with base 40% and bear 28% the expected return is about -20%, not -28%. Nor is the base too bearish on energy and services: 70x EBITDA is four times BYD's 17.3x and still embeds the option, and services at a 15.9% gross margin cannot carry a 2.6% group operating margin.

### Earnings quality: not double counted, and worse than stated

The $475m credit reversal and the $3,868m payables build are not the same dollar counted twice: the first is Q3 revenue and gross profit, the second is nine-month working capital, and pricing both is compounding rather than double counting. Two corrections run the other way. Adding back the reversal gives $1,193m of operating income and a 4.2% margin rather than 2.6%, but only if regulatory credits stop falling; credit revenue fell from $2.76bn in 2024 to $1.99bn in 2025. More important, interest income of $1,301m was 69% of the $1,883m nine-month free cash flow, so free cash flow before interest is about $582m and before the payables benefit it is negative [S8, S11]. Adjusted EBITDA excludes interest, so 103x is clean; the 439x P/E and 0.2% free-cash-flow yield are not. The earnings-quality leg of the Sell is stronger than the thesis states.

### Stress tests: a de-rating, not a default

A market 50% smaller — 11.5m electric units instead of 23.0m — leaves Tesla about 885,000 units at 7.7% share, $37.5bn of auto revenue and $6.8bn of gross profit at 18.1%; group gross profit near $14bn against $16.3bn of operating cost is a $2.3bn operating loss, and auto at 0.7x sales falls from $52.5bn to $26bn, taking the SOTP to about $125bn, or $32 a share, 2% below the current price. That is the point: the market-size test moves the floor by 8% and the price by 2%, because the price is not earnings. A doubled CAC does bite: SG&A of $7,485m over 1.77m units is $4,229 a vehicle, and doubling the demand-generation half adds about $2,100 a vehicle, $3.7bn, equal to the $3.47bn trailing operating income. Revenue 30% lower leaves $72.5bn at 19.3% gross margin, $14.0bn of gross profit against $16.3bn of cost, an operating loss; at 40x on about $8bn of EBITDA the equity is near $356bn, $90 a share (-77%). A six-month financing delay is not a solvency event: $36.18bn of net cash, $30.0bn of undrawn facilities and $9.27bn of debt repricing 200bp cost $185m more interest against $1.3bn of interest income; the cost is to the option, halving the chance of a 2026-27 proof and taking about 2.7 points off expected return [S8, S9]. Multiples compress is the base case; free cash flow 30% lower changes nothing at a 0.2% yield but raises the odds of a facility draw. The bear case is a 40x multiple, not a balance-sheet failure.

### Policy is priced as a timetable

The regulatory risks are dated and public, which makes them detectable before the 10-Q. US credit repeal has already taken 30.3% out of the pool; an EU 2035 target cut to 90% would slow the only growing vehicle market; NHTSA's EA26002 covers 3,203,754 vehicles with nine incidents and one fatality and is the last step before a recall, and a remedy at $100-1,000 a car is $320m-3.2bn plus an operating-domain restriction that would delay paid service [S87, S89]. California's list on 2026-10-23 still shows Tesla Robotaxi LLC only under testing with a safety driver, absent from driverless testing and deployment while Waymo, Nuro and Mercedes hold deployment authorisations; a permit application is reported, but an application is not an authorisation [S89, S10]. Two regulatory events set the distribution: a recall that narrows the domain (medium probability, 10-20% of the autonomy option) and a permit grant (medium-low, +25-30%). The undisclosed items — robotaxi revenue, trips and cost per trip, FSD churn, the energy backlog's contracted price, the SpaceX exchange ratio and the 50%-vote count — are where the unknown unknowns sit, and the related-party flow is disclosed but not priced: SpaceX bought $626m of Megapacks in nine months, 7.4% of energy revenue, with $588m of the receivable billed for units not yet delivered.

It is defensible as a de-rating call on a 103x multiple; it is not defensible as a liquidation call, because the reported businesses are a floor near $40-50 a share rather than a target; and it is not defensible as a claim that no buyer exists. SpaceX traded at $147.79 for a $2.01tn market value against Tesla's $373.71 and $1.48tn on 2026-10-20, and both boards have formed independent committees to study a combination [S154]. The exit arithmetic is right about General Motors, Ford and Rivian — $137.0bn between them cannot buy a $1.58tn company — and wrong about the buyer set: RBC and JPMorgan expect a 20-35% premium for Tesla holders, holders would own about 42% of a combined company at market parity and 47-50% with that premium, and approval needs 50% of all shares outstanding, with no merger vote at the 2026-12-03 annual meeting [S154]. At $399.81 a 20-35% premium is $480-540, above the $506.05 first award gate and above the bull case. The process can fail — no exchange ratio, a conflicted CEO on both sides, abstentions counted against — but a short that treats the exit as absent is short a dated, public, premium-bearing catalyst, and the expression should be a capped short with a stop at $506.05.

### The SOTP is a floor, not a twelve-month target

Where the SOTP overstates the downside is at the edges. Energy at 2.5-3.0x $12.3bn of sales ignores a 41% growth pool and a 30% gross margin; at 3.5-4.0x it is worth $12bn more. Services at 1.5x $16.3bn ignores 32% growth and a record $734m of gross profit; at 2.0x it is worth $8bn more. FSD's roughly $1bn run rate is carried at zero and is worth about $20bn at 20x, though part already sits inside services [S152, S8]. Those adjustments take the SOTP to $40-50 a share, not $35-40, and still leave 88-90% of the price unexplained. The larger problem is the framework: the SOTP implies -90%, the bear case -60% and the base case -27%, because the base applies 70x to $16.0bn of EBITDA and therefore embeds about $1.0tn of autonomy value. Tesla has never traded on SOTP, so $161-292 is the tradable range and $35-40 is the liquidation floor; a reader who takes $35-40 as the twelve-month target is handed a downside the recommendation does not forecast.

### Probabilities: right on the business, low on the event

The 20% bull weight is not too low on fundamentals. The 1.74m FSD count is company-reported and includes upfront buyers as well as monthly subscribers, only half the base is on subscriptions by the CFO's account, and management's run rate is about $1bn, under 1% of revenue [S152]; the 2.0m unsupervised miles are company-reported and equal 0.9% of Waymo's 220.6m rider-only miles at March 2026, not the 1.2% a 170m comparison implies [S151, S9]; Texas has 1,051 authorised vehicles against roughly 3,700 Waymo vehicles; and "almost sold out" for 2027 is a call statement, company-only, in a quarter when energy revenue fell 16% and revenue per GWh fell 23%. Four conjunctive conditions — a California permit, a robotaxi revenue line, energy above 30% and capex at $20bn — are not a 20% event. The event branch is where the weight is too low: a 10-12% merger weight at +27% lifts the upside to 30-32%, and with base 40% and bear 28% the expected return is about -20%, not -28%. Nor is the base too bearish on energy and services: 70x EBITDA is four times BYD's 17.3x and still embeds the option, and a 15.9% services gross margin cannot carry a 2.6% group operating margin.

### Earnings quality: not double counted, and worse than stated

The $475m credit reversal and the $3,868m payables build are not the same dollar counted twice: the first is Q3 revenue and gross profit, the second is nine-month working capital, so pricing both is compounding, not double counting. Two corrections run the other way. Adding back the reversal gives $1,193m of operating income and a 4.2% margin rather than 2.6%, but only if regulatory credits stop falling; credit revenue fell from $2.76bn in 2024 to $1.99bn in 2025. More important, interest income of $1,301m was 69% of the $1,883m nine-month free cash flow, so free cash flow before interest is about $582m and before the payables benefit it is negative [S8, S11]. Adjusted EBITDA excludes interest, so 103x is clean; the 439x P/E and 0.2% free-cash-flow yield are not. The earnings-quality leg of the Sell is stronger than the thesis states.

### Stress tests: a de-rating, not a default

A market 50% smaller — 11.5m electric units instead of 23.0m — leaves Tesla about 885,000 units at 7.7% share, $37.5bn of auto revenue and $6.8bn of gross profit at 18.1%; group gross profit near $14bn against $16.3bn of operating cost is a $2.3bn operating loss, and auto at 0.7x sales falls from $52.5bn to $26bn, taking the SOTP to about $125bn, or $32 a share, 2% below the current price. The market-size test moves the floor by 8% and the price by 2%, because the price is not earnings. A doubled CAC does bite: SG&A of $7,485m over 1.77m units is $4,229 a vehicle, and doubling the demand-generation half adds about $2,100 a vehicle, $3.7bn, equal to the $3.47bn trailing operating income. Revenue 30% lower leaves $72.5bn at 19.3% gross margin, $14.0bn of gross profit against $16.3bn of cost, an operating loss; at 40x on about $8bn of EBITDA the equity is near $356bn, $90 a share (-77%). A six-month financing delay is not a solvency event: $36.18bn of net cash, $30.0bn of undrawn facilities and $9.27bn of debt repricing 200bp cost $185m more interest against $1.3bn of interest income; the cost is to the option, halving the chance of a 2026-27 proof and taking about 2.7 points off expected return [S8, S9]. Multiples compress is the base case; free cash flow 30% lower changes nothing at a 0.2% yield but raises the odds of a facility draw. The bear case is a 40x multiple, not a balance-sheet failure.

### Policy is priced as a timetable

The regulatory risks are dated and public, so they are detectable before the 10-Q. US credit repeal has already taken 30.3% out of the pool; an EU 2035 target cut to 90% would slow the only growing vehicle market; NHTSA's EA26002 covers 3,203,754 vehicles with nine incidents and one fatality and is the last step before a recall, and a remedy at $100-1,000 a car is $320m-3.2bn plus an operating-domain restriction that would delay paid service [S87, S89]. California's list on 2026-10-23 still shows Tesla Robotaxi LLC only under testing with a safety driver, absent from driverless testing and deployment while Waymo, Nuro and Mercedes hold deployment authorisations; a permit application is reported, but an application is not an authorisation [S89, S10]. Two regulatory events set the distribution: a recall that narrows the domain (medium probability, 10-20% of the autonomy option) and a permit grant (medium-low, +25-30%). The undisclosed items — robotaxi revenue, trips and cost per trip, FSD churn, the energy backlog's contracted price, the SpaceX exchange ratio and the 50%-vote count — are where the unknown unknowns sit, and the related-party flow is disclosed but not priced: SpaceX bought $626m of Megapacks in nine months, 7.4% of energy revenue, with $588m of the receivable billed for units not yet delivered.

Impact is stated on equity value; for a short position the positive rows are losses.

| US and China demand and policy | Medium | 10-15% of revenue | Medium | 6-18 months | US EV registrations; China NEV retail | Weight Europe and storage | S139, S145 |
| Related-party concentration and governance | High, structural | 3-5% of energy value; multiple discount | Medium | Ongoing | 10-Q related-party note; SpaceX receivable | Independent review of related-party terms | S8, S10 |

arguments.markdown:
The Sell at $399.81 survives the red-team pass, but not in the form the scenario table states it. It is defensible as a de-rating call on a 103x multiple, not as a liquidation call (the reported businesses are a $40-50 floor, not a target) and not as a claim that no buyer exists. SpaceX traded at $147.79 for a $2.01tn market value against Tesla's $373.71 and $1.48tn on 2026-10-20, and both boards have formed independent committees to study a combination [S154]. General Motors, Ford and Rivian cannot buy a $1.58tn company, but SpaceX can: RBC and JPMorgan expect a 20-35% premium for Tesla holders, holders would own 42% of a combined company at parity and 47-50% with that premium, and approval needs 50% of all shares outstanding. At $399.81 a 20-35% premium is $480-540, above the $506.05 first award gate. The process can fail — no exchange ratio, a conflicted CEO, abstentions counted against — but a short that treats the exit as absent is short a dated, public, premium-bearing catalyst, and the expression should be a capped short with a stop at $506.05.

### The SOTP is a floor, not a twelve-month target

The SOTP overstates the downside at the edges. Energy at 2.5-3.0x $12.3bn of sales ignores a 41% growth pool and a 30% gross margin; at 3.5-4.0x it is worth $12bn more. Services at 1.5x $16.3bn ignores 32% growth and a record $734m of gross profit; at 2.0x it is worth $8bn more. FSD's $1bn run rate is carried at zero and is worth $20bn at 20x [S152, S8]. Those adjustments take the SOTP to $40-50 a share, not $35-40. The larger problem is the framework: the SOTP implies -90%, the bear case -60% and the base case -27%, because the base applies 70x to $16.0bn of EBITDA and so embeds $1.0tn of autonomy value. Tesla has never traded on SOTP: $161-292 is the tradable range, $35-40 the liquidation floor, and taking the floor as the twelve-month target hands the reader a downside the recommendation does not forecast.

### Probabilities: right on the business, low on the event

The 20% bull weight is not too low on fundamentals. The 1.74m FSD count is company-reported and includes upfront buyers as well as monthly subscribers, only half the base is on subscriptions by the CFO's account, and management's run rate is $1bn, under 1% of revenue; the 2.0m unsupervised miles are company-reported and equal 0.9% of Waymo's 220.6m rider-only miles at March 2026, not the 1.2% a 170m comparison implies; Texas has 1,051 authorised vehicles against 3,700 Waymo vehicles; and the call's "almost sold out" for 2027 is company-only, in a quarter when energy revenue fell 16% and revenue per GWh fell 23% [S152, S151, S9]. Four conjunctive conditions — a California permit, a robotaxi revenue line, energy above 30% and capex at $20bn — are not a 20% event. A 10-12% merger weight at +27% lifts the upside to 30-32%, and with base 40% and bear 28% the expected return is -20%, not -28%. The base is not too bearish: 70x EBITDA is four times BYD's 17.3x and still embeds the option.

### Earnings quality: not double counted, and worse than stated

The $475m credit reversal and the $3,868m payables build are not the same dollar counted twice: the first is Q3 revenue and gross profit, the second is nine-month working capital, so pricing both is compounding, not double counting. Adding back the reversal gives $1,193m of operating income and a 4.2% margin rather than 2.6%, but only if regulatory credits stop falling; credit revenue fell from $2.76bn in 2024 to $1.99bn in 2025. More important, interest income of $1,301m was 69% of the $1,883m nine-month free cash flow, so free cash flow before interest is $582m and before the payables benefit it is negative [S8, S11]. Adjusted EBITDA excludes interest, so 103x is clean; the 439x P/E and 0.2% free-cash-flow yield are not.

### Stress tests: a de-rating, not a default

A market 50% smaller — 11.5m electric units instead of 23.0m — leaves Tesla 885,000 units at 7.7% share, $37.5bn of auto revenue and $6.8bn of gross profit at 18.1%; group gross profit of $14bn against $16.3bn of operating cost is a $2.3bn operating loss, and auto at 0.7x sales falls from $52.5bn to $26bn, taking the SOTP to $125bn, or $32 a share, 2% below the current price. The market-size test moves the floor by 8% and the price by 2%, because the price is not earnings. A doubled CAC does bite: SG&A of $7,485m over 1.77m units is $4,229 a vehicle, and doubling the demand-generation half adds $2,100 a vehicle, $3.7bn, equal to the $3.47bn trailing operating income. Revenue 30% lower leaves $72.5bn at 19.3% gross margin, $14.0bn of gross profit against $16.3bn of cost, an operating loss; at 40x on $8bn of EBITDA the equity is $356bn, $90 a share (-77%). A six-month financing delay is not a solvency event: $36.18bn of net cash and $30.0bn of undrawn facilities mean the cost falls on the option, halving the chance of a 2026-27 proof and taking 2.7 points off expected return [S8, S9]. Free cash flow 30% lower changes nothing at a 0.2% yield. The bear case is a 40x multiple, not a balance-sheet failure.

### Policy is priced as a timetable

The regulatory risks are dated and public. US credit repeal has already taken 30.3% out of the pool; an EU 2035 target cut to 90% would slow the only growing vehicle market; NHTSA's EA26002 covers 3,203,754 vehicles with nine incidents and one fatality and is the last step before a recall, and a remedy at $100-1,000 a car is $320m-3.2bn plus an operating-domain restriction that would delay paid service. California's list on 2026-10-23 still shows Tesla Robotaxi LLC only under testing with a safety driver, while Waymo, Nuro and Mercedes hold deployment authorisations; a permit application is reported, but an application is not an authorisation. The undisclosed items — robotaxi revenue, trips and cost per trip, FSD churn, the energy backlog's contracted price, the SpaceX exchange ratio and the 50%-vote count — are where the unknown unknowns sit; the related-party flow is disclosed but not priced, with SpaceX buying $626m of Megapacks in nine months, 7.4% of energy revenue, and $588m of the receivable billed for units not yet delivered [S87, S89, S10].

### Ranked risks

Positive rows are losses for a short position.

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SpaceX combination at a 20-35% premium | Medium-low, 15-20% | +20-35% to the stock | Critical | 6-18 months | Exchange ratio; committee statement | Cap at 1-2% of NAV; stop at $506.05 | S154 |
| Multiple de-rates from 103x to 40x | High | -60%, $161 a share | Critical | 0-12 months | 10-year Treasury above 5%; Q4 miss | Sell or underweight; no long exposure | S11, S8 |
| California permit plus robotaxi revenue line | Medium-low | +25-30%, bull case $506 | High | 6-12 months | DMV deployment list; Q4 segment line | Stop at $506.05; reassess on the Q4 10-Q | S89, S152 |
| NHTSA EA26002 recall or ODD restriction | Medium | $0.3-3.2bn; 10-20% of autonomy option | High | 3-12 months | EA closure; recall notice | Price the remedy; demand take-rate data | S87 |
| Robotaxi teleoperation and insurance costs | High | 10-20% of autonomy value | Medium | 12-24 months | SGO crash reports; intervention disclosure | Demand trip and cost-per-trip data | S153 |
| Payables reverse and interest income falls | Medium-high | 10-15% of equity at 40x | Medium | Q4 2026 | Q4 free cash flow ex-working capital | Read the Q4 cash-flow statement | S8 |
| Capex guidance credibility and debt funding | Medium | 5-10% | Medium | 2027 | Q4 capex above $7bn; facility draw | Ask for 2027 capex and facility terms | S8 |
| US and China demand and policy | Medium | 10-15% of revenue | Medium | 6-18 months | US EV registrations; China NEV retail | Weight Europe and storage | S139, S145 |
| Related-party concentration and governance | High, structural | 3-5% of energy value | Medium | Ongoing | 10-Q related-party note; receivable | Independent review of related-party terms | S8, S10 |
:::

::: info danger
**The thesis breaks on an exit, not on a car.** A listed SpaceX at $2.01tn, two special committees and a 20-35% premium expected by RBC and JPMorgan would hand Tesla holders $480-540 a share, above the bull case. The 50%-of-outstanding vote and the CEO's conflict make it uncertain, but a short that ignores the branch is exposed to a 20-35% gap on a headline; 2.19% of float and 2.2 days to cover mean the move comes from news, not positioning. Source S154, S155.
:::

The open diligence items are the SpaceX exchange ratio, the 50%-of-outstanding vote and the contracted price in the energy backlog; the cheapest falsifier is the Q4 2026 10-Q in the last week of January 2027, where a robotaxi revenue line, or a California deployment entry before it, would re-open the Sell.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 3 by Valuation Analyst, 7,235 characters)
No buyer can pay $1,580.4bn and the company returns no cash, so the 12-month exit from Tesla at $399.81 is a sale into the market at whatever multiple prevails: with 103x trailing adjusted EBITDA, every 10 turns is $37.95 a share, 9.5% of the price. That makes the distribution roughly -60% to +27%, around a consensus target of $408.61 that is 2.2% above spot, and the only genuine change-of-control path — a share-for-share combination with SpaceX now under committee study — would hand holders an unlisted security rather than cash [S8, S11].

| Exit route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Market sale | NasdaqGS, $13.8bn traded a day | the only certain route; 20-day average 36.30m shares | any session | certain | S11 |
| Re-rating to the first award gate | public market, $2,000bn capitalisation | first 2025 award tranche crystallises at $506.05 a share | 12-36 months | low | S10, S127 |
| Share-for-share combination | SpaceX | separate board committees since 2026-10; SpaceX revenue $14.575bn in Q3 2026 | undated | low to medium | S126, S129 |
| Trade sale | General Motors, Ford, Rivian, BYD | the three US peers are worth $137.0bn together, 8.7% of Tesla | none | very low | S15, S17, S19 |
| Capital return | Tesla's board | no dividend ever declared, no repurchase programme disclosed | none | very low | S1 |
| Separation of robotaxi or energy | not disclosed | no filed plan, no registration statement | none | not disclosed | S1 |

The acquirer set is empty by arithmetic, not by preference. General Motors at $73.7bn, Ford at $45.7bn and Rivian at $17.6bn are worth $137.0bn between them, and BYD, the volume leader among listed electric-vehicle makers, earns 21.2x trailing and 13x forward — none of them can finance a $1.58tn purchase at any premium. That leaves SpaceX, the one Musk company of comparable scale, whose Q3 2026 revenue was $14.575bn across Space, Connectivity and Super Intelligence, and which disclosed with Tesla that committees are examining a combination with no decision, no agreement and no exchange ratio [S126, S129]. The mechanics matter for exit: a combination would be a share exchange into a private company, so a holder's liquidity would fall rather than rise, and the disclosed approval gates are SpaceX's special committee, its board and its controlling shareholder. No antitrust or foreign-investment filing has been disclosed, and the Chinese exposure of Tesla's Shanghai plant inside a group that also owns launch and satellite businesses is a policy test the filings have not addressed.

| Precedent | Year | Value | Multiple | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 5 by Product Analyst, 8,734 characters)
Tesla's technology position in 2026 is two facts usually merged in the narrative: the largest supervised-driving data pool and one of the cheapest large-scale EV manufacturing bases in the industry, and almost no verified driverless revenue. Active FSD subscriptions reached 1.74 million at 30 September 2026 against 10.2 million vehicles delivered to date — 17.1% of the lifetime fleet, up from 12.4% at 31 December 2025 — while cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles were "nearly two million", 1.2% of the 170 million-plus rider-only miles Waymo reports [S9]. That gap, not the subscription count, is what twelve months must close.

### What Tesla actually sells

| Product | Stage | Revenue or share | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FSD (Supervised) | Commercial, 9 EU countries | 1.74m subscriptions; revenue not disclosed | Unsupervised release | S9, S1 |
| Robotaxi / Cybercab | Commercial in Texas metros | Not disclosed inside $4.605bn services | Paid-trip disclosure | S9 |
| Model 3 / Model Y | Mature | 478,237 units, Q3 2026; 19.6% group gross margin | Next-gen platform | S9 |
| Cybertruck, Semi, Roadster | Ramp / design | 8,295 other-model units, Q3 2026 | Semi ramp; Roadster launch | S9 |
| Megapack, Powerwall | Scaling | $2.881bn in Q3 2026; 13.7 GWh | 50 GWh Texas ramp | S9, S60 |
| Optimus | Internal production | Zero external revenue | External pilot sale | S9, S99 |

### Mechanism: end-to-end vision and a one-sided flywheel

Tesla removed radar and now maps camera pixels directly to driving commands with an end-to-end neural network, trained on clips harvested from the fleet and run on in-house inference silicon. Training runs on two in-house clusters at Gigafactory Texas, with a company-built fab for inference and training silicon under construction. The flywheel is real but overwhelmingly *supervised*: the Q3 2026 update charts cumulative FSD miles on a 0-16 billion axis, against 2.0 million unsupervised miles [S60]. Supervised miles teach perception; they do not certify that the network can be left alone, which is why the federal safety file matters more than the mileage chart.

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active FSD subscriptions | 1.74m (2026-09-30) | Company count | S9 |
| FSD penetration of fleet | 17.1% | 1.74m / 10.2m deliveries | S9 |
| Cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles | 2.0m, 8x QoQ | Company count | S9 |
| Installed AI training compute | 225+ MW | Company nameplate | S9 |
| 4680 capacity, Texas | 40+ GWh/yr, dry electrode both sides | Company nameplate | S60 |
| Storage deployed | 13.7 GWh Q3; 36.0 GWh 9M | Company deliveries | S9 |
| Optimus units in service | 1,000-1,200 | Independent estimate | S99 |

### The safety file is the binding constraint

NHTSA's Office of Defects Investigation opened Engineering Analysis EA26002 on 18 March 2026 into whether FSD detects degraded visibility — glare, fog, dust — and warns the driver in time, covering an estimated 3,203,754 vehicles from model years 2016-2026, after nine confirmed incidents including one pedestrian fatality; two further FSD probes remain open, one on traffic-law violations across 2,882,566 vehicles with 80 incidents [S87]. Tesla's own analysis reportedly found its degradation-detection update "may have affected" only 3 of 9 incidents, which points to an architectural limit of camera-only sensing rather than a tuning defect. An engineering analysis is the last step before a recall; a recall would narrow the operating domain or force hardware across millions of cars, at a company that self-insures product liability.

::: evidence
**The camera-only bet is being tested by the regulator, not the market.** EA26002 covers 3.2 million FSD-equipped vehicles and Tesla's fix reportedly addresses a third of the reviewed incidents [S87, S88, S100]. The filings confirm the investigation but give no remedy or timetable, which is the largest un-priced technical risk in the autonomy option.
:::

### Comparison: three different autonomy businesses

| Dimension | Tesla | Waymo | Chinese L3 OEMs | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sensing | Camera-only, in-house chip | Lidar + radar + camera | Camera + lidar, Nvidia compute | S9, S101 |
| Verified driverless scale | 2.0m cumulative miles | 170m+ rider-only miles; 500,000 paid rides/week | L3 conditional approvals since 2025-12 | S101, S103 |
| Regulatory position | Paid driverless in Texas under SB 2807 and TxDMV authorisation (required from 2026-05-28); California paid rides on a limousine permit, no autonomous-service authorisation | California deployment authorised | MIIT eight-department L3 pilot | S89, S90, S91 |
| Cost model | Owned fleet, self-insured | Owned fleet, partner-owned vehicles | Consumer cars, driver liable | S89, S103 |

### Moat: accumulation, not exclusion

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Supervised fleet data | 8 | 10.2m cars; FSD miles charted to 16bn | 4-6 years | S9 |
| Driverless operating experience | 5 | 2.0m unsupervised miles only | 2-3 years | S9 |
| Dry-electrode cell process | 7 | Battery Day 2020 to Austin output in 2026 | 3-4 years | S60 |
| Manufacturing and integration | 8 | 134,785 employees; cells, cathode, refining in-house | 5+ years | S1 |
| Training compute | 6 | 225+ MW against more than $20bn of 2026 capex | 2-3 years | S9, S8 |
| State permits | 6 | Bilateral and political; not purchasable | 1-3 years | S89, S91 |
| Composite | 6.5/10 | Minimum 3-year lead on a geofenced service | — | S9, S60 |

The replication test is unflattering to a patent story: 50 funded engineers with every published Tesla patent could build a geofenced driverless service in two to three years — Waymo needed eleven years from its 2009 start — but could not reproduce the fleet data or the factories. Tesla's 10-K concedes the point by design, pledging irrevocably not to sue any party acting in good faith for infringing its electric-vehicle patents. California is the harder gate: on 23 October 2026 the DMV lists Tesla Robotaxi LLC only as a testing-permit holder requiring a safety driver, and the state's regulator confirmed in March 2026 that Tesla is not operating an autonomous vehicle service, its paid rides running on a limousine permit [S1, S89, S90].

| IP instrument | Covers | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Patent non-assertion pledge | EV and related-equipment patents | Irrevocable for good-faith users | Removes patents as a barrier | S1 |
| Trade secrets, NDAs | Cell process, manufacturing know-how | In force | Protects dry-electrode yield | S1 |
| In-house inference silicon; Samsung US foundry deal | AI4/AI5 design and fabrication | Austin fab commissioning 2027 | Cost and performance control | S1, S9 |
| Patent portfolio (AI, batteries, robotics) | Not enumerated in filings | Counts not publicly disclosed | Cannot be assessed publicly | — |

Tesla publishes no patent count or list, so a patent-number-level table cannot be built from its disclosures; a USPTO assignee search is the source that would settle portfolio size and freedom-to-operate risk, and it has been requested.

### Optimus is a research programme with a production line

Tesla began Optimus production in Fremont in Q3 2026 and calls the process "suitable for a commercial product", but discloses no units, cycle times, error rates or customers; independent estimates put 1,000-1,200 units across Fremont and Giga Texas with zero external sales, and the CEO described early units as "primarily for learning and data collection" [S99]. Figure AI has logged 1,250+ hours at BMW and Agility Robotics 65,000+ hours across nine sites, both with paying customers — smaller companies with weaker balance sheets but better evidence. Optimus should carry no revenue in a 12-month model.

Tesla's manufacturing and supervised-data advantages are real and hard to buy, but the priced asset is unsupervised autonomy, which in 2026 has a fatality-linked engineering analysis, a single authorising state, a pilot fleet and no disclosed revenue. Confidence is high on filings and regulator records, medium on driverless scale, low on Optimus and robotaxi unit economics, where disclosure is absent rather than adverse. Three questions would move this: Robotaxi revenue, paid trips and cost per trip disclosed quarterly; a California driverless deployment permit; and 4680 cell cost per kWh against the purchased-cell benchmark. If the first and third come good while EA26002 closes without a hardware remedy, the option is worth materially more than a pilot; if the analysis converts to a recall that restricts the operating domain, the revenue bridge loses its main support [S9, S89]."}],"isError":false}

{"url":"https://spaceandsky.com/spacex-stock-spcx-ipo-price-filings/","title":"SpaceX stock: Yes, SPCX trades on Nasdaq, and here is what the filings say","text":"Figures checked against official announcements and filings on October 17, 2026.
Yes, SpaceX stock can be bought. Space Exploration Technologies Corp. went public on June 12, 2026, and its Class A common stock trades on the Nasdaq Global Select Market and Nasdaq Texas under the ticker SPCX. Shares are bought through an ordinary brokerage account, like any other listed stock.
The IPO was priced at $135 per share. A live price is not given here, because it changes every second; the official places to check are listed below.
Image: NASA/Kim Shiflett
SPCX is the ticker, and any broker that offers Nasdaq stocks can trade it
According to the IPO pricing announcement (carried by IREI Newsline on June 12, 2026), the company priced 555,555,555 shares of Class A common stock at $135 each. The shares were expected to begin trading on June 12, with the offering expected to close on June 15. Underwriters, the banks that sell the shares to investors, also received a 30-day option to buy up to 83,333,333 additional shares at the IPO price.
The same ticker is used for every search variant people type: “spacex ticker,” “spacex stock symbol” and “spacex ticker symbol” all point to SPCX.
Image: NASA/Tony Gray
Steps to buy a listed stock, in general terms:

Open an account with a brokerage that offers US-listed stocks in your country.
Search for SPCX and confirm the company name is Space Exploration Technologies Corp.
Check the quote and the order type your broker offers, and read its fee schedule.
Place the order during Nasdaq trading hours or as your broker allows.

Shares of the company before the IPO were private. Offers to sell “pre-IPO SpaceX shares” today refer to something different from the listed stock and carry their own risks.
How to check the SpaceX share price today without relying on a copied number
The company’s investor relations site has a Stock Information page (ir.spacex.com/stock-information) with a quote, a chart and a historical price lookup. Those fields load dynamically, so they only show in a browser. Nasdaq also publishes a quote page for SPCX.
Searches such as “spacex stock price today,” “spacex stock price live” and “spacex price per share” are answered by those pages, not by an article. A static article cannot show a live price, and none is stated here.
For context only: according to CNBC, shares closed at $161 on the first trading day, June 12, 2026, up 19% from the IPO price. That is a historical closing price, not a current one.
What the SEC filings confirm about the offering
SpaceX files with the US Securities and Exchange Commission under CIK 0001181412. The filings that exist on EDGAR include:

An S-1 registration statement, publicly filed on May 20, 2026 according to press coverage, and amended; the amendment No. 2 states the company applied to list Class A common stock on Nasdaq and Nasdaq Texas under the symbol “SPCX.”
A final prospectus on Form 424B4, dated June 12, 2026 (file number 333-296070).
Eight current reports on Form 8-K between June 15 and August 14, 2026, including the Q2 2026 earnings release on August 4.

The Q2 2026 release, filed as an exhibit to the August 4 8-K, reports the following for the quarter ended June 30, 2026:

Revenue of $7.8 billion, up 92% from $4.1 billion.
Net loss of $541 million, compared with a net loss of $1.0 billion a year earlier.
Adjusted EBITDA, a profit measure that leaves out interest, taxes and certain accounting charges, of $3.5 billion.
About $100 billion of cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities, and $47.5 billion in backlog.
Three segments: Space, Connectivity and AI.

The release contains no forward guidance. The balance sheet shows 7,607 million Class A shares and 5,569 million Class B shares outstanding at June 30, 2026.
Valuation history from the xAI merger to the IPO and Cursor
“SpaceX valuation,” “SpaceX net worth” and “SpaceX worth” have no single official answer. A valuation is either a price set in a transaction or a market capitalization that moves with the stock. The table lists the events with a number attached.

Figures checked on October 17, 2026. The Bloomberg figure comes from its February 2, 2026 report on the xAI deal. The pricing announcement figures come from the June 12, 2026 release as carried by IREI Newsline. The $1.77 trillion and $161 close are from CNBC and Fortune reporting and are not figures read on an SEC page. The Cursor rows come from SpaceX’s 8-K filings of June 16 and August 14, 2026.
“SpaceX IPO valuation” is therefore reported as roughly $1.75 to $1.77 trillion in press coverage. The $135 price and the share count are the company’s own figures; the trillion-dollar total is a calculation by the press.
The Cursor deal is closed, and it was paid in SpaceX stock
The search “spacex buys cursor” is answered by SEC filings. In an 8-K filed June 16, 2026, SpaceX disclosed an Agreement and Plan of Merger with Anysphere, Inc. (Cursor), with consideration in Class A stock based on an implied equity value of $60.0 billion for Cursor.
A second 8-K, filed August 14, 2026, reports the merger was completed that day. Cursor became a wholly owned subsidiary. Cursor’s common and preferred stock converted into 389,289,254 Class A shares, and vested restricted stock units into 1,752,426 more. Unvested units and options were assumed and converted into about 29.1 million SpaceX RSUs and about 44.4 million options.
This matters for anyone looking at share counts: the Cursor payment added new shares, so the total outstanding grew after the IPO.
What is official, and what is only reported or speculated
Official, from filings or company pages: the ticker SPCX, the exchanges, the $135 IPO price, the number of shares offered, the Q2 2026 results, and the Cursor merger terms.
Reported, not an SEC fact:

The $1.77 trillion IPO valuation and the $161 first-day close (CNBC).
The xAI combination value of $1.25 trillion (Bloomberg).
A raise of about $75 billion: the announced price and share count multiply to roughly that figure, but outlets differ on the total with the greenshoe included.

Speculation: neither company has announced any plan for SpaceX to buy Tesla. News outlets have reported that an analyst, Dan Ives, linked the Tesla Roadster reveal to merger speculation. That is an analyst view, not an announcement by either company.
The same applies to “spacex stock price prediction,” “spacex stock forecast” and “will spacex stock go up.” Analyst price targets exist in press reports, but they are opinions of the firms that publish them, and none is repeated here.
Which listed companies disclose a stake or contract with SpaceX
A stake or a contract counts only when the company discloses it itself. Two sources are the reliable route:

SpaceX’s own filings, which name major holders and related-party arrangements in the prospectus and in later reports.
Each investor’s own SEC filings, such as 13F holdings reports and annual reports, which show a stake in SPCX if one exists.

For the operating side, what SpaceX launches and when is on the public schedule: see the live rocket launch schedule.

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's technology position in 2026 is two facts usually merged in the narrative: the largest supervised-driving data pool and one of the cheapest large-scale EV manufacturing bases in the industry, and almost no verified driverless revenue. Active FSD subscriptions reached 1.74 million at 30 September 2026 against 10.2 million vehicles delivered to date — 17.1% of the lifetime fleet, up from 12.4% at 31 December 2025 — while cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles were "nearly two million", 0.9% of the 220.6 million rider-only miles Waymo had logged through March 2026 [S9, S151]. That gap, not the subscription count, is what twelve months must close.

### What Tesla actually sells

| Product | Stage | Revenue or share | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FSD (Supervised) | Commercial, 9 EU countries | 1.74m subscriptions; revenue not disclosed | Unsupervised release | S9, S1 |
| Robotaxi / Cybercab | Commercial in Texas metros | Not disclosed inside $4.605bn services | Paid-trip disclosure | S9 |
| Model 3 / Model Y | Mature | 478,237 units, Q3 2026; 19.6% group gross margin | Next-gen platform | S9 |
| Cybertruck, Semi, Roadster | Ramp / design | 8,295 other-model units, Q3 2026 | Semi ramp; Roadster launch | S9 |
| Megapack, Powerwall | Scaling | $2.881bn in Q3 2026; 13.7 GWh | 50 GWh Texas ramp | S9, S60 |
| Optimus | Internal production | Zero external revenue | External pilot sale | S9, S99 |

### Mechanism: end-to-end vision and a one-sided flywheel

Tesla removed radar and now maps camera pixels directly to driving commands with an end-to-end neural network, trained on clips harvested from the fleet and run on in-house inference silicon. Training runs on two in-house clusters at Gigafactory Texas, with a company-built fab for inference and training silicon under construction. The flywheel is real but overwhelmingly *supervised*: the Q3 2026 update charts cumulative FSD miles on a 0-16 billion axis, against 2.0 million unsupervised miles [S60]. Supervised miles teach perception; they do not certify that the network can be left alone, which is why the federal safety file matters more than the mileage chart.

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active FSD subscriptions | 1.74m (2026-09-30) | Company count | S9 |
| FSD penetration of fleet | 17.1% | 1.74m / 10.2m deliveries | S9 |
| Cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles | 2.0m, 8x QoQ | Company count | S9 |
| Installed AI training compute | 225+ MW | Company nameplate | S9 |
| 4680 capacity, Texas | 40+ GWh/yr, dry electrode both sides | Company nameplate | S60 |
| Storage deployed | 13.7 GWh Q3; 36.0 GWh 9M | Company deliveries | S9 |
| Optimus units in service | 1,000-1,200 | Independent estimate | S99 |

### The safety file is the binding constraint

NHTSA's Office of Defects Investigation opened Engineering Analysis EA26002 on 18 March 2026 into whether FSD detects degraded visibility — glare, fog, dust — and warns the driver in time, covering an estimated 3,203,754 vehicles from model years 2016-2026, after nine confirmed incidents including one pedestrian fatality; two further FSD probes remain open, one on traffic-law violations across 2,882,566 vehicles with 80 incidents [S87]. Tesla's own analysis reportedly found its degradation-detection update "may have affected" only 3 of 9 incidents, which points to an architectural limit of camera-only sensing rather than a tuning defect. An engineering analysis is the last step before a recall; a recall would narrow the operating domain or force hardware across millions of cars, at a company that self-insures product liability.

::: evidence
**The camera-only bet is being tested by the regulator, not the market.** EA26002 covers 3.2 million FSD-equipped vehicles and Tesla's fix reportedly addresses a third of the reviewed incidents [S87, S88, S100]. The filings confirm the investigation but give no remedy or timetable, which is the largest un-priced technical risk in the autonomy option.
:::

### Comparison: three different autonomy businesses

| Dimension | Tesla | Waymo | Chinese L3 OEMs | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sensing | Camera-only, in-house chip | Lidar + radar + camera | Camera + lidar, Nvidia compute | S9, S101 |
| Verified driverless scale | 2.0m cumulative miles | 220.6m rider-only miles through 2026-03; 500,000 paid rides/week | L3 conditional approvals since 2025-12 | S151, S101, S103 |
| Regulatory position | Paid driverless in Texas under SB 2807 and TxDMV authorisation (required from 2026-05-28); California paid rides on a limousine permit, no autonomous-service authorisation | California deployment authorised | MIIT eight-department L3 pilot | S89, S90, S91 |
| Cost model | Owned fleet, self-insured | Owned fleet, partner-owned vehicles | Consumer cars, driver liable | S89, S103 |

### Moat: accumulation, not exclusion

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Supervised fleet data | 8 | 10.2m cars; FSD miles charted to 16bn | 4-6 years | S9 |
| Driverless operating experience | 5 | 2.0m unsupervised miles only | 2-3 years | S9 |
| Dry-electrode cell process | 7 | Battery Day 2020 to Austin output in 2026 | 3-4 years | S60 |
| Manufacturing and integration | 8 | 134,785 employees; cells, cathode, refining in-house | 5+ years | S1 |
| Training compute | 6 | 225+ MW against more than $20bn of 2026 capex | 2-3 years | S9, S8 |
| State permits | 6 | Bilateral and political; not purchasable | 1-3 years | S89, S91 |
| Composite | 6.5/10 | Minimum 3-year lead on a geofenced service | — | S9, S60 |

The replication test is unflattering to a patent story: 50 funded engineers with every published Tesla patent could build a geofenced driverless service in two to three years — Waymo needed eleven years from its 2009 start — but could not reproduce the fleet data or the factories. Tesla's 10-K concedes the point by design, pledging irrevocably not to sue any party acting in good faith for infringing its electric-vehicle patents. California is the harder gate: on 23 October 2026 the DMV lists Tesla Robotaxi LLC only as a testing-permit holder requiring a safety driver, and the state's regulator confirmed in March 2026 that Tesla is not operating an autonomous vehicle service, its paid rides running on a limousine permit [S1, S89, S90].

| IP instrument | Covers | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Patent non-assertion pledge | EV and related-equipment patents | Irrevocable for good-faith users | Removes patents as a barrier | S1 |
| Trade secrets, NDAs | Cell process, manufacturing know-how | In force | Protects dry-electrode yield | S1 |
| In-house inference silicon; Samsung US foundry deal | AI4/AI5 design and fabrication | Austin fab commissioning 2027 | Cost and performance control | S1, S9 |
| Patent portfolio (AI, batteries, robotics) | Not enumerated in filings | Counts not publicly disclosed | Cannot be assessed publicly | — |

Tesla publishes no patent count or list, so a patent-number-level table cannot be built from its disclosures; a USPTO assignee search is the source that would settle portfolio size and freedom-to-operate risk, and it has been requested.

### Optimus is a research programme with a production line

Tesla began Optimus production in Fremont in Q3 2026 and calls the process "suitable for a commercial product", but discloses no units, cycle times, error rates or customers; independent estimates put 1,000-1,200 units across Fremont and Giga Texas with zero external sales, and the CEO described early units as "primarily for learning and data collection" [S99]. Figure AI has logged 1,250+ hours at BMW and Agility Robotics 65,000+ hours across nine sites, both with paying customers — smaller companies with weaker balance sheets but better evidence. Optimus should carry no revenue in a 12-month model.

Tesla's manufacturing and supervised-data advantages are real and hard to buy, but the priced asset is unsupervised autonomy, which in 2026 has a fatality-linked engineering analysis, a single authorising state, a pilot fleet and no disclosed revenue. Confidence is high on filings and regulator records, medium on driverless scale, low on Optimus and robotaxi unit economics, where disclosure is absent rather than adverse. Three questions would move this: Robotaxi revenue, paid trips and cost per trip disclosed quarterly; a California driverless deployment permit; and 4680 cell cost per kWh against the purchased-cell benchmark. If the first and third come good while EA26002 closes without a hardware remedy, the option is worth materially more than a pilot; if the analysis converts to a recall that restricts the operating domain, the revenue bridge loses its main support.

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's technology position in 2026 is two facts usually merged in the narrative: the largest supervised-driving data pool and one of the cheapest large-scale EV manufacturing bases in the industry, and almost no verified driverless revenue. Active FSD subscriptions reached 1.74 million at 30 September 2026 against 10.2 million vehicles delivered to date — 17.1% of the lifetime fleet, up from 12.4% at 31 December 2025 — while cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles were "nearly two million", 0.9% of the 220.6 million rider-only miles Waymo had logged through March 2026 [S9, S151]. That gap, not the subscription count, is what twelve months must close.

### What Tesla actually sells

| Product | Stage | Revenue or share | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FSD (Supervised) | Commercial, 9 EU countries | 1.74m subscriptions; revenue not disclosed | Unsupervised release | S9, S1 |
| Robotaxi / Cybercab | Commercial in Texas metros | Not disclosed inside $4.605bn services | Paid-trip disclosure | S9 |
| Model 3 / Model Y | Mature | 478,237 units, Q3 2026; 19.6% group gross margin | Next-gen platform | S9 |
| Cybertruck, Semi, Roadster | Ramp / design | 8,295 other-model units, Q3 2026 | Semi ramp; Roadster launch | S9 |
| Megapack, Powerwall | Scaling | $2.881bn in Q3 2026; 13.7 GWh | 50 GWh Texas ramp | S9, S60 |
| Optimus | Internal production | Zero external revenue | External pilot sale | S9, S99 |

### Mechanism: end-to-end vision and a one-sided flywheel

Tesla removed radar and now maps camera pixels directly to driving commands with an end-to-end neural network, trained on clips harvested from the fleet and run on in-house inference silicon. Training runs on two in-house clusters at Gigafactory Texas, with a company-built fab for inference and training silicon under construction. The flywheel is real but overwhelmingly *supervised*: the Q3 2026 update charts cumulative FSD miles on a 0-16 billion axis, against 2.0 million unsupervised miles [S60]. Supervised miles teach perception; they do not certify that the network can be left alone, which is why the federal safety file matters more than the mileage chart.

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active FSD subscriptions | 1.74m (2026-09-30) | Company count | S9 |
| FSD penetration of fleet | 17.1% | 1.74m / 10.2m deliveries | S9 |
| Cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles | 2.0m, 8x QoQ | Company count | S9 |
| Installed AI training compute | 225+ MW | Company nameplate | S9 |
| 4680 capacity, Texas | 40+ GWh/yr, dry electrode both sides | Company nameplate | S60 |
| Storage deployed | 13.7 GWh Q3; 36.0 GWh 9M | Company deliveries | S9 |
| Optimus units in service | 1,000-1,200 | Independent estimate | S99 |

### The safety file is the binding constraint

NHTSA's Office of Defects Investigation opened Engineering Analysis EA26002 on 18 March 2026 into whether FSD detects degraded visibility — glare, fog, dust — and warns the driver in time, covering an estimated 3,203,754 vehicles from model years 2016-2026, after nine confirmed incidents including one pedestrian fatality; two further FSD probes remain open, one on traffic-law violations across 2,882,566 vehicles with 80 incidents [S87]. Tesla's own analysis reportedly found its degradation-detection update "may have affected" only 3 of 9 incidents, which points to an architectural limit of camera-only sensing rather than a tuning defect. An engineering analysis is the last step before a recall; a recall would narrow the operating domain or force hardware across millions of cars, at a company that self-insures product liability.

::: evidence
**The camera-only bet is being tested by the regulator, not the market.** EA26002 covers 3.2 million FSD-equipped vehicles and Tesla's fix reportedly addresses a third of the reviewed incidents [S87, S88, S100]. The filings confirm the investigation but give no remedy or timetable, which is the largest un-priced technical risk in the autonomy option.
:::

### Comparison: three different autonomy businesses

| Dimension | Tesla | Waymo | Chinese L3 OEMs | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sensing | Camera-only, in-house chip | Lidar + radar + camera | Camera + lidar, Nvidia compute | S9, S101 |
| Verified driverless scale | 2.0m cumulative miles | 220.6m rider-only miles through 2026-03; 500,000 paid rides/week | L3 conditional approvals since 2025-12 | S151, S101, S103 |
| Regulatory position | Paid driverless in Texas under SB 2807 and TxDMV authorisation (required from 2026-05-28); California paid rides on a limousine permit, no autonomous-service authorisation | California deployment authorised | MIIT eight-department L3 pilot | S89, S90, S91 |
| Cost model | Owned fleet, self-insured | Owned fleet, partner-owned vehicles | Consumer cars, driver liable | S89, S103 |

### Moat: accumulation, not exclusion

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Supervised fleet data | 8 | 10.2m cars; FSD miles charted to 16bn | 4-6 years | S9 |
| Driverless operating experience | 5 | 2.0m unsupervised miles only | 2-3 years | S9 |
| Dry-electrode cell process | 7 | Battery Day 2020 to Austin output in 2026 | 3-4 years | S60 |
| Manufacturing and integration | 8 | 134,785 employees; cells, cathode, refining in-house | 5+ years | S1 |
| Training compute | 6 | 225+ MW against more than $20bn of 2026 capex | 2-3 years | S9, S8 |
| State permits | 6 | Bilateral and political; not purchasable | 1-3 years | S89, S91 |
| Composite | 6.5/10 | Minimum 3-year lead on a geofenced service | — | S9, S60 |

The replication test is unflattering to a patent story: 50 funded engineers with every published Tesla patent could build a geofenced driverless service in two to three years — Waymo needed eleven years from its 2009 start — but could not reproduce the fleet data or the factories. Tesla's 10-K concedes the point by design, pledging irrevocably not to sue any party acting in good faith for infringing its electric-vehicle patents. California is the harder gate: on 23 October 2026 the DMV lists Tesla Robotaxi LLC only as a testing-permit holder requiring a safety driver, and the state's regulator confirmed in March 2026 that Tesla is not operating an autonomous vehicle service, its paid rides running on a limousine permit [S1, S89, S90].

| IP instrument | Covers | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Patent non-assertion pledge | EV and related-equipment patents | Irrevocable for good-faith users | Removes patents as a barrier | S1 |
| Trade secrets, NDAs | Cell process, manufacturing know-how | In force | Protects dry-electrode yield | S1 |
| In-house inference silicon; Samsung US foundry deal | AI4/AI5 design and fabrication | Austin fab commissioning 2027 | Cost and performance control | S1, S9 |
| Patent portfolio (AI, batteries, robotics) | Not enumerated in filings | Counts not publicly disclosed | Cannot be assessed publicly | — |

Tesla publishes no patent count or list, so a patent-number-level table cannot be built from its disclosures; a USPTO assignee search is the source that would settle portfolio size and freedom-to-operate risk, and it has been requested.

### Optimus is a research programme with a production line

Tesla began Optimus production in Fremont in Q3 2026 and calls the process "suitable for a commercial product", but discloses no units, cycle times, error rates or customers; independent estimates put 1,000-1,200 units across Fremont and Giga Texas with zero external sales, and the CEO described early units as "primarily for learning and data collection" [S99]. Figure AI has logged 1,250+ hours at BMW and Agility Robotics 65,000+ hours across nine sites, both with paying customers — smaller companies with weaker balance sheets but better evidence. Optimus should carry no revenue in a 12-month model.

Tesla's manufacturing and supervised-data advantages are real and hard to buy, but the priced asset is unsupervised autonomy, which today carries a fatality-linked engineering analysis, a single authorising state, a pilot fleet and no disclosed revenue. Confidence is high on filings and regulator records, medium on driverless scale, low on Optimus and robotaxi unit economics, where disclosure is absent rather than adverse. The disclosures that would move this: Robotaxi revenue, paid trips and cost per trip reported quarterly; a California driverless deployment permit; and dry-electrode cell cost per kWh against the purchased-cell benchmark. If the first and third come good while the engineering analysis closes without a hardware remedy, the option is worth materially more than a pilot; if it converts to a recall that restricts the operating domain, the revenue bridge loses its main support.

The 12-month exit is therefore two-sided: a sale into a 103x multiple, and a minority-probability bid that pays a premium in another listed stock. Prediction markets put 18% on an announced merger by 2026-12-31 and 67% by 2027-12-31, no terms are agreed, and Tesla's approval needs a majority of all shares outstanding. Weighted across the branches, the expected 12-month return is between -6% and +3% depending on the deal probability: better than the -17% the standalone businesses offer, but not a return that pays for a 60% drawdown [S154, S156, S158, S8].

| Separation of robotaxi or energy | not disclosed | no filed plan, no registration statement | none | not disclosed | S1 |

The acquirer arithmetic has changed; the carmakers' indifference has not. General Motors at $73.7bn, Ford at $45.7bn and Rivian at $17.6bn are worth $137.0bn between them, 8.7% of Tesla, and BYD earns 21.2x trailing, so none can finance $1.58tn at any premium. At parity Tesla holders would own 42-43% of the combined company and 47-50% with the premium. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financial Analysis (financials, revision 4 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,910 characters)
Tesla converted $1,531M of free cash flow in Q3 2026, but the statements no longer show it earning its cost of capital: a 5.5% trailing return on invested capital sits 57 basis points above the ten-year Treasury, $41,778M of capex since 2023 has coincided with a 61% fall in operating income, and the profit that remains leans on interest from the cash pile and a payables build rather than on operations [S8, S12, S11].

### Revenue recovered, operating profit did not

| Line item ($M unless stated) | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | 9M 2026 | TTM to 2026-09-30 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 96,773 | 97,690 | 94,827 | 78,669 | 103,570 | S12, S13, S1, S8 |

| Research and development | 3,969 | 4,540 | 6,411 | 7,078 | 8,861 | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Selling, general and administrative | 4,800 | 5,150 | 5,834 | 5,830 | 7,485 | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Operating income | 8,891 | 7,076 | 4,355 | 2,057 | 3,466 | S12, S13, S1, S8 |

Revenue fell for two years before the 2026 rebound while operating income fell throughout, from $8,891M in FY2023 to $3,466M trailing, because research and development rose from $3,969M to $8,861M and selling and administrative cost from $4,800M to $7,485M against gross profit that stayed between $17.1B and $20.0B. The Q3 2026 operating margin of 2.6% came on revenue flat year on year with deliveries down 2% to 486,532 from 497,099, so price, mix and a weaker dollar carried the top line. Reported against adjusted: Q3 2026 GAAP net income of $787M against non-GAAP of $1,697M, and diluted EPS of $0.22 against $0.48. The quarter also absorbed a $475M reversal of previously recognised regulatory credit revenue for returned credits, so the 2.6% operating margin understates the underlying figure by 1.7 points [S12, S13, S1, S8].

### Free cash flow is a payables loan and a capex pause

Nine-month operating cash flow of $14,897M exceeded the $13,014M of capital expenditure to leave $1,883M of free cash flow, against $6,220M for FY2025. Two facts weaken the conversion. Management attributes $3.51 billion of the $3.96 billion year-on-year operating-cash-flow increase to working capital, and in Q3 2026 alone free cash flow of $1,531M rested on a $2,590M working-capital inflow, of which accounts payable supplied $1,920M and accrued liabilities $1,950M; stripping it out, quarterly free cash flow was -$1,059M, and $3,670M of capex sat in liabilities at 2026-09-30. Across the nine months, payables rose $3,868M from 2025-12-31 to $17,239M and the cash conversion cycle fell to 2.6 days from 13.0, so without the payables build nine-month free cash flow would have been -$1,985M. Capital expenditure nearly doubled from $6,134M a year earlier, and the 2026 plan was restated between filings — "in excess of $25 billion" in the July 2026 report, "in excess of $20 billion" in the October 2026 one, and $20 billion on the Q3 2026 call — leaving full-year 2026 free cash flow between -$1,290M and +$1,160M depending on whether Q4 operating cash flow matches Q4 2025's $3,813M or Q3 2026's $6,263M [S8, S9, S83, S102].

### The balance sheet carries the plan; the off-balance items carry the risk
