| Tesla Robotaxi, LLC | Texas, US | LLC | Robotaxi operations | 100% | Tesla, Inc. | S1 |

### The dilution path runs through a $2 trillion gate

Musk holds 699,580,882 shares, or 19.8%, including 286,428,773 restricted shares from the 2018 award, and 207,498,721 of his shares are pledged against personal borrowings. The 2018 award was exercised in full on 2026-06-16 for 303,960,630 shares, which is why the count rose 202m, or 5.4%, in the nine months to 2026-09-30. Forward dilution is the 2025 CEO Performance Award: 423,743,904 shares, 10.7% of the current count, in 12 equal tranches, none earned as of 2026-10-19. Each earned share carries a $334.09 offset payable in cash or shares, a five-year holding requirement, and every tranche needs a market-cap milestone before any operating milestone counts, starting at $2 trillion — 26.6% above the 2026-10-30 value — then nine $500bn and two $1tn increments to $8.5 trillion. The economics sit closer to a premium-struck option than a free grant: at $399.81 the gross spread is $65.72 a share, and at the plan's top the transfer is $769.6bn net of offsets, 9.1% of an $8.5 trillion capitalisation [S10, S107].

### What the customer actually buys

The business is three P&Ls sold to different budget owners. Automotive ($69.53bn of FY2025 revenue, 73% of the total) sells vehicles to consumers, leasing companies and fleets, and monetises the installed base through Supercharging, service, parts, used cars and insurance; the software layer is FSD (Supervised), with 1.74m active subscriptions at 2026-09-30. Energy ($12.77bn, 13.5% of revenue, 29.8% gross margin) sells Megapack and Powerwall to utilities, developers, industrial sites and, increasingly, data-centre operators whose budget is a power-availability capex line rather than a transport one. Services ($12.53bn, +19% in FY2025) is largely a captive aftermarket on Tesla's own parc. Growth has shifted from unit volume — Q3 2026 deliveries were 486,532, down 2% year on year — to storage deployment (13.7 GWh in Q3 2026), software attach and the Robotaxi and Optimus optionality the pay award is designed to reward [S1, S9].

### Capacity is built; volume is the question

Tesla runs eight primary plants: Fremont (Model 3/Y, more than 550,000 units), Shanghai (more than 950,000), Berlin (more than 375,000), Texas (Model Y more than 375,000, Cybertruck and Cybercab more than 125,000 each) and Nevada (Semi 25,000), plus Megapack plants in California (40 GWh), Shanghai (20 GWh) and Texas (50 GWh). Headcount was 134,785 at 2025-12-31. Nameplate vehicle capacity of 2.53m units against an annualised Q3 2026 run rate of 1.95m leaves a fifth of the system idle, while Semi, Cybercab and Optimus lines add depreciation before revenue; that is the mechanism by which a flat revenue year becomes either margin expansion or further compression [S9, S1].

### No payout, and a board that cannot be replaced

Tesla has never paid a dividend, has no repurchase authorisation and made no purchases in FY2025, while holding $45.45bn of cash and short-term investments; with no distribution, a holder's 12-month total return is the share price alone. Governance reinforces retention: the board has three classes, a 2025 management proposal to remove supermajority voting requirements won 39.4% of shares outstanding and failed, and the 2026-12-03 meeting asks holders only to elect three Class I directors, cast a say-on-pay vote and ratify the auditor. The counter-evidence is real — one share class is more minority-proportional than Rivian's ten-vote Class B, seven of nine directors are independent, the CEO takes no salary, and unearned award shares carry no independent votes because an irrevocable proxy votes them with the rest of the stock — but none of it returns cash or lets a majority change the charter. For a holder at $399.81 the structure therefore offers no cash yield, caps the upside above $2 trillion by 9.1%, and gives no route to force a change of capital-return policy: that argues for sizing the position as a price-only bet, not for rejecting the equity. The open question is whether a $1.58 trillion price for $94.83bn of revenue and a 16.2% automotive gross margin leaves anything after that gate is crossed [S1, S10, S114].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Founding Team & Key Personnel (team, revision 4 by Company Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,630 characters)
Tesla's board is majority independent on paper, but the three decisions that mattered in 2024-2026 — a $2.0bn investment in the CEO's own AI company after shareholders rejected the measure, a pay award that can reach 423.7m shares, and the retention of a classified board — all went against the minority's expressed preference, so key-person and capital-allocation risk are real, formally disclosed, and only partly offset by the award's extreme vesting gates [S10].

### Independence is not the same as accountability

Nine directors sit on the board, seven of them independent under Nasdaq rules, with Robyn Denholm as independent chair since November 2018 and all four committees composed solely of independents. The structure that matters is elsewhere: three staggered classes with three-year terms, supermajority voting requirements that a 2025 management proposal failed to remove with 39.4% of shares outstanding in favour, and two family directors — Elon and Kimbal Musk — in the room. Compensation Committee chair Ira Ehrenpreis has also served on SpaceX's board since February 2026, the counterparty to Tesla's $2.0bn investment and $143.3m of 2025 revenue, a relationship the proxy calls immaterial [S10].

### Pay is gated on market value, not on operating return

The 2025 CEO Performance Award is 423,743,904 shares in 12 equal tranches. Each tranche needs a market-capitalisation milestone first — from $2 trillion, 26.6% above the 2026-10-30 value, through nine $500bn and two $1tn steps to $8.5 trillion — and one of 12 operational milestones: four strategic-product goals (10m active FSD subscriptions, 1m bots delivered, 1m Robotaxis in commercial operation among them) or eight Adjusted EBITDA goals. Each earned share carries a $334.09 offset and a five-year hold, and tranches 11 and 12 also require a board-approved CEO succession framework, the only formal succession mechanism disclosed. Against that, General Motors paid Mary Barra $48.2m of realized compensation in 2025, and Musk has taken no salary since 2019 and has no employment agreement or severance; reported 2025 total compensation of $158.36bn was an accounting value, with realized pay at $0 [S10, S107, S109].

### The xAI vote is the test the board failed

At the 2025-11-06 meeting shareholders approved the pay award with 1,892,235,822 votes for, 564,940,908 against and 12,227,846 abstentions, 76.6% of votes cast. A separate non-binding measure authorising funding for xAI drew 1.06bn votes for and 916.3m against but was recorded as rejected because Tesla's bylaws count abstentions as votes against; on 2026-01-16 the company nonetheless agreed to invest $2.0bn in xAI, completing on 2026-03-12 as SpaceX Class A stock after the SpaceX-xAI merger. The Audit Committee reviews related-person transactions above $120,000 under a written policy, but the sequence shows the review is procedural: a holder should assume future flows to Musk-controlled companies are a board decision, not a shareholder one [S59, S104, S105].

### One person carries the strategy; the bench is uneven

The 10-K says Musk "does not devote his full time and attention to Tesla" and lists management roles at SpaceX, xAI, Neuralink and The Boring Company, while the proxy records that xAI became a SpaceX subsidiary in February 2026 and that Musk is SpaceX's CEO, CTO and chairman. The operating bench is strongest in manufacturing and finance: Tom Zhu, SVP APAC and global vehicle manufacturing since June 2025, joined in 2014 and built Gigafactory Shanghai; Vaibhav Taneja has been CFO since August 2023 and inside Tesla's finance function since 2017. Demand execution is the weak spot: Omead Afshar left in June 2025, Troy Jones was dismissed as head of North American sales in July 2025, the North American service head left in August 2025 and Raj Jegannathan departed in February 2026 after 13 years. Headcount was 134,785 at 2025-12-31; the attrition is concentrated in senior commercial roles [S1, S111, S124].

### What the record confirms, and what diligence must settle

Public records confirm the founder-market fit: Musk co-founded Zip2 (sold to Compaq in 1999) and PayPal (sold to eBay in 2002), has run Tesla since October 2008, and still owns 19.8% with 207,498,721 shares pledged. They also confirm the concentration: no chief operating officer, no permanent North American sales leader, a board with no director who has run a vehicle programme at another OEM, and a CEO whose other companies are now suppliers, investees and counterparties. The gaps a diligence team should close are the succession plan behind tranches 11-12, the terms and lenders behind the pledge, the fairness opinion, if any, for the $2.0bn xAI/SpaceX purchase, and references on Zhu and Taneja from SolarCity and Shanghai. For a 12-month holder the concentration is not a separately observable discount in the share price: it argues for a smaller position and for demanding evidence that Zhu and Taneja can run the operating business while Musk is elsewhere [S10, S2].

::: evidence
**The strongest proof of execution is a manufacturing ramp the founder did not personally run; the strongest doubt is a board that proceeded with a related-party investment after shareholders rejected it.**

Tom Zhu built Gigafactory Shanghai, the largest plant in the system at more than 950,000 units, and Berlin set a quarterly production record in Q3 2026; Tesla passed 10.2m cumulative vehicles. The counterweight is procedural: an xAI funding measure lost on a 1.06bn-to-916.3m vote, yet $2.0bn was committed five weeks later, and the Compensation Committee chair sits on SpaceX's board (sources S9, S104, S10).
:::

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Development Strategy (strategy, revision 3 by Product Analyst, changed since the previous version, 7,921 characters)
Tesla's strategy is no longer self-funded, and the filings now say so. With 2026 capital expenditure guided above $20 billion against $15.0 billion of trailing Adjusted EBITDA (Q4 2025 to Q3 2026), Tesla signed three credit agreements totalling $30 billion in September 2026 and states that heightened capital spending "will necessitate additional funding beyond our operating cash flow" [S8]. That sentence, not the robotaxi narrative, is the strategy disclosure that matters for the next twelve months: the autonomy, energy and robotics options are now financed partly with balance-sheet capacity.

### The plan has three pillars and one new capital sink

The stated plan, carried in the 10-K and in the 2025 CEO Performance Award, is to convert a hardware business into an autonomy and robotics business: FSD (Supervised) and Robotaxi, energy storage, and Optimus, funded by a vehicle business that delivered 1.32 million units in the first nine months of 2026 [S10]. What is new is the depth of vertical integration behind it — 225+ MW of training compute, an in-house inference chip, a Samsung foundry collaboration and a company semiconductor fab commissioning equipment in 2027 — which turns a software roadmap into a fixed-cost programme closer to a foundry than to an automaker.

### The track record is mixed, and the split is informative

Energy and manufacturing promises have largely been kept: Megafactory Texas started production in Q3 2026, Optimus production began in Fremont ahead of the January 2026 target to start before the end of 2026, and 36.0 GWh of storage was deployed in nine months against 46.7 GWh for all of 2025. Autonomy promises have not: the 2025 award still lists "1 million Robotaxis in commercial operation" and "10 million active FSD subscriptions" as unmet operational milestones, against 300+ claimed Cybercabs and 1.74 million subscriptions, and none of the 423.7 million shares has been earned because the first tranche also needs $2.0 trillion of market capitalisation plus one operational milestone [S9, S10]. The pattern is that Tesla ships physical products within a quarter or two of plan and ships software-defined promises years late — which is why the robotaxi timeline should be discounted but the Megapack and Semi timelines should not.

### Resources fit the plan only at the low end

Nine-month capex of $13.01 billion against guidance of "in excess of $20 billion" leaves $7.0 billion for the fourth quarter, after a Q2 spike of $5.79 billion; the guidance was cut from "more than $25 billion" in the 10-Q rather than in the shareholder letter. Free cash flow of $1.53 billion in Q3 2026 depended on $2.59 billion of working-capital inflow, and $3.67 billion of equipment and construction spend sat unpaid in liabilities. Against that, $45.45 billion of cash and $30 billion of undrawn facilities mean the plan is affordable — just not self-funded [S8, S102]. The mechanism matters: borrowing to fund a call option on autonomy converts equity risk into refinancing risk, and the return on that borrowing depends on Robotaxi revenue the company does not yet disclose, so the cost of the strategy now appears in interest and covenants rather than in a share count.

The related-party lines deserve emphasis. SpaceX bought $626 million of Megapacks in the first nine months of 2026, 7.4% of $8.43 billion of energy revenue, and $588 million of the receivable was billed for units not yet delivered — revenue quality a third-party backlog would not show. That is capital allocation and customer concentration inside the second engine, and it means the energy story is more dependent on one related buyer than the order-rate language implies.

### What the second curves are actually worth

Energy is the one adjacency already at scale and profitable: 13.7 GWh deployed in Q3 2026 alone, 50 GWh of new Texas capacity and record order rates, which is why it deserves to be valued as a business with a discount for the related-party share. Robotaxi is an option whose value is capped by permits and by the federal safety file rather than by manufacturing capacity — 300+ claimed Cybercabs is a pilot, and neither trips nor revenue are disclosed inside $4.605 billion of services revenue. Optimus is further still, with zero external sales and no published throughput, and the semiconductor fab adds a foundry's fixed-cost risk to a company already guiding more than $20 billion of capex. Margins carry the bill: Q3 2026 operating income was $718 million on $28.05 billion of revenue, a 2.6% operating margin, while regulatory credits, the highest-margin revenue line, fell from $2.76 billion in 2024 to $1.99 billion in 2025 [S1, S9]. For an investor this is the crux — the plan's returns sit in businesses with no disclosed revenue, while its costs land on a 2.6%-margin income statement.

### What must be true in twelve months

Three things must hold for the strategy to stay credible without new equity: Robotaxi revenue must be disclosed as its own line with paid trips growing outside Texas; capex must land at or below the guided floor with free cash flow positive before working-capital swings; and energy must keep compounding with third-party demand large enough to absorb the new capacity. The signposts are a California driverless deployment permit, a quarterly Robotaxi revenue disclosure, the close or escalation of NHTSA's EA26002, and whether the credit facilities are drawn at all. If all four move positively, the strategy is self-sustaining on debt and the option value is real; if none does, the company is borrowing against a low-margin auto business to fund revenue it cannot yet show, and the right posture is to wait for the Robotaxi line rather than pay for it in advance."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG Assessment (esg, revision 1 by Regulatory Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,956 characters)
Tesla's ESG and policy position has already cost it real money in 2026 — a US consumer credit that vanished, a regulatory-credit line that halved and then reversed $475 million — but the binding constraint on the next twelve months is not reputational: Tesla holds no California permit to run a driverless paid service and faces a 3,203,754-vehicle NHTSA engineering analysis. Automotive regulatory credits earned $1,993 million in 2025 against $2,763 million in 2024, then $639 million in the first nine months of 2026 against $1,451 million a year earlier; the contracted credit backlog fell to $384 million at 2026-09-30 from $841 million at 2025-12-31 [S1, S8]. Credits were sold against compliance shortfalls created by federal and state programmes, so when the 2025 budget law restricted them the shortfalls shrank and delivered credits became returnable — which is why a reversal exists at all. On the 2026 run rate the line is worth roughly $850 million a year of near-pure gross margin; models that restore it toward the 2024 peak overstate revenue and automotive margin.

### Permits, not software, cap the paid robotaxi market

The California DMV's list, updated 2026-10-23, places TESLA ROBOTAXI LLC among holders of an autonomous-vehicle testing permit **with a safety driver**; Tesla appears on neither the driverless-testing list (2026-10-22) nor the deployment list, which names only Mercedes-Benz, Nuro and Waymo. The California Public Utilities Commission said in March 2026 that the state's Tesla "Robotaxi" runs on a limousine permit, outside autonomous-vehicle passenger-service rules. In Texas, Senate Bill 2807 — not 2809 — requires Texas DMV authorisation for commercial automated vehicles from 2026-05-28, with a public lookup and a complaint process, but it is a registration regime rather than a volume cap [S89, S91]. A testing permit with a driver cannot generate driverless ride revenue, so the paid-service market for twelve months is permissive states only, and California needs two further approvals against Waymo's multi-year precedent.

### Safety enforcement is the sharper exposure

NHTSA's Office of Defects Investigation opened Engineering Analysis EA26002 on 2026-03-18 into Tesla's FSD degradation-detection system in reduced-visibility conditions, escalating Preliminary Evaluation PE24031 and covering model years 2016 to 2026. An Engineering Analysis is the last administrative step before the agency can seek a mandatory recall. The direct cash cost of a software recall is small because the remedy ships over the air; the indirect cost is not, because agency findings become exhibits in the product-liability cases Tesla already defends and a recall is the one event that can interrupt the autonomy narrative carrying most of the equity value. Tesla discloses no NHTSA consent order, which would be the materially worse outcome. Separately, NHTSA records eight recall campaigns on the 2026 Model Y between 2025-05-30 and 2026-09-01, including front-suspension fasteners (26V558000) — high for one nameplate in sixteen months [S87, S88, S47].

### Governance: the tail shrank, the concentration did not

On 2025-12-19 the Delaware Supreme Court reversed the Chancery rescission of Mr Musk's 2018 pay award, reinstating it with $1 in nominal damages and a reduced fee award, after 72% of disinterested shares voted to ratify in 2024. That removes an overhang priced since January 2024 and is, on balance, favourable. Concentration remains: Mr Musk holds 699,580,882 shares, 19.8% of 3,952,648,559 outstanding, of which 207,498,721 are pledged as loan collateral — a forced-selling channel in a drawdown. The 2025 CEO Performance Award covers 423,743,904 restricted shares, 10.7% of those outstanding, and because unearned shares vote proportionally to other holders the control effect is smaller than the dilution effect. The 2026 escalation is capital allocation: Tesla agreed in January 2026 to invest approximately $2.00 billion in xAI Holdings, the right converted into SpaceX Class A stock when SpaceX acquired xAI Holdings on 2026-02-02, and Tesla completed the purchase on 2026-03-12 [S1, S10]. That investment is the governance fact most likely to move institutional demand within a year.

### Social: enforcement is mixed, and the largest case just closed

The California Civil Rights Department's race-discrimination action ran its first, equitable-relief trial phase from 2026-09-21 to a scheduled close on 2026-10-30 in Alameda County Superior Court, while the EEOC's parallel race-harassment and retaliation suit, filed 2023-09-28, sits in discovery with no trial date. Against that, the National Labor Relations Board dismissed a complaint over Buffalo plant IT rules on 2026-10-29 [S8, S96]. The exposure that matters is injunctive rather than monetary: a finding would impose monitoring and reporting obligations on plant management and raise the cost of state incentives where Tesla builds, whereas cash damages are undisclosed and unlikely to be material.

### The environmental case does not price in twelve months

Tesla's 2025 Impact Report claims nearly 37 million tonnes of CO2e avoided by customers in 2025 and a 2040 net-zero commitment across the value chain; both are company material and unverified, and its Scope 1, 2 and 3 totals could not be read because the file would not load. The one environmental rule with a hard compliance cost for a battery maker has been deferred: Regulation (EU) 2025/1561 pushed supply-chain due diligence from 18 August 2025 to 18 August 2027, and the battery passport starts on 18 February 2027 — both outside the horizon [S95, S97].

Key P/M fit gaps:
- The hardest thing about selling robotaxi is not the tech: it is insurance and remote supervision cost per paid mile, plus the permit chain. No section quantifies insurance/teleop cost per mile; the report says "10-20% of autonomy value" in the risk matrix without a basis. The one-question is contribution after insurance, depreciation and remote supervision — but the report never establishes even a benchmark range for those three costs (e.g., Waymo's reported cost per mile estimates, AV insurance premiums, teleop ratios: 1 remote operator per N vehicles). So the one-question can't be answered even directionally. That's a real gap.
- Budget owner for energy is described (utility/developer/data-centre capex line) ✓ good.
- Lost deals: no evidence anywhere of lost deals. For energy: Tesla lost the big data-centre deals? There were reports of Tesla losing storage share to Chinese integrators in 2026. For FSD: churn not disclosed. For vehicles: the report shows volume losses but does not describe why buyers chose BYD etc. (partly in competition: price).
- Adoption: why isn't FSD adopted faster? 17.1% penetration; the report doesn't test price elasticity or the free-alternative (fold into pass 3 item partly).
- Megapack backlog: company-only, with 7.4% of energy revenue to a related party (SpaceX) and $588m billed for undelivered units — that's revenue quality; the section labels it. But there's an important P/M fit question: is the "nearly sold out through 2027" demand third-party? The report says record order rate. Could ask: how much of the unsatisfied obligations of $10.73bn is SpaceX/related party and how much is contracted at fixed price. That's partly diligence question already in thesis.

items.action: Publish one distribution and derive everything from it. items.issue: The report's central quantitative claim, the expected twelve-month return, is stated four different ways and the probability of its main upside event four more. items.action: Add the bridge as a table in thesis (or financials): TTM adjusted EBITDA $14,995m, plus or minus each segment's contribution, arriving at $16.0bn, with the energy line shown both at the 33.1% Q3 margin and at the ex-refund margin, since those two assumptions move the base case by more than the Tesla-specific growth assumed. items.issue: The base case rests on $16.0bn of adjusted EBITDA, $1.0bn above the $14,995m trailing figure, and no section shows how the $1.0bn is earned — yet thesis assumption 3 has energy normalising to 25-30% from 33.1%, and the ex-refund margin is nearer 14.8%, so the two assumptions may point in opposite directions. arguments.notes: Number stress-test arithmetic, version 1. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 2 by Lead Analyst, 8,736 characters)
Tesla is the industry's strongest capability attached to its most expensive claim on it. At $399.81 on 2026-10-30 the equity is capitalised at $1,580.4bn on $3.47bn of trailing operating income, while the businesses the filings describe — cars, storage and services — are worth $139-160bn, or $35-40 a share, on peer multiples [S8, S9, S11]. The judgement is Sell, and it is a de-rating call rather than a liquidation call: the reported value is a floor of $40-50 a share, the tradable range is $161-292, and 90-91% of the price is an option on revenue the quarterly report does not book.

The conditional form makes the call testable. If the need is real — 23.0m electric units in 2026, 28% of global light-vehicle sales — and if the capability is defensible — 1.74m active FSD subscriptions and a 33.1% storage gross margin against Fluence's 5.1% — then the economics still do not scale to this price. The residual $1,420-1,441bn needs $105bn of 2030 operating income at 20x, or 2.1-4.2m robotaxis at a 25% margin, against 1,051 authorised vehicles in Texas on 2026-10-27 and 125,000 units of annual Cybercab capacity [S125, S127, S137, S61]. The outcome is attractive only if the price falls toward the base case or the option converts into a disclosed revenue line; at $399.81 neither holds.

Consensus is Hold, not Sell: 24 buy, 1 strong buy, 20 hold and 3 sell across 48 firms, with an average target of $408.61, 2.2% above the close. The difference is not about the car; it is about the option. The market prices autonomy as a 2028 cash flow, while the record shows 2.0m cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles — 0.9% of the 220.6m rider-only miles Waymo had logged through March 2026 — a California permit that allows testing with a safety driver and nothing driverless, and a Texas service of 1,051 vehicles against Waymo's 500,000 paid rides a week across ten cities [S128, S151, S142, S89]. A 2.2% consensus upside and a -27% base case are two prices for the same option; the gap is the thesis.

The mechanism is the multiple, not the earnings. Tesla trades at 103x trailing adjusted EBITDA of $14,995m and 439.4x earnings, against a peer median of 19.1x and BYD's 17.3x; one turn of the multiple is $15.0bn, three years of net income. The operating margin was 2.6% in Q3 2026, interest income was 46.5% of pre-tax profit, nine-month free cash flow of $1,883m was smaller than the $3,868m payables build that produced it, and a 5.5% ROIC sits 57bp above a 4.93% ten-year Treasury [S11, S131, S15, S9, S8, S22]. A delay in autonomy compresses the rating, not the earnings, so the drawdown does not require a bad quarter.

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 31% | A California driverless deployment permit, a quarterly Robotaxi revenue line with positive contribution, energy gross margin above 30% and capex at $20bn; or a SpaceX share-for-share combination at a 20-35% premium | $506.05 a share, +26.6%, the first 2025 award gate at a $2,000bn capitalisation and 131x adjusted EBITDA; a combination at $480-540 pays the same band | DMV deployment list; Q4 2026 segment disclosure; exchange ratio | S89, S127, S154, S156 |
| Base | 40% | No robotaxi monetisation before 2028, the US pool stays near 6-7% of sales, energy revenue per GWh keeps falling and the multiple compresses toward 70x | $292 a share, -27%: 70x on $16.0bn of adjusted EBITDA plus $36.18bn of net cash | Q4 2026 results without a robotaxi line; US EV registrations below 250,000 a quarter | S8, S9, S139 |
| Bear | 29% | EA26002 converts to a recall that restricts the operating domain, California stays closed, China and US share erode, capex overruns force a facility draw and the multiple de-rates to 40x | $161 a share, -60%; a 25x case is $104, -74% | NHTSA engineering-analysis closure or recall notice; capex above $7bn in Q4; payables reversal | S87, S8, S11 |
:::

The probabilities are the thesis in numbers: 31% bull, 40% base and 29% bear give an expected 12-month return of -19.8%, with a 29% chance of a 60% loss against a 31% chance of a 27% gain. The bull case is deliberately generous: it requires four conjunctive conditions — a California permit, a robotaxi revenue line, energy above 30% and capex at $20bn — and it also absorbs the SpaceX branch, because a 20-35% premium pays the same band as the first award gate. That substitution is the point: the merger raises the floor, it does not raise the expected return, and because the premium is paid in SPCX paper trading at 143x annualised second-quarter 2026 adjusted EBITDA, it swaps one crowded multiple for another. The bear case is a 40x multiple, not a balance-sheet failure: $36.18bn of net cash and $30.0bn of undrawn facilities mean a financing delay costs the option, not the company [S8, S154, S157].

| Rank | Assumption | Confidence | What would disprove it | Impact if wrong | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Autonomy stays unmonetised through 2027: no robotaxi revenue line is disclosed and the paid service stays in Texas | High | A quarterly robotaxi revenue line with positive contribution, or a California driverless deployment permit, inside twelve months | The bull case, +27%, replaces the base case, -27% | Q4 2026 results in the last week of January 2027 pass without a robotaxi line | S89, S151 |
| 2 | The equity multiple holds above 40x adjusted EBITDA despite a 4.93% ten-year Treasury and a VIX in its 77th percentile | Low | A move to 40x or below | -60%, $161 a share; 25x gives $104 | Ten-year Treasury above 5%; a quarterly miss against consensus | S8, S11, S22 |
| 3 | Energy gross margin normalises to 25-30% once the $526m of Q3 2026 tariff refunds and warranty true-ups roll off | Medium | Two consecutive quarters above 30% with no tariff refunds and Megapack price per kWh stabilising | $1.5bn of EBITDA, $9-10 a share at 25x | Energy revenue per GWh below $200m, or margin below 25% in Q4 2026 | S9, S61 |
| 4 | Capital expenditure lands at or below $20bn and free cash flow is non-negative before working-capital swings | Medium | Q4 capex above $7bn, a third guidance change, or a second quarter of negative free cash flow ex-working capital | $5bn of free cash flow, $31 a share at 25x | A draw on the $30bn facilities; payables growth above 20% year on year | S8, S83 |
| 5 | A SpaceX combination is attempted at a 20-35% premium, with a probability of 25-45% inside twelve months | Medium | The committees end without terms, or the vote threshold fails | +20% to +35% adverse to a short; the expected return moves from -19.8% to -6% to +3% | A filed exchange ratio; the 50%-of-outstanding vote count | S154, S156, S158 |

|---|---|---|---|---|

Tesla is at 0.9% of the miles with no driverless deployment permit | S142, S151, S130 |

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Company Overview (company_overview, revision 5 by Company Analyst, 8,950 characters)
Tesla's legal and ownership structure is unusually plain for a founder-led company — one class of stock, a Texas parent with no VIE or dual-class layer, and a CEO who owns 19.8% — so what constrains a 12-month equity return is not the charter but a 10.7% contingent dilution struck at market capitalisations from $2 trillion upward, no dividend or buyback, and a classified board that minority holders cannot replace. Tesla, Inc. trades on Nasdaq under TSLA; 3,952,648,559 shares were outstanding at 2026-09-30 and market capitalisation was $1.58 trillion at the $399.81 close on 2026-10-30 [S10, S112].

### One operating group, no holding-company layer

The registrant was incorporated in Delaware on 2003-07-01 and converted to a Texas corporation on 2024-06-13. The structure is flat: country operating companies, single-purpose solar and lease vehicles and insurance captives, with no contractual-control or variable-interest layer separating legal from economic ownership. The filings disclose no separate intellectual-property holding company; the listed parent files the group's consolidated accounts, while the operating subsidiaries hold the plants, local licences and financing books [S1, S58].

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership | Controller | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tesla, Inc. | Texas, US | Listed corporation | Registrant; consolidated group; public equity | 100% of subsidiaries | Board; Musk 19.8% | S1, S58 |
| Tesla (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. | China | Limited liability company | Gigafactory and Megafactory Shanghai operating entity | 100% | Tesla, Inc. | S1 |
| Tesla Manufacturing Brandenburg SE | Germany | European company | Gigafactory Berlin-Brandenburg | 100% | Tesla, Inc. | S1 |
| Tesla Robotaxi, LLC | Texas, US | LLC | Robotaxi operations | 100% | Tesla, Inc. | S1 |

### The dilution path runs through a $2 trillion gate

Musk holds 699,580,882 shares, or 19.8%, including 286,428,773 restricted shares from the 2018 award, and 207,498,721 of his shares are pledged against personal borrowings. The 2018 award was exercised in full on 2026-06-16 for 303,960,630 shares, which is why the count rose 202m, or 5.4%, in the nine months to 2026-09-30. Forward dilution is the 2025 CEO Performance Award: 423,743,904 shares, 10.7% of the current count, in 12 equal tranches, none earned as of 2026-10-19. Each earned share carries a $334.09 offset payable in cash or shares, a five-year holding requirement, and every tranche needs a market-cap milestone before any operating milestone counts, starting at $2 trillion — 26.6% above the 2026-10-30 value — then nine $500bn and two $1tn increments to $8.5 trillion. The economics sit closer to a premium-struck option than a free grant: at $399.81 the gross spread is $65.72 a share, and at the plan's top the transfer is $769.6bn net of offsets, 9.1% of an $8.5 trillion capitalisation [S10, S107].

| Holder | Class | Shares | % of shares | % of votes | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Elon Musk (CEO, director) | Common | 699,580,882 | 19.8% | 19.8% | S10 |
| Vanguard Capital Management | Common | 210,796,512 | 5.3% | 5.3% | S10 |
| All directors and officers (11 persons) | Common | 706,496,615 | 20.0% | 20.0% | S10 |
| Public float, calculated (excludes insider shares and 423.7m unvested restricted shares) | Common | 2,822,408,040 | 71.4% | 71.4% | S10 |

### What the customer actually buys

The business is three P&Ls sold to different budget owners. Automotive ($69.53bn of FY2025 revenue, 73% of the total) sells vehicles to consumers, leasing companies and fleets, and monetises the installed base through Supercharging, service, parts, used cars and insurance; the software layer is FSD (Supervised), with 1.74m active subscriptions at 2026-09-30. Energy ($12.77bn, 13.5% of revenue, 29.8% gross margin) sells Megapack and Powerwall to utilities, developers, industrial sites and, increasingly, data-centre operators whose budget is a power-availability capex line rather than a transport one. Services ($12.53bn, +19% in FY2025) is largely a captive aftermarket on Tesla's own parc. Growth has shifted from unit volume — Q3 2026 deliveries were 486,532, down 2% year on year — to storage deployment (13.7 GWh in Q3 2026), software attach and the Robotaxi and Optimus optionality the pay award is designed to reward [S1, S9].

### Capacity is built; volume is the question

Tesla runs eight primary plants: Fremont (Model 3/Y, more than 550,000 units), Shanghai (more than 950,000), Berlin (more than 375,000), Texas (Model Y more than 375,000, Cybertruck and Cybercab more than 125,000 each) and Nevada (Semi 25,000), plus Megapack plants in California (40 GWh), Shanghai (20 GWh) and Texas (50 GWh). Headcount was 134,785 at 2025-12-31. Nameplate vehicle capacity of 2.53m units against an annualised Q3 2026 run rate of 1.95m leaves a fifth of the system idle, while Semi, Cybercab and Optimus lines add depreciation before revenue; that is the mechanism by which a flat revenue year becomes either margin expansion or further compression [S9, S1].

### No payout, and a board that cannot be replaced

Tesla has never paid a dividend, has no repurchase authorisation and made no purchases in FY2025, while holding $45.45bn of cash and short-term investments; with no distribution, a holder's 12-month total return is the share price alone. Governance reinforces retention: the board has three classes, a 2025 management proposal to remove supermajority voting requirements won 39.4% of shares outstanding and failed, and the 2026-12-03 meeting asks holders only to elect three Class I directors, cast a say-on-pay vote and ratify the auditor. The counter-evidence is real — one share class is more minority-proportional than Rivian's ten-vote Class B, seven of nine directors are independent, the CEO takes no salary, and unearned award shares carry no independent votes because an irrevocable proxy votes them with the rest of the stock — but none of it returns cash or lets a majority change the charter. For a holder at $399.81 the structure therefore offers no cash yield, caps the upside above $2 trillion by 9.1%, and gives no route to force a change of capital-return policy: that argues for sizing the position as a price-only bet, not for rejecting the equity. The open question is whether a $1.58 trillion price for $94.83bn of revenue and a 16.2% automotive gross margin leaves anything after that gate is crossed [S1, S10, S114].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 2 by Market Analyst, 8,840 characters)
Tesla is winning the market that is shrinking and losing the one that is growing. It holds the US electric-vehicle market at a share no rival approaches while that market contracts, ranks fourth among China's new-energy brands in a domestic pool that is itself shrinking, and its European recovery has come inside a pool growing faster than it. What Tesla owns is narrower than the narrative: the charging standard every major automaker has licensed, an installed base of paid FSD subscriptions, and a storage gross margin materially above the nearest listed integrator's.

### In the United States, Tesla sets the price because it holds the pool
Tesla sold 144,094 US electric vehicles in Q3 2026 for 54% of the market, and 386,194 in nine months for 52.9%, with its own US volume down 14.4% against a market down 30.3%. Share gains inside a contracting pool flatter the position: the absolute US revenue base is smaller than in 2025. The mechanism is distribution: when a $7,500 credit disappears, the brand with the densest charging footprint keeps the remaining buyers. The competitive question for the next twelve months is not who takes US share from Tesla but whether Tesla can hold price, and it has — automotive gross margin rose to 18.5% in Q3 2026 from 17.0% a year earlier while regulatory-credit revenue fell 73% to $113 million [S8, S9].

### China is where Tesla is the price taker
BYD sold 456,713 passenger cars in September 2026, 273,143 of them battery-electric, and 3,078,490 in nine months — 2.3 times Tesla's 1,324,681 [S138, S146, S149]. Around Tesla sat Geely at 119,682 retail units, Leapmotor at 78,202 and Xiaomi at 40,015, the last at 269,000 in nine months against a 550,000 target. The price evidence is in the margins: BYD earned 19.46% gross margin overseas against 16.66% at home in 2025, a revealed domestic ceiling Tesla cannot price above without losing volume. Tesla's China retail of 64,837 was 3.8 times smaller than BYD's in September while Chinese battery-electric wholesale still grew 18.3%: the pool was there and Tesla did not take it.

### Europe: growth in units, no evidence of share
EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,931,465 in January-September 2026 at a 22.7% share, with September at 29.9%, so the pool expanded 49% while Tesla's European deliveries recovered from a 2025 slump and Giga Berlin set a production record [S140, S147, S150]. A recovery off a collapsed base inside a pool growing that fast is not share gain, and Tesla discloses no EU unit count; ACEA's manufacturer table would settle it. There the buyer chooses between compliance-driven models from Volkswagen, Renault, Stellantis and Hyundai-Kia and imported Chinese BEVs that carry a tariff but still undercut on price. Tesla's advantage is software and charging density; its handicap is a two-model line-up against a broader compliant field, with Model 3/Y accounting for 478,237 of 486,532 deliveries in Q3 2026.

### Storage is the one position Tesla clearly owns
Tesla's energy segment earned 33.1% gross margin in Q3 2026 on 13.7 GWh, against Fluence's 5.1% in the June 2026 quarter and 13.1% for its 2025 fiscal year, while Tesla's storage revenue per GWh fell to $210 million from $273 million [S8, S9, S61]. That sixfold gap is the clearest unrivaled cost position in the case: in-house cells, one-piece assembly and Autobidder dispatch compress installed cost, while the integrator without cells absorbs the price decline. Two cautions. Q3 2026 energy margin was flattered by $526 million of IEEPA tariff refunds booked against energy cost of revenue, so the underlying gap is narrower than 28 points; and CATL and Sungrow supply the cells and inverters Tesla must buy, which caps how long the integration premium survives as system prices fall.

### In paid autonomy, Tesla is the challenger with the permits to prove it
Waymo ran 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities by March 2026 with 3,000 vehicles and more than 170 million rider-only miles, and raised $16 billion in February 2026 at a $126 billion post-money valuation [S89, S101, S125, S142, S130, S9]. Tesla began Cybercab rides in Austin on 2026-09-03, held 1,051 Texas-authorised Robotaxi vehicles on 2026-10-27 (544 Cybercab, 507 Model Y) against 739 on 2026-10-09, and reports 2.0 million cumulative unsupervised miles; it is absent from California's driverless deployment permits, where Waymo is authorised, and discloses no ride count or fare. The most dangerous competitor is therefore Waymo, not BYD: BYD competes for the same buyer at a price Tesla can match with cost, while Waymo competes for the same regulatory permission and is nearly two orders of magnitude ahead in paid miles.

::: evidence
**Tesla's defensible positions are the charging standard, FSD subscriptions and storage margin — not vehicle share.**

Its 18.5% automotive and 33.1% energy gross margins were earned while regulatory credits fell 73% and Chinese battery-electric wholesale grew 18.3%, which says Tesla can hold price in the US and in storage while losing volume in China [S8, S138, S9]. The counter-evidence runs the other way in autonomy: 2.0 million unsupervised miles against Waymo's 170 million-plus, and no California deployment permit, leave the option carrying the equity premium as the one where Tesla trails most.

Tesla is a high-margin incumbent in a shrinking US pool, sub-scale in the largest battery-electric market, and a trailing challenger in paid autonomy. Its wedge — vertical integration, the charging standard and storage cost — protects margin rather than volume, which argues for underwriting unit growth below the market's and tracking China retail share, storage revenue per GWh and Texas Robotaxi authorisations."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Founding Team & Key Personnel (team, revision 4 by Company Analyst, 8,630 characters)
Tesla's board is majority independent on paper, but the three decisions that mattered in 2024-2026 — a $2.0bn investment in the CEO's own AI company after shareholders rejected the measure, a pay award that can reach 423.7m shares, and the retention of a classified board — all went against the minority's expressed preference, so key-person and capital-allocation risk are real, formally disclosed, and only partly offset by the award's extreme vesting gates [S10].

### Independence is not the same as accountability

Nine directors sit on the board, seven of them independent under Nasdaq rules, with Robyn Denholm as independent chair since November 2018 and all four committees composed solely of independents. The structure that matters is elsewhere: three staggered classes with three-year terms, supermajority voting requirements that a 2025 management proposal failed to remove with 39.4% of shares outstanding in favour, and two family directors — Elon and Kimbal Musk — in the room. Compensation Committee chair Ira Ehrenpreis has also served on SpaceX's board since February 2026, the counterparty to Tesla's $2.0bn investment and $143.3m of 2025 revenue, a relationship the proxy calls immaterial [S10].

### Pay is gated on market value, not on operating return

The 2025 CEO Performance Award is 423,743,904 shares in 12 equal tranches. Each tranche needs a market-capitalisation milestone first — from $2 trillion, 26.6% above the 2026-10-30 value, through nine $500bn and two $1tn steps to $8.5 trillion — and one of 12 operational milestones: four strategic-product goals (10m active FSD subscriptions, 1m bots delivered, 1m Robotaxis in commercial operation among them) or eight Adjusted EBITDA goals. Each earned share carries a $334.09 offset and a five-year hold, and tranches 11 and 12 also require a board-approved CEO succession framework, the only formal succession mechanism disclosed. Against that, General Motors paid Mary Barra $48.2m of realized compensation in 2025, and Musk has taken no salary since 2019 and has no employment agreement or severance; reported 2025 total compensation of $158.36bn was an accounting value, with realized pay at $0 [S10, S107, S109].

### The xAI vote is the test the board failed

At the 2025-11-06 meeting shareholders approved the pay award with 1,892,235,822 votes for, 564,940,908 against and 12,227,846 abstentions, 76.6% of votes cast. A separate non-binding measure authorising funding for xAI drew 1.06bn votes for and 916.3m against but was recorded as rejected because Tesla's bylaws count abstentions as votes against; on 2026-01-16 the company nonetheless agreed to invest $2.0bn in xAI, completing on 2026-03-12 as SpaceX Class A stock after the SpaceX-xAI merger. The Audit Committee reviews related-person transactions above $120,000 under a written policy, but the sequence shows the review is procedural: a holder should assume future flows to Musk-controlled companies are a board decision, not a shareholder one [S59, S104, S105].

### One person carries the strategy; the bench is uneven

The 10-K says Musk "does not devote his full time and attention to Tesla" and lists management roles at SpaceX, xAI, Neuralink and The Boring Company, while the proxy records that xAI became a SpaceX subsidiary in February 2026 and that Musk is SpaceX's CEO, CTO and chairman. The operating bench is strongest in manufacturing and finance: Tom Zhu, SVP APAC and global vehicle manufacturing since June 2025, joined in 2014 and built Gigafactory Shanghai; Vaibhav Taneja has been CFO since August 2023 and inside Tesla's finance function since 2017. Demand execution is the weak spot: Omead Afshar left in June 2025, Troy Jones was dismissed as head of North American sales in July 2025, the North American service head left in August 2025 and Raj Jegannathan departed in February 2026 after 13 years. Headcount was 134,785 at 2025-12-31; the attrition is concentrated in senior commercial roles [S1, S111, S124].

### What the record confirms, and what diligence must settle

Public records confirm the founder-market fit: Musk co-founded Zip2 (sold to Compaq in 1999) and PayPal (sold to eBay in 2002), has run Tesla since October 2008, and still owns 19.8% with 207,498,721 shares pledged. They also confirm the concentration: no chief operating officer, no permanent North American sales leader, a board with no director who has run a vehicle programme at another OEM, and a CEO whose other companies are now suppliers, investees and counterparties. The gaps a diligence team should close are the succession plan behind tranches 11-12, the terms and lenders behind the pledge, the fairness opinion, if any, for the $2.0bn xAI/SpaceX purchase, and references on Zhu and Taneja from SolarCity and Shanghai. For a 12-month holder the concentration is not a separately observable discount in the share price: it argues for a smaller position and for demanding evidence that Zhu and Taneja can run the operating business while Musk is elsewhere [S10, S2].

::: evidence
**The strongest proof of execution is a manufacturing ramp the founder did not personally run; the strongest doubt is a board that proceeded with a related-party investment after shareholders rejected it.**

Tom Zhu built Gigafactory Shanghai, the largest plant in the system at more than 950,000 units, and Berlin set a quarterly production record in Q3 2026; Tesla passed 10.2m cumulative vehicles. The counterweight is procedural: an xAI funding measure lost on a 1.06bn-to-916.3m vote, yet $2.0bn was committed five weeks later, and the Compensation Committee chair sits on SpaceX's board (sources S9, S104, S10).
:::

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 3 by Market Analyst, 8,595 characters)
Tesla's problem is not that its markets are small; it is that the two that made it are contracting while the two that grow are priced per unit, not per promise. Global electric-car sales are expected to reach 23.0 million units in 2026, 28% of all car sales, from more than 20 million in 2025, and the IEA projects half of global sales by 2035 [S9, S137]. Dividing 23.0 million by 28% implies 82 million light vehicles, so the electric pool is the whole case: Tesla delivered 1,324,681 vehicles in the first nine months of 2026 (358,023; 480,126; 486,532) — a run-rate of 1.77 million, or 7.7% of the 2026 electric pool and 2.2% of all cars. Unit growth of 15% in 2026 slows to a 7.7% CAGR to 2035 on the IEA's own 50%-share projection, while Tesla's third quarter fell 2% year on year. That is a share problem inside a decelerating market: what an investor buys is not category growth but the price Tesla can hold for a differentiated slice of it.

**Market size, top-down and bottom-up**

| Layer | 2026 size | How derived | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAM — global light vehicles | 82m units | 23.0m electric ÷ 28% share | S137 |
| SAM — global electric cars (BEV+PHEV) | 23.0m units | IEA forecast, 28% of sales | S137 |
| SOM — Tesla deliveries | 1.32m in 9M 2026; 1.77m run-rate (7.7% of SAM) | Quarterly delivery table | S9 |
| TAM — global storage deployments | 158 GW / 459 GWh | BloombergNEF 2026 forecast | S141 |
| SOM — Tesla storage | 36.0 GWh in 9M 2026 (7.8% of 2026E) | 10-Q plus deployment table | S8, S9 |
| TAM — paid robotaxi revenue | $0.3-0.5bn fare-based, against $3.5-5.5bn third-party | 500k rides/week × 52 × $12-18 assumed fare | S142, S144 |

### The two largest pools shrank by policy, not by demand

Removing the $7,500 federal credit on 2025-09-30 cut the US electric pool by 30.3% year to date: sales fell 36% year on year in Q4 2025 and 27% in Q1 2026 to 216,399 units, and were still 30.3% below the prior year through September 2026 even after a 7.7% sequential rebound to 266,630 in Q3, when electric cars were 6.4% of US new-vehicle sales and Tesla's own US volume fell 14.4%. China's new-energy retail fell 16.7% year on year to 1.084 million in September 2026, the ninth consecutive decline, and 12.8% to 7.758 million in nine months, while penetration hit a record 67.0% only because total passenger-car retail fell 28.0%; battery-electric retail fell 7.4%, plug-in hybrid retail 35.6% and range-extended electric 19.3%, while battery-electric wholesale rose 18.3% and NEV exports 163.5% to 558,000. Tightening China's purchase-tax preference and withdrawing local subsidies raised the cash price of the cheapest cars first and pushed production abroad. Tesla held 52.9% of the smaller US pool and was China's fourth-largest NEV brand by retail at 64,837 units: US equity value is now a bet on a 6-7% electric share of the US market in 2027, and China is a capped, price-deflationary market whose growth reaches Tesla through exports that carry tariffs [S138, S139, S145].

### Europe is the only vehicle market growing fast enough to matter

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,931,465 in January-September 2026, a 22.7% share against 16.1% a year earlier, and September alone ran at 290,117 units and a 29.9% share, up 72.9% year on year on a total market up 5.7% [S140, S147]. On those two shares the electric pool grew 49% in units, the only large market where Tesla can add volume without cutting price. EU demand is regulation-created: the 2025-2027 CO2 step forces fleet averages down, and the Commission's 2025-12-16 proposal to replace the 100% 2035 target with a 90% cut has moved the long-dated backstop into Parliament and Council, where ministers remain split. Europe carries Tesla's 2026 volume growth (Berlin posted record production in Q3 2026), and that growth is capped by a policy being renegotiated while it is relied upon.

### Storage compounds in volume and deflates in price

Global storage installations reached 112 GW in 2025 and are forecast at 158 GW and 459 GWh in 2026, a 41% annual increase, with BloombergNEF seeing 3.1 TW cumulative by 2036 [S141, S8]. Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in the first nine months of 2026, 7.8% of the forecast 2026 pool, but its storage revenue per GWh fell to $210 million from $273 million a year earlier — a 23% decline — because Q3 energy revenue fell 16% while deployments rose 9.6%. The market is increasingly structural: Tesla reported its highest-ever order rate and backlog and ties demand to data-centre load growth, not subsidies. But model the segment on revenue per GWh falling faster than volume rises. At 2026 unit prices the 459 GWh pool is worth $69-107 billion depending on whether Chinese or Tesla-level pricing is assumed, and that gap is the segment's whole margin question.

### Paid robotaxi is a Waymo-sized business, not a market yet

The only scaled paid autonomous service is Waymo's: 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities as of 2026-03-27, which is 26 million a year and, at an assumed $12-18 average fare, a $0.3-0.5 billion business [S142, S144, S125]. Third-party research puts the 2026 robotaxi market at $3.5-5.5 billion and 2030 estimates span $27-204 billion, a 7.3x spread that marks sizes built from ride-hailing spend rather than observed fares. Tesla is scaling from a smaller base: Texas regulators listed 1,051 authorised Robotaxi vehicles on 2026-10-27 (544 Cybercab, 507 Model Y), up from 739 on 2026-10-09, against roughly 3,000 Waymo vehicles, and Tesla reports about 2 million cumulative unsupervised miles against Waymo's 170 million-plus. Tesla discloses no ride count, fare or robotaxi revenue. The serviceable market by 2028 is therefore set by permits and per-mile safety evidence, not TAM studies: a $50 billion 2028 robotaxi line would require Tesla to overtake the incumbent and multiply the 2026 paid market more than twenty-fold.

**Where the growth is, and where Tesla stands**

| Region | Market size (2026) | Growth | Tesla's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States | 266,630 EVs in Q3 2026; 6.4% of new-vehicle sales | −30.3% year to date; +7.7% QoQ in Q3 | Entered, 52.9% of the EV pool; US volume −14.4% | Credit repealed 2025-09-30; tariff and content rules under OBBBA | Ford, GM, Hyundai-Kia, Rivian, Toyota hybrids | S139, S145 |
| China | 7.758m NEV retail in 9M 2026; 67.0% penetration in September | −12.8% in 9M; BEV retail −7.4%, PHEV −35.6% | Entered; fourth-largest NEV brand at 64,837 in September | Purchase-tax preference tightened; local-brand cost advantage; export tariffs | BYD, Geely, Leapmotor, Xiaomi, Changan | S138 |
| European Union | 1,931,465 BEVs in 9M 2026; 22.7% share (29.9% in September) | 49% BEV unit growth in 9M; total market +5.7% | Entered; recovering off a weak 2025, Berlin at record output | CO2 2035 target under renegotiation; country-level incentives | Volkswagen, Renault, Stellantis, Hyundai-Kia, BYD | S140, S147 |
| Rest of world | Not disclosed by Tesla; Chinese NEV exports 3.887m in 9M 2026 (+138.8%) | Chinese NEV exports +163.5% in September | Entered; record quarterly deliveries in Canada, Australia, Japan and Taiwan | Tariffs on Chinese-built cars; charging build-out | BYD, Geely, Leapmotor, Toyota | S138, S9 |
| Storage (global) | 158 GW / 459 GWh in 2026E | +41% in GW after +48% in 2025 | Entered; 36.0 GWh in 9M 2026, 7.8% of 2026E | Cell supply, tariffs on Chinese cells, interconnection queues | CATL, Sungrow, Fluence, BYD | S141, S8 |

::: evidence
**The demand Tesla is priced for grows everywhere except where it sells most.**

The IEA's 23 million-unit 2026 forecast is carried by Europe (20% growth) and by Chinese exports (163.5% in September), while the United States and China — the sources of most of Tesla's 2024-2025 revenue — are down 30.3% and 12.8% year to date [S137, S138, S145]. The counterweight is Tesla's own disclosure that battery availability, not orders, limited Q3 2026 volume, alongside its largest backlog in four years: the next two quarters may be supply-constrained rather than demand-constrained.
:::

The implication is allocation, not enthusiasm: weight the case toward storage, Tesla's highest-margin segment and its fastest-growing pool, and toward Europe; treat US vehicle revenue as share defence at a lower market level; and value paid autonomy at zero until rides and fares are disclosed. What would move this assessment: Tesla's 2026 regional unit split, the contracted price per MWh in its storage backlog, and its Austin Robotaxi ride count and average fare."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 7 by Product Analyst, 8,794 characters)
Tesla's technology position in 2026 is two facts usually merged in the narrative: the largest supervised-driving data pool and one of the cheapest large-scale EV manufacturing bases in the industry, and almost no verified driverless revenue. Active FSD subscriptions reached 1.74 million at 30 September 2026 against 10.2 million vehicles delivered to date — 17.1% of the lifetime fleet, up from 12.4% at 31 December 2025 — while cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles were "nearly two million", 0.9% of the 220.6 million rider-only miles Waymo had logged through March 2026 [S9, S151]. That gap, not the subscription count, is what twelve months must close.

### What Tesla actually sells

| Product | Stage | Revenue or share | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FSD (Supervised) | Commercial, 9 EU countries | 1.74m subscriptions; revenue not disclosed | Unsupervised release | S9, S1 |
| Robotaxi / Cybercab | Commercial in Texas metros | Not disclosed inside $4.605bn services | Paid-trip disclosure | S9 |
| Model 3 / Model Y | Mature | 478,237 units, Q3 2026; 19.6% group gross margin | Next-gen platform | S9 |
| Cybertruck, Semi, Roadster | Ramp / design | 8,295 other-model units, Q3 2026 | Semi ramp; Roadster launch | S9 |
| Megapack, Powerwall | Scaling | $2.881bn in Q3 2026; 13.7 GWh | 50 GWh Texas ramp | S9, S60 |
| Optimus | Internal production | Zero external revenue | External pilot sale | S9, S99 |

### Mechanism: end-to-end vision and a one-sided flywheel

Tesla removed radar and now maps camera pixels directly to driving commands with an end-to-end neural network, trained on clips harvested from the fleet and run on in-house inference silicon. Training runs on two in-house clusters at Gigafactory Texas, with a company-built fab for inference and training silicon under construction. The flywheel is real but overwhelmingly *supervised*: the Q3 2026 update charts cumulative FSD miles on a 0-16 billion axis, against 2.0 million unsupervised miles [S60]. Supervised miles teach perception; they do not certify that the network can be left alone, which is why the federal safety file matters more than the mileage chart.

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active FSD subscriptions | 1.74m (2026-09-30) | Company count | S9 |
| FSD penetration of fleet | 17.1% | 1.74m / 10.2m deliveries | S9 |
| Cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles | 2.0m, 8x QoQ | Company count | S9 |
| Installed AI training compute | 225+ MW | Company nameplate | S9 |
| 4680 capacity, Texas | 40+ GWh/yr, dry electrode both sides | Company nameplate | S60 |
| Storage deployed | 13.7 GWh Q3; 36.0 GWh 9M | Company deliveries | S9 |
| Optimus units in service | 1,000-1,200 | Independent estimate | S99 |

### The safety file is the binding constraint

NHTSA's Office of Defects Investigation opened Engineering Analysis EA26002 on 18 March 2026 into whether FSD detects degraded visibility — glare, fog, dust — and warns the driver in time, covering an estimated 3,203,754 vehicles from model years 2016-2026, after nine confirmed incidents including one pedestrian fatality; two further FSD probes remain open, one on traffic-law violations across 2,882,566 vehicles with 80 incidents [S87]. Tesla's own analysis reportedly found its degradation-detection update "may have affected" only 3 of 9 incidents, which points to an architectural limit of camera-only sensing rather than a tuning defect. An engineering analysis is the last step before a recall; a recall would narrow the operating domain or force hardware across millions of cars, at a company that self-insures product liability.

::: evidence
**The camera-only bet is being tested by the regulator, not the market.** EA26002 covers 3.2 million FSD-equipped vehicles and Tesla's fix reportedly addresses a third of the reviewed incidents [S87, S88, S100]. The filings confirm the investigation but give no remedy or timetable, which is the largest un-priced technical risk in the autonomy option.
:::

### Comparison: three different autonomy businesses

| Dimension | Tesla | Waymo | Chinese L3 OEMs | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sensing | Camera-only, in-house chip | Lidar + radar + camera | Camera + lidar, Nvidia compute | S9, S101 |
| Verified driverless scale | 2.0m cumulative miles | 220.6m rider-only miles through 2026-03; 500,000 paid rides/week | L3 conditional approvals since 2025-12 | S151, S101, S103 |
| Regulatory position | Paid driverless in Texas under SB 2807 and TxDMV authorisation (required from 2026-05-28); California paid rides on a limousine permit, no autonomous-service authorisation | California deployment authorised | MIIT eight-department L3 pilot | S89, S90, S91 |
| Cost model | Owned fleet, self-insured | Owned fleet, partner-owned vehicles | Consumer cars, driver liable | S89, S103 |

### Moat: accumulation, not exclusion

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Supervised fleet data | 8 | 10.2m cars; FSD miles charted to 16bn | 4-6 years | S9 |
| Driverless operating experience | 5 | 2.0m unsupervised miles only | 2-3 years | S9 |
| Dry-electrode cell process | 7 | Battery Day 2020 to Austin output in 2026 | 3-4 years | S60 |
| Manufacturing and integration | 8 | 134,785 employees; cells, cathode, refining in-house | 5+ years | S1 |
| Training compute | 6 | 225+ MW against more than $20bn of 2026 capex | 2-3 years | S9, S8 |
| State permits | 6 | Bilateral and political; not purchasable | 1-3 years | S89, S91 |
| Composite | 6.5/10 | Minimum 3-year lead on a geofenced service | — | S9, S60 |

The replication test is unflattering to a patent story: 50 funded engineers with every published Tesla patent could build a geofenced driverless service in two to three years — Waymo needed eleven years from its 2009 start — but could not reproduce the fleet data or the factories. Tesla's 10-K concedes the point by design, pledging irrevocably not to sue any party acting in good faith for infringing its electric-vehicle patents. California is the harder gate: on 23 October 2026 the DMV lists Tesla Robotaxi LLC only as a testing-permit holder requiring a safety driver, and the state's regulator confirmed in March 2026 that Tesla is not operating an autonomous vehicle service, its paid rides running on a limousine permit [S1, S89, S90].

| IP instrument | Covers | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Patent non-assertion pledge | EV and related-equipment patents | Irrevocable for good-faith users | Removes patents as a barrier | S1 |
| Trade secrets, NDAs | Cell process, manufacturing know-how | In force | Protects dry-electrode yield | S1 |
| In-house inference silicon; Samsung US foundry deal | AI4/AI5 design and fabrication | Austin fab commissioning 2027 | Cost and performance control | S1, S9 |
| Patent portfolio (AI, batteries, robotics) | Not enumerated in filings | Counts not publicly disclosed | Cannot be assessed publicly | — |

Tesla publishes no patent count or list, so a patent-number-level table cannot be built from its disclosures; a USPTO assignee search is the source that would settle portfolio size and freedom-to-operate risk, and it has been requested.

### Optimus is a research programme with a production line

Tesla began Optimus production in Fremont in Q3 2026 and calls the process "suitable for a commercial product", but discloses no units, cycle times, error rates or customers; independent estimates put 1,000-1,200 units across Fremont and Giga Texas with zero external sales, and the CEO described early units as "primarily for learning and data collection" [S99]. Figure AI has logged 1,250+ hours at BMW and Agility Robotics 65,000+ hours across nine sites, both with paying customers — smaller companies with weaker balance sheets but better evidence. Optimus should carry no revenue in a 12-month model.

Tesla's manufacturing and supervised-data advantages are real and hard to buy, but the priced asset is unsupervised autonomy, which today carries a fatality-linked engineering analysis, a single authorising state, a pilot fleet and no disclosed revenue. Confidence is high on filings and regulator records, medium on driverless scale, low on Optimus and robotaxi unit economics, where disclosure is absent rather than adverse. The disclosures that would move this: Robotaxi revenue, paid trips and cost per trip reported quarterly; a California driverless deployment permit; and dry-electrode cell cost per kWh against the purchased-cell benchmark. If the first and third come good while the engineering analysis closes without a hardware remedy, the option is worth materially more than a pilot; if it converts to a recall that restricts the operating domain, the revenue bridge loses its main support."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Risk Assessment (risk, revision 3 by Red Team Analyst, 8,896 characters)
The Sell at $399.81 survives the red-team pass, but not in the form the scenario table states it. It is defensible as a de-rating call on a 103x multiple, not as a liquidation call (the reported businesses are a $40-50 floor, not a target) and not as a claim that no buyer exists. SpaceX traded at $147.79 for a $2.01tn market value against Tesla's $373.71 and $1.48tn on 2026-10-20, and both boards have formed independent committees to study a combination [S154]. General Motors, Ford and Rivian cannot buy a $1.58tn company, but SpaceX can: RBC and JPMorgan expect a 20-35% premium for Tesla holders, holders would own 42% of a combined company at parity and 47-50% with that premium, and approval needs 50% of all shares outstanding. At $399.81 a 20-35% premium is $480-540, above the $506.05 first award gate. The process can fail — no exchange ratio, a conflicted CEO, abstentions counted against — but a short that treats the exit as absent is short a dated, public, premium-bearing catalyst, and the expression should be a capped short with a stop at $506.05.

### The SOTP is a floor, not a twelve-month target

The SOTP overstates the downside at the edges. Energy at 2.5-3.0x $12.3bn of sales ignores a 41% growth pool and a 30% gross margin; at 3.5-4.0x it is worth $12bn more. Services at 1.5x $16.3bn ignores 32% growth and a record $734m of gross profit; at 2.0x it is worth $8bn more. FSD's $1bn run rate is carried at zero and is worth $20bn at 20x [S152, S8]. Those adjustments take the SOTP to $40-50 a share, not $35-40. The larger problem is the framework: the SOTP implies -90%, the bear case -60% and the base case -27%, because the base applies 70x to $16.0bn of EBITDA and so embeds $1.0tn of autonomy value. Tesla has never traded on SOTP: $161-292 is the tradable range, $35-40 the liquidation floor, and taking the floor as the twelve-month target hands the reader a downside the recommendation does not forecast.

### Probabilities: right on the business, low on the event

The 20% probability assigned to the bull case is not too low on fundamentals. The 1.74m FSD count is company-reported and includes upfront buyers as well as monthly subscribers, only half the base is on subscriptions by the CFO's account, and management's run rate is $1bn, under 1% of revenue; the 2.0m unsupervised miles are company-reported and equal 0.9% of Waymo's 220.6m rider-only miles at March 2026, not the 1.2% a 170m comparison implies; Texas has 1,051 authorised vehicles against 3,700 Waymo vehicles; and the call's "almost sold out" for 2027 is company-only, in a quarter when energy revenue fell 16% and revenue per GWh fell 23% [S152, S151, S9]. Four conjunctive conditions — a California permit, a robotaxi revenue line, energy above 30% and capex at $20bn — are not a 20% event. A merger branch with a 10-12% probability at +27% lifts the upside to 30-32%, and with base 40% and bear 28% the expected return is -20%, not -28%. The base is not too bearish: 70x EBITDA is four times BYD's 17.3x and still embeds the option.

### Earnings quality: not double counted, and worse than stated

The $475m credit reversal and the $3,868m payables build are not the same dollar counted twice: the first is Q3 revenue and gross profit, the second is nine-month working capital, so pricing both is compounding, not double counting. Adding back the reversal gives $1,193m of operating income and a 4.2% margin rather than 2.6%, but only if regulatory credits stop falling; credit revenue fell from $2.76bn in 2024 to $1.99bn in 2025. More important, interest income of $1,301m was 69% of the $1,883m nine-month free cash flow, so free cash flow before interest is $582m and before the payables benefit it is negative [S8, S11]. Adjusted EBITDA excludes interest, so 103x is clean; the 439x P/E and 0.2% free-cash-flow yield are not.

### Stress tests: a de-rating, not a default

A market 50% smaller — 11.5m electric units instead of 23.0m — leaves Tesla 885,000 units at 7.7% share, $37.5bn of auto revenue and $6.8bn of gross profit at 18.1%; group gross profit of $14bn against $16.3bn of operating cost is a $2.3bn operating loss, and auto at 0.7x sales falls from $52.5bn to $26bn, taking the SOTP to $125bn, or $32 a share, 2% below the current price. The market-size test moves the floor by 8% and the price by 2%, because the price is not earnings. A doubled CAC does bite: SG&A of $7,485m over 1.77m units is $4,229 a vehicle, and doubling the demand-generation half adds $2,100 a vehicle, $3.7bn, equal to the $3.47bn trailing operating income. Revenue 30% lower leaves $72.5bn at 19.3% gross margin, $14.0bn of gross profit against $16.3bn of cost, an operating loss; at 40x on $8bn of EBITDA the equity is $356bn, $90 a share (-77%). A six-month financing delay is not a solvency event: $36.18bn of net cash and $30.0bn of undrawn facilities mean the cost falls on the option, halving the chance of a 2026-27 proof and taking 2.7 points off expected return [S8, S9]. Free cash flow 30% lower changes nothing at a 0.2% yield. The bear case is a 40x multiple, not a balance-sheet failure.

### Policy is priced as a timetable

The regulatory risks are dated and public. US credit repeal has already taken 30.3% out of the pool; an EU 2035 target cut to 90% would slow the only growing vehicle market; NHTSA's EA26002 covers 3,203,754 vehicles with nine incidents and one fatality and is the last step before a recall, and a remedy at $100-1,000 a car is $320m-3.2bn plus an operating-domain restriction that would delay paid service. California's list on 2026-10-23 still shows Tesla Robotaxi LLC only under testing with a safety driver, while Waymo, Nuro and Mercedes hold deployment authorisations; a permit application is reported, but an application is not an authorisation. The undisclosed items — robotaxi revenue, trips and cost per trip, FSD churn, the energy backlog's contracted price, the SpaceX exchange ratio and the 50%-vote count — are where the unknown unknowns sit; the related-party flow is disclosed but not priced, with SpaceX buying $626m of Megapacks in nine months, 7.4% of energy revenue, and $588m of the receivable billed for units not yet delivered [S87, S89, S10].

### Ranked risks

Positive rows are losses for a short position.

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SpaceX combination at a 20-35% premium | Medium-low, 15-20% | +20-35% to the stock | Critical | 6-18 months | Exchange ratio; committee statement | Cap at 1-2% of NAV; stop at $506.05 | S154 |
| Multiple de-rates from 103x to 40x | High | -60%, $161 a share | Critical | 0-12 months | 10-year Treasury above 5%; Q4 miss | Sell or underweight; no long exposure | S11, S8 |
| California permit plus robotaxi revenue line | Medium-low | +25-30%, bull case $506 | High | 6-12 months | DMV deployment list; Q4 segment line | Stop at $506.05; reassess on the Q4 10-Q | S89, S152 |
| NHTSA EA26002 recall or ODD restriction | Medium | $0.3-3.2bn; 10-20% of autonomy option | High | 3-12 months | EA closure; recall notice | Price the remedy; demand take-rate data | S87 |
| Robotaxi teleoperation and insurance costs | High | 10-20% of autonomy value | Medium | 12-24 months | SGO crash reports; intervention disclosure | Demand trip and cost-per-trip data | S153 |
| Payables reverse and interest income falls | Medium-high | 10-15% of equity at 40x | Medium | Q4 2026 | Q4 free cash flow ex-working capital | Read the Q4 cash-flow statement | S8 |
| Capex guidance credibility and debt funding | Medium | 5-10% | Medium | 2027 | Q4 capex above $7bn; facility draw | Ask for 2027 capex and facility terms | S8 |
| US and China demand and policy | Medium | 10-15% of revenue | Medium | 6-18 months | US EV registrations; China NEV retail | Weight Europe and storage | S139, S145 |
| Related-party concentration and governance | High, structural | 3-5% of energy value | Medium | Ongoing | 10-Q related-party note; receivable | Independent review of related-party terms | S8, S10 |
:::

::: info danger
**The thesis breaks on an exit, not on a car.** A listed SpaceX at $2.01tn, two special committees and a 20-35% premium expected by RBC and JPMorgan would hand Tesla holders $480-540 a share, above the bull case. The 50%-of-outstanding vote and the CEO's conflict make it uncertain, but a short that ignores the branch is exposed to a 20-35% gap on a headline; 2.19% of float and 2.2 days to cover mean the move comes from news, not positioning. Source S154, S155.
:::

The open diligence items are the SpaceX exchange ratio, the vote threshold and the contracted price in the energy backlog; the cheapest falsifier is the Q4 2026 10-Q in the last week of January 2027, where a robotaxi revenue line, or a California deployment entry before it, would re-open the Sell. Source S154, S89."}],"isError":false}
