{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 3 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,214 characters)
Tesla's reported segments describe a vehicle business whose gross margin does not cover group research and development and selling costs, a storage business and a services business that together earn the group's operating profit, and a third quarter of 2026 in which both of those profit pools were helped by tariff refunds and warranty true-ups — the return is earned on storage and on the cash pile, not on the car.

### Three segments, three ways of getting paid

The automotive segment took 73.3% of third-quarter 2026 revenue ($20,560M of $28,046M), services and other 16.4% ($4,605M) and energy generation and storage 10.3% ($2,881M). The buyer differs in each: a retail or fleet customer pays cash or finances a car when control transfers; an energy customer — a utility, developer or data-centre operator — pays on project milestones across quarters; a service customer pays per transaction for collision repair, maintenance or a Supercharging session; another automaker pays for regulatory credits at transfer of title. The mix has moved: energy was 6.2% of FY2023 revenue ($6,035M) and 13.5% in FY2025 ($12,771M), while automotive revenue fell from $82,419M to $69,526M. The only recurring software charge is FSD (Supervised) at $99 a month, with 1.74 million active subscriptions on 2026-09-30 against 1.04 million a year earlier [S8, S1, S121].

### The vehicle does not pay for the research budget

| Per unit (one vehicle delivered), Q3 2026 | USD per unit | Note | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive revenue | 42,259 | $20,560M ÷ 486,532 deliveries | S9 |
| Cost of automotive revenue | (34,436) | materials, labour, overhead, warranty, tariffs | S8 |
| Automotive gross profit | 7,823 | 18.5% margin | S8 |
| Regulatory credits inside that profit | 232 | $113M ÷ 486,532; no matching cost | S8 |
| Automotive gross profit excluding credits | 7,590 | 18.1% of $20,447M ex-credit revenue | S8 |
| Group R&D and SG&A per unit | (9,817) | $4,776M ÷ 486,532, all charged to the car | S9 |
| Automotive-only operating contribution | (1,994) | a loss before energy and services | derived |
| Energy and services gross profit per unit | 3,470 | $1,688M ÷ 486,532 | S8 |
| Group operating profit per unit | 1,476 | $718M ÷ 486,532 | S9 |
| Interest income per unit | 915 | $445M ÷ 486,532 | S8 |
| Pre-tax profit per unit | 1,965 | $956M ÷ 486,532 | S8 |

A delivered car carried $42,259 of automotive revenue and $34,436 of cost, leaving $7,823 of gross profit, or $7,590 once regulatory credits are removed; spreading $4,776M of group research and development and selling cost over 486,532 deliveries costs $9,817 a vehicle, so the automotive line alone runs at roughly -$1,994 a vehicle. Energy and services add $3,470 a vehicle and turn that into $1,476 of operating profit and, with $445M of interest income, $1,965 of pre-tax profit. Cost per vehicle was $33,666 in Q4 2025, $35,786 in Q1 2026 and $34,436 in Q3 2026, so unit cost is not falling; the rise in ex-credit automotive margin from 15.4% to 18.1% year on year arrived with a richer Asia-Pacific delivery mix in Q3 2026, not from the factory [S9, S8].

::: evidence
**The reported credit collapse is a clawback of past revenue, not yet a collapse in current demand — but the contracted backlog says it is coming.**

Reported credit revenue fell from $542M in Q4 2025 to $380M in Q1 2026, $146M in Q2 2026 and $113M in Q3 2026, after $1,993M in FY2025 and $2,763M in FY2024. The Q3 2026 figure is net of a $475M reversal of previously recognised credit revenue for contractual return of already-delivered credits, so gross credit sales in the quarter were about $588M — higher than Q4 2025 — and the reported line overstates the speed of the decline. The forward indicator is worse: contracted credit obligations with original terms over one year fell to $384M at 2026-09-30 from $841M at 2025-12-31, only $201M of it due within twelve months, against $1,993M earned in FY2025. Toyota and Stellantis left Tesla's European CO2 pool for 2026, with Subaru also reported out, and UBS put the pool at more than €1 billion of annual revenue. Tesla names no credit buyer in its filings [S8, S83, S1, S123].
:::

### Storage earns the best margin and the least predictable one

Energy generation and storage produced $954M of gross profit on $2,881M of revenue in Q3 2026 (33.1%), after 20.4% in Q2 2026 and 39.5% in Q1 2026. Revenue per GWh deployed fell from $274 per kWh in Q1 2026 to $210 per kWh in Q3 2026, and gross profit per kWh went $108, $47, $70 across the three quarters, so the segment's margin moves with Megapack pricing, cell cost, tariff recoveries and warranty true-ups. Demand evidence is strong: $10.73 billion of unsatisfied energy obligations at 2026-09-30 with $4.80 billion due within twelve months, and a Megapack book management described as nearly sold out through 2027. The counter-evidence is that part of that growth is a related party: SpaceX bought $626M of Megapacks in the first nine months of 2026 ($221M in Q3), left $729M of receivables at 2026-09-30 — $588M of it for units not yet delivered — and $648M of deferred revenue, so energy's fastest-growing account is the chief executive's other company [S8, S1, S117].

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vehicles | per vehicle delivered, blended across models | $42,259 revenue, $34,436 cost | Q3 2026 | S9 |
| Regulatory credits | per credit sold to another automaker | not disclosed; $113M net of a $475M reversal | Q3 2026 | S8 |
| Energy storage | per kWh deployed, Megapack and Powerwall blended | $210/kWh revenue, $70/kWh gross profit | Q3 2026 | S9 |
| FSD (Supervised) | per vehicle per month | $99 | 2026-10 | S121 |
| Megapack to SpaceX | per project, milestone billed | not disclosed; $626M of revenue | 9M 2026 | S8 |
| Vehicle leasing | per vehicle per month | not disclosed; $353M leasing revenue | Q3 2026 | S8 |
| Supercharging | per session or per kWh | not disclosed | Q3 2026 | S8 |
| Robotaxi and Cybercab | per ride | not disclosed | Q3 2026 | S9 |

### Services is the quiet second engine

Services and other grew revenue 33% year on year to $4,605M and lifted gross profit to $734M, a 15.9% margin against 10.5% in Q3 2025 and an all-time high. Behind it are used-vehicle sales, collision and non-warranty maintenance, paid Supercharging across 8,904 stations and 84,465 connectors, and an insurance book — parts-and-labour businesses with largely variable costs riding on a charging network with largely fixed ones, so utilisation lifts the marginal margin. Rivian's software and services segment earned 42% on $605M of revenue in the same quarter, so Tesla's margin is well below the best comparable but on 7.6 times the revenue, and services now supplies 13.4% of group gross profit from 16.4% of revenue. The risk sits in the used-car and collision lines, which depend on the resale values that also underpin Tesla's lease residuals and insurance claims [S9, S120].

### What breaks even, and what cannot be measured

At Q3 2026 unit economics and constant group cost, the automotive line covers its share of the group only at about 611,000 deliveries a quarter, 26% above the 486,532 delivered. Tesla discloses no customer-acquisition cost — there is no marketing line in the statements — so SG&A at 7.2% of revenue is the nearest proxy and a CAC payback or LTV:CAC ratio cannot be computed from the filings; that limit matters, because the claim that Tesla acquires buyers more cheaply than Ford or GM is untested. Judged on operating margin, Tesla's 2.6% sits below GM's 8.2% EBIT-adjusted and Ford's 5.5%, while its 18.1% ex-credit gross margin is level with BYD's 18%: the difference is the operating cost line, not the car. For an investor underwriting the shares at the current quote, the implication is that the next twelve months pay for a storage margin that has printed anywhere between 20% and 40% and a software attach that carries no disclosed revenue — the diligence question is what FSD subscription revenue and Megapack-only margin actually are, because those two numbers decide whether the group earns more than its cost of capital [S115, S116, S119]."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financial Analysis (financials, revision 4 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,910 characters)
Tesla converted $1,531M of free cash flow in Q3 2026, but the statements no longer show it earning its cost of capital: a 5.5% trailing return on invested capital sits 57 basis points above the ten-year Treasury, $41,778M of capex since 2023 has coincided with a 61% fall in operating income, and the profit that remains leans on interest from the cash pile and a payables build rather than on operations [S8, S12, S11].

### Revenue recovered, operating profit did not

| Line item ($M unless stated) | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | 9M 2026 | TTM to 2026-09-30 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 96,773 | 97,690 | 94,827 | 78,669 | 103,570 | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Gross profit | 17,660 | 17,450 | 17,094 | 14,965 | 19,974 | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Gross margin | 18.2% | 17.9% | 18.0% | 19.0% | 19.3% | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Research and development | 3,969 | 4,540 | 6,411 | 7,078 | 8,861 | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Selling, general and administrative | 4,800 | 5,150 | 5,834 | 5,830 | 7,485 | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Operating income | 8,891 | 7,076 | 4,355 | 2,057 | 3,466 | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Operating margin | 9.2% | 7.2% | 4.6% | 2.6% | 3.3% | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Net income | 14,997 | 7,091 | 3,794 | 2,378 | 3,218 | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Diluted EPS ($) | 4.30 | 2.04 | 1.08 | 0.67 | 0.91 | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Operating cash flow | 13,256 | 14,923 | 14,747 | 14,897 | 18,710 | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Capital expenditure | 8,898 | 11,339 | 8,527 | 13,014 | 15,407 | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Free cash flow | 4,358 | 3,584 | 6,220 | 1,883 | 3,296 | S12, S13, S1, S8 |

Revenue fell for two years before the 2026 rebound while operating income fell throughout, from $8,891M in FY2023 to $3,466M trailing, because research and development rose from $3,969M to $8,861M and selling and administrative cost from $4,800M to $7,485M against gross profit that stayed between $17.1B and $20.0B. The Q3 2026 operating margin of 2.6% came on revenue flat year on year with deliveries down 2% to 486,532 from 497,099, so price, mix and a weaker dollar carried the top line. Reported against adjusted: Q3 2026 GAAP net income of $787M against non-GAAP of $1,697M, and diluted EPS of $0.22 against $0.48. The quarter also absorbed a $475M reversal of previously recognised regulatory credit revenue for returned credits, so the 2.6% operating margin understates the underlying figure by 1.7 points [S12, S13, S1, S8].

### Free cash flow is a payables loan and a capex pause

Nine-month operating cash flow of $14,897M exceeded the $13,014M of capital expenditure to leave $1,883M of free cash flow, against $6,220M for FY2025. Two facts weaken the conversion. Management attributes $3.51 billion of the $3.96 billion year-on-year operating-cash-flow increase to working capital, and in Q3 2026 alone free cash flow of $1,531M rested on a $2,590M working-capital inflow, of which accounts payable supplied $1,920M and accrued liabilities $1,950M; stripping it out, quarterly free cash flow was -$1,059M, and $3,670M of capex sat in liabilities at 2026-09-30. Across the nine months, payables rose $3,868M from 2025-12-31 to $17,239M and the cash conversion cycle fell to 2.6 days from 13.0, so without the payables build nine-month free cash flow would have been -$1,985M. Capital expenditure nearly doubled from $6,134M a year earlier, and the 2026 plan was restated between filings — "in excess of $25 billion" in the July 2026 report, "in excess of $20 billion" in the October 2026 one, and $20 billion on the Q3 2026 call — leaving full-year 2026 free cash flow between -$1,290M and +$1,160M depending on whether Q4 operating cash flow matches Q4 2025's $3,813M or Q3 2026's $6,263M [S8, S9, S83, S102].

### The balance sheet carries the plan; the off-balance items carry the risk

| Metric | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | TTM to 2026-09-30 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Return on invested capital | 28.3% | 13.7% | 7.0% | 5.5% | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Return on equity | 27.9% | 10.5% | 4.9% | 3.8% | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Return on assets | 15.9% | 6.2% | 2.9% | 2.2% | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Days sales outstanding | 13.2 | 16.5 | 17.6 | 16.3 | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Days inventory outstanding | 62.9 | 54.7 | 58.2 | 61.5 | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Days payables outstanding | 66.6 | 56.7 | 62.8 | 75.3 | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Cash conversion cycle (days) | 9.5 | 14.4 | 13.0 | 2.6 | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Interest coverage | 56.99x | 20.22x | 12.88x | 9.96x | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Stock-based compensation / revenue | 1.9% | 2.0% | 3.0% | 4.2% | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Capital expenditure / revenue | 9.2% | 11.6% | 9.0% | 16.5% (9M) | S12, S13, S1, S8 |
| Net cash | 24,437 | 28,685 | 35,906 | 36,180 | S12, S13, S1, S8 |

Cash of $17,853M and short-term investments of $27,594M against $9,267M of debt gave $36,180M of net cash at 2026-09-30, and three credit agreements signed in September 2026 lifted unused committed facilities to $30.00B from $6.43B at 2025-12-31, so the $20B capex year is funded several times over without equity. The obligations outside the debt line matter more: $7,955M of minimum lease payments at 2025-12-31, of which $1,320M falls due within twelve months; an accrued warranty reserve of $7,414M that grew 20.9% in nine months against 10% delivery growth; and $7,055M of deferred revenue. Goodwill and intangibles of $381M are 0.2% of assets, so there is no acquisition accounting to discount, and interest coverage of 9.96x is ample but has fallen from 56.99x in FY2023 as operating income shrank [S8, S1].

### The capital is not earning its keep

Returns have fallen faster than margins. Return on invested capital went from 28.3% in FY2023 to 13.7%, 7.0% and 5.5% trailing, and return on equity from 27.9% to 3.8%; the 5.5% compares with a 4.93% ten-year Treasury yield on 2026-10-30, leaving 57 basis points for equity risk in a business whose operating margin has halved twice in three years. The capex record explains it: $41,778M spent in FY2023, FY2024, FY2025 and the first nine months of 2026 against a $5,425M fall in operating income over the same span — from FY2022's peak of $13,656M the fall is $10,190M — an incremental return that is negative at group level. Nothing has been returned to shareholders: no dividend and no repurchase from FY2021 to Q3 2026, while $2,000M of cash went into the xAI investment agreed in January 2026, converted into SpaceX Class A stock on 2026-03-12, and media reported the investment went ahead against a shareholder vote. GM authorised a $20B repurchase in the same quarter [S1, S8, S10, S115, S104].

### What flatters the number, and what would change it

Four items soften the reported result. Interest income of $1,301M was 42.9% of nine-month pre-tax income, and $445M was 46.5% of the Q3 2026 figure, against 17.5% in FY2024. Stock-based compensation of $3,346M in nine months is 4.3% of revenue and the main reason non-GAAP profit more than doubles GAAP profit; EPS is struck on 3,240M basic and 3,541M diluted weighted-average shares against 3,952,648,559 shares outstanding at 2026-09-30, and the 713M difference is the 423.7M unvested shares of the 2025 CEO award plus 286.4M restricted shares from the 2018 award, both excluded until earned — so dividing earnings by the diluted count understates the share base by 12%, and the award, if earned, lifts the count by a further 12%. An effective tax rate of 20% against 27% was helped by a smaller valuation-allowance release in Q2 2026, and cost of automotive sales benefited from what management calls warranty adjustments while the warranty reserve rose 20.9%. Sensitivity: a percentage point of ex-credit automotive margin is worth $800M a year on $80,000M of automotive revenue, 6.4 times a point of energy margin at $12,500M, and each $1B of capex is $1B of free cash flow. Base case FY2027 free cash flow of $2,000M assumes operating cash flow of $22,000M less capex of $20,000M with energy at 30% and automotive at 18%; energy back at Q2 2026's 20.4% and automotive at 15.4% removes $3,360M and turns it into -$1,360M; energy held at 33.1% adds $390M. The variable that moves the outcome most is capex, a management decision worth $5B in a single restatement between July and October 2026 — more than six points of automotive margin. The diligence question is what the 2027 capex number is and whether the payables build reflects renegotiated terms or deferred payments [S8, S83, S1, S117, S102].

::: info danger
The most serious red flag is the composition of free cash flow rather than its level: nine-month free cash flow is smaller than the rise in payables that produced it, capital expenditure was re-scoped in the same quarter that new credit lines were arranged, and the cash balance generating almost half of pre-tax profit is the only reason reported earnings look positive at the operating level. Reported free cash flow is a ceiling, not a run-rate.
:::"}],"isError":false}

As a result of rapidly evolving trade and fiscal policy and geopolitical conflicts, uncertainty in the automotive and energy markets continues, posing risks to our global supply chain and cost structure which could have a meaningfully adverse impact on demand for our products and our profitability. The current tariff regime will have a relatively larger impact on our energy generation and storage business compared to our automotive business. While we prepare for near-term challenges to our business under current policies, we are focused on long-term growth opportunities as we continue to further vertically integrate and localize our supply chain and make prudent investments in infrastructure.
These plans are subject to uncertainties inherent in establishing and ramping manufacturing operations, which may be exacerbated by new product and manufacturing technologies we introduce, the number of concurrent international projects, any industry-wide component constraints, labor shortages and any future impact from events outside of our control. For example, changes to fiscal and trade policy with respect to tariffs, export controls and other restrictions may impact our global supply chain cost structure and availability, affecting not only vehicle production, but also facility expansions. Furthermore, scaling autonomy operations presents significant challenges due to evolving regulations, the resources required for SI inference and training, and operational and infrastructure support required, any of which could adversely affect our timelines and results. Moreover, we have set ambitious technological targets with our plans for battery cells as well as for iterative manufacturing and design improvements for our vehicles.
Changes in government and economic policies, incentives or tariffs may also impact our production, cost structure and the competitive landscape. For instance, while the final scope and application of recently announced changes in trade policy remain uncertain at this time, tariffs on imports and subsequent retaliatory tariffs could impact consumer spending and demand for durable goods and related services. We will continue to adjust accordingly to such developments, and we believe our ongoing cost reduction efforts, including through production innovation, process improvements and logistics optimization, and focus on operating leverage, vertical integration and supply chain localization will continue to benefit us in relation to our competitors. Our new products, production capacity, infrastructure investments and advances in autonomy and robotics, position us for future growth.
The long-term success of this business is dependent upon incremental volume growth. arguments.markdown:
Tesla is the industry's strongest capability attached to its most expensive claim on it. At $399.81 on 2026-10-30 the equity is capitalised at $1,580.4bn on $3.47bn of trailing operating income, while the businesses the filings describe — cars, storage and services — are worth $139-160bn, or $35-40 a share, on peer multiples [S8, S9, S11]. The judgement is Sell, and it is a de-rating call rather than a liquidation call: the reported value is a floor of $35-50 a share, the twelve-month range runs from $64 in a full de-rating to $506.05 at the award gate, and 90-91% of the price is an option on revenue the quarterly report does not book.

The conditional form makes the call testable. If the need is real — 23.0m electric units in 2026, 28% of global light-vehicle sales — and if the capability is defensible — 1.74m active FSD subscriptions and a 14.8% ex-refund storage gross margin against Fluence's 13.1% fiscal-2025 figure — then the economics still do not scale. The residual $1,420-1,441bn needs $105bn of 2030 operating income at 20x, or 2.1-4.2m robotaxis at a 25% margin, against 1,051 authorised vehicles in Texas on 2026-10-27 and 125,000 units of annual Cybercab capacity [S125, S127, S137, S61]. The outcome is attractive only if the price falls toward the base case or the option converts into a disclosed revenue line; at $399.81 neither holds.

Consensus is Hold, not Sell: 24 buy, 1 strong buy, 20 hold and 3 sell across 48 firms, with an average target of $408.61, 2.2% above the close. The difference is not about the car; it is about the option. The market prices autonomy as a 2028 cash flow, while the record shows 2.0m cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles — 0.9% of the 220.6m rider-only miles Waymo had logged through March 2026 — a California permit that allows testing with a safety driver and nothing driverless, and a Texas service of 1,051 vehicles against Waymo's 500,000 paid rides a week across ten cities [S128, S151, S142, S89]. A 2.2% consensus upside and a -33.5% base case are two prices for the same option; the gap is the thesis.

The mechanism is the multiple, not the earnings. Tesla trades at 103x trailing adjusted EBITDA of $14,995m and 439.4x earnings, against a peer median of 19.1x and BYD's 17.3x. The operating margin was 2.6% in Q3 2026, interest income was 46.5% of pre-tax profit, nine-month free cash flow of $1,883m was smaller than the $3,868m payables build that produced it, and a 5.5% ROIC sits 57bp above a 4.93% ten-year Treasury [S11, S131, S15, S9, S8, S22]. A delay in autonomy compresses the rating, not the earnings, so the drawdown does not require a bad quarter.

The base case is built from the trailing number, not from a forecast. Q3 2026 energy gross profit of $954m included $526m of IEEPA tariff refunds and warranty true-ups; ex-refund it was about $428m on $2,881m of revenue, or 14.8%, close to Fluence's 13.1% fiscal-2025 margin rather than six times its 5.1% June quarter [S9, S61]. Stripping the one-off gives the figure the valuation rests on:

| Step | Adjusted EBITDA | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trailing twelve months to 2026-09-30 | $14,995m | as reported | S9 |
| Less Q3 2026 tariff refunds and warranty true-ups | -$526m | inside energy cost of revenue, one-off | S9, S61 |
| Trailing, ex-one-offs | $14,469m | the bear multiple's base | S9 |
| Base case, next twelve months | $14,500m | credits fall, energy at 14-18%, no robotaxi revenue | S9, S61 |

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 30% | 15% autonomy proof — a California driverless deployment permit and a disclosed robotaxi revenue line with positive contribution; 15% a SpaceX share-for-share combination at a 20-35% premium | $506.05, +26.6%, the first 2025 award gate at a $2,000bn capitalisation; a combination at $480-540 pays the same band | DMV deployment list; Q4 2026 segment disclosure; filed exchange ratio | S89, S127, S154, S156 |
| Base | 40% | No robotaxi monetisation before 2028, the US pool near 6-7% of sales, energy revenue per GWh falling and margin at 14-18%, multiple at 70x | $266, -33.5%: 70x on $14.5bn of adjusted EBITDA plus $36.18bn of net cash | Q4 2026 results without a robotaxi line; energy margin below 14% | S8, S9, S139 |
| Bear | 22% | EA26002 converts to a restricting recall, California stays closed, US and China share erode, capex overruns force a facility draw, multiple at 40x | $156, -61%: 40x on $14.47bn of ex-one-off EBITDA plus net cash | NHTSA closure or recall notice; capex above $7bn in Q4; payables reversal | S87, S8, S11 |
| Full de-rating | 8% | The multiple converges on the reported businesses at 15-25x, with autonomy carried at zero | $64-101, midpoint $82, -79% | Ten-year Treasury above 5.5%; two quarters of negative free cash flow ex-working capital | S8, S9, S22 |
:::

The probabilities are the thesis in numbers: 30% bull, 40% base, 22% bear and 8% full de-rating give an expected twelve-month return of -25.2%, with a 30% chance of a 26.6% gain against a 30% chance of a 61% loss or worse. The bull price is not an EBITDA output at all: $506.05 across 3,952.6m shares is $2,000bn, the first award gate, which is 131x the $15.3bn of EBITDA the same case assumes — the award sets that price, not the cash flow. The bull is also deliberately generous: four conjunctive conditions, or the merger, which substitutes for the first because a 20-35% premium pays the same band. The combination raises the floor, not the expected return, and because the premium is paid in SPCX paper trading at 143x annualised second-quarter 2026 adjusted EBITDA, it swaps one crowded multiple for another [S154, S157]. The bear is a multiple event, not a solvency event: $36.18bn of net cash and $30.0bn of undrawn facilities mean a financing delay costs the option, not the company [S8].

| Rank | Assumption | Confidence | What would disprove it | Impact if wrong | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Autonomy stays unmonetised through 2027: no robotaxi revenue line is disclosed and the paid service stays in Texas | High | A quarterly robotaxi revenue line with positive contribution, or a California driverless permit, inside twelve months | The bull case, +26.6%, replaces the base case, -33.5% | Q4 2026 results pass without a robotaxi line | S89, S151 |
| 2 | The equity multiple holds above 40x adjusted EBITDA despite a 4.93% ten-year Treasury | Low | A move to 40x or below | -61% at 40x, $156; the 15-25x branch gives $64-101 | Ten-year Treasury above 5%; a quarterly miss | S8, S11, S22 |
| 3 | Energy gross margin normalises to 14-18% once the $526m of Q3 2026 refunds and warranty true-ups roll off | Medium | Two quarters above 20% with no tariff refunds and Megapack price per kWh stabilising | $1.5bn of EBITDA, $9-10 a share at 25x | Energy revenue per GWh below $200m, or margin below 14% in Q4 2026 | S9, S61 |
| 4 | Capex lands at or below $20bn and free cash flow is non-negative before working capital | Medium | Q4 capex above $7bn, a third guidance change, or a second quarter of negative free cash flow ex-working capital | $5bn of free cash flow, $31 a share at 25x | A draw on the $30bn facilities; payables growth above 20% | S8, S83 |
| 5 | A SpaceX combination is attempted at a 20-35% premium, with a 15% probability inside twelve months | Medium | The committees end without terms, or the vote threshold fails | +20% to +35% adverse to a short | A filed exchange ratio; the 50%-of-outstanding vote | S154, S156, S158 |

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Waymo | Best | 2009-2026 | 500,000 paid rides a week across ten cities and 220.6m rider-only miles by March 2026, after a 2009 start and a $16bn round at a $126bn post-money: paid autonomy took eleven years and is still city-by-city. Tesla is at 0.9% of the miles with no driverless permit | S142, S151, S130 |
| Tesla's 2022 de-rating | Cautionary | 2021-2022 | The shares fell 65.5% in twelve months as the multiple compressed while revenue kept growing; when the multiple carries the price, the drawdown is the return | S11, S161 |
| SpaceX (SPCX) | Cautionary | 2026 | $2.01tn at 143x annualised Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA after a 2026-06-12 IPO at $135; a premium paid in the most expensive listed currency is not cash | S154, S157 |
:::

The case turns unattractive above $266, where 70x already capitalises roughly $0.9tn of autonomy value the filings do not show, and attractive only below the reported-business value of $35-40 a share or once the option is proven. Sell now; do not initiate a long into the Q4 2026 report in the last week of January 2027; if short, cap the notional at 2.9% of NAV, so a 35% merger gap costs 1.0% of NAV, with $506.05 — the first award gate and the bottom of the premium band — as a reference stop that a gap can trade through [S8, S127, S154]. One diligence item remains open: the Q4 2026 10-Q segment disclosure, because until it lands robotaxi revenue per vehicle-week is not disclosed; whether it is positive at the contribution level after insurance, depreciation and remote supervision is the only number that can convert 90-91% of the price into cash flow.

Which is the right "ex-refund" adjustment?

Careful. The reported energy gross profit $954M = revenue $2,881M (net of $339M refund pass-through) − cost $1,927M (net of $526M refund). If we strip the refunds entirely (i.e., assume no IEEPA refunds at all), revenue would be $2,881M + $339M = $3,220M and cost $1,927M + $526M = $2,453M, gross profit = $767M, margin 23.8%. Hmm, that's the "without any refund" basis. But the Lead's $428M = $954M − $526M, which subtracts the cost-side benefit only but doesn't add back the revenue reduction. That would be inconsistent... unless the $526M is the net benefit after the $339M pass-through? No — the 10-Q clearly says $526M reduction to cost and $339M reduction to revenue.

Wait, maybe the Lead's "$526M of IEEPA tariff refunds and warranty true-ups" is a different figure: a company-sourced statement that energy gross profit included $526M of one-time benefits from tariff refunds AND warranty true-ups. The 10-Q gives $526M tariff refund to energy cost. So perhaps the $526M in the Lead's message is just tariff refunds, and warranty true-ups are separate (not quantified in the filing). Hmm.

The Lead said: "Q3 2026 energy gross profit $954m on $2,881m of revenue is 33.1%; strip the $526m of IEEPA tariff refunds and warranty true-ups and it is $428m, about 14.8%." and "with the $526m split between tariff refunds and warranty true-ups (the quantum is company-sourced and appears in no filing as a segment line — say so)."

So the Lead believes $526M is a combined figure split between tariff refunds and warranty true-ups. But the 10-Q says $526M is exactly the energy cost-of-revenue IEEPA refund. There may also be warranty true-ups of some amount, making the combined one-off larger than $526M. Or maybe the company on the earnings call said energy gross profit included "$526M of one-time benefits, primarily tariff refunds and warranty true-ups" — and the 10-Q's $526M is coincidentally the tariff refund number. Need to check the shareholder deck/earnings call transcript. The 8-K exhibit pages 3-4 may have a slide "Q3 2026 financial summary" with a note. Let me read 8-K page 3 and 4.

Also, there's a subtlety: energy revenue includes $339M reduction for customer refunds. But economically, if we remove the tariff refund event, the customer refunds wouldn't exist either, so revenue would be higher by $339M and cost higher by $526M: gross profit = $954M − $526M + $339M = $767M (23.8% of $3,220M). Hmm. But maybe the company's "one-time benefit" figure nets these: $526M − $339M = $187M. Then ex-one-off gross profit = $767M (23.8%). That doesn't match 14.8%.

This webcast will also be available for replay for approximately one year thereafter. CERTAIN TERMS When used in this update, certain terms have the following meanings. Our vehicle deliveries include only vehicles that have been transferred to end customers with all paperwork correctly completed. Our energy product deployment volume includes both customer units when installed and equipment sales at time of delivery. “Net income attributable to common stockholders (non-GAAP)" is equal to (i) net income attributable to common stockholders before (ii)(a) stock-based compensation expense, net of tax, (b) digital assets unrealized (gain) loss, net of tax, (c) SpaceX equity investment unrealized (gain) loss, net of tax and (d) certain tax items. "Adjusted EBITDA (non-GAAP)" is equal to (i) net income attributable to common stockholders before (ii)(a) interest expense, (b) provision for (benefit from) income taxes, (c) depreciation, amortization and impairment, (d) stock-based compensation expense (e) digital assets unrealized (gain) loss and (f) SpaceX equity investment unrealized (gain) loss. "Free cash flow" is operating cash flow less capital expenditures. Average cost per vehicle is cost of automotive sales divided by new vehicle deliveries (excluding operating leases). “Days sales outstanding” is equal to (i) average accounts receivable, net for the period divided by (ii) total revenues and multiplied by (iii) the number of days in the period. “Days payable outstanding” is equal to (i) average accounts payable for the period divided by (ii) total cost of revenues and multiplied by (iii) the number of days in the period. “Days of supply” is calculated by dividing new car ending inventory by the relevant period's deliveries and using trading days. Constant currency impacts are calculated by comparing actuals against current results converted into USD using average exchange rates from the prior period. NON-GAAP FINANCIAL INFORMATION Consolidated financial information has been presented in accordance with GAAP as well as on a non-GAAP basis to supplement our consolidated financial results. Our non-GAAP financial measures include non-GAAP net income (loss) attributable to common stockholders, non-GAAP net income (loss) attributable to common stockholders on a diluted per share basis (calculated using weighted average shares for GAAP diluted net income (loss) attributable to common stockholders), Adjusted EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA margin, non-GAAP automotive gross margin and free cash flow. These non-GAAP financial measures also facilitate management’s internal comparisons to Tesla’s historical performance as well as comparisons to the operating results of other companies. Management believes that it is useful to supplement its GAAP financial statements with this non-GAAP information because management uses such information internally for its operating, budgeting and financial planning purposes. Management also believes that presentation of the non-GAAP financial measures provides useful information to our investors regarding our financial condition and results of operations, so that investors can see through the eyes of Tesla management regarding important financial metrics that Tesla uses to run the business and allowing investors to better understand Tesla’s performance. Non-GAAP information is not prepared under a comprehensive set of accounting rules and therefore, should only be read in conjunction with financial information reported under U.S. GAAP when understanding Tesla’s operating performance. A reconciliation between GAAP and non-GAAP financial information is provided above. FORWARD-LOOKING STATEMENTS Certain statements in this update, including, but not limited to, statements in the “Outlook” section; statements relating to the development, strategy, ramp, production and capacity, demand and market growth, cost, pricing and profitability, investment, deliveries, deployment, availability and other features and improvements and timing of existing and future Tesla products and services and supporting infrastructure; statements regarding operating margin, operating profits, spending and liquidity; and statements regarding expansion, improvements and/or ramp and related timing at our facilities are “forward-looking statements” within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Future results may differ materially from those expressed in any forward-looking statement. The following important factors, without limitation, could cause actual results to differ materially from those in the forward-looking statements: the risk of delays in launching and/or manufacturing our products, services and features cost-effectively; our ability to build and/or grow our products and services, sales, delivery, installation, servicing and charging capabilities and effectively manage this growth; our ability to successfully and timely develop, introduce and scale, as well as our consumers’ demand for, products and services based on super intelligence, robotics and automation, electric vehicles, advanced driver assistance systems, and ride-hailing services generally and our vehicles and services specifically; the ability of suppliers to deliver components according to schedules, prices, quality and volumes acceptable to us, and our ability to manage such components effectively; any issues with lithium-ion cells or other components manufactured at our factories; our ability to ramp our factories in accordance with our plans; our ability to procure supply of battery cells, including through our own manufacturing; risks relating to international operations and expansion, including unfavorable and uncertain regulatory, political, economic, tax, tariff, export controls and labor conditions; any failures by Tesla products to perform as expected or if product recalls occur; the risk of product liability claims; competition in the automotive, transportation and energy product and services and robotics markets; our ability to maintain public credibility and confidence in our long-term business prospects; our ability to manage risks relating to our various product financing programs; the status of government and economic incentives for electric vehicles and energy products; our ability to attract, hire and retain key employees and qualified personnel; our ability to maintain the security of our information and production and product systems; our compliance with various regulations and laws applicable to our operations and products, which may evolve from time to time; risks relating to our indebtedness and financing strategies; and adverse foreign exchange movements. More information on potential factors that could affect our financial results is included from time to time in our Securities and Exchange Commission filings and reports, including the risks identified under the section captioned “Risk Factors” in our annual report on Form 10-K filed with the SEC on January 28, 2026 and subsequent quarterly reports on Form 10-Q. - Musk footnote: includes 413,152,109 trust shares + 286,428,773 restricted shares issued on 2018 award exercise (issued and outstanding, voting, service-based forfeiture). So the beneficial-ownership percentage column uses a base of 3,952,648,559 adjusted by adding options exercisable within 60 days for the person (and presumably excluding the 423.7m unearned shares from the denominator? "Corresponding adjustments have been made to the shares outstanding" — this is ambiguous: since the 423.7m restricted shares are issued and outstanding (granted), are they in the 3,952,648,559? Let me think.

Actually, were the 423,743,904 shares granted in 2025 issued and outstanding? The proxy says "shares of restricted stock granted to Mr. Musk pursuant to the 2025 CEO Performance Award" — restricted stock is typically issued and outstanding when granted, unless it's a restricted stock unit. Interesting! So indeed the proxy's 19.8% uses a reduced denominator. That aligns with the Lead's request: "show Musk at 17.7% of issued shares and 19.8% of issued excluding unvested restricted shares, with the basis stated once." Hmm, "19.8% of issued excluding unvested restricted shares" — i.e., excluding the 423.7m. So 699,580,882/(3,952,648,559−423,743,904) = 19.82%.

Wait but is the 286,428,773 restricted stock from 2018 included in both numerator and denominator? Yes, issued and outstanding, voting rights exercisable by Musk. Alternatively, at 2025-12-31 shares = 3,751m did NOT include the 423.7m award shares (not yet issued), and the 304m exercise minus ~102m withheld for taxes gives 3,953m. Then the 423.7m restricted stock granted under the 2025 award is NOT in the 3,952,648,559 count. But then why "corresponding adjustments have been made to the shares outstanding" for Musk? Hmm.

Wait — actually maybe the 423.7m shares WERE issued and outstanding at grant (Sept 2025), so at 2025-12-31, 3,751m included them. Then ex-award = 3,327m. Then the 2026 exercise added 304m, less tax withholding of ~102m... 3,327 + 304 − 102 = 3,529m. But reported 3,952.6m. Not matching either.

arguments.markdown:
Tesla is the industry's strongest capability attached to its most expensive claim on it. At $399.81 on 2026-10-30 the equity is capitalised at $1,580.4bn on $3.47bn of trailing operating income, while the businesses the filings describe — cars, storage and services — are worth $139-160bn, or $35-40 a share, on peer multiples [S8, S9, S11]. The judgement is Sell, and it is a de-rating call rather than a liquidation call: the reported value is a floor of $35-50 a share, the twelve-month range runs from $64 in a full de-rating to $506.05 at the award gate, and 90-91% of the price is an option on revenue the quarterly report does not book.

The conditional form makes the call testable. If the need is real — 23.0m electric units in 2026, 28% of global light-vehicle sales — and if the capability is defensible — 1.74m active FSD subscriptions and a 14.8% ex-refund storage gross margin against Fluence's 13.1% fiscal-2025 figure — then the economics still do not scale. The residual $1,420-1,441bn needs $105bn of 2030 operating income at 20x, or 2.1-4.2m robotaxis at a 25% margin, against 1,051 authorised vehicles in Texas on 2026-10-27 and 125,000 units of annual Cybercab capacity [S125, S127, S137, S61]. At $399.81 the case is attractive only if the price falls toward the base case.

Consensus is Hold, not Sell: 24 buy, 1 strong buy, 20 hold and 3 sell across 48 firms, with an average target of $408.61, 2.2% above the close. The difference is not about the car; it is about the option. The market prices autonomy as a 2028 cash flow, while the record shows 2.0m cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles — 0.9% of the 220.6m rider-only miles Waymo had logged through March 2026 — a California permit that allows testing with a safety driver and nothing driverless, and a Texas service of 1,051 vehicles against Waymo's 500,000 paid rides a week across ten cities [S128, S151, S142, S89]. A 2.2% consensus upside and a -33.5% base case are two prices for the same option.

The mechanism is the multiple, not the earnings. Tesla trades at 103x trailing adjusted EBITDA of $14,995m and 439.4x earnings, against a peer median of 19.1x and BYD's 17.3x. The operating margin was 2.6% in Q3 2026, interest income was 46.5% of pre-tax profit, nine-month free cash flow of $1,883m was smaller than the $3,868m payables build that produced it, and a 5.5% ROIC sits 57bp above a 4.93% ten-year Treasury [S11, S131, S15, S9, S8, S22]. A delay in autonomy compresses the rating, not the earnings, so the drawdown does not require a bad quarter.

The base case is built from the trailing number, not from a forecast. Q3 2026 energy gross profit of $954m included $526m of IEEPA tariff refunds and warranty true-ups; ex-refund it was about $428m on $2,881m of revenue, or 14.8%, close to Fluence's 13.1% fiscal-2025 margin rather than six times its 5.1% June quarter [S9, S61]. {"url":"https://mgrid.org/2026/10/23/tesla-deploys-13-7-gwh-in-q3-but-books-16-less-storage-revenue-as-526-million-of-tariff-refunds-lift-margin-to-33-1/","title":"Tesla Deploys 13.7 GWh in Q3 but Books 16% Less Storage Revenue, as $526 Million of Tariff Refunds Lift Margin to 33.1%","text":"Q3 2026 storage deployed: 13.7 GWhEnergy generation and storage revenue: $2.88 billionRevenue change year over year: -16%IEEPA tariff refund to energy cost of revenue: $526 millionEnergy gross margin: 33.1%

Tesla deployed 13.7 GWh of energy storage in the third quarter of 2026 and booked $2.88 billion of energy generation and storage revenue, down $534 million, or 16%, from a year earlier. The Austin, Texas company reported the results on October 21, 2026 in its quarterly filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Deployments rose from 12.5 GWh in the third quarter of 2025 and 13.5 GWh in the second quarter of 2026, yet revenue fell. Tesla attributes the drop mainly to tariff refunds for certain Megapack customers, a lower average selling price per Megapack unit, fewer Powerwall deployments and fewer solar retrofit cash deployments, partly offset by more Megapack deployments.

The tariff story runs through both lines of the energy income statement. In February 2026 the Supreme Court invalidated certain tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, which made Tesla eligible for refunds on imported goods. In the quarter, Tesla recognized $526 million of IEEPA tariff refunds as a reduction to energy generation and storage cost of revenues, and $339 million as a reduction to energy revenue for refunds it owes certain storage customers under contract. Automotive sales took a $260 million cost reduction from the same ruling. Tesla says the amounts recognized in the first half of 2026 were immaterial.

The refunds flattered margin. Cost of energy generation and storage revenue fell $415 million, or 18%, and energy gross margin rose to 33.1% from 31.4% a year earlier. Tesla credits deployment fluctuations, the tariff refunds and a lower average cost per Megapack unit. Energy gross profit still slipped to $954 million from $1.07 billion, according to Electrek’s reading of the shareholder letter. Over nine months, energy revenue is down $506 million, or 6%, and gross margin is flat at 30.2% against 30.3%.

Deployments missed the Street. Electrek reports that analysts expected roughly 15.9 GWh for the quarter. Tesla says Megapack deployments vary meaningfully quarter to quarter with the timing of project milestones and logistics. Through the third quarter, Tesla has deployed 36.0 GWh of storage in 2026. The filing says the company is ramping its Megafactories in Shanghai and Lathrop, California, and that a new Megafactory near Houston, Texas began production in the third quarter. Tesla started Megapack 3 production in Texas in September.

One customer stands out in the filing. SpaceX bought $221 million of Megapacks in the quarter and $626 million over nine months, at a cost of revenue of $171 million and $478 million. Tesla’s accounts receivable from SpaceX stood at $729 million at quarter end, including milestone billings and capacity reservations for Megapacks not yet delivered, and deferred revenue on those SpaceX contracts was $648 million. Across all customers, deferred revenue from customer payments reached $3.30 billion, up from $2.04 billion at the end of 2025. Tesla’s remaining performance obligations on contracts longer than a year total $10.73 billion, with $4.80 billion expected in the next 12 months.

The energy segment sits inside a flat company quarter. Total revenue was $28.05 billion, essentially unchanged from a year earlier, and operating income fell 56% to $718 million as research and development spending rose 69% to $2.76 billion. Services and other revenue grew 33% to $4.61 billion. Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles and produced 464,391.

Why It Matters

Strip out the tariff accounting and the storage business looks different. The $339 million revenue reduction is a one-time pass-through to customers. Adding it back still leaves energy revenue below last year’s quarter despite 10% more gigawatt-hours, so the lower average selling price per Megapack is doing real work on the top line. The $526 million cost refund is also one-time. Without it, cost of energy revenue would have risen rather than fallen, and the 33.1% margin would not have held. Investors who read this quarter’s margin as a Megapack cost story are reading a tariff story.

The second thing the filing shows is concentration. SpaceX accounts for $221 million of the quarter’s energy revenue and holds $729 million of receivables and reservations, more than any customer Tesla has named. Tesla’s first-quarter 2026 energy results showed revenue and deployments falling together. This quarter deployments grew and revenue fell anyway. The 36.0 GWh deployed through September, with Houston now producing, is the number to watch against the fourth quarter, and the filing gives no deployment guidance.

Critical Perspective
Tesla deployed 13.7 GWh and still booked 16% less energy revenue, and $526 million of the margin story is a tariff refund the Supreme Court handed it, not a cost it took out of a Megapack. CATL, the largest cell maker, told investors this week that storage is a rising share of its sales even as its profit growth slowed to 15%, so falling revenue per unit is a market condition and not a Tesla problem alone. When Tesla folded SolarCity in 2016, solar deployments fell for two straight years while management described each quarter as a transition, and the Powerwall and solar retrofit declines in this filing read the same way. With SpaceX holding $729 million of receivables and reservations, how much of Tesla’s storage backlog is one related party buying from another?

That is the useful comparison for a buyer in 2026: where each system is designed to work, how it watches the driver, and what its manufacturer promises. There is not enough comparable public data to name a safety winner.

Safety note: These are Level 2 driver-assistance systems, not autonomous vehicles. NHTSA says the driver remains responsible when a Level 2 system controls steering and speed. Keep watching the road and be ready to brake or steer immediately. Features and eligible roads can change by vehicle, hardware, region, and software version.

Key takeaways

Super Cruise and BlueCruise permit hands-off driving only on compatible mapped roads; FSD (Supervised) is intended for a wider variety of roads.
GM says Super Cruise works on about 750,000 miles of compatible roads in the United States and Canada. Ford says its Blue Zones cover more than 130,000 miles of North American roads. Those figures use different definitions and should not be treated as a controlled test.
All three use a driver-facing camera for attention monitoring in current implementations, although the exact hardware and alerts vary by model and software version.
FSD (Supervised) is the subject of an open NHTSA Engineering Analysis into degraded-visibility detection. An open investigation is not a finding that every vehicle has a defect or that a recall is required.
Public crash-report counts cannot establish a safety ranking because NHTSA says the data are not normalized for fleet size, miles driven, or operating conditions.

How we evaluated the systems
This comparison was updated on August 11, 2026. It is a document-based review, not a Chariotz road test. We compared current manufacturer descriptions, owner guidance, compatible-road claims, driver-monitoring requirements, and open NHTSA actions. We did not convert manufacturer-reported miles or crash counts into safety rates.
That last limitation matters. NHTSA’s Standing General Order data page says Level 2 crash reports are not normalized by vehicle count or miles traveled and that manufacturers have different access to telemetry. Raw report totals therefore cannot support a fair brand-to-brand safety ranking.

Chief Financial Officer Vaibhav Taneja told investors on the Q3 earnings call that the proceeds are going back into U.S. production capacity, according to Benzinga’s coverage of the call. The refunds matter for two reasons. They flattered the energy business, where gross margin jumped from 20.4% to 33.1% in one quarter. And they landed in the middle of a spending cycle that spans robotaxis, humanoid robots, solar, AI compute and a chip fab. We covered the revenue side of this quarter in our earlier report on Tesla energy revenue dropping 16% on tariff refunds. This piece focuses on the other half of the ledger: where the refund money is headed and what it signals for hardware supply chains.

One caution before the numbers. The phrase “Trump tariff refunds” is a headline shorthand. Tesla’s own filing describes refunds tied to tariffs that the U.S. Supreme Court invalidated under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). We use the filing’s framing in the analysis below and flag where the headline label goes further than the paperwork.

The core disclosure is simple. Tesla recognized US$786 million in tariff refunds in the quarter. Of that, US$526 million reduced cost of revenues in the energy generation and storage segment, and US$260 million reduced cost of revenues in automotive. Those figures come from Tesla’s quarterly filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, which is posted on the SEC’s EDGAR system.

Taneja then explained the intent on the call. The money, he said, is being reinvested to expand production capacity in the United States. He named five destinations: more robotaxis in the fleet, more production capacity for Optimus, new solar manufacturing capacity, additional AI compute infrastructure, and a semiconductor fab. He did not attach dollar amounts to any of them, so any split of the US$786 million across those projects is unconfirmed.

Elon Musk, Tesla’s chief executive, did not make a separate statement about the refunds in the material we reviewed. The framing came from the CFO. That fits the pattern of the call, where Taneja handled the cash and margin questions while Musk spoke about long-range manufacturing scale.

The US$786 Million Breakdown by Segment

Splitting the total by segment shows where the tariff burden had been sitting. Energy took two thirds of the benefit even though it is the smaller of Tesla’s two big hardware businesses. That tilt makes sense for a segment that imports battery cells and related components, and it explains why the margin swing showed up there first.

Source: Tesla quarterly filing and Q3 earnings call. The net figure in the last row is our own subtraction of US$339 million from US$786 million. Tesla did not publish it as a combined number, so treat it as an analytical estimate of the economic benefit rather than a reported result.

Why “Trump Tariff Refunds” Is a Label, Not Tesla’s Wording

Benzinga’s headline calls the money “Trump tariff refunds.” Several other outlets used similar phrasing in their coverage of the call. The shorthand is understandable, since the tariffs in question were a signature trade policy. But Tesla’s filing does not use that label. It ties the refunds to tariffs invalidated under IEEPA, and that is the precise legal hook.

The distinction matters for accuracy. A reader who sees “Trump tariff refunds” could assume every tariff Tesla ever paid is now recoverable. The filing says no such thing. It ties the refunds to the tariffs invalidated under IEEPA, and it does not describe any wider category of duties as refundable.

We therefore describe the money as IEEPA tariff refunds throughout this report, and we treat the political label as a reader-facing shorthand. If Tesla or the government publishes a fuller accounting of which duties were refunded, the picture could shift, but the current record supports nothing broader.

How the February 2026 Supreme Court Ruling Set This Up

Tesla’s filing states that the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in February 2026 that certain tariffs imposed under IEEPA were invalid. Tesla’s Q3 refund recognition is the dollar figure that flows from that decision in its books.

The timeline is short to state. The ruling came in February 2026, and by the third quarter Tesla had recognized US$786 million. The filing does not walk through the steps in between, so we will not guess at the administrative path. What the record shows is a gap of several months between the court decision and the quarter in which Tesla booked the benefit.

Our research found no verified dollar amounts from other automakers or hardware companies for the same period. That does not mean peers have no claims. It means we cannot responsibly compare Tesla’s figure to a competitor’s. If other manufacturers disclose their own refunds in coming earnings reports, a side-by-side table will become possible.

The US$339 Million Customer Refund Offset

The refund story has a second side that many headlines skipped. Tesla reported a US$339 million reduction in energy generation and storage revenue tied to refunds owed to customers under contract. In plain terms, some of the tariff cost had been passed through to buyers of energy products, and when Tesla got money back, it owed a share to those customers.

That pass-through is why gross margin and revenue moved in opposite directions. Cost of revenues fell by US$526 million in energy, which lifted margin. Revenue fell too, because of the customer refunds. The result was lower reported revenue alongside much higher margin, which is exactly what the energy numbers showed this quarter. The trade publication Energy-Storage.News reported that revenues fell even as Tesla posted its second-highest quarterly deployment total, which Taneja put at 13.7 gigawatt-hours.

arguments.markdown:
Tesla is the industry's strongest capability attached to its most expensive claim on it. At $399.81 on 2026-10-30 the equity is capitalised at $1,580.4bn on $3.47bn of trailing operating income, while the businesses the filings describe — cars, storage and services — are worth $139-160bn, or $35-40 a share, on peer multiples. The judgement is Sell, and it is a de-rating call rather than a liquidation call: the reported value is a floor of $35-50 a share, the twelve-month range runs from $64 in a full de-rating to $506.05 at the award gate, and 90-91% of the price is an option on revenue the quarterly report does not book. If the need is real — 23.0m electric units in 2026, 28% of global light-vehicle sales — and if the capability is defensible — 1.74m active FSD subscriptions and a 14.8% ex-refund storage gross margin against Fluence's 13.1% fiscal-2025 figure — then the economics still do not scale. The residual $1,420-1,441bn needs $105bn of 2030 operating income at 20x, or 2.1-4.2m robotaxis at a 25% margin, against 1,051 authorised vehicles in Texas on 2026-10-27 and 125,000 units of annual Cybercab capacity. At $399.81 the case is attractive only if the price falls toward the base case [S8, S9, S11, S125, S127, S137, S61].

Consensus is Hold, not Sell: 24 buy, 1 strong buy, 20 hold and 3 sell across 48 firms, with an average target of $408.61, 2.2% above the close. The market prices autonomy as a 2028 cash flow, while the record shows 2.0m cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles — 0.9% of the 220.6m rider-only miles Waymo had logged through March 2026 — a California permit that allows testing with a safety driver and nothing driverless, and a Texas service of 1,051 vehicles against Waymo's 500,000 paid rides a week across ten cities [S128, S151, S142, S89]. A 2.2% consensus upside and a -33.5% base case are two prices for the same option.

The mechanism is the multiple, not the earnings. Tesla trades at 103x trailing adjusted EBITDA of $14,995m and 439.4x earnings, against a peer median of 19.1x and BYD's 17.3x. The operating margin was 2.6% in Q3 2026, interest income was 46.5% of pre-tax profit, nine-month free cash flow of $1,883m was smaller than the $3,868m payables build that produced it, and a 5.5% ROIC sits 57bp above a 4.93% ten-year Treasury [S11, S131, S15, S9, S8, S22]. A delay in autonomy compresses the rating, not the earnings, so the drawdown does not require a bad quarter.

The base case is built from the trailing number, not from a forecast. Q3 2026 energy gross profit of $954m included $526m of IEEPA tariff refunds and warranty true-ups; ex-refund it was about $428m on $2,881m of revenue, or 14.8%, close to Fluence's 13.1% fiscal-2025 margin rather than six times its 5.1% June quarter [S9, S61]. The bridge:

| Step | Adjusted EBITDA | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trailing twelve months to 2026-09-30 | $14,995m | as reported | S9 |
| Less Q3 2026 tariff refunds and warranty true-ups | -$526m | one-off, energy cost of revenue | S9, S61 |
| Trailing, ex-one-offs | $14,469m | the bear multiple's base | S9 |
| Base case, next twelve months | $14,500m | credits fall, energy at 14-18%, no robotaxi revenue | S9, S61 |

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 30% | 15% autonomy proof — a California driverless deployment permit and a disclosed robotaxi revenue line with positive contribution; 15% a SpaceX share-for-share combination at a 20-35% premium | $506.05, +26.6%, the first 2025 award gate at $2,000bn; a combination at $480-540 pays the same band | DMV deployment list; Q4 2026 segment disclosure; filed exchange ratio | S89, S127, S154, S156 |
| Base | 40% | No robotaxi monetisation before 2028, the US pool near 6-7% of sales, energy revenue per GWh falling and margin at 14-18%, multiple at 70x | $266, -33.5%: 70x on $14.5bn of adjusted EBITDA plus $36.18bn of net cash | Q4 2026 results without a robotaxi line; energy margin below 14% | S8, S9, S139 |
| Bear | 22% | EA26002 converts to a restricting recall, California stays closed, US and China share erode, capex overruns force a facility draw, multiple at 40x | $156, -61%: 40x on $14.47bn of ex-one-off EBITDA plus net cash | NHTSA closure or recall notice; capex above $7bn in Q4; payables reversal | S87, S8, S11 |
| Full de-rating | 8% | The multiple converges on the reported businesses at 15-25x, with autonomy carried at zero | $64-101, midpoint $82, -79% | Ten-year Treasury above 5.5%; two quarters of negative free cash flow ex-working capital | S8, S9, S22 |
:::

The probabilities are the thesis in numbers: 30% bull, 40% base, 22% bear and 8% full de-rating give an expected twelve-month return of -25.2%, with a 30% chance of a 26.6% gain against a 30% chance of a 61% loss or worse. The bull price is not an EBITDA output: $506.05 across 3,952.6m shares is $2,000bn, the first award gate, which is 131x the $15.3bn of EBITDA the same case assumes — the award sets that price, not the cash flow. The bull is generous: four conjunctive conditions, or the merger, which pays the same band. The combination raises the floor, not the expected return, and because the premium is paid in SPCX paper trading at 143x annualised second-quarter 2026 adjusted EBITDA, it swaps one crowded multiple for another. The counter-evidence is real: energy and services are compounding, the balance sheet holds $36.18bn of net cash, and a premium bid can gap the shares at any time [S154, S157].

| 2 | The equity multiple holds above 40x adjusted EBITDA despite a 4.93% ten-year Treasury | Low | A move to 40x or below | -61% at 40x, $156; the 15-25x branch gives $64-101 | Ten-year Treasury above 5%; a quarterly miss | S8, S11, S22 |
| 3 | Energy gross margin normalises to 14-18% once the $526m of Q3 2026 refunds and warranty true-ups roll off | Medium | Two quarters above 20% with no tariff refunds and Megapack price per kWh stabilising | $1.5bn of EBITDA, $9-10 a share at 25x | Energy revenue per GWh below $200m, or margin below 14% in Q4 2026 | S9, S61 |
| 4 | Capex lands at or below $20bn and free cash flow is non-negative before working capital | Medium | Q4 capex above $7bn, a third guidance change, or a second quarter of negative free cash flow ex-working capital | $5bn of free cash flow, $31 a share at 25x | A draw on the $30bn facilities; payables growth above 20% | S8, S83 |
| 5 | A SpaceX combination is attempted at a 20-35% premium, with a 15% probability inside twelve months | Medium | The committees end without terms, or the vote threshold fails | +20% to +35% adverse to a short | A filed exchange ratio; the 50%-of-outstanding vote | S154, S156, S158 |

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Waymo | Best | 2009-2026 | 500,000 paid rides a week and 220.6m rider-only miles by March 2026, after a 2009 start and a $16bn round at a $126bn post-money: paid autonomy took eleven years and is still city-by-city. Tesla is at 0.9% of the miles with no driverless permit | S142, S151, S130 |
| Tesla's 2022 de-rating | Cautionary | 2021-2022 | The shares fell 65.5% in twelve months as the multiple compressed while revenue grew; when the multiple carries the price, the drawdown is the return | S11, S161 |
| SpaceX (SPCX) | Cautionary | 2026 | $2.01tn at 143x annualised Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA after a 2026-06-12 IPO at $135; a premium paid in the most expensive listed currency is not cash | S154, S157 |
:::

The case turns attractive only below the reported-business value of $35-40 a share or once the option is proven; above $266 the price already capitalises roughly $0.9tn of autonomy value the filings do not show. arguments.markdown:
The weighted score is 3.8 out of 10, the average of the dimensions below at their stated weights, and the recommendation is Sell. Valuation carries a 20% weight and scores 2: the reported car, storage and services businesses are worth $139-160bn, or $35-40 a share, against a $1,580.4bn capitalisation at $399.81 on 2026-10-30, and the equity trades at 103x trailing adjusted EBITDA of $14,995m against BYD's 17.3x [S8, S9, S11, S131].

| Dimension | Weight | Score (1-10) | Rationale | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Valuation and margin of safety | 20% | 2 | $35-40 a share of reported value against $399.81; 103x against BYD's 17.3x; 439.4x earnings against 19.1x | S8, S9, S11, S131, S15 |
| Business quality and unit economics | 15% | 4 | Automotive at -$1,994 a vehicle after group R&D and SG&A; energy at 14.8% ex-refund against Fluence's 13.1% fiscal 2025, but 12% of revenue | S9, S61, S8 |
| Market growth and timing | 10% | 4 | US EV sales -30.3% YTD and China NEV retail -12.8%; Europe +49%; storage demand of 158 GW/459 GWh | S139, S138, S140, S141 |
| Competitive position | 15% | 5 | 52.9% US EV share, fourth in China at 64,837 units against BYD's 246,816; autonomy at 0.9% of Waymo's 220.6m miles | S145, S146, S151 |
| Earnings quality and cash conversion | 10% | 3 | 9M free cash flow of $1,883m below a $3,868m payables build; interest income 46.5% of Q3 2026 pre-tax profit | S8, S22 |
| Balance sheet and funding | 10% | 6 | Net cash $36,180m and $30.0bn undrawn, against $7,955m of leases and a $7,414m warranty reserve | S8 |
| Management and capital allocation | 10% | 3 | $2.0bn to xAI after a 1.06bn to 916.3m vote against it; compensation chair on SpaceX's board | S10, S104, S107 |
| Catalysts and exit path | 5% | 4 | SpaceX committees and a 20-35% premium implying $480-540; no dividend and no buyback | S154, S156, S162 |
| ESG and regulatory licence | 5% | 4 | Credits down to $1,993m from $2,763m; EA26002 covers 3,203,754 vehicles | S8, S87 |

The composite is not close to neutral, and no single dimension rescues it. The dimensions that could offset a stretched multiple — market growth and the balance sheet — carry modest weights, while the one that cannot be argued away, the gap between price and reported value, carries the largest.

Business quality scores 4. Q3 2026 automotive revenue of $42,259 a vehicle against $34,436 of cost leaves $7,823 of gross profit, or $7,590 excluding credits, below the $9,817 a vehicle of group research, development, selling and administrative cost, so the car runs at -$1,994 a vehicle and energy plus services pay the operating cost. Energy is the best business, but its Q3 2026 gross margin of 33.1% contains $526m of IEEPA tariff refunds and warranty true-ups; ex-refund it is about $428m on $2,881m of revenue, or 14.8%, against Fluence's 13.1% fiscal 2025 and 5.1% June quarter — a real manufacturing advantage, not a sixfold one — and energy is 12% of revenue, down 16% year on year. Earnings quality scores 3 because nine-month free cash flow of $1,883m is smaller than the $3,868m payables build, interest income was 46.5% of Q3 2026 pre-tax profit, and a 5.5% ROIC sits 57bp above a 4.93% ten-year Treasury. The balance sheet is the one dimension above neutral at 6: $36,180m of net cash and $30.0bn of undrawn facilities fund the $20bn capex plan without equity [S8, S9, S22, S61].

Market growth scores 4 and competitive position 5. The pools that pay Tesla's bills are shrinking by policy in the United States and China while the growing pool, Europe and grid storage, is smaller and priced per unit; the company holds the largest share of America's electric-vehicle market yet is fourth in China, and its autonomy mileage is 0.9% of the incumbent's. The score is not lower because Tesla still sets the US price and builds storage at a lower cost than listed integrators; it is not higher because none of those advantages compounds into the revenue line the price requires.

Management and governance scores 3: the board committed $2.0bn to xAI after a shareholder measure against it drew 1.06bn votes to 916.3m, the compensation committee chair also sits on SpaceX's board, and the 423,743,904-share award is gated from a $2,000bn market capitalisation, so dilution arrives only in up states. Catalysts and exit score 4 because a listed SpaceX at $2.01tn, with both boards' committees and a 20-35% broker premium, implies $480-540 a share, a real exit that substitutes for rather than adds to the bull case. ESG and regulatory licence score 4: automotive credits fell to $1,993m in FY2025 from $2,763m, NHTSA's EA26002 covers 3,203,754 vehicles, and the NLRB dismissed its Buffalo complaint on 2026-10-29 [S10, S96, S154].

The recommendation does not change in any branch of the distribution, and it changes only on an event, not on a lower price. The report uses one set: bull 30% — 15% autonomy proof and 15% a SpaceX combination — at $506.05, +26.6%; base 40% at $266, -33.5%, which is 70x on $14.5bn of adjusted EBITDA plus $36.18bn of net cash; bear 22% at $156, -61%; and a full de-rating at 8%, $64-101, -79%. The expected twelve-month return is -25.2%. The base-case EBITDA is the trailing $14,995m less $526m of Q3 one-offs, held at $14.5bn on an energy margin of 14-18%; the bull price is not an EBITDA output at all, because $506.05 across 3,952.6m shares is the $2,000bn award gate. A merger announced at a premium would end the standalone short at the exchange ratio; a disclosed robotaxi revenue line with positive contribution, or a California driverless deployment entry, would move autonomy into the valuation and force a re-underwrite.

Position sizing is zero long and, at most, a capped short. With that distribution the Kelly fraction for a long is negative, so there is no case for owning the shares. The short's problem is the gap: a premium bid can arrive outside market hours and trade through any stop, so the position is sized to the event rather than to the chart. Cap the short notional at 2.9% of NAV, which makes a 35% gap cost 1.0% of NAV, with $506.05 — the first award gate — as a reference stop. The market regime compounds the de-rating case: volatility sits near the top of its range for the past year and long-term Treasury yields are close to their highs for the year, so the multiple has no rate cushion.

| Measure | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Long position | Zero | S8, S11 |
| Short notional cap | 2.9% of NAV; a 35% gap costs 1.0% of NAV | S154 |
| Stop reference | $506.05, the first award gate | S127 |
| Expected 12-month return | -25.2% | S8, S9, S11 |
| Market regime | VIX 19.42 at the 77th percentile; 10-year Treasury 4.93%; high-yield spread 326bp; energy +17.6% over three months against technology +2.4% | S21, S22, S46, S37, S32 |

The next diligence actions are specific and none is met at the current price: the Q4 2026 report must disclose a robotaxi revenue line and free cash flow before working capital; the California DMV deployment list must add Tesla; NHTSA must close or recall EA26002, with a remedy cost of $0.3-3.2bn; and a SpaceX exchange ratio and vote threshold must be filed. The conditions for investing are a disclosed robotaxi revenue line with positive contribution, a driverless deployment permit, an energy margin above 14% without tariff refunds, and capex inside the plan with positive free cash flow before working capital.

::: sensitivity
| Rank | Assumption | Base | What would disprove it | Impact on value | Impact level | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The equity multiple holds above 40x adjusted EBITDA | 103x trailing | A move to 40x or below | -61% at 40x, $156; the 15-25x branch gives $64-101, -79% | high | 10-year Treasury above 5%; a quarterly miss | S8, S11, S22 |
| 2 | Autonomy stays unmonetised through 2027 | No robotaxi revenue line | A quarterly line with positive contribution, or a California permit | +26.6% at $506.05 replaces the base | high | Q4 2026 results without a line | S89, S151 |
| 3 | Energy gross margin normalises to 14-18% | 14.8% in Q3 2026 ex-refund | Two quarters above 20% without tariff refunds | $1.5bn of EBITDA, $9-10 a share at 25x | medium | Energy revenue per GWh below $200m | S9, S61 |
| 4 | Capex lands at or below $20bn with non-negative free cash flow | $20bn | Q4 capex above $7bn or a third guidance change | $5bn of free cash flow, $31 a share at 25x | medium | A draw on the $30bn facilities | S8, S83 |
| 5 | A SpaceX combination is attempted at a 20-35% premium | No filed terms; 15% probability | Committees end without terms, or the vote fails | +20% to +35% adverse to a short | medium | A filed exchange ratio | S154, S156, S158 |
:::

::: takeaways
1. Sell at $399.81: $139-160bn of reported-business value, or $35-40 a share, sits against a $1,580.4bn capitalisation, so 90-91% of the price is an option the filings do not book [S8, S9].
2. The rating is carried by the multiple: 103x trailing adjusted EBITDA against BYD's 17.3x, a base case of $266 at 70x on $14.5bn of EBITDA, and an expected twelve-month return of -25.2% [S11, S131, S9].
3. Size for the exit, not the chart: a 20-35% SpaceX premium implies $480-540, so cap any short at 2.9% of NAV notional, where a 35% gap costs 1.0% of NAV, and re-underwrite only on a disclosed robotaxi revenue line or a California deployment permit [S154, S89].
:::

{"url":"https://global.chinadaily.com.cn/a/202301/10/WS63bcc320a31057c47eba8aa5.html","title":"Tesla's new No 2 revved up Shanghai Gigafactory","text":"FILE PHOTO: Tesla's China chief Tom Zhu speaks at a delivery ceremony for China-made Tesla Model 3 vehicles in the Shanghai Gigafactory of the US electric car maker in Shanghai, China December 30, 2019. [Photo/Xinhua]

Tom Zhu has delivered for Tesla in China, and now Elon Musk has moved him into the No 2 spot at the electric-vehicle maker.
Described as a hard worker who keeps a low profile, Zhu has been promoted to take direct oversight of the automaker's US assembly plants as well as sales operations in North America and Europe, according to Reuters.
Zhu, who was born in China but now holds a New Zealand passport, joined Tesla in 2014. He previously was a project manager at a company started by his MBA classmates at Duke University, advising Chinese contractors who were working on infrastructure projects in Africa.
According to Zhu's social media accounts, he earned a bachelor's degree from the Auckland University of Technology in 2004 and an MBA from the Fuqua School of Business at Duke University.
The Tesla internal posting showed that Zhu's title of vice-president for Greater China had not changed and that he also kept his responsibilities as Tesla's most senior executive for sales in the rest of Asia, as of Jan 3. The move makes Zhu the highest-profile executive at Tesla after CEO Musk.
Reuters reviewed the organizational chart that had been posted internally by Tesla and confirmed the change with two people who had seen it.
"Tesla teams led by Tom Zhu have the best world-class executions probably in the history of the world for large manufacturing companies," the Tesla Synopsis account posted on Twitter on Sunday.
"Tom Zhu is the Tim Cook of Tesla," said the Twitter account Big Tesla on Jan 2, comparing him with the Apple CEO.
Zhu and a team of people reporting to him were brought in by Tesla late last year to troubleshoot production issues in the US, fueling an expectation among colleagues then that he was being prepared for a larger role.
Global role
Zhu's appointment to a global role comes while Musk has been occupied by his acquisition of social media platform Twitter, and Tesla analysts and investors have urged action that would bolster the senior executive ranks and allow the multi-billionaire to focus on Tesla.
During Shanghai's lockdown for COVID-19, Zhu was among the first group of employees sleeping in the factory as they worked to keep it running, people who work with him have said.
The Shanghai Gigafactory was built in 10 months in 2019, and it was 65 percent less costly to build than the Model 3 production plant in the US, according to Forbes. A few years later, it became the largest EV production plant in the world.
When Tesla delivered 936,000 vehicles worldwide in 2021, more than half of the vehicles came from the Shanghai factory, it was reported.
Zhu is taking charge of Tesla's main production hubs while the company prepares the launch of Cybertruck and a revamped version of its Model 3 sedan.
"Zhu is a core leader at Tesla and a linchpin to its success, especially in China," Daniel Ives, managing director and senior equity research analyst covering the tech industry at Wedbush Securities, was reported as saying by CNN.
Agencies contributed to this story.","truncated":false}
