Tesla's legal and ownership structure is plain for a founder-led company — one class of stock, a Texas parent with no VIE or dual-class layer, and a CEO who owns 17.7% of the 3,952,648,559 issued shares (19.8% on the proxy's ex-award basis) — so what constrains a 12-month equity return is not the charter but a 10.7% unearned award struck at market capitalisations from $2 trillion upward, no dividend or buyback, and a classified board that minority holders cannot replace. Tesla trades on Nasdaq under TSLA; market capitalisation was $1.58tn at the $399.81 close on 2026-10-30 [S10, S112].

### One operating group, no holding-company layer

The registrant was incorporated in Delaware on 2003-07-01 and converted to a Texas corporation on 2024-06-13. The structure is flat — country operating companies, single-purpose solar and lease vehicles and insurance captives — with no contractual-control or variable-interest layer between legal and economic ownership. No separate IP holding company is disclosed; the parent files consolidated accounts, while the subsidiaries hold the plants, licences and financing books [S1, S58].

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership | Controller | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tesla, Inc. | Texas, US | Listed corporation | Registrant; consolidated group; public equity | 100% of subsidiaries | Board; Musk 17.7% | S1, S58 |
| Tesla (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. | China | Limited liability company | Shanghai vehicle and Megapack plants | 100% | Tesla, Inc. | S1 |
| Tesla Manufacturing Brandenburg SE | Germany | European company | Berlin vehicle plant | 100% | Tesla, Inc. | S1 |

### The award runs through a $2 trillion gate

Musk holds 699,580,882 shares, 17.7% of the issued count, including 286,428,773 unvested 2018-award shares; 207,498,721 are pledged against personal borrowings. The 2018 award was exercised in full on 2026-06-16 for 303,960,630 shares, lifting the count 202m, or 5.4%, in the nine months to 2026-09-30. The 2025 CEO Performance Award adds 423,743,904 shares, 10.7% of the count, in 12 equal tranches, none earned at 2026-10-19; the proxy shows they are already issued and outstanding, voted by irrevocable proxy and excluded from earnings per share until earned, so vesting dilutes earnings and Musk's economic share without issuing new stock. Each earned share carries a $334.09 offset and a five-year hold, and every tranche needs a market-cap milestone before any operating milestone counts, starting at $2 trillion — 26.6% above the 2026-10-30 value — then nine $500bn and two $1tn increments to $8.5 trillion. At $399.81 the gross spread is $65.72 a share; at the top the transfer is $769.6bn net of offsets, 9.1% of an $8.5 trillion capitalisation. The mechanism favours the holder in a flat tape: below $2tn no tranche earns, so no value transfers and no dilution occurs [S10, S8, S107].

### The cap table reconciles on one denominator

The proxy computes beneficial ownership on the 3,952,648,559 shares outstanding at 2026-09-30, adds options exercisable within 60 days to each holder's own percentage, and subtracts the 423,743,904 unearned shares for Musk and the officer-director group, giving a 3,528,904,655 denominator and his 19.8%. It publishes no float figure and does not say how those shares enter a float calculation; the table below is our residual calculation, and the non-insider float including Vanguard is 2,822,408,040 shares, 71.4% of the issued count [S10].

| Holder | Class | Shares | % of issued | % of votes | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Elon Musk | Common | 699,580,882 | 17.7% | 17.7% | S10 |
| Other directors and officers (10 persons) | Common | 6,915,733 | 0.2% | 0.2% | S10 |
| Vanguard Capital Management | Common | 210,796,512 | 5.3% | 5.3% | S10 |
| 2025 award shares, issued but unearned | Common | 423,743,904 | 10.7% | voted proportionally | S10 |
| Other public holders (residual) | Common | 2,611,611,528 | 66.1% | 66.1% | S10 |
| Total issued and outstanding | Common | 3,952,648,559 | 100.0% | 100.0% | S10 |

### Three P&Ls, and capacity ahead of volume

Three P&Ls have different buyers. Automotive ($69.53bn of FY2025 revenue, 73%) sells vehicles to consumers, lessors and fleets and monetises the installed base through Supercharging, service, parts, used cars and insurance; software is FSD (Supervised), with 1.74m active subscriptions at 2026-09-30. Energy ($12.77bn, 13.5%, 29.8% gross margin) sells Megapack and Powerwall to utilities, developers, industrial sites and data-centre operators whose budget is a power-availability capex line. Services ($12.53bn, +19%) is a captive aftermarket on Tesla's own parc. Growth has shifted from volume — Q3 2026 deliveries were 486,532, down 2% year on year — to storage (13.7 GWh in Q3 2026), software attach and Robotaxi and Optimus optionality. Tesla runs eight plants: Fremont (more than 550,000 units), Shanghai (more than 950,000), Berlin (more than 375,000), Texas (Model Y more than 375,000; Cybertruck and Cybercab more than 125,000 each) and Nevada (Semi 25,000), plus Megapack plants in California (40 GWh), Shanghai (20 GWh) and Texas (50 GWh). Headcount was 134,785 at 2025-12-31; nameplate capacity of 2.53m units against an annualised Q3 2026 run rate of 1.95m leaves a fifth of the system idle, while Semi, Cybercab and Optimus lines add depreciation before revenue [S1, S9].

### No payout, and a board that cannot be replaced

Tesla has never paid a dividend, has no repurchase authorisation and made no purchases in FY2025, while holding $45.45bn of cash and short-term investments; with no distribution, a holder's 12-month total return is the share price alone. Governance reinforces retention: three board classes, a 2025 management proposal to remove supermajority voting won 39.4% of shares outstanding and failed, and the 2026-12-03 meeting asks holders only to elect three Class I directors, cast a say-on-pay vote and ratify the auditor. The counter-evidence is real — one share class is cleaner than Rivian's ten-vote Class B, seven of nine directors are independent, the CEO takes no salary — but none of it returns cash or lets a majority change the charter. For a holder at $399.81 the structure offers no cash yield, caps the upside above $2tn by 9.1%, and gives no route to force a change in capital-return policy: that argues for sizing the position as a price-only bet, not for rejecting the equity. Because a minority holder owns an earnings claim and a vote that cannot change the board, the 12-month return is a bet on the share price; the only discipline is the decision to hold or sell. The open question is whether $1.58tn for $94.83bn of revenue and a 16.2% automotive gross margin leaves anything after that gate is crossed [S1, S10, S114].

arguments.markdown:
Tesla is winning the market that is shrinking and losing the one that is growing. It holds the US electric-vehicle market at a share no rival approaches while that market contracts, ranks fourth among China's new-energy brands in a pool that is itself shrinking, and its European recovery has come inside a pool growing faster than it. What Tesla owns is narrower than the narrative: the charging standard every major automaker has licensed, 1.74 million paid FSD subscriptions, and a storage business whose 33.1% reported gross margin falls to 14.8% once $526 million of tariff refunds and warranty true-ups are removed — mid-pack against CATL and Sungrow, not ahead of them [S8, S9, S167].

### In the United States, Tesla sets the price because it holds the pool

Tesla sold 144,094 US electric vehicles in Q3 2026 for 54% of the market, and 386,194 in nine months for 52.9%, with its own US volume down 14.4% against a market down 30.3%. Share gains inside a contracting pool flatter the position: absolute US revenue is smaller than in 2025. When a $7,500 credit disappears, the brand with the densest charging footprint keeps the remaining buyers. The competitive question is not who takes US share from Tesla but whether Tesla can hold price, and it has — automotive gross margin rose to 18.5% in Q3 2026 from 17.0% while regulatory-credit revenue fell 73% to $113 million [S145, S8].

### China is where Tesla is the price taker

BYD sold 456,713 passenger cars in September 2026, 273,143 of them battery-electric, and 3,078,490 in nine months — 2.3 times Tesla's 1,324,681. Geely sold 119,682 retail units, Leapmotor 78,202 and Xiaomi 40,015 in September. BYD earned 19.46% gross margin overseas against 16.66% at home in 2025, a revealed domestic ceiling Tesla cannot price above without losing volume; Tesla's China retail of 64,837 was 3.8 times smaller than BYD's in September while Chinese battery-electric wholesale grew 18.3%. In driver assistance, Huawei and Momenta together supply more than 80% of China's urban NOA systems, Momenta alone 65% [S138, S146, S149, S168].

### Europe: growth in units, no evidence of share

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,931,465 in January-September 2026 at a 22.7% share, with September at 29.9%, so the pool expanded 49% while Tesla's European deliveries recovered from a 2025 slump. A recovery off a collapsed base inside a pool growing that fast is not share gain; Tesla discloses no EU unit count, and ACEA's manufacturer table would settle it. Buyers choose between compliance models from Volkswagen, Renault, Stellantis and Hyundai-Kia and tariffed Chinese BEVs that still undercut on price. Tesla's handicap is a two-model line-up: Model 3/Y were 478,237 of 486,532 deliveries in Q3 2026 [S140, S147].

### Storage: integration, not a cost moat

The 33.1% energy gross margin Tesla reported for Q3 2026 is not comparable with an integrator's clean number: $526 million of IEEPA tariff refunds and warranty true-ups sit inside cost of revenue, so the underlying margin is $428 million on $2,881 million, or 14.8%. On that basis Tesla is mid-pack: Fluence earned 13.1% in fiscal 2025 and 5.1% in the June 2026 quarter, CATL's energy-storage segment 23.96% in H1 2026, Sungrow's storage segment 32.43%, and LG Energy Solution a 1.5% operating margin in Q2 2026 [S8, S9, S61, S66, S167, S166, S172, S169]. Integration does not show up as a margin outlier, and revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million as system prices deflated. The "sixfold" gap to Fluence was an artefact of the refund; what remains is a volume business where Tesla's advantage is software, not cost per kWh.

### In paid autonomy Tesla trails, and in driver assistance it is no longer alone

Waymo ran 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities by March 2026 with about 3,700 vehicles and had logged 220.6 million rider-only miles through March 2026. Tesla began Cybercab rides in Austin on 2026-09-03 and stood at 1,051 vehicles on the Texas authorisation list on 2026-10-27 (544 Cybercab, 507 Model Y), up from 739 on 2026-10-09 on the same list; it reports 2.0 million cumulative unsupervised miles, 0.9% of Waymo's rider-only total, is absent from California's driverless deployment permits, and discloses no ride count or fare. Baidu's Apollo Go ran 3.4 million trips in Q4 2025, up 200%, and Pony.ai passed 1,400 vehicles on 2026-03-25 against a 3,000 target for end-2026. Insurance, remote supervision and cost per paid mile are undisclosed for all three; a 10-20% swing in autonomy value turns on them. The supervised market is not Tesla's either: GM's Super Cruise is hands-free on about 750,000 compatible miles in the US and Canada, Ford's BlueCruise on more than 130,000 Blue Zone miles at Level 2, and comma.ai's openpilot sells aftermarket kits with no OEM fleet. Tesla's 1.74 million FSD subscriptions remain the largest single pool, but hands-free highway driving is now a $40-50 a month OEM feature, which caps what Tesla can charge and explains a 17.1% attach rate [S151, S125, S142, S171, S130, S170].

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| Waymo | Waymo One | Driverless deployment permits in 10 US cities | 500,000 paid rides a week; 220.6m rider-only miles; ~3,700 vehicles | Only scaled US operator | Permits, safety record, $16bn raised | No vehicle manufacturing; city-by-city cost | S151, S142, S130 |
| Baidu / Pony.ai | Apollo Go, Pony robotaxi | Chinese L4 pilot cities | 3.4m Apollo trips in Q4 2025; Pony 1,400+ vehicles in March 2026 | China leaders | Fleet scale; cost per mile | Geofenced, subsidy-dependent | S171 |

::: evidence
**Tesla's defensible positions are the charging standard, FSD subscriptions and storage integration — not vehicle share or a storage cost lead.**

Its 18.5% automotive margin was earned while regulatory credits fell 73%, which says Tesla can hold price in the US; but its energy margin ex-refund (14.8%) sits below CATL's ESS segment (23.96%) and Sungrow's storage segment (32.43%), so the storage cost moat does not survive a like-for-like benchmark. In autonomy, 2.0 million unsupervised miles against Waymo's 220.6 million and no California permit leave the autonomy option the one where Tesla trails most. [S8, S167, S166, S172, S151]

| Weaknesses | Fourth in China at 6.0% of NEV retail; energy gross margin 14.8% ex-refund against CATL's 23.96% and Sungrow's 32.43%; no disclosed EU unit share; no California driverless permit; no robotaxi revenue | S138, S8, S167, S166, S172 |

| Threats | Waymo's 220.6m rider-only miles, ~3,700 vehicles and $16bn raise; BYD exports up 154% to 180,700 in September 2026; Huawei and Momenta over 80% of China urban NOA; hybrids at 36.3% of EU registrations | S151, S146, S168, S140 |
:::

Tesla is a high-margin incumbent in a shrinking US pool, sub-scale in the largest battery-electric market, and a distant challenger to Waymo and Baidu in autonomy. Its wedge — vertical integration, the charging standard and storage software — protects margin rather than volume: underwrite unit growth below the market's and track China retail share, storage revenue per GWh and Texas authorisations.

Tesla closes at $399.81 on NasdaqGS on 2026-10-30, a $1,580.4bn market capitalisation and $1,544.2bn enterprise value; on the businesses its filings describe — cars, storage, services — it is worth $139-160bn, or $35-40 a share. The other $1,420-1,441bn, 90-91% of the equity, rests on robotaxi, FSD and Optimus revenue the quarterly report does not yet book, and the buyer pays 103x trailing adjusted EBITDA for the whole. The reported businesses cannot carry the price; the shares are a claim on a multiple, not earnings [S8, S9].

| Metric | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Last price | $399.81 at 2026-10-30 20:00 UTC, NasdaqGS, USD | S11 |

| Returns | 1M +12.7%, 3M +28.5%, 12M -12.4% against the S&P 500's -0.9%, +1.2%, +10.8% | S11, S20 |
| Liquidity | $13.8bn a day, 20-day average 36.30m shares | S11 |
| Trailing P/E | 439.4x against a peer median of 19.1x | S8, S11, S15 |
| EV/adjusted EBITDA | 103.0x on $14,995m trailing | S9, S11 |
| Free-cash-flow yield | 0.2% on $3,303m trailing | S9, S11 |
| Active FSD subscriptions | 1.74m at 2026-09-30, +67%; company-defined to include about 870k one-time buyers held in deferred revenue and about 870k monthly subscribers | S9, S8, S152, S173 |
| Insider activity, 6 months | no purchases; 19 sales of $13.32m, 17 under 10b5-1 plans | S2 |

### The price pays for a multiple, not for earnings

Trailing revenue is $103.6bn, adjusted EBITDA $15.0bn, operating income $3.47bn and free cash flow $3.3bn after $15.4bn of capital expenditure. That is 445x EV/operating income, a 0.2% free-cash-flow yield and 14.9x sales, against 17.3x EV/EBITDA for BYD and 19.1x earnings for General Motors below. The EBITDA the company prefers adds back $4.3bn of stock compensation, up from $2.8bn in FY2025, so 103x becomes 144x before that add-back. One turn is worth $15.0bn: the price is a rating, and a delay in autonomy compresses the rating, not the earnings. The capital structure has added supply, not raised capital: no external equity since the 2010 IPO; the nine months to 2026-09-30 were funded from $14,897m of operating cash flow, $5,834m of debt and $314m of option proceeds, and 202m new shares lifted the count to 3,953m — $80.8bn of new equity at the closing price [S8, S9, S2].

| Dividends and buybacks | since 2010 | none | no dividend ever declared, no repurchase programme | S1 |

### What the reported businesses are worth

| Method | Inputs | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive and regulatory credits | $75.0bn trailing revenue at 0.6-0.8x EV/sales, above GM and Ford's multiples | $45-60bn | S9, S15, S17 |
| Energy generation and storage | $12.3bn trailing revenue, 30.2% nine-month gross margin, at 2.5-3.0x sales; CATL earns 19.8x | $31-37bn | S9, S133 |
| Services and other | $16.3bn trailing revenue, +32% year on year, at 1.5x sales | $24bn | S9 |
| Net cash at 2026-09-30 | $45,447m cash and short-term investments less $9,267m debt | $36,180m | S8 |
| SpaceX equity stake | $2,002m bought in Q1 2026 plus $863m unrealised gain | $2,865m | S9 |

The split matters more than the total. Energy, the best-margin segment at 33.1% gross, is 12% of trailing revenue and fell 16% year on year as Megapack prices fell; services grew 32% and set a record $734m of gross profit. Neither stretches to a trillion dollars at peer multiples. A generous automotive recovery — 10% operating margin on $75bn at 25x — lifts the total to $288bn, $73 a share, and still leaves 82% of the price unexplained [S9].

### What the price requires by 2030

Inverting the price gives the same answer. The residual $1,441bn, discounted at 10% and valued at 20x 2030 operating income, needs $105bn of 2030 operating income; at 40x, $53bn. At a 25% robotaxi margin and $100,000 of revenue per vehicle-year, that is 2.1-4.2m vehicles by 2030, against 1,051 authorised robotaxis in Texas on 2026-10-27 and 125,000 units of installed Cybercab capacity a year: 17-34 years of factory output and two to four times the one-million-robotaxi milestone the board paired with a $3.5tn market capitalisation [S125, S127]. The ladder is less demanding than the price: the $4.0tn tranche implies 80x, below the 103x the shares carry.

| CATL | 19.8x | n/d | n/d | n/d | S133 |
| Fluence Energy | n/m | n/m | n/m | -14.6% | S61, S62 |

Tesla's own history agrees. The P/E was 34.0x at the end of 2022, 57.8x in 2023, 204.6x in 2024 and 420.8x in 2025 as diluted EPS fell from $4.90 to $1.08, and is 439.4x now; EV/sales, the steadier measure, is 14.9x inside a 14.7-16.5x band, because revenue doubled while the shares returned -0.8% over five years. A 4.93% ten-year Treasury yield, a VIX at its 77th percentile and a 326bp high-yield spread make a 439x earnings multiple harder to hold than it was in 2021 [S11, S12, S22].

### Consensus, guidance and the dates that reset the multiple

Consensus is Hold — 24 buy, 1 strong buy, 20 hold and 3 sell across 48 firms — with an average target of $408.61, 2.2% above the close; an 83-analyst sample gives $442.13, 10.6% above. Targets run from Jefferies at $400 to RBC at $480, and Q3 2026 adjusted EPS was $0.48 against $0.45 expected. Tesla gives no numeric revenue or EPS guidance, promises only "hardware-related profits accompanied by an acceleration of SI, software and fleet-based profits", and cut capital expenditure to about $20bn from more than $25bn. The dates that reset the multiple are the fourth-quarter 2026 results in the last week of January 2027, on the pattern of the FY2025 10-K filed 2026-01-29, the first Cybercab deployment outside Austin, and the SpaceX committee process. The counter-argument is that the premium buys an option that is maturing: 1.74m active FSD subscriptions, an attach rate above 75% of North American deliveries, nearly 2m unsupervised Robotaxi miles, and a fleet that grew from 739 to 1,051 vehicles in eighteen days. The 1.74m is company-sourced, not a recurring-revenue base: free trials are excluded and the CFO put half the paid base on monthly plans on 2026-10-21, so about 870,000 buyers paid once — cash held in $4.08bn of deferred revenue that includes FSD — and about 870,000 pay $99 a month. The "approaching $1 billion" FSD run-rate is therefore arithmetic on the monthly half at US list, about $1.03bn a year, not audited revenue, under 1% of the $103.6bn top line, a ceiling before regional pricing and churn [S9, S8, S152, S173]. If robotaxi unit economics are proven in 2027, 103x on today's EBITDA is a discount to what the business would then earn. The weak version fails — energy caps at $37bn — and no company in the peer table pairs a 30% energy gross margin with 32% services growth above 30x earnings. Confidence in the arithmetic is high, in the multiple's durability low, because durability rests on evidence the company has not disclosed. For a buyer at $399.81 the implication is that the return depends on a re-rating that robotaxi disclosure would have to earn, while the downside is carried by the multiple; on this arithmetic there is no margin of safety in the price, and the three questions that would change that are revenue per robotaxi-week in Austin, the energy segment's operating margin, and whether a capital-return policy ever replaces permanent dilution [S128, S9, S125].

arguments.markdown:
Tesla is winning the market that is shrinking and losing the one that is growing. It holds the US electric-vehicle market at a share no rival approaches while that market contracts, ranks fourth among China's new-energy brands in a pool that is itself shrinking, and its European recovery has come inside a pool growing faster than it. What Tesla owns is narrower than the narrative: the charging standard every major automaker has licensed, 1.74 million paid FSD subscriptions, and a storage business whose 33.1% reported gross margin falls to 14.8% once $526 million of tariff refunds and warranty true-ups are removed — mid-pack against CATL and Sungrow, not ahead of them [S8, S9, S167].

### In the United States, Tesla sets the price because it holds the pool

Tesla sold 144,094 US electric vehicles in Q3 2026 for 54% of the market, and 386,194 in nine months for 52.9%, with its own US volume down 14.4% against a market down 30.3%. Share gains inside a contracting pool flatter the position: absolute US revenue is smaller than in 2025. When a $7,500 credit disappears, the brand with the densest charging footprint keeps the remaining buyers. The question is not who takes US share but whether Tesla can hold price, and it has — automotive gross margin rose to 18.5% in Q3 2026 from 17.0% while regulatory-credit revenue fell 73% to $113 million [S145, S8].

### China is where Tesla is the price taker

BYD sold 456,713 passenger cars in September 2026, 273,143 of them battery-electric, and 3,078,490 in nine months — 2.3 times Tesla's 1,324,681. Geely sold 119,682 retail units, Leapmotor 78,202 and Xiaomi 40,015 in September. BYD earned 19.46% gross margin overseas against 16.66% at home in 2025, a domestic ceiling Tesla cannot price above without losing volume; Tesla's China retail of 64,837 was 3.8 times smaller than BYD's in September while Chinese battery-electric wholesale grew 18.3%. In driver assistance, Huawei and Momenta together supply more than 80% of China's urban NOA systems, Momenta alone 65% [S138, S146, S149, S168].

### Europe: growth in units, no evidence of share

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,931,465 in January-September 2026 at a 22.7% share, with September at 29.9%, so the pool expanded 49% while Tesla's European deliveries recovered from a 2025 slump. A recovery off a collapsed base inside a pool growing that fast is not share gain; Tesla discloses no EU unit count, and ACEA's manufacturer table would settle it. Buyers choose between compliance models from Volkswagen, Renault, Stellantis and Hyundai-Kia and tariffed Chinese BEVs that undercut on price. Tesla's handicap is a two-model line-up: Model 3/Y were 478,237 of 486,532 deliveries in Q3 2026 [S140, S147].

### Storage: integration, not a cost moat

The 33.1% energy gross margin Tesla reported for Q3 2026 is not comparable with an integrator's clean number: $526 million of IEEPA tariff refunds and warranty true-ups sit inside cost of revenue, so the underlying margin is $428 million on $2,881 million, or 14.8%. On that basis Tesla is mid-pack: Fluence earned 13.1% in fiscal 2025 and 5.1% in the June 2026 quarter, CATL's energy-storage segment 23.96% in H1 2026, Sungrow's storage segment 32.43%, and LG Energy Solution a 1.5% operating margin in Q2 2026 [S8, S9, S61, S66, S167, S166, S172, S169]. Integration does not show up as a margin outlier, and revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million as system prices deflated. The "sixfold" gap to Fluence was an artefact of the refund; what remains is a volume business where Tesla's advantage is software, not cost per kWh.

### In paid autonomy Tesla trails, and in driver assistance it is no longer alone

Waymo ran 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities by March 2026 with about 3,700 vehicles and had logged 220.6 million rider-only miles through March 2026. Tesla began Cybercab rides in Austin on 2026-09-03 and stood at 1,051 vehicles on the Texas authorisation list on 2026-10-27 (544 Cybercab, 507 Model Y), up from 739 on 2026-10-09 on the same list; it reports 2.0 million cumulative unsupervised miles, 0.9% of Waymo's rider-only total, is absent from California's driverless deployment permits, and discloses no ride count or fare. Baidu's Apollo Go ran 3.4 million trips in Q4 2025 and Pony.ai passed 1,400 vehicles on 2026-03-25 against a 3,000 year-end target. Insurance, remote supervision and cost per paid mile are undisclosed; a 10-20% swing in autonomy value turns on them. The supervised market is not Tesla's either: GM's Super Cruise is hands-free on about 750,000 compatible miles in the US and Canada, Ford's BlueCruise on more than 130,000 Blue Zone miles at Level 2, and comma.ai's openpilot sells aftermarket kits with no OEM fleet. FSD's 1.74 million subscriptions are the largest single pool, but hands-free highway driving is now a $40-50 a month OEM feature, which caps what Tesla can charge and explains a 17.1% attach rate [S151, S125, S142, S171, S130, S170].

**Tesla's defensible positions are the charging standard, FSD subscriptions and storage integration — not vehicle share or a storage cost lead.**

Its 18.5% automotive margin was earned while regulatory credits fell 73%, which says Tesla can hold price in the US; but its energy margin ex-refund (14.8%) sits below CATL's ESS segment (23.96%) and Sungrow's storage segment (32.43%), so the storage cost moat does not survive a like-for-like benchmark. In autonomy, 2.0 million unsupervised miles against Waymo's 220.6 million and no California permit leave the autonomy option the one where Tesla trails most. [S8, S167, S166, S172, S151]

Tesla is a high-margin incumbent in a shrinking US pool, sub-scale in the largest battery-electric market, and a distant challenger to Waymo and Baidu in autonomy. Nine directors sit on the board, seven of them independent under Nasdaq rules, with Robyn Denholm as independent chair since November 2018 and all four committees composed solely of independents. At the 2025-11-06 meeting shareholders approved the pay award with 1,892,235,822 votes for and 564,940,908 against, 76.6% of votes cast. arguments.markdown:
Tesla is winning the market that is shrinking and losing the one that is growing. It holds the US electric-vehicle market at a share no rival approaches while that market contracts, ranks fourth among China's new-energy brands in a pool that is itself shrinking, and its European recovery has come inside a pool growing faster than it. What Tesla owns is narrower than the narrative: the charging standard every major automaker has licensed, 1.74 million paid FSD subscriptions, and a storage business whose 33.1% reported gross margin falls to 14.8% once $526 million of tariff refunds and warranty true-ups are removed — mid-pack against CATL and Sungrow, not ahead of them [S8, S9, S167].

### In the United States, Tesla sets the price because it holds the pool

Tesla sold 144,094 US electric vehicles in Q3 2026 for 54% of the market, and 386,194 in nine months for 52.9%, with its own US volume down 14.4% against a market down 30.3%. Share gains inside a contracting pool flatter the position: absolute US revenue is smaller than in 2025. When a $7,500 credit disappears, the brand with the densest charging footprint keeps the remaining buyers. The question is whether Tesla can hold price, and it has — automotive gross margin rose to 18.5% in Q3 2026 from 17.0% while regulatory-credit revenue fell 73% to $113 million [S145, S8].

### China is where Tesla is the price taker

BYD sold 456,713 passenger cars in September 2026, 273,143 of them battery-electric, and 3,078,490 in nine months — 2.3 times Tesla's 1,324,681. Geely sold 119,682 retail units, Leapmotor 78,202 and Xiaomi 40,015 in September. BYD earned 19.46% gross margin overseas against 16.66% at home in 2025, a domestic ceiling Tesla cannot price above; Tesla's China retail of 64,837 was 3.8 times smaller than BYD's in September while Chinese battery-electric wholesale grew 18.3%. In driver assistance, Huawei and Momenta together supply more than 80% of China's urban NOA systems, Momenta alone 65% [S138, S146, S149, S168].

### Europe: growth in units, no evidence of share

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,931,465 in January-September 2026 at a 22.7% share, with September at 29.9%, so the pool expanded 49% while Tesla's European deliveries recovered from a 2025 slump. A recovery off a collapsed base inside a pool growing that fast is not share gain; Tesla discloses no EU unit count, and ACEA's manufacturer table would settle it. Buyers choose between compliance models from Volkswagen, Renault, Stellantis and Hyundai-Kia and tariffed Chinese BEVs that undercut. Tesla's handicap is a two-model line-up: Model 3/Y were 478,237 of 486,532 deliveries in Q3 2026 [S140, S147].

### Storage: integration, not a cost moat

The 33.1% energy gross margin Tesla reported for Q3 2026 is not comparable with an integrator's clean number: $526 million of IEEPA tariff refunds and warranty true-ups sit inside cost of revenue, so the underlying margin is $428 million on $2,881 million, or 14.8%. On that basis Tesla is mid-pack: Fluence earned 13.1% in fiscal 2025 and 5.1% in the June 2026 quarter, CATL's energy-storage segment 23.96% in H1 2026, Sungrow's storage segment 32.43%, and LG Energy Solution a 1.5% operating margin in Q2 2026 [S8, S9, S61, S66, S167, S166, S172, S169]. Integration does not show up as a margin outlier, and revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million as system prices deflated. The "sixfold" gap to Fluence was an artefact of the refund; what remains is a volume business where Tesla's advantage is software, not cost per kWh.

### In paid autonomy Tesla trails, and in driver assistance it is no longer alone

Waymo ran 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities by March 2026 with about 3,700 vehicles and had logged 220.6 million rider-only miles through March 2026. Tesla began Cybercab rides in Austin on 2026-09-03 and stood at 1,051 vehicles on the Texas authorisation list on 2026-10-27 (544 Cybercab, 507 Model Y), up from 739 on 2026-10-09 on the same list; it reports 2.0 million cumulative unsupervised miles, 0.9% of Waymo's rider-only total, is absent from California's driverless deployment permits, and discloses no ride count or fare. Baidu's Apollo Go ran 3.4 million trips in Q4 2025 and Pony.ai passed 1,400 vehicles on 2026-03-25 against a 3,000 year-end target. Insurance, teleoperation and cost per paid mile are undisclosed; a 10-20% swing in autonomy value turns on them. The supervised market is not Tesla's either: GM's Super Cruise is hands-free on about 750,000 compatible miles in the US and Canada, Ford's BlueCruise on more than 130,000 Blue Zone miles at Level 2, and comma.ai's openpilot sells aftermarket kits with no OEM fleet. FSD's 1.74 million subscriptions are the largest single pool, but hands-free highway driving is now a $40-50 a month OEM feature, which caps what Tesla can charge and explains a 17.1% attach rate [S151, S125, S142, S171, S130, S170].

::: evidence
**Tesla's defensible positions are the charging standard, FSD subscriptions and storage integration — not vehicle share or a storage cost lead.**

Its 18.5% automotive margin was earned while regulatory credits fell 73%, which says Tesla can hold price in the US; but its energy margin ex-refund (14.8%) sits below CATL's ESS segment (23.96%) and Sungrow's storage segment (32.43%), so the storage cost moat does not survive a like-for-like benchmark. In autonomy, 2.0 million unsupervised miles against Waymo's 220.6 million and no California permit leave the autonomy option the one where Tesla trails most. [S8, S167, S166, S172, S151]
:::

::: quad
| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | 52.9% US EV share in 9M 2026; 1.74m active FSD subscriptions; 18.5% automotive gross margin with credits down 73%; NACS licensing; 36.0 GWh storage in 9M 2026 | S8, S9, S145 |
| Weaknesses | Fourth in China at 6.0% of NEV retail; energy gross margin 14.8% ex-refund against CATL's 23.96% and Sungrow's 32.43%; no disclosed EU unit share; no California driverless permit; no robotaxi revenue | S138, S8, S167, S166, S172 |
| Opportunities | 459 GWh global storage pool in 2026; Texas authorisations up from 739 to 1,051 in 18 days; EU BEV registrations up 49% year on year | S141, S125, S147 |
| Threats | Waymo's 220.6m rider-only miles, ~3,700 vehicles and $16bn raise; BYD exports up 154% to 180,700 in September 2026; Huawei and Momenta over 80% of China urban NOA; hybrids at 36.3% of EU registrations | S151, S146, S168, S140 |
:::

Tesla is a high-margin incumbent in a shrinking US pool, sub-scale in the largest battery-electric market, and a distant challenger to Waymo and Baidu in autonomy. Its wedge — vertical integration, the charging standard and storage software — protects margin rather than volume: underwrite unit growth below the market's and track China retail share, storage revenue per GWh and Texas authorisations.

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's board is majority independent on paper, but the three decisions that mattered in 2024-2026 — a $2.0bn investment in the CEO's own AI company after shareholders rejected the measure, a pay award that can reach 423.7m shares, and the retention of a classified board — all went against the minority's expressed preference, so key-person and capital-allocation risk are real, disclosed, and only partly offset by the award's extreme vesting gates [S10].

### Independence is not the same as accountability

Nine directors sit, seven independent under Nasdaq rules, with Robyn Denholm as independent chair since November 2018 and all four committees independent-only. What matters is elsewhere: three staggered classes, supermajority voting requirements a 2025 management proposal failed to remove with 39.4% of shares outstanding in favour, and two family directors — Elon and Kimbal Musk. Compensation Committee chair Ira Ehrenpreis has also served on SpaceX's board since February 2026, the counterparty to Tesla's $2.0bn investment and $143.3m of 2025 revenue, a relationship the proxy calls immaterial [S10].

### Pay is gated on market value, not on operating return

The 2025 CEO Performance Award is 423,743,904 shares in 12 equal tranches. Each tranche needs a market-cap milestone first — from $2 trillion, 26.6% above the 2026-10-30 value, through nine $500bn and two $1tn steps to $8.5 trillion — and one of 12 operating milestones: four product goals (10m FSD subscriptions, 1m bots delivered, 1m Robotaxis in commercial operation) or eight Adjusted EBITDA goals. Each earned share carries a $334.09 offset and a five-year hold, and tranches 11 and 12 also require a board-approved CEO succession framework, the only formal succession mechanism disclosed. Against that, GM paid Mary Barra $48.2m of realized pay in 2025, while Musk has taken no salary since 2019 and has no employment agreement or severance; reported 2025 total compensation of $158.36bn was an accounting value, realized pay $0 [S10, S107, S109].

### The xAI vote is the test the board failed

At the 2025-11-06 meeting shareholders approved the pay award with 1,892,235,822 votes for and 564,940,908 against, 76.6% of votes cast. A non-binding measure authorising funding for xAI drew 1.06bn for and 916.3m against but was recorded as rejected because Tesla's bylaws count abstentions as votes against; on 2026-01-16 the company nonetheless agreed to invest $2.0bn in xAI, converted to SpaceX Class A stock on 2026-03-12 after the merger. The Audit Committee reviews related-person transactions above $120,000 under a written policy, but the sequence shows the review is procedural: a holder should assume future flows to Musk-controlled companies are a board decision, not a shareholder one [S59, S104, S105].

### One person carries the strategy; the bench is uneven

The 10-K says Musk "does not devote his full time and attention to Tesla" and lists roles at SpaceX, xAI, Neuralink and The Boring Company; the proxy records that xAI became a SpaceX subsidiary in February 2026 and that Musk is SpaceX's CEO, CTO and chairman. The operating bench is strongest in manufacturing and finance: Tom Zhu, SVP APAC and global vehicle manufacturing since June 2025, joined in 2014 and built Gigafactory Shanghai; Vaibhav Taneja has been CFO since August 2023 and inside Tesla's finance function since 2017. Demand execution is the weak spot: Omead Afshar left in June 2025, Troy Jones was dismissed as North American sales head in July 2025, the service head left in August 2025 and Raj Jegannathan departed in February 2026 after 13 years. Headcount was 134,785 at 2025-12-31; the attrition is concentrated in senior commercial roles [S1, S111, S124].

### What the record confirms, and what diligence must settle

Public records confirm founder-market fit: Musk co-founded Zip2 (sold to Compaq in 1999) and PayPal (sold to eBay in 2002), has run Tesla since October 2008, and still owns 17.7% of the issued count (19.8% on the proxy's basis) with 207,498,721 shares pledged. They also confirm the concentration: no chief operating officer, no permanent North American sales leader, a board with no director who has run a vehicle programme at another OEM, and a CEO whose other companies are now suppliers, investees and counterparties. Diligence should close the succession plan behind tranches 11-12, the lenders behind the pledge, the fairness opinion, if any, for the $2.0bn xAI/SpaceX purchase, and references on Zhu and Taneja. For a 12-month holder the concentration is not a separately observable discount in the share price: it argues for a smaller position and for demanding evidence that Zhu and Taneja can run the operating business while Musk is elsewhere [S10, S2].

::: evidence
**Execution is proven in manufacturing, not the boardroom: Shanghai ramped while a related-party investment proceeded after shareholders rejected it.**

Tom Zhu built Gigafactory Shanghai, the largest plant at more than 950,000 units, and Berlin set a quarterly production record in Q3 2026; Tesla passed 10.2m cumulative vehicles. The counterweight is procedural: an xAI funding measure lost 1.06bn to 916.3m, yet $2.0bn was committed five weeks later, and the Compensation Committee chair sits on SpaceX's board (S9, S104, S10).
:::

arguments.markdown:
Tesla is winning the market that is shrinking and losing the one that is growing. It holds the US electric-vehicle market at a share no rival approaches while that market contracts, ranks fourth among China's new-energy brands in a pool that is itself shrinking, and its European recovery has come inside a pool growing faster than it. What Tesla owns is narrower than the narrative: the charging standard every major automaker has licensed, 1.74 million paid FSD subscriptions, and a storage business whose 33.1% reported gross margin falls to 14.8% once $526 million of tariff refunds and warranty true-ups are removed — mid-pack against CATL and Sungrow, not ahead of them [S8, S9, S167].

### In the United States, Tesla sets the price because it holds the pool

Tesla sold 144,094 US electric vehicles in Q3 2026 for 54% of the market, and 386,194 in nine months for 52.9%, with US volume down 14.4% against a market down 30.3%. Share gains inside a contracting pool flatter the position: absolute US revenue is smaller than in 2025. When a $7,500 credit disappears, the brand with the densest charging footprint keeps the remaining buyers. The question is whether Tesla can hold price, and it has — automotive gross margin rose to 18.5% in Q3 2026 from 17.0% while regulatory-credit revenue fell 73% to $113 million [S145, S8].

### China is where Tesla is the price taker

BYD sold 456,713 passenger cars in September 2026, 273,143 of them battery-electric, and 3,078,490 in nine months — 2.3 times Tesla's 1,324,681. Geely sold 119,682 retail units, Leapmotor 78,202 and Xiaomi 40,015 in September. BYD earned 19.46% gross margin overseas against 16.66% at home in 2025, a domestic ceiling Tesla cannot price above; Tesla's China retail of 64,837 was 3.8 times smaller than BYD's in September while Chinese battery-electric wholesale grew 18.3%. In driver assistance, Huawei and Momenta together supply more than 80% of China's urban NOA systems, Momenta alone 65% [S138, S146, S149, S168].

### Europe: growth in units, no evidence of share

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,931,465 in January-September 2026 at a 22.7% share, with September at 29.9%, so the pool expanded 49% while Tesla's European deliveries recovered from a 2025 slump. A recovery off a collapsed base inside a pool growing that fast is not share gain; Tesla discloses no EU unit count, and ACEA's manufacturer table would settle it. Buyers choose between compliance models from Volkswagen, Renault, Stellantis and Hyundai-Kia and tariffed Chinese BEVs that undercut. Tesla's handicap is a two-model line-up: Model 3/Y were 478,237 of 486,532 deliveries in Q3 2026 [S140, S147].

### Storage: integration, not a cost moat

The 33.1% energy gross margin Tesla reported for Q3 2026 is not comparable with an integrator's clean number: $526 million of IEEPA tariff refunds and warranty true-ups sit inside cost of revenue, so the underlying margin is $428 million on $2,881 million, or 14.8%. On that basis Tesla is mid-pack: Fluence earned 13.1% in fiscal 2025 and 5.1% in the June 2026 quarter, CATL's energy-storage segment 23.96% in H1 2026, Sungrow's storage segment 32.43%, and LG Energy Solution a 1.5% operating margin in Q2 2026 [S8, S9, S61, S66, S167, S166, S172, S169]. Integration does not show up as a margin outlier, and revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million as system prices deflated. The "sixfold" gap to Fluence was an artefact of the refund; what remains is a volume business where Tesla's advantage is software, not cost per kWh.

### In paid autonomy Tesla trails, and in driver assistance it is no longer alone

Waymo ran 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities by March 2026 with about 3,700 vehicles and had logged 220.6 million rider-only miles through March 2026. Tesla began Cybercab rides in Austin on 2026-09-03 and stood at 1,051 vehicles on the Texas authorisation list on 2026-10-27 (544 Cybercab, 507 Model Y), up from 739 on 2026-10-09 on the same list; it reports 2.0 million cumulative unsupervised miles, 0.9% of Waymo's rider-only total, is absent from California's driverless deployment permits, and discloses no ride count or fare. Baidu's Apollo Go ran 3.4 million trips in Q4 2025 and Pony.ai passed 1,400 vehicles on 2026-03-25 against a 3,000 year-end target. Insurance, teleoperation and cost per paid mile are undisclosed; a 10-20% swing in autonomy value turns on them. The supervised market is not Tesla's either: GM's Super Cruise is hands-free on about 750,000 compatible miles in the US and Canada, Ford's BlueCruise on more than 130,000 Blue Zone miles at Level 2, and comma.ai's openpilot sells aftermarket kits with no OEM fleet. FSD's 1.74 million subscriptions are the largest single pool, but hands-free highway driving is now a $40-50 a month OEM feature, which caps what Tesla can charge and explains a 17.1% attach rate [S151, S125, S142, S171, S130, S170].

| Paid robotaxi (challenger) | Waymo (500,000 rides a week) | Baidu Apollo Go (3.4m trips in Q4 2025) | Pony.ai, WeRide | Tesla (1,051 Texas vehicles) | S151, S171, S125 |

::: evidence
**Tesla's defensible positions are the charging standard, FSD subscriptions and storage integration — not vehicle share or a storage cost lead.**

Its 18.5% automotive margin was earned while regulatory credits fell 73%, which says Tesla can hold price in the US; but its energy margin ex-refund (14.8%) sits below CATL's ESS segment (23.96%) and Sungrow's storage segment (32.43%), so the storage cost moat does not survive a like-for-like benchmark. In autonomy, 2.0 million unsupervised miles against Waymo's 220.6 million and no California permit leave the autonomy option the one where Tesla trails most. [S8, S167, S166, S172, S151]
:::

| Weaknesses | Fourth in China at 6.0% of NEV retail; energy gross margin 14.8% ex-refund against CATL's 23.96% and Sungrow's 32.43%; no disclosed EU unit share; no California driverless permit; no robotaxi revenue | S138, S8, S167, S166, S172 |
| Opportunities | 459 GWh global storage pool in 2026; Texas authorisations up from 739 to 1,051 in 18 days; EU BEV registrations up 49% year on year | S141, S125, S147 |
| Threats | Waymo's 220.6m rider-only miles, ~3,700 vehicles and $16bn raise; BYD exports up 154% to 180,700 in September 2026; Huawei and Momenta over 80% of China urban NOA; hybrids at 36.3% of EU registrations | S151, S146, S168, S140 |
:::

Tesla is a high-margin incumbent in a shrinking US pool, sub-scale in the largest battery-electric market, and a distant challenger to Waymo and Baidu in autonomy. Its wedge — vertical integration, the charging standard and storage software — protects margin rather than volume: underwrite unit growth below the market's and track China retail share, storage revenue per GWh and Texas authorisations.

The autonomy half needs a permit and a positive-contribution P&L; the merger half needs two boards, an exchange ratio and 50% of all shares. A 30% combined weight is defensible; the 15% autonomy leg is the more generous of the two.
The base is not too bearish. It applies 70x to $14.5bn of adjusted EBITDA — four times BYD's 17.3x — and still lands at $266, -33.5%, because 70x is itself an autonomy multiple. arguments.markdown:
Tesla's board is majority independent on paper, but the three decisions that mattered in 2024-2026 — a $2.0bn investment in the CEO's own AI company after shareholders rejected the measure, a pay award that can reach 423.7m shares, and the retention of a classified board — all went against the minority's expressed preference, so key-person and capital-allocation risk are real, disclosed, and only partly offset by the award's extreme vesting gates [S10].

### Independence is not the same as accountability

Nine directors sit, seven independent under Nasdaq rules, with Robyn Denholm as independent chair since November 2018 and all four committees independent-only. What matters is elsewhere: three staggered classes, supermajority voting requirements a 2025 management proposal failed to remove with 39.4% of shares outstanding in favour, and two family directors — Elon and Kimbal Musk. Compensation Committee chair Ira Ehrenpreis has also served on SpaceX's board since February 2026, the counterparty to Tesla's $2.0bn investment and $143.3m of 2025 revenue, a relationship the proxy calls immaterial [S10].

### Pay is gated on market value, not on operating return

The 2025 CEO Performance Award is 423,743,904 shares in 12 equal tranches. Each tranche needs a market-cap milestone first — from $2 trillion, 26.6% above the 2026-10-30 value, through nine $500bn and two $1tn steps to $8.5 trillion — and one of 12 operating milestones: four product goals (10m FSD subscriptions, 1m bots delivered, 1m Robotaxis in commercial operation) or eight Adjusted EBITDA goals. Each earned share carries a $334.09 offset and a five-year hold, and tranches 11 and 12 also require a board-approved CEO succession framework, the only formal succession mechanism disclosed. Against that, GM paid Mary Barra $48.2m of realized pay in 2025, while Musk has taken no salary since 2019 and has no employment agreement or severance; reported 2025 total compensation of $158.36bn was an accounting value, realized pay $0 [S10, S107, S109].

### The xAI vote is the test the board failed

At the 2025-11-06 meeting shareholders approved the pay award with 1,892,235,822 votes for and 564,940,908 against, 76.6% of votes cast. A non-binding measure authorising funding for xAI drew 1.06bn for and 916.3m against but was recorded as rejected because Tesla's bylaws count abstentions as votes against; on 2026-01-16 the company nonetheless agreed to invest $2.0bn in xAI, converted to SpaceX Class A stock on 2026-03-12 after the merger. The Audit Committee reviews related-person transactions above $120,000 under a written policy, but the sequence shows the review is procedural: a holder should assume future flows to Musk-controlled companies are a board decision, not a shareholder one [S59, S104, S105].

### One person carries the strategy; the bench is uneven

The 10-K says Musk "does not devote his full time and attention to Tesla" and lists roles at SpaceX, xAI, Neuralink and The Boring Company; the proxy records that xAI became a SpaceX subsidiary in February 2026 and that Musk is SpaceX's CEO, CTO and chairman. The operating bench is strongest in manufacturing and finance: Tom Zhu, SVP APAC and global vehicle manufacturing since June 2025, joined in 2014 and built Gigafactory Shanghai; Vaibhav Taneja has been CFO since August 2023 and inside Tesla's finance function since 2017. Demand execution is the weak spot: Omead Afshar left in June 2025, Troy Jones was dismissed as North American sales head in July 2025, the service head left in August 2025 and Raj Jegannathan departed in February 2026 after 13 years. Headcount was 134,785 at 2025-12-31; the attrition is concentrated in senior commercial roles [S1, S111, S124].

### What the record confirms, and what diligence must settle

Public records confirm founder-market fit: Musk co-founded Zip2 (sold to Compaq in 1999) and PayPal (sold to eBay in 2002), has run Tesla since October 2008, and still owns 17.7% of the issued count (19.8% on the proxy's basis) with 207,498,721 shares pledged. They also confirm the concentration: no chief operating officer, no permanent North American sales leader, a board with no director who has run a vehicle programme at another OEM, and a CEO whose other companies are now suppliers, investees and counterparties. Diligence should close the succession plan behind tranches 11-12, the lenders behind the pledge, the fairness opinion, if any, for the $2.0bn xAI/SpaceX purchase, and references on Zhu and Taneja. For a 12-month holder the concentration is not a separately observable discount in the share price: it argues for a smaller position and for demanding evidence that Zhu and Taneja can run the operating business while Musk is elsewhere [S10, S2].

::: evidence
**Execution is proven in manufacturing, not the boardroom: Shanghai ramped while a related-party investment proceeded after shareholders rejected it.**

Tom Zhu built Gigafactory Shanghai, the largest plant at more than 950,000 units, and Berlin set a quarterly production record in Q3 2026; Tesla passed 10.2m cumulative vehicles. The counterweight is procedural: an xAI funding measure lost 1.06bn to 916.3m, yet $2.0bn was committed five weeks later, and the Compensation Committee chair sits on SpaceX's board (S9, S104, S10).
:::

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's board is majority independent on paper, but the three decisions that mattered in 2024-2026 — a $2.0bn investment in the CEO's own AI company after shareholders rejected the measure, a pay award that can reach 423.7m shares, and the retention of a classified board — all went against the minority's expressed preference, so key-person and capital-allocation risk are real, disclosed, and only partly offset by the award's extreme vesting gates [S10].

### Independence is not the same as accountability

Nine directors sit, seven independent under Nasdaq rules, with Robyn Denholm as independent chair since November 2018 and all four committees independent-only. What matters is elsewhere: three staggered classes, supermajority voting requirements a 2025 management proposal failed to remove with 39.4% of shares outstanding in favour, and two family directors — Elon and Kimbal Musk. Compensation Committee chair Ira Ehrenpreis has also served on SpaceX's board since February 2026, the counterparty to Tesla's $2.0bn investment and $143.3m of 2025 revenue, a relationship the proxy calls immaterial [S10].

### Pay is gated on market value, not on operating return

The 2025 CEO Performance Award is 423,743,904 shares in 12 equal tranches. Each tranche needs a market-cap milestone first — from $2 trillion, 26.6% above the 2026-10-30 value, through nine $500bn and two $1tn steps to $8.5 trillion — and one of 12 operating milestones: four product goals (10m FSD subscriptions, 1m bots delivered, 1m Robotaxis in commercial operation) or eight Adjusted EBITDA goals. Each earned share carries a $334.09 offset and a five-year hold, and tranches 11 and 12 also require a board-approved CEO succession framework, the only formal succession mechanism disclosed. Against that, GM paid Mary Barra $48.2m of realized pay in 2025, while Musk has taken no salary since 2019 and has no employment agreement or severance; reported 2025 total compensation of $158.36bn was an accounting value, realized pay $0 [S10, S107, S109].

### The xAI vote is the test the board failed

At the 2025-11-06 meeting shareholders approved the pay award with 1,892,235,822 votes for and 564,940,908 against, 76.6% of votes cast. A non-binding measure authorising funding for xAI drew 1.06bn for and 916.3m against but was recorded as rejected because Tesla's bylaws count abstentions as votes against; on 2026-01-16 the company nonetheless agreed to invest $2.0bn in xAI, converted to SpaceX Class A stock on 2026-03-12 after the merger. The Audit Committee reviews related-person transactions above $120,000 under a written policy, but the sequence shows the review is procedural: a holder should assume future flows to Musk-controlled companies are a board decision, not a shareholder one [S59, S104, S105].

### One person carries the strategy; the bench is uneven

The 10-K says Musk "does not devote his full time and attention to Tesla" and lists roles at SpaceX, xAI, Neuralink and The Boring Company; the proxy records that xAI became a SpaceX subsidiary in February 2026 and that Musk is SpaceX's CEO, CTO and chairman. The operating bench is strongest in manufacturing and finance: Tom Zhu, SVP APAC and global vehicle manufacturing since June 2025, joined in 2014 and built Gigafactory Shanghai; Vaibhav Taneja has been CFO since August 2023 and inside Tesla's finance function since 2017. Demand execution is the weak spot: Omead Afshar left in June 2025, Troy Jones was dismissed as North American sales head in July 2025, the service head left in August 2025 and Raj Jegannathan departed in February 2026 after 13 years. Headcount was 134,785 at 2025-12-31; the attrition is concentrated in senior commercial roles [S1, S111, S124].

### What the record confirms, and what diligence must settle

Public records confirm founder-market fit: Musk co-founded Zip2 (sold to Compaq in 1999) and PayPal (sold to eBay in 2002), has run Tesla since October 2008, and still owns 17.7% of the issued count (19.8% on the proxy's basis) with 207,498,721 shares pledged. They also confirm the concentration: no chief operating officer, no permanent North American sales leader, a board with no director who has run a vehicle programme at another OEM, and a CEO whose other companies are now suppliers, investees and counterparties. Diligence should close the succession plan behind tranches 11-12, the lenders behind the pledge, the fairness opinion, if any, for the $2.0bn xAI/SpaceX purchase, and references on Zhu and Taneja. For a 12-month holder the concentration is not a separately observable discount in the share price: it argues for a smaller position and for demanding evidence that Zhu and Taneja can run the operating business while Musk is elsewhere [S10, S2].

::: evidence
**Execution is proven in manufacturing, not the boardroom: Shanghai ramped while a related-party investment proceeded after shareholders rejected it.**

Tom Zhu built Gigafactory Shanghai, the largest plant at more than 950,000 units, and Berlin set a quarterly production record in Q3 2026; Tesla passed 10.2m cumulative vehicles. The counterweight is procedural: an xAI funding measure lost 1.06bn to 916.3m, yet $2.0bn was committed five weeks later, and the Compensation Committee chair sits on SpaceX's board (S9, S104, S10).
:::

arguments.markdown:
Tesla is winning the market that is shrinking and losing the one that is growing. It holds the US electric-vehicle market at a share no rival approaches while that market contracts, ranks fourth among China's new-energy brands in a pool that is itself shrinking, and its European recovery has come inside a pool growing faster than it. What Tesla owns is narrower than the narrative: the charging standard every major automaker has licensed, 1.74 million paid FSD subscriptions, and a storage business whose 33.1% reported gross margin falls to 14.8% once $526 million of tariff refunds and warranty true-ups are removed — mid-pack against CATL and Sungrow, not ahead of them [S8, S9, S167].

### In the United States, Tesla sets the price because it holds the pool

Tesla sold 144,094 US electric vehicles in Q3 2026 for 54% of the market, and 386,194 in nine months for 52.9%, with US volume down 14.4% against a market down 30.3%. Share gains inside a contracting pool flatter the position: absolute US revenue is smaller. When a $7,500 credit disappears, the brand with the densest charging footprint keeps the remaining buyers. The question is whether Tesla can hold price, and it has — automotive gross margin rose to 18.5% in Q3 2026 from 17.0% [S145, S8].

### China is where Tesla is the price taker

BYD sold 456,713 passenger cars in September 2026, 273,143 of them battery-electric, and 3,078,490 in nine months — 2.3 times Tesla's 1,324,681. Geely sold 119,682 and Xiaomi 40,015 retail units in September. BYD earned 19.46% gross margin overseas against 16.66% at home in 2025, a domestic ceiling Tesla cannot price above; Tesla's China retail of 64,837 was 3.8 times smaller than BYD's in September while Chinese battery-electric wholesale grew 18.3%. In driver assistance, Huawei and Momenta together supply more than 80% of China's urban NOA systems, Momenta alone 65% [S138, S146, S149, S168].

### Europe: growth in units, no evidence of share

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,931,465 in January-September 2026 at a 22.7% share, with September at 29.9%, so the pool expanded 49% while Tesla's European deliveries recovered from a 2025 slump. A recovery off a collapsed base inside a pool growing that fast is not share gain; Tesla discloses no EU unit count, and ACEA's manufacturer table would settle it. Volkswagen, Renault, Stellantis and Hyundai-Kia sell compliance models, and tariffed Chinese BEVs undercut. Tesla's handicap is a two-model line-up: Model 3/Y were 478,237 of 486,532 deliveries in Q3 2026 [S140, S147].

### Storage: integration, not a cost moat

The 33.1% energy gross margin Tesla reported for Q3 2026 is not comparable with an integrator's clean number: $526 million of IEEPA tariff refunds and warranty true-ups sit inside cost of revenue, so the underlying margin is $428 million on $2,881 million, or 14.8%. On that basis Tesla is mid-pack: Fluence earned 13.1% in fiscal 2025 and 5.1% in the June 2026 quarter, CATL's energy-storage segment 23.96% in H1 2026, Sungrow's storage segment 32.43%, and LG Energy Solution a 1.5% operating margin in Q2 2026 [S8, S9, S61, S66, S167, S166, S172, S169]. Integration does not show up as a margin outlier, and revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million as system prices deflated. The counter-evidence to the margin reset is scale: 36.0 GWh in nine months and Autobidder dispatch may still give Tesla the lowest installed cost per project even at a mid-teens gross margin, which the segment margin alone cannot disprove.

### In paid autonomy Tesla trails, and in driver assistance it is no longer alone

Waymo ran 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities by March 2026 with about 3,700 vehicles and had logged 220.6 million rider-only miles through March 2026. Tesla began Cybercab rides in Austin on 2026-09-03 and stood at 1,051 vehicles on the Texas authorisation list on 2026-10-27 (544 Cybercab, 507 Model Y); it reports 2.0 million cumulative unsupervised miles, 0.9% of Waymo's rider-only total, is absent from California's driverless deployment permits, and discloses no ride count or fare. Baidu's Apollo Go ran 3.4 million trips in Q4 2025; Pony.ai passed 1,400 vehicles in March 2026. Insurance, teleoperation and cost per paid mile are undisclosed; a 10-20% swing in autonomy value turns on them. The supervised market is not Tesla's either: GM's Super Cruise is hands-free on about 750,000 compatible miles in the US and Canada, Ford's BlueCruise on more than 130,000 Blue Zone miles, and comma.ai's openpilot sells aftermarket kits with no OEM fleet. FSD's 1.74 million subscriptions are the largest single pool, but hands-free highway driving is now a $40-50 a month OEM feature, which caps what Tesla can charge and explains a 17.1% attach rate [S151, S125, S142, S171, S130, S170].

::: evidence
**Tesla's defensible positions are the charging standard, FSD subscriptions and storage integration — not vehicle share or a storage cost lead.**

Its 18.5% automotive margin was earned while regulatory credits fell 73%; but its energy margin ex-refund (14.8%) sits below CATL's ESS segment (23.96%) and Sungrow's storage segment (32.43%), so the storage cost moat does not survive a like-for-like benchmark. In autonomy, 2.0 million unsupervised miles against Waymo's 220.6 million and no California permit leave the autonomy option the one where Tesla trails most. Sources: S8, S167, S166, S172, S151.
:::

:::

Tesla is a high-margin incumbent in a shrinking US pool, sub-scale in the largest battery-electric market, and a distant challenger to Waymo and Baidu in autonomy. Its wedge — vertical integration, the charging standard and storage software — protects margin rather than volume: underwrite unit growth below the market's and track China retail share, storage revenue per GWh and Texas authorisations. What would settle this: a disclosed robotaxi revenue line and cost per paid mile, Tesla's EU registrations in ACEA's manufacturer table, and Megapack's price per MWh against CATL and Sungrow tenders.

arguments.markdown:
Tesla is winning the market that is shrinking and losing the one that is growing. It holds the US electric-vehicle market at a share no rival approaches while that market contracts, ranks fourth among China's new-energy brands in a pool that is itself shrinking, and its European recovery has come inside a pool growing faster than it. What Tesla owns is narrower than the narrative: the charging standard every major automaker has licensed, 1.74 million paid FSD subscriptions, and a storage business whose 33.1% reported gross margin falls to 14.8% once $526 million of tariff refunds and warranty true-ups are removed — mid-pack against CATL and Sungrow, not ahead of them [S8, S9, S167].

### In the United States, Tesla sets the price because it holds the pool

Tesla sold 144,094 US electric vehicles in Q3 2026 for 54% of the market, and 386,194 in nine months for 52.9%, with US volume down 14.4% against a market down 30.3%. Share gains inside a contracting pool flatter the position: absolute US revenue is smaller. When a $7,500 credit disappears, the brand with the densest charging footprint keeps the remaining buyers. The question is whether Tesla can hold price, and it has — automotive gross margin rose to 18.5% in Q3 2026 from 17.0% [S145, S8].

### China is where Tesla is the price taker

BYD sold 456,713 passenger cars in September 2026, 273,143 of them battery-electric, and 3,078,490 in nine months — 2.3 times Tesla's 1,324,681. Geely sold 119,682 and Xiaomi 40,015 retail units in September. BYD earned 19.46% gross margin overseas against 16.66% at home in 2025, a domestic ceiling Tesla cannot price above; Tesla's China retail of 64,837 was 3.8 times smaller than BYD's in September while Chinese battery-electric wholesale grew 18.3%. In driver assistance, Huawei and Momenta together supply more than 80% of China's urban NOA systems, Momenta alone 65% [S138, S146, S149, S168].

### Europe: growth in units, no evidence of share

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,931,465 in January-September 2026 at a 22.7% share, with September at 29.9%, so the pool expanded 49% while Tesla's European deliveries recovered from a 2025 slump. A recovery off a collapsed base inside a pool growing that fast is not share gain; Tesla discloses no EU unit count, and ACEA's manufacturer table would settle it. Volkswagen, Renault, Stellantis and Hyundai-Kia sell compliance models, and tariffed Chinese BEVs undercut. Tesla's handicap is a two-model line-up: Model 3/Y were 478,237 of 486,532 deliveries in Q3 2026 [S140, S147].

### Storage: integration, not a cost moat

The 33.1% energy gross margin Tesla reported for Q3 2026 is not comparable with an integrator's clean number: $526 million of IEEPA tariff refunds and warranty true-ups sit inside cost of revenue, so the underlying margin is $428 million on $2,881 million, or 14.8%. On that basis Tesla is mid-pack: Fluence earned 13.1% in fiscal 2025 and 5.1% in the June 2026 quarter, CATL's energy-storage segment 23.96% in H1 2026, Sungrow's storage segment 32.43%, and LG Energy Solution a 1.5% operating margin in Q2 2026 [S8, S9, S61, S66, S167, S166, S172, S169]. Integration does not show up as a margin outlier, and revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million as system prices deflated. The counter-evidence is scale: 36.0 GWh in nine months and Autobidder dispatch may still give Tesla the lowest installed cost per project even at a mid-teens margin, which the segment margin cannot disprove.

### In paid autonomy Tesla trails, and in driver assistance it is no longer alone

Waymo ran 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities by March 2026 with about 3,700 vehicles and had logged 220.6 million rider-only miles through March 2026. Tesla is winning the market that is shrinking and losing the one that is growing. It holds the US electric-vehicle market at a share no rival approaches while that market contracts, ranks fourth among China's new-energy brands in a pool that is itself shrinking, and its European recovery has come inside a pool growing faster than it. What Tesla owns is narrower than the narrative: the charging standard every major automaker has licensed, 1.74 million paid FSD subscriptions, and a storage business whose 33.1% reported gross margin falls to 14.8% once $526 million of tariff refunds and warranty true-ups are removed — mid-pack against CATL and Sungrow, not ahead of them [S8, S9, S167].

### In the United States, Tesla sets the price because it holds the pool

Tesla sold 144,094 US electric vehicles in Q3 2026 for 54% of the market, and 386,194 in nine months for 52.9%, with US volume down 14.4% against a market down 30.3%. Share gains in a contracting pool flatter the position. When a $7,500 credit disappears, the brand with the densest charging footprint keeps the remaining buyers. The question is whether Tesla can hold price, and it has — automotive gross margin rose to 18.5% in Q3 2026 from 17.0% [S145, S8].

### China is where Tesla is the price taker

BYD sold 456,713 passenger cars in September 2026, 273,143 of them battery-electric, and 3,078,490 in nine months — 2.3 times Tesla's 1,324,681. Geely sold 119,682 and Xiaomi 40,015 retail units in September. BYD earned 19.46% gross margin overseas against 16.66% at home in 2025, a domestic ceiling Tesla cannot price above; Tesla's China retail of 64,837 was 3.8 times smaller than BYD's in September while Chinese battery-electric wholesale grew 18.3%. In driver assistance, Huawei and Momenta together supply more than 80% of China's urban NOA systems, Momenta alone 65% [S138, S146, S149, S168].

### Europe: growth in units, no evidence of share

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,931,465 in January-September 2026 at a 22.7% share, with September at 29.9%, so the pool expanded 49% while Tesla's European deliveries recovered from a 2025 slump. A recovery off a collapsed base inside a pool growing that fast is not share gain; Tesla discloses no EU unit count, and ACEA's manufacturer table would settle it. Volkswagen, Renault, Stellantis and Hyundai-Kia sell compliance models; tariffed Chinese BEVs undercut. Tesla's handicap is a two-model line-up: Model 3/Y were 478,237 of 486,532 deliveries in Q3 2026 [S140, S147].

### Storage: integration, not a cost moat

The 33.1% energy gross margin Tesla reported for Q3 2026 is not comparable with an integrator's clean number: $526 million of IEEPA tariff refunds and warranty true-ups sit inside cost of revenue, so the underlying margin is $428 million on $2,881 million, or 14.8%. On that basis Tesla is mid-pack: Fluence earned 13.1% in fiscal 2025 and 5.1% in the June 2026 quarter, CATL's energy-storage segment 23.96% in H1 2026, Sungrow's storage segment 32.43%, and LG Energy Solution a 1.5% operating margin in Q2 2026 [S8, S9, S61, S66, S167, S166, S172, S169]. Integration does not show up as a margin outlier, and revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million as system prices deflated. The counter-evidence is scale: 36.0 GWh in nine months and Autobidder may still give Tesla the lowest installed cost per project even at a mid-teens margin.

Waymo ran 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities by March 2026 with about 3,700 vehicles and had logged 220.6 million rider-only miles through March 2026. Energy and services are compounding, but the clean energy margin is 14.8% ex-refund, not 33.1%, revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210m, and services' record $734m of gross profit on $4.605bn of revenue is a 15.9% margin; valuing energy at 3.5-4.0x sales and services at 2.0x adds about $20bn, $5 a share, against a $399.81 price [S152, S151, S9, S131, S8].

### The SOTP is a floor, not a target

The SOTP overstates the downside at the edges. Energy at 2.5-3.0x $12.3bn of sales ignores a 41% growth pool and a clean 14.8% margin; at 3.5-4.0x it is worth $12bn more. Services at 1.5x $16.3bn ignores 32% growth and a record $734m of gross profit; at 2.0x it is worth $8bn more. FSD's $1bn run rate is carried at zero and is worth $20bn at 20x. Net cash of $36.18bn is verified and the $2.87bn SpaceX stake is a minor line, so the deliberate conservatism is autonomy at zero; FSD alone puts $5 a share back. Those adjustments take the floor to $40-50 a share, not $35-40. The larger problem is the framework: the SOTP implies -87% to -90%, the base case -33.5% and the full de-rating -79%, because the base applies 70x to $14.5bn of EBITDA and so embeds about $1.0tn of autonomy value. A $40-50 floor beside a $266 base is a 5-7x gap, and taking the floor as the twelve-month target hands the reader a downside the recommendation does not forecast. Tesla has never traded on SOTP: $266 is the base, $156 the bear, $82 the full de-rating, $40-50 the liquidation floor [S152, S8, S9].

### Earnings quality: not double counted, and worse than stated

The $475m credit reversal and the $3,868m payables build are not the same dollar counted twice: the first is Q3 2026 revenue and gross profit, the second is nine-month working capital, so pricing both is compounding, not double counting. Adding back the reversal gives $1,193m of operating income and a 4.2% margin rather than 2.6%, but only if regulatory credits stop falling; credit revenue fell from $2.76bn in 2024 to $1.99bn in 2025. More important, interest income of $1,301m was 69% of the $1,883m nine-month free cash flow, so free cash flow before interest is $582m and before the payables benefit it is negative. Adjusted EBITDA excludes interest, so 103x is clean; the 439x P/E and 0.2% free-cash-flow yield are not [S8, S11].

### Robotaxi cost per paid mile is the missing number

The bull case treats the autonomy branch as a permit event; it is a unit-economics event. Tesla discloses no robotaxi revenue, ride count, average fare, insurance cost, remote-supervision ratio or cost per paid mile, and no operator discloses the last three. The only public signal is adverse: remote operators have been reported crashing the vehicles, a cost and safety channel rather than a scaling one. The 15% autonomy branch requires a disclosed revenue line with positive contribution; if cost per paid mile exceeds fare, the branch is worth zero even with a California permit, and the distribution becomes 15% merger, 55% base, 22% bear and 8% de-rating, an expected return of about -34.2%, not -25.2%. The $506.05 outcome is not costless: it needs a cost stack that has never been published, which is why the branch is 15% and not higher [S153, S89].

### Stress tests: a de-rating, not a default

A market 50% smaller — 11.5m electric units instead of 23.0m — leaves Tesla 885,000 units at 7.7% share, $37.5bn of auto revenue and $6.8bn of gross profit at 18.1%; group gross profit of $14bn against $16.3bn of operating cost is a $2.3bn operating loss, and auto at 0.7x sales falls from $52.5bn to $26bn, taking the SOTP to $120-126bn, or $30-32 a share, 92% below the current price and 10-21% below the $139-160bn floor. The Sell survives; the base case's 70x on $14.5bn does not. A doubled CAC does bite: SG&A of $7,485m over 1.77m units is $4,229 a vehicle, and doubling the demand-generation half adds $2,100 a vehicle, $3.7bn, equal to the $3.47bn trailing operating income. Revenue 30% lower leaves $72.5bn at 19.3% gross margin, $14.0bn of gross profit against $16.3bn of cost, an operating loss; at 40x on $8bn of EBITDA the equity is $356bn, $90 a share (-77%). A six-month financing delay is not a solvency event: $36.18bn of net cash and $30.0bn of undrawn facilities mean the cost falls on the option, delaying the proof and trimming the bull weight. Free cash flow 30% lower changes nothing at a 0.2% yield. The bear case is a 40x multiple, not a balance-sheet failure [S8, S9].

### Policy and the related party are priced as a timetable

The regulatory risks are dated and public. US credit repeal has already taken 30.3% out of the pool; an EU 2035 target cut to 90% would slow the only growing vehicle market; NHTSA's EA26002 covers 3,203,754 vehicles with nine incidents and one fatality and is the last step before a recall, and a remedy at $100-1,000 a car is $320m-3.2bn plus an operating-domain restriction that would delay paid service. California's list on 2026-10-23 still shows Tesla Robotaxi LLC only under testing with a safety driver, while Waymo, Nuro and Mercedes hold deployment authorisations; a permit application is reported, but an application is not an authorisation. The undisclosed items — robotaxi revenue, trips and cost per mile, FSD churn, the energy backlog's contracted price, the SpaceX exchange ratio and the 50%-vote count — are where the unknown unknowns sit. The related-party flow is disclosed but not priced: SpaceX bought $626m of Megapacks in nine months, 7.4% of energy revenue, and $588m of the receivable was billed for units not yet delivered. Source S87, S89, S10.
