rows.finding: Automotive regulatory credits earned $1,993M in FY2025 vs $2,763M in FY2024, and $639M in 9M 2026 vs $1,451M in 9M 2025; contracted credit backlog $384M at 2026-09-30 vs $841M at 2025-12-31; $475M of previously delivered credits reversed in 2026.
rows.mechanism: Credits monetise compliance shortfalls created by federal and state programmes; when the 2025 budget law narrowed those programmes, shortfalls and deliverable credits shrank, shrinking a near-pure-margin revenue line.
rows.benchmark: FY2024 peak of $2,763M; 9M 2025 run rate of $1,451M.
rows.weakens: Q3 2026 gross credit sales were about $588M once the $475M reversal is added back, above Q4 2025's $542M, so the reported decline overstates the demand fall.
rows.implication: Model no recovery toward the 2024 peak; a 2026 run rate near $850M is the realistic base.
rows.confidence: high — two primary filings.
rows.follow_up: What portion of the $384M contracted obligation ($201M within 12 months) is at risk of further reversal?

rows.finding: California DMV's 2026-10-23 list places TESLA ROBOTAXI LLC only among testing-permit holders requiring a safety driver; Tesla is absent from the driverless-testing list (2026-10-22) and the deployment list, which names only Mercedes-Benz, Nuro and Waymo.
rows.mechanism: A testing permit with a safety driver cannot carry paying passengers without a driver, so California paid driverless revenue requires a driverless testing permit and then a deployment permit.
rows.benchmark: Waymo, Mercedes-Benz and Nuro hold California deployment authorisations; Tesla has none.
rows.weakens: Tesla runs paid rides in California on a limousine permit, which supports revenue but not driverless operation.
rows.implication: The twelve-month paid driverless market is permissive states only; California needs two further approvals.
rows.confidence: high — regulator's own list.
rows.follow_up: When did Tesla last apply for a driverless testing permit, and what did the DMV require?

rows.finding: Texas SB 2807 (not 2809) has required TxDMV authorisation for commercial automated vehicles since 2026-05-28; 1,051 vehicles held that authorisation on 2026-10-27.
rows.mechanism: Texas operates a registration-and-complaint regime rather than a volume cap, so authorised fleet size is the binding number, not a permit quota.
rows.benchmark: Zero Tesla vehicles authorised for driverless commercial operation in California on 2026-10-23.
rows.weakens: The earlier framing that Texas authorisation was unanswerable is superseded; the count is public and dated.
rows.implication: Texas is the only scaled paid driverless market in the record, at 1,051 authorised vehicles.
rows.confidence: medium — TxDMV programme page plus independent tally.
rows.follow_up: How fast is the authorised count growing, and what share is Cybercab vs Model Y?

rows.finding: Waymo had logged 220.6M rider-only miles through March 2026; Tesla's cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles were about 2.0M, 0.9% of Waymo's base.
rows.mechanism: Verified driverless miles are the output metric regulators, insurers and fleet partners underwrite; a 0.9% ratio shows the autonomy option is priced on supervised fleet data, not driverless experience.
rows.benchmark: Waymo 220.6M rider-only miles through 2026-03.
rows.weakens: Tesla's supervised FSD miles (charted to 16bn) are far larger but do not certify driverless capability.
rows.implication: Any valuation that capitalises Tesla as a scaled robotaxi operator is ahead of verified miles by two orders of magnitude.
rows.confidence: medium — company count for Tesla, independent compilation for Waymo.
rows.follow_up: What is Tesla's paid driverless miles per month and its disengagement rate?

rows.finding: NHTSA's Engineering Analysis EA26002, opened 2026-03-18, covers an estimated 3,203,754 Tesla vehicles (MY2016-2026) over FSD degradation detection in reduced visibility; no NHTSA consent order is disclosed.
rows.mechanism: An Engineering Analysis is the last administrative step before a mandatory recall; a recall can restrict the operating domain of the software that carries most of the equity value.
rows.benchmark: Escalated from Preliminary Evaluation PE24031; eight 2026 Model Y recall campaigns between 2025-05-30 and 2026-09-01.
rows.weakens: An over-the-air remedy would make the direct cash cost small; no consent order has been imposed.
rows.implication: Price a recall as a narrative and litigation-cost event rather than a cash event.
rows.confidence: high on the investigation, medium on outcome.
rows.follow_up: What remedy scope would NHTSA accept, and does it require hardware?

rows.finding: On 2025-12-19 the Delaware Supreme Court reversed the Chancery rescission of the 2018 CEO pay award, reinstating it with $1 nominal damages and a reduced fee award after 72% of disinterested shares ratified in 2024.
rows.mechanism: Litigation over the pay award created a governance discount from January 2024; the reversal removes the rescission risk and most of the fee exposure.
rows.benchmark: 2024 Chancery rescission of the $55.8bn package.
rows.weakens: The result validates a very large related-party pay outcome and does not address concentration.
rows.implication: Remove the pay-litigation discount; keep a key-person and related-party discount.
rows.confidence: high — court outcome reflected in the 10-K.
rows.follow_up: What fee award remains, and does any appeal or new derivative claim survive?

rows.finding: Tesla agreed in January 2026 to invest about $2.00bn in xAI Holdings; the right converted into SpaceX Class A stock when SpaceX acquired xAI Holdings on 2026-02-02, and Tesla completed the purchase on 2026-03-12.
rows.mechanism: A related-party capital allocation moves cash to entities controlled by the CEO, converting an operating company into a holding of another Musk vehicle and creating a vote flashpoint.
rows.benchmark: Tesla's stated capital-allocation priorities (capex above $20bn in 2026).
rows.weakens: The stake is marked to a listed SpaceX Class A price, so value is observable rather than written off.
rows.implication: Raises the odds of an adverse vote at the 2026-12-03 annual meeting and strengthens the governance discount.
rows.confidence: high — proxy and independent reporting agree.
rows.follow_up: How is the SpaceX stake marked, and what information rights do Tesla holders get?

rows.finding: The US federal clean-vehicle consumer credit ended for vehicles acquired after 2025-09-30; US EV sales fell 24% in H1 2026 and 46.9% year on year in August 2026.
rows.mechanism: Removing a $7,500 point-of-sale credit raises the effective price of a Tesla by roughly 15-20% on a $40,000 car, and the demand response shows in registrations within two quarters.
rows.benchmark: Pre-termination US EV growth; H1 2026 decline.
rows.weakens: State rebates (California $3,500) and cheaper trims partly offset the loss.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite a US demand recovery from policy in the next twelve months.
rows.confidence: high — IRS notice plus independent sales data.
rows.follow_up: What is Tesla's US unit decline net of price cuts, and how much is mix?

rows.finding: China's NEV purchase tax is a 5% half-rate capped at RMB 15,000 for 2026-2027, replacing full exemption.
rows.mechanism: A capped half-rate raises the transaction price of most Tesla models modestly and narrows the advantage over ICE, but keeps NEVs advantaged.
rows.benchmark: Full purchase-tax exemption through 2025.
rows.weakens: Local production and price cuts can absorb the change.
rows.implication: Modest headwind to China volume, not a step change.
rows.confidence: medium — secondary report of a fiscal rule.
rows.follow_up: What is the per-model tax increase for Model 3 and Model Y in China?

rows.finding: EU CO2 targets run on a 2025-2027 three-year average, and a December 2025 proposal would cut the 2035 target to 90%; EU battery due diligence was deferred to 2027-08-18 and the battery passport starts 2027-02-18.
rows.mechanism: Three-year averaging preserves the compliance-credit pool through 2027, while weakening the 2035 target reduces the long-run value of over-compliance.
rows.benchmark: Original 2025 single-year target and 100% 2035 ban.
rows.weakens: Toyota and Stellantis left Tesla's EU CO2 pool in March 2026, shrinking the buyer base.
rows.implication: Credit income persists near term but shrinks structurally; battery compliance costs fall outside the twelve-month horizon.
rows.confidence: high on the flexibility, medium on the 2035 proposal.
rows.follow_up: Will the 2035 90% target survive Parliament, and who remains in Tesla's CO2 pool?

rows.finding: Tesla's total recordable case rate and days-away rate, and any GM, Ford or BYD comparison, cannot be read: the 2025 Impact Report file returned no content, and establishment-level OSHA 300A data requires an establishment query that is outstanding (user data request U1).
rows.mechanism: Injury rates drive state incentive conditions, insurer pricing and permit challenges at the plants where Tesla is expanding capacity, so their absence leaves the social pillar qualitative.
rows.benchmark: BLS industry incidence rates; GM, Ford and BYD plant-level disclosure (not in the record).
rows.weakens: Tesla's safety claims are company material only and could not be tested.
rows.implication: Treat workplace safety as an unmeasured licence-to-operate risk rather than a clean bill.
rows.confidence: low — data gap, stated as a limitation.
rows.follow_up: What are Fremont and Austin TRC and DART rates for 2023-2025 against GM and Ford plants?

plan.decision_question: Do environmental, social and governance factors change Tesla's cost of capital, demand or licence to operate over the next twelve months?
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla's ESG and policy position has already removed a material profit stream and leaves its highest-value product gated by permits and a live safety investigation, so ESG lowers, rather than raises, the multiple a twelve-month buyer should pay.
plan.why_different: The other sections price demand, technology and financing; this one prices the rules — credits, permits, enforcement, litigation and governance — that determine what Tesla may sell, where, and at what discount rate.
plan.mechanism: Regulatory programmes create the compliance shortfalls Tesla monetises as credits; when the rules narrow, credit revenue and the permitted operating domain shrink together, while enforcement and related-party governance shift the discount rate.
plan.comparison_set: Waymo (California deployment versus Tesla testing-with-driver), GM/Ford/BYD (credit buyers, workplace-safety benchmarks), and the 2024 credit peak against the 2026 run rate.
plan.counter_evidence: Policy still favours Tesla: Texas commercial authorisation (1,051 vehicles at 2026-10-27), EU three-year CO2 averaging through 2027, the NLRB dismissal, and a pay-litigation overhang removed by the Delaware Supreme Court in December 2025.
plan.visual: Regulatory record table plus the policy impact matrix, with the credit-revenue bridge in the opening paragraph.
plan.prohibited: 'huge market', 'strong team', 'high barriers to entry', 'clear business model', 'fierce competition', 'risks are manageable', 'well positioned'; vague counts; unlabelled company claims.

rows.finding: Active FSD subscriptions reached 1.74 million at 2026-09-30 versus 1.04 million a year earlier (+67%), against 10.2 million cumulative vehicles delivered — a 17.1% penetration of the lifetime fleet, up from 12.4% at 2025-12-31.
rows.mechanism: Software monetisation of an installed base: each incremental point of attach adds recurring revenue at near-zero marginal cost, and the attach rate is rising without a price cut disclosed in filings.
rows.benchmark: Waymo sells no consumer software; Chinese OEMs bundle L2+ at zero incremental price (God's Eye on BYD), so paid attach is Tesla-specific.
rows.weakens: Tesla does not disclose FSD revenue separately, so attach is a unit count, not a revenue number; $904 million of the $3.867 billion automotive deferred-revenue balance was to be recognised in the 12 months after 2025-12-31, which caps the near-term software P&L effect.
rows.implication: Supports a services-multiple argument, but too small in dollars to justify the equity on its own; diligence should ask for FSD revenue and churn by cohort.
rows.confidence: high — both figures are company-reported operating metrics in SEC filings
rows.follow_up: What is FSD subscription revenue and monthly churn, and how many subscriptions are monthly versus upfront purchases?

rows.finding: Tesla reached nearly 2 million cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles by 2026-09-30 (8x quarter on quarter) with Cybercab rides starting in Austin on 2026-09-03; management claimed 300+ Cybercabs in Austin on 2026-10-10.
rows.mechanism: Cumulative unsupervised miles are the only disclosed proxy for driverless operating experience; at ~2 million miles the fleet has roughly a week's worth of Waymo-scale experience, so safety statistics remain statistically thin.
rows.benchmark: Waymo is reported at about 500,000 paid rides a week on 3,000+ vehicles with 170m+ rider-only miles — roughly 85-100x Tesla's cumulative unsupervised miles.
rows.weakens: Miles, not rides or revenue: Tesla discloses neither paid trips, revenue per trip, nor utilisation, and registered Cybercabs (349 in Texas) are not proven operating vehicles.
rows.implication: Twelve-month monetisation requires roughly two orders of magnitude of scale-up from a base that is still a pilot; price the robotaxi option at a discount to the narrative.
rows.confidence: medium — miles are company-reported; the Waymo comparator is a press aggregation, not a filing
rows.follow_up: How many paid Robotaxi trips and what gross bookings per week, and what share of the fleet is revenue-earning on a given day?

rows.finding: California's DMV lists Tesla Robotaxi LLC only as a testing-permit holder with a safety driver (page updated 2026-10-23); Tesla is absent from the driverless-testing authorisation list and from the deployment list, where Waymo, Nuro, Zoox and Mercedes appear.
rows.mechanism: Autonomous ride-hailing is gated state by state; California requires a DMV driverless/deployment permit plus a CPUC passenger-service authorisation, so absence from the list is a hard block on paid driverless revenue in the largest US AV market.
rows.benchmark: Waymo holds deployment authorisation in California; Teslas paid driverless service is confined to permissive states, led by Texas.
rows.weakens: Texas has no equivalent state permit gate, so Tesla can and does run paid driverless service in Austin; the California block limits scale and valuation, not existence.
rows.implication: Geography is the binding constraint on the 12-month revenue ramp; the investment case needs a dated California or other gated-market permit as a signpost.
rows.confidence: high — primary regulator list read directly
rows.follow_up: Has Tesla filed for a California driverless testing or deployment permit, and what is the CPUC status of its ride-hailing authorisation?

rows.finding: NHTSA opened Engineering Analysis EA26002 on 2026-03-18 into FSD's degradation-detection system, covering about 3,203,754 vehicles (2016-2026 Model S/3/X/Y, Cybertruck) after 9 confirmed incidents including one pedestrian fatality; two further FSD-related probes are open (PE25012 with 80 incidents, AQ25002 crash-reporting audit).
rows.mechanism: An engineering analysis is the last stage before a forced recall; a recall on a camera-only architecture either forces a software restriction on the operating domain or a hardware change across millions of cars, both of which slow the unsupervised roadmap and raise product-liability exposure that Tesla largely self-insures.
rows.benchmark: Tesla's December 2023 Autopilot remedy (recall 23V838, about 2 million vehicles) was closed by an over-the-air update; the reported finding that its visibility fix may address only 3 of 9 incidents suggests an OTA remedy may not close this one.
rows.weakens: The section's safety case rests on an aggregator's reading of the ODI file because the ODI PDF text did not extract; the primary filing confirms the investigation and its subject, not every count.
rows.implication: Material downside risk to the autonomy option: budget for a recall and for a narrower unsupervised operating domain; ask counsel-grade diligence on the EA timing.
rows.confidence: medium — investigation existence and subject are primary; counts are secondary
rows.follow_up: What is the EA26002 timetable and has Tesla proposed a remedy that NHTSA has accepted?

rows.finding: Tesla produces dry-electrode 4680 cells with both anode and cathode made in Austin (stated January 2026), at more than 40 GWh of installed annual Texas capacity, alongside 10 GWh of cathode material, 7 GWh of LFP cells in Nevada and 30 GWh of lithium refining in early ramp — yet the Q3 2026 update still calls battery availability the limiting factor on vehicle volumes.
rows.mechanism: Cell cost is the largest single variable in vehicle gross margin; in-house dry-electrode production removes a purchased-cell markup and a supplier allocation constraint, but only if yield holds at volume — which the company does not disclose.
rows.benchmark: BYD and CATL supply themselves and third parties at scale; Tesla still buys cells for most vehicles, and its disclosed constraint is availability, not demand.
rows.weakens: No cost-per-kWh, yield or scrap figure is disclosed anywhere in the filings, so the 'cheapest cell per kWh' claim in trade coverage is unverified; the 40 GWh nameplate is capacity, not output.
rows.implication: A genuine manufacturing option but not yet a proven cost advantage; margin diligence should target 4680 yield and the purchased-versus-in-house cost spread.
rows.confidence: medium-high — dry-electrode process and capacity are company statements; economics are unverified
rows.follow_up: What is 4680 cell cost per kWh versus the purchased-cell benchmark, and what is the dry-electrode line yield?

rows.finding: Energy storage deployed 36.0 GWh in the first nine months of 2026 (13.7 GWh in Q3) against 46.7 GWh in all of 2025, with installed annual Megapack capacity of 40 GWh (California), 20 GWh (Shanghai) and 50 GWh (Texas, started Q3 2026); SpaceX, a related party, accounted for $626 million of Megapack revenue in 9M 2026, about 7% of energy revenue.
rows.mechanism: Storage is a manufacturing business with a shorter sales cycle and higher growth than autos; but part of the demand is internal to the CEO's other company, and $588 million of the $729 million SpaceX receivable was for Megapacks not yet delivered.
rows.benchmark: Megapack competes with CATL, BYD and Fluence on $/kWh and delivery time; Tesla's advantage is integration and 110 GWh of announced capacity, not proprietary chemistry.
rows.weakens: Related-party revenue flatters the order book, and the segment is exposed to tariffs on imported cells under OBBBA, which the 10-Q flags as a cost risk.
rows.implication: The strongest genuinely-verified second engine, but quality of demand needs adjusting for the related-party share before capitalising the backlog.
rows.confidence: high — capacity, deployments and the related-party note are all in SEC filings
rows.follow_up: What share of the energy backlog is unrelated third parties, and what is Megapack gross margin excluding SpaceX?

rows.finding: Optimus production began in Fremont in Q3 2026 and Tesla calls the process 'suitable for a commercial product', but the company discloses no units, no throughput, no uptime and no external customer; independent estimates put 1,000-1,200 units at Fremont and Giga Texas with zero external sales.
rows.mechanism: Humanoid robots are a data-and-manufacturing problem with a 10,000-component bill of materials; until tasks are specified with cycle times and error rates, the product is an R&D programme, not a revenue line.
rows.benchmark: Figure AI has 1,250+ documented operating hours at BMW and Agility Robotics 65,000+ hours across nine sites, both with paying customers; Unitree shipped 5,500+ humanoid units in 2025 at consumer prices.
rows.weakens: Tesla's claim of commercial readiness is unverified by any operating metric and its own CEO described early units as learning devices; estimated unit cost of $50,000-100,000 is far above the stated sub-$20,000 consumer target.
rows.implication: Assign no revenue in the 12-month model; treat Optimus as a free option whose value depends on 2027-2028 evidence.
rows.confidence: high that no external evidence exists; medium on unit counts
rows.follow_up: What tasks does Optimus perform unsupervised, at what cycle time and error rate, and when is the first external sale?

rows.finding: Tesla's IP position is deliberately not patent-shaped: the 10-K states an irrevocable pledge not to sue any party acting in good faith for infringing its patents in electric vehicles or related equipment, while claiming protection mainly through trade secrets, proprietary data, in-house inference silicon and manufacturing know-how; the Q3 2026 update puts installed AI training compute at Cortex 1 >105 MW and Cortex 2 >120 MW, with a 400 MW year-end target.
rows.mechanism: Without enforceable patents the moat must come from accumulation — fleet data, training compute, cell process know-how and vertical integration — which is slow for a rival to copy but not legally defensible, so it protects margin only while the leader keeps spending.
rows.benchmark: Waymo protects its stack with trade secrets, lidar hardware and a decade of driverless miles; Chinese OEMs compete on cost and regulation rather than IP. Tesla's patent pledge is unique among them.
rows.weakens: The pledge is limited to EVs and good-faith users, and AI/robotics patents are outside it; still, no public count or quality metric of Tesla's portfolio is disclosed, so a patent-level table cannot be built from filings.
rows.implication: The replication test is capital- and time-based, not legal: a funded team could match hardware in 2-3 years but not 15 billion supervised miles or 225+ MW of training compute.
rows.confidence: medium-high — the pledge is quoted from the 10-K; compute figures are company-reported
rows.follow_up: What is Tesla's granted-patent count by jurisdiction in AI, batteries and robotics, and are any third-party patents blocking Cybercab or Optimus?

plan.decision_question: Is Tesla's product and technology position actually ahead in 2026, and is unsupervised autonomy monetizable within 12 months?
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla in 2026 leads the world in supervised driving data and low-cost electric-vehicle manufacturing, but its autonomy is still a supervised product plus a roughly 300-car Texas pilot, so the 12-month question is whether paid driverless scale compounds from a very small base while a 3.2-million-vehicle federal safety probe and a missing California permit cap how far it can go.
plan.why_different: Unlike the market, competition and financial sections, this one tests the company's technical claims against regulator records, product versions and independent operating evidence, and separates what is proven from what is asserted.
plan.mechanism: Cumulative supervised miles and in-house compute lower the cost of each autonomy increment; but driverless revenue is gated by state permits and by NHTSA defect findings, so technical progress converts into cash only where a permit exists — which is why Texas revenue is real and California revenue is not yet.
plan.comparison_set: Waymo (deployment permits, about 500,000 weekly paid rides, 170m+ rider-only miles), Chinese OEMs with L3 conditional approvals since December 2025, Figure AI and Agility Robotics on humanoid operating hours, CATL/BYD on storage and cell cost.
plan.counter_evidence: EA26002 covers 3.2 million vehicles with one fatality and Tesla's own fix may address only 3 of 9 incidents; California lists Tesla only for supervised testing; Optimus has zero external customers; FSD and Robotaxi revenue are not separately disclosed; battery availability, not demand, limits vehicle output.
plan.visual: Technology comparison table (Tesla vs Waymo vs Chinese L3 OEMs) plus the moat/replication table; supported by the product-inventory table.
plan.prohibited: No 'self-driving' without a supervised/unsupervised qualifier; no 'industry-leading', 'best-in-class', 'huge market', 'strong moat', 'well positioned'; no vague counts ('many patents', 'about 300') where a filed number exists; no claim of driverless service in California.

rows.finding: The 1.74m active FSD subscriptions at 2026-09-30 are a company-defined count that includes upfront purchases and monthly subscriptions and excludes free trials; management put about half the paid base on monthly plans on 2026-10-21, implying ~870,000 subscribers and ~870,000 one-time buyers worth about $1.0bn a year at the $99 US list price.
rows.mechanism: Merging one-time software purchases with recurring subscriptions makes the metric look like an annuity; only half the base is recurring, and $4.08bn of deferred revenue also covers connectivity, Supercharging and OTA, so FSD cash cannot be isolated.
rows.benchmark: Tesla's own 10 million active FSD subscription milestone in the 2025 CEO Performance Award; the 1.74m count is 17.4% of that target.
rows.weakens: The split is call commentary, not a filed figure; the $4.08bn deferred revenue bucket is not FSD-specific, so the recurring base may be smaller than 'half'.
rows.implication: Treat FSD subscription revenue as under 1% of revenue and not yet an annuity; do not pay for 1.74m as if all were recurring.
rows.confidence: medium - count is filed, split is commentary
rows.follow_up: Will Tesla disclose monthly versus upfront FSD revenue in the 10-K revenue note?

rows.finding: Robotaxi insurance, teleoperation and cost per paid mile are not disclosed; the disclosed pieces are 1,051 Texas-authorised vehicles at 2026-10-27, Cybercab entry on 2026-09-03, Austin hours of 06:00-24:00, and remote operators implicated in crashes. Pony.ai's $8.6m Q1 2026 robotaxi revenue on 1,776 vehicles implies about $4,800 per vehicle per quarter.
rows.mechanism: A paid driverless mile earns money only if fare exceeds insurance, teleoperation, depreciation, charging and cleaning; without those lines the contribution margin cannot be computed, and the disclosed fleet is too small to matter at group scale.
rows.benchmark: Pony.ai $4,800 per vehicle per quarter; 1,051 Tesla vehicles at that rate would produce about $5m a quarter against $28.0bn of group quarterly revenue.
rows.weakens: Pony's revenue includes service lines and its fleet is not all in paid service, so per-vehicle revenue is a rough upper bound; Tesla's fare and utilisation are unknown.
rows.implication: Value robotaxi at option value, not on near-term unit economics; the model's largest gap is the cost stack, not demand.
rows.confidence: medium - arithmetic on disclosed figures, no Tesla cost data
rows.follow_up: What does Tesla charge per Robotaxi trip in Austin, and what utilisation does the 1,051-vehicle fleet run at?

rows.finding: Verified driverless scale: Waymo 220.6m rider-only miles to 2026-03 and about 500,000 paid rides a week; Baidu 3.2m fully driverless rides in Q1 2026 and over 22m cumulative; Pony.ai 1,776 vehicles produced by 2026-05-24; WeRide about 1,300 robotaxis globally at 2026-04-30; Huawei and Momenta hold more than 80% of China's urban NOA market.
rows.mechanism: Autonomy scale is being built in geofenced city fleets abroad while Tesla's verified driverless base is 2.0m miles in Texas; Chinese NOA suppliers monetise consumer L2+ through OEM licences instead of owning fleets.
rows.benchmark: Tesla 2.0m cumulative unsupervised miles = 0.9% of Waymo's 220.6m rider-only miles.
rows.weakens: Operating domains and definitions differ (rider-only miles versus unsupervised miles, rides versus miles), so the ratios are directional, not like-for-like; Chinese figures are company-reported.
rows.implication: Tesla is a challenger in driverless operation, not the leader; the leadership claim rests on supervised data and manufacturing.
rows.confidence: high on Waymo/Tesla filings and coverage, medium on Chinese company-reported figures
rows.follow_up: Will Waymo or Baidu publish cost per paid mile before Tesla discloses robotaxi revenue?

rows.finding: The assisted-driving set is converging on hands-off, eyes-on: GM Super Cruise and Ford BlueCruise are supervised highway systems with no driverless revenue, and comma.ai's aftermarket openpilot is under an NHTSA preliminary evaluation opened in 2026-09 after five crashes causing three deaths.
rows.mechanism: Supervised assistance is a feature sold on subscription or a $999 device, not a transportation service; safety investigations attach to all hands-off systems, not only Tesla's.
rows.benchmark: Tesla FSD (Supervised) versus Super Cruise, BlueCruise and openpilot on supervision requirement and driverless revenue.
rows.weakens: openpilot is an aftermarket product with a different liability chain, so its crash record does not transfer to Tesla; it does show the regulatory pattern.
rows.implication: Do not price FSD (Supervised) as autonomy; its value is option value on a later unsupervised release.
rows.confidence: medium - qualitative comparison, no common test protocol
rows.follow_up: Does NHTSA's comma.ai probe change the approval path for Tesla's FSD degradation fix?

rows.finding: NHTSA Engineering Analysis EA26002 (opened 2026-03-18) covers 3,203,754 model-year 2016-2026 vehicles over degraded-visibility detection after nine incidents including one pedestrian fatality; a second FSD probe covers 2,882,566 vehicles and 80 traffic-law incidents.
rows.mechanism: An engineering analysis is the last step before a recall; a recall that narrows the operating domain or requires hardware would raise the cost of the unsupervised option across millions of cars.
rows.benchmark: Tesla's reported finding that its degradation-detection update may have affected 3 of 9 incidents.
rows.weakens: No remedy or timetable is published, so the probability and cost of a recall cannot be quantified.
rows.implication: The federal safety file is the binding constraint on autonomous revenue in the next 12 months; it caps the option value.
rows.confidence: high on the filing, low on outcome
rows.follow_up: Will EA26002 escalate to a recall, and would the remedy be software-only?

rows.finding: Texas fleet counts differ by basis: 349 registrations at 2026-10-15 versus 1,051 authorised vehicles at 2026-10-27; the report uses 1,051 authorised as the single basis.
rows.mechanism: Registration counts and authorisation counts measure different things (vehicles registered for operation versus vehicles authorised under the state programme), so mixing them understates the fleet.
rows.benchmark: 349 registrations versus 1,051 authorised vehicles.
rows.weakens: Neither figure discloses how many vehicles are actually in paid service at a given hour.
rows.implication: Use 1,051 authorised vehicles; do not present it as paid-trip scale.
rows.confidence: medium - single independent report on the state programme
rows.follow_up: Will TxDMV publish its authorised-vehicle list directly?

plan.decision_question: Is Tesla's product and technology position actually ahead in 2026, and is unsupervised autonomy monetizable within 12 months?
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla's technology lead in 2026 is real in supervised driving, battery process and manufacturing and unproven in driverless operation: 2.0 million cumulative unsupervised miles against 220.6 million Waymo rider-only miles, one authorising state and no disclosed robotaxi revenue, with the federal safety file the binding constraint on the option.
plan.why_different: This section judges what is proven versus claimed in the technology and products themselves; the market section sizes the opportunity and the financial section prices the P&L, so this section must supply the technical evidence and the missing-data map.
plan.mechanism: End-to-end vision turns fleet miles into training data, but supervised miles do not certify driverless operation; driverless revenue requires a regulatory authorisation and a per-mile cost stack (insurance, teleoperation, depreciation) that Tesla does not disclose.
plan.comparison_set: Waymo (220.6m rider-only miles, 500k paid rides/week); Chinese L4 operators Pony.ai (1,776 vehicles, $8.6m Q1 robotaxi revenue), WeRide (~1,300 robotaxis) and Baidu (3.2m driverless rides in Q1 2026); Chinese NOA suppliers Huawei/Momenta (>80% of urban NOA); assisted systems Super Cruise, BlueCruise and openpilot.
plan.counter_evidence: Tesla's 1.74m FSD subscriptions, fully dry-electrode 4680 output and 13.7 GWh quarterly storage are real and hard to replicate; the Chinese and Waymo comparisons are geofenced and use different definitions, and Tesla's 2.0m unsupervised miles grew eightfold in a quarter from a small base.
plan.visual: The operator comparison table and the robotaxi unit-economics disclosure table.
plan.prohibited: FSD is autonomous; Tesla leads autonomy; huge market; strong moat; well positioned; about/hundreds of.

rows.finding: Tesla expects capital expenditures 'in excess of $20 billion in 2026', cut in the Q3 2026 10-Q from 'more than $25 billion' guided since April 2026; $13.01 billion was spent in the first nine months, implying about $7 billion in Q4.
rows.mechanism: Capex is the input to the autonomy, Optimus and energy ramps; a guidance cut either defers the revenue those lines were meant to produce or reveals that spending discipline is overriding the roadmap.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 capex was $8.53bn and FY2024 $11.34bn; capex is therefore more than doubling year on year, the opposite of the 2024-2025 trend.
rows.weakens: Guidance has moved twice in six months, so the $20bn floor itself has low reliability; unpaid capex in liabilities was $3.67bn at quarter-end, meaning cash spend lags the reported number.
rows.implication: The plan is affordable only at the lower end; the cut is a signal that either projects slipped or cash is being protected — both weaken the 2027 revenue bridge.
rows.confidence: high — all figures from SEC filings
rows.follow_up: Which projects were deferred from 2026 into 2027, and what is the capex plan for 2027?

rows.finding: In September 2026 Tesla entered three credit agreements with aggregate commitments of $30 billion ($20 billion delayed-draw term loan maturing 2029 plus $10 billion revolver replacing a $5 billion facility), undrawn at 2026-09-30, and the 10-Q states that heightened capital expenditure 'will necessitate additional funding beyond our operating cash flow'.
rows.mechanism: Arranging $30bn of committed debt before spending it converts an equity-funding question into a leverage question: management can pursue the plan without dilution, but the plan's cash burn now carries a fixed cost and a maturity date.
rows.benchmark: Tesla had $45.45bn of cash and investments and had been net-cash positive; the new facilities take gross debt capacity up by $30bn in a single quarter.
rows.weakens: Facilities are commitments, not drawn debt; Tesla still holds $45.45bn of liquid assets, so near-term solvency is not in question.
rows.implication: The strategy is now partly debt-financed; the equity case loses its 'fortress balance sheet funds the future' pillar and gains interest cost and covenant questions.
rows.confidence: high — disclosed in the 10-Q
rows.follow_up: How much of the $30bn will be drawn in 2027, and at what all-in cost?

rows.finding: Q3 2026 free cash flow of $1.53 billion depended on $2.59 billion of working-capital inflow (accounts payable +$1.92bn, accrued liabilities +$1.95bn); excluding it, free cash flow would have been about -$1.06 billion, and on an 'as spent' basis including $1.03bn of unpaid capex it was closer to $0.5 billion.
rows.mechanism: Working-capital timing shifts cash between quarters without changing economics; a quarter's free cash flow driven by unpaid bills reverses when the invoices land, so the sustainable cash generation is far below the headline.
rows.benchmark: Q2 2026 free cash flow was -$1.09bn; Q1 2026 $1.44bn; Q4 2025 $1.42bn — the business swings around zero after capex.
rows.weakens: The $2.59bn working-capital figure and the 'as spent' calculation come from a trade analysis of the 10-Q, not from the filing itself.
rows.implication: The auto cash engine is thinner than the narrative: it funds neither the doubling of capex nor the options without help from suppliers' credit or the new facilities.
rows.confidence: high for the reported figures; medium for the adjusted calculation
rows.follow_up: What is trailing-twelve-month free cash flow excluding working-capital swings, and when do the accrued invoices reverse?

rows.finding: The auto cash engine is flat to shrinking: FY2025 revenue fell $2.86bn to $94.83bn and net income fell $3.30bn to $3.79bn, while automotive regulatory credits fell from $2,763m to $1,993m; 9M 2026 revenue rose $8.74bn to $78.67bn but net income fell $576m to $2.38bn, and Q3 2026 operating income was $718m on $28.05bn of revenue (2.6%).
rows.mechanism: Credits were pure-margin revenue; losing them while revenue grows means every incremental dollar of sales carries more cost, so operating leverage runs the wrong way exactly when capex peaks.
rows.benchmark: FY2024 regulatory credits were $2,763m and FY2023 $1,790m, so 2025's $1,993m is a 28% fall from the peak; OBBBA cut remaining performance obligations by $3.84bn.
rows.weakens: Q3 2026 gross margin improved 160bp year on year and energy gross profit is at record levels, so mix is partly offsetting the credit loss.
rows.implication: A shrinking-margin auto business cannot carry a $20bn+ capex programme and a $30bn debt facility without either volume growth or external capital — the central tension of the strategy.
rows.confidence: high — figures from the 10-K notes
rows.follow_up: What is automotive gross margin excluding credits and FSD deferral releases for each of the last eight quarters?

rows.finding: The 2025 CEO Performance Award sets 12 tranches tied to market capitalisation from $2.0 trillion to $8.5 trillion plus 12 operational milestones (20 million vehicles delivered, 10 million active FSD subscriptions, 1 million bots delivered, 1 million robotaxis in commercial operation, and Adjusted EBITDA of $50bn/$80bn/$130bn/$210bn/$300bn/$400bn); as of the 2026 proxy none of the 423.7 million shares had been earned, while trailing Adjusted EBITDA was about $15.0bn and cumulative deliveries 10.2 million.
rows.mechanism: A pay plan is a public statement of management's own targets; measuring delivery against it converts narrative into a scorecard and shows how far the current business is from the first hurdle.
rows.benchmark: The 2018 award, by contrast, was earned in full; the first 2025 tranche needs $50bn of Adjusted EBITDA, 3.3x the current $15.0bn, and a $2.0 trillion market capitalisation.
rows.weakens: The market-capitalisation hurdles make early tranches partly a stock-price test rather than an operating one, so slow certification does not prove operating failure.
rows.implication: The company's own incentive document implies a plan several times larger than the current business; investors are paying for tranches the board has not certified, which supports a wait-for-evidence stance rather than paying for the full plan.
rows.confidence: high — award terms and status from the proxy and the quarterly update
rows.follow_up: Which single operational milestone does management expect to certify first, and on what evidence?

rows.finding: Robotaxi is owned-fleet capital intensity: Tesla carries vehicle depreciation, depot, cleaning, charging, teleoperation and insurance costs on its own balance sheet, with 300+ Cybercabs claimed in Austin and about 2 million cumulative unsupervised miles — while paid Robotaxi revenue is not disclosed separately inside $4.605bn of Q3 2026 services and other revenue.
rows.mechanism: Owning the fleet converts a software margin into an asset-heavy transport margin; returns then depend on utilisation and depreciation, not on licence fees, so scale must be large before the option is worth its capital.
rows.benchmark: Waymo's licensing-and-fleet model spreads capital across Alphabet and partners; Tesla owns the fleet, the depreciation and the depot infrastructure, and disclosed that it is building cleaning, charging, teleoperations and fleet-management capacity.
rows.weakens: Tesla's existing 10.2 million-vehicle fleet and Supercharger network lower the incremental cost of depots and charging relative to a new entrant, which is a real cost advantage.
rows.implication: The strategy's most valuable option also consumes the most capital per unit of proven revenue; without per-trip disclosure the market cannot distinguish a subsidy from a business.
rows.confidence: medium — capital intensity is described qualitatively in filings; no robotaxi capex figure is disclosed
rows.follow_up: What is Robotaxi revenue, cost per trip and vehicle utilisation, and what capex is allocated to the fleet?

rows.finding: Energy is the one second curve already at scale: 46.7 GWh deployed in 2025 and 36.0 GWh in 9M 2026, Megafactory Texas (planned 50 GWh) began production in Q3 2026, Q3 2026 energy revenue was $2.881bn, and SpaceX — a related party — bought $626m of Megapacks in 9M 2026 (about 7% of energy revenue), with $588m of the $729m receivable for undelivered units.
rows.mechanism: Storage revenue is recognised on delivery, so billing a related party for undelivered units builds receivables and deferred revenue without cash; that flatters the order book and the cash conversion.
rows.benchmark: Megapack competes with CATL, BYD and Fluence; Tesla's differentiator is 110 GWh of announced annual capacity (40 GWh California, 20 GWh Shanghai, 50 GWh Texas) and software, not proprietary chemistry.
rows.weakens: Even excluding SpaceX, energy revenue grew and Q3 2026 gross profit reached records; the segment is genuinely profitable, unlike robotaxi or Optimus.
rows.implication: Energy deserves a real multiple, but the related-party share and the undelivered billing mean the 'record backlog' should be discounted before it is capitalised.
rows.confidence: high on capacity and revenue; medium on the backlog claim
rows.follow_up: What is the third-party backlog excluding SpaceX, and what is Megapack gross margin?

plan.decision_question: Does the stated strategy (autonomy, energy, Optimus) fund itself from the auto cash flow, or does it require external capital?
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla's strategy is no longer self-funded: with 2026 capex guided above $20bn against roughly $15bn of trailing Adjusted EBITDA, the company signed $30bn of credit facilities in September 2026 and its own filing says the plan will require funding beyond operating cash flow — so the autonomy and robotics options are now financed with balance-sheet risk, not just auto profits.
plan.why_different: The financial section measures what happened; this section tests whether the stated plan is affordable, whether dated promises were kept, and which 12-month signposts would confirm or kill the strategy.
plan.mechanism: The auto business generates about $15bn of Adjusted EBITDA and low free cash flow after a doubling of capex; the $30bn of new credit lines converts the strategy from self-funded to debt-funded, which shifts the risk from dilution to leverage and turns 2027 milestones into covenant-relevant events rather than narrative ones.
plan.comparison_set: Waymo/Alphabet (capital-light licensing versus owned fleet, deployment permits), BYD (self-funded volume and vertical integration), Chinese OEMs with L3 approvals, and Tesla's own 2018 award, which was earned in full while this one has earned zero of twelve tranches.

plan.prohibited: No 'well funded', 'self-funding', 'massive addressable market', 'clear path to profitability'; no undated 'soon'; no claim that robotaxi or Optimus revenue is material without a disclosed figure.

rows.finding: Tesla, Inc. is a Texas corporation (converted from Delaware on 2024-06-13), headquartered in Austin, with one class of common stock (3,952,648,559 shares at 2026-09-30; 6,000m authorised) and 100m authorised preferred shares of which none are issued. Market capitalisation was $1.58tn at the $399.81 close on 2026-10-30.
rows.mechanism: A single share class means votes and cash-flow rights are proportional: the CEO's 19.8% cannot outvote the 80.2% float, so control runs through the classified board and the charter, not through supervoting stock. Preferred stock authorised but unissued is latent defensive capacity.
rows.benchmark: Rivian, a listed EV peer, has Class A (1 vote) and Class B (10 votes); Tesla's structure is simpler and more minority-proportional than the founder-controlled peer.
rows.weakens: Texas law (Bus. Orgs. Code 21.606), a three-class board and supermajority bylaw provisions still let the board block a takeover or activist programme; proportionality of votes does not equal influence.
rows.implication: The legal wrapper is not the constraint on a 12-month return; an investor owns the whole operating group with no VIE, nominee or minority-interest leakage at the top.
rows.confidence: high - primary filings for entity, share count and charter; dated market data for price
rows.follow_up: Confirm with the Texas Secretary of State that the 2024 conversion and the current certificate of formation are as filed, and whether any blank-check preferred designation has been created since 2026-09-30.

rows.finding: Shares outstanding rose from 3,751m at 2025-12-31 to 3,953m at 2026-09-30 (+202m, +5.4%) as Musk exercised all 303,960,630 options of the 2018 award on 2026-06-16. The 2025 CEO Performance Award adds up to 423,743,904 shares, 10.7% of the 2026-09-30 count; none of its 12 tranches had been earned as of 2026-10-19.
rows.mechanism: The award is closer to an option than to a grant: each earned share carries an offset of $334.09 (cash or shares), so at $399.81 the gross spread is only about $66 per share. Every tranche also requires a market-cap gate beginning at $2tn, about 27% above the 2026-10-30 capitalisation, so dilution arrives only in states where holders have already gained.
rows.benchmark: The 2018 award was 303,960,630 shares (about 12% of the then count) with a $100bn first market-cap gate and 12 tranches; the 2025 award repeats the architecture at $2tn, nine $500bn steps and two $1tn steps to roughly $8.5tn.
rows.weakens: At the top of the plan the transfer is large: 423.7m shares at an $8.5tn capitalisation is about $911bn gross, roughly $770bn net of the $334.09 offsets, close to 9% of that market value - exactly the states in which an equity holder's return is strongest.
rows.implication: Treat the award as a convex claim on the upside: it caps the tail of the return distribution by about 9-10% above $2tn, but it costs nothing at today's price and the voting agreement neutralises its votes until tranches are earned.
rows.confidence: high - share counts, offset and tranche terms all from the proxy or 10-Q; the $8.5tn endpoint rests on a Reuters account of the milestones
rows.follow_up: Obtain the full 2025 CEO Performance Award agreement (Exhibit 10.2 to the 2025-11-07 8-K) and confirm the 12 market-cap levels and the treatment of the $334.09 offset in a change of control.

rows.finding: Musk beneficially owns 699,580,882 shares, 19.8% of the company, of which 207,498,721 shares (29.7% of his stake) are pledged as collateral for personal indebtedness. All directors and officers together hold 20.0%. Insiders sold $87.69m of stock in the 12 months to 2026-10-09 with no open-market purchases: Kathleen Wilson-Thompson $29.95m, James Murdoch $26.72m, Kimbal Musk $25.61m, CFO Vaibhav Taneja $5.41m.
rows.mechanism: A 19.8% founder stake with a pledged block creates a forced-seller channel that is correlated with bad news: a sharp price fall can trigger margin sales that deepen the fall. Board policy caps pledging for the CEO at the lesser of $3.5bn and 25% of pledged value, so the constraint is the loan amount, not the share count.
rows.benchmark: No purchases against $87.69m of sales is a weak signal for a management team asking holders to underwrite a $1.58tn capitalisation; the sales are mostly 10b5-1 or tax-withholding transactions, which reduces the informational content.
rows.weakens: Sales equal about 0.04% of Musk's stake and 0.006% of market value; Wilson-Thompson and Murdoch are exiting directors with planned programmes, so the signal is weaker than the headline suggests.
rows.implication: Pledge risk is a tail event to price, not a reason to avoid; the absence of any insider buying at $360-450 is a modest negative on management's own view of the 12-month return.
rows.confidence: high for holdings and pledges (proxy), medium for interpretation of sales
rows.follow_up: Ask for the loan-to-value terms and lenders behind the 207.5m pledged shares, and whether any pledge was added after 2026-09-30.

rows.finding: FY2025 revenue was $94.83bn, down 3% from $97.69bn: automotive $69.53bn (-10%), energy generation and storage $12.77bn (+27%, 29.8% gross margin) and services $12.53bn (+19%). Q3 2026 revenue was $28.05bn, flat year on year, with energy down 16% to $2.88bn, gross profit $5.49bn, operating income $718m and net income $787m.
rows.mechanism: Automotive is still 73% of FY2025 revenue at a 16.2% gross margin, so group profit is geared to vehicle price and volume, not to the faster-growing storage line; storage adds margin (29.8%) but fell 16% in Q3 2026 on lower Megapack prices and fewer Powerwall deployments.
rows.benchmark: Energy rose from 10.3% of FY2024 revenue to 13.5% in FY2025, yet group gross margin fell from 17.9% to 18.0% before opex and operating income compressed; the mix shift has not yet changed the profit pool.
rows.weakens: Q3 2026 gross margin rose 160bp year on year and services grew to $4.61bn, so the mix is improving even as reported revenue is flat.
rows.implication: A 12-month holder is buying an auto-margin business with an optionality overlay; the segment disclosure, not the holding structure, is where the return is made or lost.
rows.confidence: high - audited annual figures and reviewed quarterly figures
rows.follow_up: Separate regulatory-credit revenue from vehicle gross profit in FY2026 to see how much of the 16.2% automotive margin is policy-dependent.

rows.finding: Tesla runs eight primary manufacturing sites: Fremont (Model 3/Y, >550,000 units), Shanghai (>950,000), Berlin (>375,000), Texas (Model Y >375,000, Cybertruck >125,000, Cybercab >125,000), Nevada (Semi 25,000), plus Megapack plants in California (40 GWh), Shanghai (20 GWh) and Texas (50 GWh) and Powerwall in Nevada (>6 GWh). Headcount was 134,785 at 2025-12-31.
rows.mechanism: Installed vehicle capacity of roughly 2.5m units against Q3 2026 deliveries of 486,532 (about 1.95m annualised) leaves meaningful idle capacity; fixed-cost absorption therefore depends on volume recovery, and each new line (Semi, Cybercab, Optimus) adds depreciation before revenue.
rows.benchmark: Shanghai alone (>950,000) is nearly half of global capacity and the source of the cost base that supports export margins; Berlin set a quarterly production record in Q3 2026.
rows.weakens: Capacity is a nameplate figure that management says depends on equipment uptime and supply; battery availability, not demand, was cited as the Q3 2026 volume constraint.
rows.implication: Operating leverage is the mechanism that turns a flat revenue year into either margin expansion or further compression; it is not a structural feature an investor can rely on without volume.
rows.confidence: high for capacity and headcount (company disclosure); medium for the utilisation calculation
rows.follow_up: Get quarterly production by plant and the Semi/Cybercab ramp schedule to test the 2.5m capacity against demand.

rows.finding: Tesla has never paid a dividend, has no share-repurchase authorisation (no purchases in FY2025), holds $45.45bn of cash and short-term investments, and proposes only three items at its 2026-12-03 meeting: three Class I directors, a say-on-pay vote and auditor ratification. A 2025 management proposal to remove supermajority voting requirements won about 39.4% of shares outstanding and failed.
rows.mechanism: With no payout and no buyback, total return is the share price alone; cash is recycled into capex ($4.73bn in Q3 2026) and related-party investments ($2.0bn into xAI, converted into SpaceX stock on 2026-03-12). Supermajority requirements and a classified board mean a minority cannot force a change of capital-allocation policy.
rows.benchmark: General Motors, a single-class OEM peer, returns cash through dividends and buybacks; Tesla's retention is justified only if reinvestment earns above its cost of capital.
rows.weakens: Retaining cash is defensible when capex is $4.7bn a quarter and the balance sheet funds the AI and robotics build without external capital; the $2.0bn xAI position is only 0.13% of market value.
rows.implication: The 12-month return is a pure price bet with no carry; governance provisions make a change in capital-return policy unlikely without board initiative.
rows.confidence: high - all from the 10-K and 2026 proxy
rows.follow_up: Ask the board whether a buyback authorisation would be considered if the shares trade below the $334.09 offset level, and how the xAI/SpaceX position will be marked.

rows.finding: 3,952,648,559 shares were issued and outstanding at 2026-09-30. The count includes 423,743,904 unearned 2025 CEO Performance Award restricted shares and 286,428,773 unvested 2018 award restricted shares: Q3 2026 basic weighted-average shares were 3,240m, which equals 3,952.6m less 710.2m unvested restricted shares (within 2.4m of rounding and timing), while diluted was 3,541m.

No new shares are issued when the 2025 award tranches are earned, so the dilution is to EPS and to Musk's economic share, not to the legal count.

rows.finding: The proxy's beneficial-ownership percentages are based on 3,952,648,559 shares at 2026-09-30, adding options exercisable within 60 days to each holder's own percentage and subtracting the 423,743,904 unearned award shares from the denominator for Musk and for the officer-director group only (3,528,904,655), which yields Musk's 19.8% and the group's 20.0%; on the unadjusted count Musk is 17.7% and the group 17.9%.

rows.benchmark: Rivian reports founder ownership on the same beneficial basis, but with a 10-vote Class B that separates economic and voting percentages; Tesla's single class keeps the two identical.
rows.weakens: Any reading that Musk's stake rose to 19.8% of the company; it did not, the denominator changed.
rows.implication: Quote 17.7% when comparing Musk with other holders of the issued count and 19.8% only when reproducing the proxy; the gap is 2.1 points and entirely definitional.

rows.finding: The proxy publishes no public-float figure and does not state whether the 423,743,904 award shares enter a float calculation. The residual non-insider float including Vanguard is 2,822,408,040 shares (71.4% of the issued count); excluding Vanguard it is 2,611,611,528 (66.1%), with the 423.7m shown as its own row so the cap table sums to 100.0%.
rows.mechanism: A single-class company with a 17.9% insider block and a 10.7% unearned award block leaves about two-thirds of the count genuinely tradable; float is a computed residual, not a disclosed figure.
rows.benchmark: Nasdaq large caps typically have a free float above 80%; Tesla's 66.1-71.4% is lower but not controlled-company territory.
rows.weakens: The earlier cap table's 96.7% sum, which mixed the proxy's ex-award group percentage (20.0%) with full-count holder percentages (5.3%, 71.4%).
rows.implication: Liquidity is not the constraint; the constraint is that the 10.7% award block is issued, forfeitable and outside the float, so it cannot be voted against Musk or sold by him.
rows.confidence: medium-high: arithmetic from the proxy base, but the float definition is ours
rows.follow_up: Obtain Tesla's index-provider float file (S&P, MSCI) to see whether the unearned award shares are treated as float or as strategic holdings.

rows.finding: The 2025 CEO Performance Award is 423,743,904 shares in 12 equal tranches, 0 earned at 2026-10-19, each tranche gated first on market capitalisation from $2 trillion (26.6% above the $399.81 close on 2026-10-30) through nine $500bn and two $1tn increments to $8.5 trillion, with a $334.09 per-share offset and five-year holding requirement.
rows.mechanism: Market-cap gates transfer value only in up states, and the offset makes the award a premium-struck option: gross spread $65.72 a share at $399.81, $769.6bn net at the $8.5tn top (9.1% of that capitalisation).
rows.benchmark: The 2018 award had a $100bn first gate and no offset; GM's 2025 CEO realized pay was $48.2m with no mega-grant.
rows.weakens: The headline that shareholders approved a $1tn pay package; at the current price the in-the-money value of all 12 tranches is zero until the first gate is crossed.
rows.implication: The award is not a 12-month dilution event: the first gate is 26.6% above spot, so a flat or down year transfers nothing and the share count does not change.
rows.confidence: high: proxy and award terms
rows.follow_up: Model the probability-weighted value of the award under the valuation team's scenarios and check whether the offset is payable in cash or shares at Tesla's election.

rows.finding: Tesla has never paid a dividend, has no repurchase authorisation and made no purchases in FY2025 while holding $45.45bn of cash and short-term investments; the board is classified, and a 2025 management proposal to remove supermajority voting requirements won 39.4% of shares outstanding and failed.
rows.mechanism: With no distribution and no buyback, a holder's 12-month return is the share price alone; a classified board blocks a majority from changing that policy.
rows.benchmark: GM returned $6.3bn through buybacks and dividends in 2025; BYD pays a dividend; Tesla returns nothing.
rows.weakens: The counter-argument that $45.45bn of cash is 'available' for return: without an authorisation or a board that will propose one, the cash is not a holder's claim.
rows.implication: The absence of capital return is a structural cap on total return, not a temporary choice, and it argues for sizing the position as a price-only bet.
rows.confidence: high: 10-K and 10-Q disclosures
rows.follow_up: Ask whether the board would consider a buyback authorisation at the 2026-12-03 meeting and whether any director has proposed one.

rows.finding: FY2025 revenue was $94.83bn: automotive $69.53bn (73.3%), energy generation and storage $12.77bn (13.5%) at a 29.8% gross margin, and services $12.53bn (+19%). Q3 2026 deliveries were 486,532, down 2% year on year, while storage deployment was 13.7 GWh.
rows.mechanism: Growth has shifted from vehicle volume to storage and software, so the revenue mix is improving margin quality even while the auto top line is flat.
rows.benchmark: Energy is 13.5% of revenue but a larger share of gross profit than its revenue share implies, given the 29.8% margin against 16.2% automotive.
rows.weakens: The bear case that Tesla is only a car company with a declining margin; the energy segment grew 13.5% of revenue from 10.3% a year earlier.
rows.implication: The equity is increasingly a storage-and-software business priced as an auto-plus-optionality story; a 12-month holder needs storage growth to offset auto volume.
rows.confidence: high: 10-K segment data and 8-K results
rows.follow_up: Split FY2025 gross profit by segment to see whether energy already earns more gross profit than automotive.

plan.decision_question: Does Tesla's legal, ownership and capital structure as of 2026-10 constrain an equity holder's 12-month return?
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla's structure is shareholder-plain — one class, a Texas parent, no VIE — but a 10.7% unearned award, a $2tn first vesting gate, no capital return and a classified board mean the 12-month holder owns a price-only claim whose upside above $2tn is shared with the CEO.
plan.why_different: This section is the legal and ownership map: who owns what, how many shares exist, and which structure features move a holder's return. It does not judge products, demand or valuation.
plan.mechanism: The award shares are already issued and outstanding but unearned and outside the float; earning them dilutes EPS and Musk's economic share without changing the legal count. Market-cap gates move value only in up states, and no dividend or buyback leaves total return to the share price.
plan.comparison_set: BYD, GM, Rivian and Lucid on share classes, float, capital return and founder ownership; Tesla's single class is cleaner than Rivian's ten-vote Class B but its capital return is the weakest of the group.
plan.counter_evidence: One share class, 71.4% non-insider float, seven of nine independent directors, no salary for the CEO, and award tranches that require a 26.6% market-cap gain before any value transfers — all features that protect minority holders more than the headline pay package suggests.
plan.visual: A cap table on one denominator that sums to 100% with the unearned award shares as a separate row, plus a kpi row for the $2tn gate.
plan.prohibited: Do not call the award 'unissued'; do not mix proxy beneficial-ownership percentages with full-count percentages; no 'huge', 'strong', 'well positioned'.

team.author: Company Analyst
queries: SEC DEF 14A 2026-10-19: directors and nominees, independence determination, chair, classified board, committee membership
SEC DEF 14A 2026-10-19: compensation discussion, 2025 CEO Performance Award tranches, $334.09 offset, pay ratio, pledge policy
SEC DEF 14A 2026-10-19: related-person transactions with SpaceX and xAI, $2.0bn xAI investment converted to SpaceX stock
SEC 8-K 2025-11-07 (items 5.02, 5.07): shareholder approval of the 2025 award, 1,892,235,822 for and 564,940,908 against
SEC 10-K FY2025 item 1A: key-person risk factor, Musk does not devote full time, pledge and forced-sale risk

web search: Tesla xAI investment board approval after shareholder vote

web search: Tornetta v. Musk Delaware Supreme Court 2025 reversal

rows.finding: The board has nine directors, seven of them independent, with Robyn Denholm as independent chair since November 2018 and all four committees composed solely of independent directors. It remains a three-class board with three-year terms and supermajority voting requirements; the 2025 management proposal to remove those requirements won about 39.4% of shares outstanding and failed, and the board has said it will not repropose declassification. Elon Musk and his brother Kimbal both sit on the board.
rows.mechanism: Independence without replaceability is weak accountability: a classified board with supermajority bylaw protection cannot be changed by a majority of holders, and two family directors sit in the room where related-party terms are set.
rows.benchmark: Nasdaq requires a majority-independent board, which Tesla meets; independent-chair prevalence among large US companies is now the norm, so the chair is not a differentiator. Peer EV maker Rivian concentrates control through Class B ten-vote shares instead.
rows.weakens: Seven of nine independents, an independent chair with over 100 meetings in 2025, and the annual say-on-pay give holders real voice, and the 2025 award itself was put to a shareholder vote.
rows.implication: On paper the board can constrain the CEO; in practice the charter makes it hard for holders to replace it, so governance risk is a slow-burn discount rather than a 12-month catalyst.
rows.confidence: high - composition and committee facts from the proxy; the 39.4% figure is the company's own disclosure
rows.follow_up: Ask for the board's succession plan and the circumstances in which it would repropose declassification; check whether any nominee received below 80% support in 2025.

rows.finding: The 2025 CEO Performance Award is 423,743,904 shares in 12 equal tranches. Every tranche needs a market-capitalisation milestone starting at $2tn and one of 12 operational milestones (four strategic-product goals including 10m active FSD subscriptions, 1m bots and 1m Robotaxis, and eight Adjusted EBITDA goals), with market-cap steps of nine $500bn and two $1tn to roughly $8.5tn. Each earned share carries a $334.09 offset and a five-year holding period; tranches 11 and 12 also require a board-approved CEO succession framework.
rows.mechanism: Because the market-cap gate is necessary for every tranche, the CEO's marginal reward is a valuation event, not an operating return; the $334.09 offset and five-year hold reduce the value per share but do not change that the payout is priced off the share price.
rows.benchmark: GM CEO Mary Barra's realized 2025 compensation was $48.2m, up 61.7%; Tesla's award is worth roughly an order of magnitude more at the top end and is gated on valuation, not on relative total shareholder return.
rows.weakens: The first gate is about 27% above the 2026-10-30 capitalisation, no tranche has been earned, the votes on unearned shares are neutralised by an irrevocable proxy, and the CEO took no salary in 2025 (realized pay ratio 0.00:1).
rows.implication: The structure does align the CEO with holders on valuation, and the succession condition is a genuine key-person mitigation; but it pays most where the equity has already compounded, and it rewards a market-cap outcome the board cannot verify operationally.
rows.confidence: high for terms, medium for the calculated transfer
rows.follow_up: Model the award's transfer at each market-cap step and test whether the Adjusted EBITDA milestones are calibrated to the auto business or to a robotics outcome that does not yet exist.

rows.finding: Shareholders approved the 2025 CEO Performance Award on 2025-11-06 with 1,892,235,822 votes for, 564,940,908 against and 12,227,846 abstentions (about 76.6% of votes cast). A separate non-binding measure authorising funding for xAI drew about 1.06bn votes for and 916.3m against but was recorded as rejected because Tesla's bylaws count abstentions as votes against; on 2026-01-16 Tesla nonetheless agreed to invest $2.0bn in xAI, completing the investment on 2026-03-12 as SpaceX Class A stock after the SpaceX-xAI merger.
rows.mechanism: The xAI vote is the clearest test of whether the independent majority constrains capital allocation toward the CEO's other companies; the outcome shows the constraint is procedural (Audit Committee review) rather than binding.
rows.benchmark: The 2018 award was ratified with about 77% support in June 2024; the xAI measure drew only about 54% of votes cast and failed once abstentions were counted - a materially narrower mandate.
rows.weakens: $2.0bn is 0.13% of market value and the position was acquired on the same terms as other investors in the round; the investment is now SpaceX stock, arguably a stronger asset than an xAI preferred stake.
rows.implication: The board treats a rejected shareholder measure on a related-party transaction as advisory and proceeds; a holder should assume future related-party capital flows to Musk companies are a board decision, not a shareholder one.
rows.confidence: high for the vote tallies (8-K and proxy), medium for the motive attribution
rows.follow_up: Establish whether the Audit Committee or a special committee approved the xAI/SpaceX investment, and obtain the minutes and fairness opinion, if any.

rows.finding: The 10-K states that although Musk 'spends significant time with Tesla', he 'does not devote his full time and attention to Tesla' and holds management positions at SpaceX, xAI, Neuralink and The Boring Company. The proxy records that xAI became a SpaceX subsidiary in February 2026; Musk is SpaceX's CEO, CTO and chairman. Tesla now holds SpaceX Class A stock as a result of the $2.0bn conversion.
rows.mechanism: A CEO whose other companies are now vertically linked (SpaceX owns xAI, Tesla owns SpaceX stock) turns time allocation into a related-party conflict, not just a scheduling issue.
rows.benchmark: No CEO of a comparably sized US company runs three other operating companies; the proxy itself lists SpaceX, xAI, Neuralink and The Boring Company.
rows.weakens: The 2025 award includes a succession-framework condition on tranches 11-12, and the proxy says Musk is 'highly active' in Tesla management.
rows.implication: Key-person risk is disclosed, not mitigated: the reward for holders is that the same attention produced the Robotaxi and Optimus optionality they are paying for, and the risk is an abrupt loss of that attention.
rows.confidence: high - the risk factor and biography are explicit
rows.follow_up: Ask the board what formal time-allocation commitment it has from the CEO and how it would disclose a material increase in his time at SpaceX.

rows.finding: Sales and service leadership has been unstable: Omead Afshar (VP, North America and Europe sales and manufacturing) left in June 2025, Troy Jones (head of North American sales) was dismissed in July 2025, Tesla's North American service head left in August 2025 and Raj Jegannathan - who had taken over North American sales - departed in February 2026 after 13 years. The finance and manufacturing core is stable by contrast: Vaibhav Taneja has been CFO since 2023 and Tom Zhu, SVP APAC and global vehicle manufacturing since June 2025, joined Tesla in 2014 and built Gigafactory Shanghai.
rows.mechanism: Replacing a sales leader twice in a year transfers demand execution to Musk and a small circle, which raises the operational cost of his divided attention.
rows.benchmark: Peer OEMs also rotate sales leaders, but two North American sales heads in under twelve months and a service head leaving within two months is a rate above the norm for a company whose problem is demand.
rows.weakens: Total headcount rose to 134,785 at 2025-12-31, Zhu's manufacturing bench delivered record Berlin output and 10.2m cumulative vehicles by Q3 2026, and some departures follow the April 2024 restructuring rather than a 2025-26 deterioration.
rows.implication: The bench is deep in manufacturing and finance but thin in demand generation at the moment demand is the binding constraint; that is an execution risk a 12-month holder should price.
rows.confidence: high for names and dates, medium for the causal read on demand
rows.follow_up: Reference-check the last three North American sales leaders on mandate, resources and reasons for leaving; ask who now owns the sales number.

rows.finding: Musk holds 19.8% of the shares (699,580,882, including 286,428,773 restricted shares from the 2018 award) and has pledged 207,498,721 shares. He has taken no salary since 2019, and Tesla has no employment agreement or severance arrangement with any named executive officer. Directors and officers sold $87.69m of stock in the 12 months to 2026-09-09 with no purchases; the largest sellers were Wilson-Thompson ($29.95m), Murdoch ($26.72m) and Kimbal Musk ($25.61m).
rows.mechanism: Zero cash pay and no severance remove the usual retention levers; retention runs through the founder's own equity, so a holder's return and the CEO's retention are the same variable.
rows.benchmark: Founder-led peers with 15-25% stakes are common; what is unusual is a 19.8% stake with a $0 salary, no employment agreement, no severance and a $2tn-gated equity award all at once.
rows.weakens: The CEO's wealth is already overwhelmingly Tesla stock, which aligns him without any pay; directors' sales are small relative to holdings and mostly under 10b5-1 plans.
rows.implication: Alignment is genuine and cheap for the company (no cash pay), but the reliance on one person is total and the only formal succession mechanism sits inside an incentive award rather than in a board plan.
rows.confidence: high for holdings and pay facts, low for the inference on management's view
rows.follow_up: Run reference checks on Taneja and Zhu with former colleagues at SolarCity, PwC and Tesla Shanghai; check whether any director has a business relationship with SpaceX or xAI beyond board service.
