plan.decision_question: Is capital allocation and key-person risk adequately handled, and is it priced into the equity?
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla's board is majority independent on paper, but the three decisions that mattered in 2024-2026 - a $2.0bn investment in the CEO's own AI company after shareholders rejected the measure, a pay award that can reach 423.7m shares, and the retention of a classified board - all went against the minority's expressed preference, so key-person and capital-allocation risk are real, formally disclosed, and only partly offset by the award's extreme vesting gates.
plan.why_different: The company section maps the entity and the share count; this section judges the people who allocate the capital, the incentives that drive them and the board that is supposed to constrain them.
plan.mechanism: Pay gated by market capitalisation makes the CEO's marginal reward a valuation event rather than an operating return; a classified board with two family directors and a compensation chair who also sits on SpaceX's board weakens related-party oversight; a revolving sales bench transfers execution risk to a small group around Musk.
plan.comparison_set: GM's $48.2m realized CEO pay in 2025, Rivian's dual-class founder control, the 2018 award's $100bn first gate, and Tesla's own 2024 ratification vote (about 77%) as the base rate for shareholder support.
plan.counter_evidence: Seven of nine directors are independent with an independent chair since 2018; the pay award was approved by 76.6% of votes cast; the CEO takes no salary and no severance; tranches 11-12 require a CEO succession framework; Tom Zhu provides genuine manufacturing depth; headcount rose to 134,785.
plan.visual: Team assessment matrix plus the evidence component on the xAI vote and the pay vote.
plan.prohibited: strong team; experienced management team; proven leadership; visionary; world-class; recently; many years of experience

team.author: Company Analyst
queries: Elon Musk University of Pennsylvania 1997 BA physics BS economics independent biography
Robyn Denholm University of Sydney economics degree UNSW Master of Commerce 1999
Tom Zhu Auckland University of Technology bachelor's 2004 Duke Fuqua MBA
JB Straubel Stanford BS MS energy systems engineering graduation years
DEF 14A 2026: directors, independence, committee membership and related-party transactions
DEF 14A 2026 compensation: 2025 CEO Performance Award tranches, market-cap gates and offset
10-K FY2025: executive officers, key-person disclosure and headcount

rows.finding: Musk earned a BA in physics from Penn's School of Arts and Sciences and a BS in economics from Wharton, both awarded in 1997, and Stanford confirmed in 2024 it had no record of him enrolling in a graduate programme.
rows.mechanism: The founder's technical credibility rests on a physics degree from an Ivy League school, not on a Stanford doctorate; the proxy lists the degrees but gives no year or institution detail, which is why the independent record matters.
rows.benchmark: Among the peer CEOs, Mary Barra holds a Stanford MBA and RJ Scaringe a PhD from MIT Sloan; Musk's two bachelor's degrees are the weakest formal technical credential in that group but the longest operating record.
rows.weakens: The widely repeated claim that Musk attended or completed a Stanford PhD in applied physics.
rows.implication: Founder-market fit is real but rests on operating history, not on postgraduate science training; this does not change the investment case but stops the CV from being overstated in diligence.
rows.confidence: medium-high: independent press account, consistent with the proxy's degree list
rows.follow_up: Obtain the University of Pennsylvania registrar or alumni record confirming both degrees and the 1997 award date.

rows.finding: Tom Zhu earned a Bachelor of Commerce in information technology from Auckland University of Technology in 2004 and an MBA from Duke University's Fuqua School of Business (year not stated); he joined Tesla in 2014 and built Gigafactory Shanghai in 10 months in 2019 at 65% lower cost than the US Model 3 plant.
rows.mechanism: Zhu's manufacturing record is the strongest operating evidence in the team: a greenfield plant delivered in ten months at a large cost advantage, then scaled to the largest plant in the system.
rows.benchmark: Legacy OEM greenfield plants typically take 24-36 months; the 10-month Shanghai build is the comparison that makes Zhu a credible operating No. 2.
rows.weakens: The claim that Tesla has no operating bench behind Musk; Shanghai and Berlin were run by Zhu, not by the CEO.
rows.implication: Bench depth in manufacturing is real, which partly offsets key-person risk at the CEO level; the missing piece is commercial leadership.
rows.confidence: medium: independent press citing Zhu's own social profile; not a primary HR record
rows.follow_up: Reference-check Zhu with two Shanghai suppliers and one former Tesla China director on cost, quality and ramp decisions.

rows.finding: Robyn Denholm holds a Bachelor of Economics from the University of Sydney and a Master of Commerce from the University of New South Wales in 1999; she began her career at Arthur Andersen in Sydney in 1984 and was finance VP at Toyota Australia from 1989, before CFO roles at Juniper Networks and Telstra.
rows.mechanism: The independent chair's qualification is financial and operational, not automotive engineering; her authority is procedural (committee control) rather than technical.
rows.benchmark: GM's chair is its CEO (combined role); Tesla separates the roles but the chair has never publicly opposed a Musk proposal on a shareholder vote.
rows.weakens: The defence that an independent chair with a finance background is a check on the CEO; the xAI sequence shows the check did not bind.
rows.implication: The chair is competent to run a board process but has not used her position to block related-party capital allocation, which is the governance risk that matters.
rows.confidence: medium: Wikipedia with citations, proxy confirms degrees and roles
rows.follow_up: Read Denholm's public statements on the xAI vote and ask whether she recused herself from the SpaceX board relationship.

rows.finding: The nine-person board has seven independent directors and four independent committees, but the Compensation Committee chair (Ehrenpreis) has sat on SpaceX's board since February 2026, the counterparty to Tesla's $2.0bn investment and $143.3m of 2025 revenue.
rows.mechanism: Independence is measured by Nasdaq tests, not by counterparty relationships; a director who sits on both sides of a related-party transaction can be nominally independent and still conflicted.
rows.benchmark: S&P 500 peers typically disclose and recuse directors with counterparty board seats; Tesla's proxy calls the SpaceX relationship immaterial.
rows.weakens: The company's 'seven of nine independent' defence of its board.
rows.implication: The governance discount is justified by the composition of the committee that sets the CEO's pay, not by the number of independent directors.
rows.confidence: high: proxy discloses the SpaceX board seat
rows.follow_up: Ask for the Compensation Committee's minutes on the 2025 award and whether Ehrenpreis recused himself from the SpaceX-related votes.

rows.finding: The 2025 CEO Performance Award pays only after market-capitalisation gates from $2 trillion to $8.5 trillion and 12 operating milestones, yet the realised 2025 pay of Musk was $0 (no salary since 2019) against Mary Barra's $48.2m at GM; the award's accounting value of $158.36bn is not cash.
rows.mechanism: Pay is tied to market value first and operating metrics second, so the CEO is rewarded for multiple expansion even if margins or volumes disappoint; the offset and holding period claw back some of the upside.
rows.benchmark: GM ties 70% of Barra's pay to operating metrics and total shareholder return; Tesla's first gate is a market cap 26.6% above spot.
rows.weakens: The claim that the award is 'performance-based' in an operating sense: every tranche needs the market cap first.
rows.implication: The compensation structure does not align pay with the operating milestones a 12-month holder cares about; it aligns the CEO with a multi-year market-cap outcome.
rows.confidence: high: proxy compensation tables and award terms
rows.follow_up: Model how many operating milestones must be met at each market-cap level and whether any tranche can vest on operations alone.

rows.finding: Executive turnover in 2024-2026 is concentrated in commercial roles: Omead Afshar left in June 2025, Troy Jones was dismissed as North American sales head in July 2025, the North American service head left in August 2025 and Raj Jegannathan departed in February 2026 after 13 years, while Zhu and Taneja remain.
rows.mechanism: The operating bench is deep in manufacturing and finance but thin in demand generation and sales, exactly the functions that a flat-volume year stresses.
rows.benchmark: GM and Ford have had stable North American sales leadership through 2025-2026; Tesla has had three changes in the role in 18 months.
rows.weakens: The claim that the bench is uniformly thin; manufacturing and finance are covered.
rows.implication: The missing hire is a permanent North American sales and service leader; until it is filled, the delivery miss risk sits with Musk and Zhu.
rows.confidence: medium: press and filing disclosures, not a complete HR record
rows.follow_up: Ask who currently runs North American sales and service and whether the role reports to Zhu or to Musk.

rows.finding: Education years are not in the 2026 proxy for any director or officer; independent records give Musk 1997, Zhu 2004 and Denholm's master's 1999, while Taneja, Straubel, Ehrenpreis and Wilson-Thompson have no public graduation year we could verify.
rows.mechanism: The proxy lists institutions and degrees but not dates, so a CV table built only on it looks complete while missing the chronology that shows whether a degree preceded or followed the operating career.
rows.benchmark: Peer proxies (GM, Rivian) also omit graduation years; the gap is standard, not a Tesla-specific disclosure failure.
rows.weakens: Any table that presents 'Year: not stated' as if it were a finding about the person rather than about the proxy.
rows.implication: The education table should state its evidential limit rather than imply a date; the career table carries the chronology that matters.
rows.confidence: high: checked the proxy and independent records
rows.follow_up: Request alumni-register confirmation for Taneja (ICAI), Straubel (Stanford) and Ehrenpreis (UCLA/Stanford) if the IC asks for full CVs.

plan.decision_question: Is capital allocation and key-person risk adequately handled, and is it priced?
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla's board is majority independent on paper, but the three decisions that mattered in 2024-2026 — a $2.0bn investment in the CEO's own AI company after shareholders rejected the measure, a pay award that can reach 423.7m shares, and the retention of a classified board — all went against the minority's expressed preference, so key-person and capital-allocation risk are real, formally disclosed, and only partly offset by the award's extreme vesting gates.
plan.why_different: This section judges the people and the board: who runs the company, how they are paid, what the record says about succession and bench depth. It does not re-litigate the share count or the valuation.
plan.mechanism: A classified board and a compensation committee with a counterparty director convert shareholder votes into advisory signals; the CEO's attention is split across four companies, and the pay package pays him for market value rather than operating returns.
plan.comparison_set: GM (Barra's operating-weighted pay, combined chair/CEO), Rivian (founder control with a 10-vote class), BYD (founder-led with a concentrated but single-class structure) and Lucid (professional CEO, PIF control); Tesla's governance sits between founder control and a professional board.
plan.counter_evidence: Seven of nine directors are independent, the CEO takes no salary, the award's first gate is 26.6% above spot, Zhu's Shanghai ramp is a genuine operating bench, and there has been no CFO turnover since 2023.
plan.visual: The education table with verified years where they exist, plus an assessment matrix whose scores are defined, not asserted.
plan.prohibited: No 'strong team', no 'experienced team', no scores without a stated scale, no 'recently'.

rows.finding: Automotive gross margin was 18.5% in Q3 2026 and 18.1% excluding regulatory credits ($3,806M gross profit less $113M credits on $20,447M of ex-credit revenue), up from 16.3% ex-credits in Q2 2026 and 15.4% in Q3 2025.
rows.mechanism: Credits are pure-margin revenue, so removing them cuts the denominator as well as the numerator; the residual margin is what the vehicle itself earns before credits, and it moves with regional delivery mix, FX and one-off cost items rather than with factory efficiency.
rows.benchmark: FY2023 ex-credit automotive gross margin of 17.7% ($16,030M less $1,790M credits on $80,629M) - i.e. the 2026 recovery only returns the business to its 2023 level; BYD's Q3 2026 gross margin was 18%.
rows.weakens: Management attributed the sequential gain to a higher Asia-Pacific delivery mix; Q3 2026 also carried tariff refunds and warranty adjustments in cost of automotive sales, and Q2 2026 fell back to 16.3%, so the level is fragile.
rows.implication: Invest: the core vehicle economics are stabilising near 18%, which supports the base case that the auto business can fund itself at current volume, but not that it can fund $20B+ of annual capex.
rows.confidence: high - margin computed from filed segment tables and independently corroborated at 18.1% by the earnings call
rows.follow_up: What is the ex-credit automotive gross margin by region, and how much of the Q3 2026 improvement is the tariff refund quantified in dollars?

rows.finding: Regulatory credit revenue fell to $113M in Q3 2026 from $146M in Q2 2026, $380M in Q1 2026 and $542M in Q4 2025 - an 87% decline in three quarters - and was 15.7% of Q3 2026 operating income versus 45.8% of FY2025 operating income.
rows.mechanism: Credits carry negligible incremental cost, so each dollar is operating profit; OBBBA restricted US programmes and European pool members left, removing the buyer base rather than the supply of credits.
rows.benchmark: FY2024 credits of $2,763M and $890M in a single quarter (Q2 2024) per the Q3 2026 call; FY2025 credits of $1,993M, of which $1,451M in the first nine months.
rows.weakens: Tesla does not name the buyers, and deferred revenue on credits is immaterial, so the remaining contracted volume cannot be verified; the $3.84B fall in remaining performance obligations in 2025 suggests further attrition.
rows.implication: Price out the line: the credit collapse has already happened and the P&L absorbed it, so it is no longer a forward risk - but it also means 2026 operating profit has no credit cushion left to lose.
rows.confidence: high on the quarterly figures; low on the buyer base, which is not publicly disclosed
rows.follow_up: Who bought the $113M of Q3 2026 credits, and how much credit revenue is contracted for 2027?

rows.finding: Energy generation and storage earned $954M of gross profit on $2,881M of revenue in Q3 2026 (33.1%), after $640M on $3,139M (20.4%) in Q2 2026 and $952M on $2,408M (39.5%) in Q1 2026; revenue per GWh deployed fell from $274/kWh in Q1 2026 to $210/kWh in Q3 2026.
rows.mechanism: Storage is priced per project and per kWh, so margin swings with Megapack pricing, cell cost, tariff recoveries and warranty true-ups rather than with a stable take rate; deployment timing means revenue and cost land in different quarters.
rows.benchmark: Segment gross margin of 18.9% in FY2023, 26.2% in FY2024 and 29.8% in FY2025; trailing-twelve-month margin 29.7% on $12,265M of revenue.
rows.weakens: Management attributed the Q3 2026 jump to tariff refunds and cell-related warranty cost reimbursements and Q2 2026 fell to 20.4% on unfavourable warranty adjustments - the same mechanism in reverse.
rows.implication: Wait for confirmation: energy earns the group's best gross margin, but a segment whose margin moves between 20% and 40% within three quarters cannot yet be underwritten at 33%.
rows.confidence: high on the segment figures; medium on the per-kWh figures, which divide revenue including solar and services by GWh deployed
rows.follow_up: What is the Megapack-only gross margin and average selling price, and what share of the $10.42B of remaining energy performance obligations is priced at 2026 levels?

rows.finding: Services and other revenue rose 33% year on year to $4,605M with gross profit of $734M (15.9%), an all-time high, from $366M (10.5%) in Q3 2025.
rows.mechanism: Used vehicle sales, collision and non-warranty maintenance carry parts and labour costs, while paid Supercharging runs on a network of 8,904 stations and 84,465 connectors whose utilisation costs are largely fixed - rising utilisation lifts the marginal margin.
rows.benchmark: Rivian's software and services segment earned a 42% gross margin on $605M of revenue in the same quarter, so Tesla's services margin is lower but on 7.6 times the revenue.
rows.weakens: The mix is not broken out, so the margin gain could come from used-vehicle pricing rather than Supercharging or insurance; an ageing fleet raises warranty claims that sit in cost of automotive, not services.
rows.implication: Invest further: services is the fastest-growing line and the second-largest source of gross profit, and its margin is improving without one-off help disclosed in the filings.
rows.confidence: high on revenue and margin; low on the mix, which Tesla does not disaggregate
rows.follow_up: What are the revenue and gross margin of paid Supercharging and of Tesla Insurance separately?

rows.finding: Per vehicle in Q3 2026: automotive revenue $42,259, cost of automotive revenue $34,436, gross profit $7,823; group R&D and SG&A of $4,776M is $9,817 per vehicle, so the automotive line alone runs at about -$1,994 per vehicle before energy and services.
rows.mechanism: Group opex is largely fixed and increasingly directed at AI, robotics and chip programmes that produce no current revenue, so it is spread over whatever volume the vehicle business delivers.
rows.benchmark: Q4 2025 cost per vehicle was $33,666 and gross profit $8,639; Q1 2026 revenue per vehicle was $45,344 on a richer mix.
rows.weakens: Tesla does not disclose segment operating income in an extractable form at Q3 2026, so the opex split behind this figure is an allocation, not a reported number; part of R&D is arguably an investment in options rather than a cost of the car.
rows.implication: The operating profit is not earned by the car: it is earned by energy and services gross profit ($3,470 per vehicle) net of an opex base the car cannot cover.
rows.confidence: medium - derived by dividing filed totals by filed deliveries
rows.follow_up: What share of the $2,761M quarterly R&D is Optimus, silicon and autonomy rather than vehicle programmes?

rows.finding: Tesla's Q3 2026 operating margin of 2.6% ($718M on $28,046M) is below GM's 8.2% EBIT-adjusted margin and Ford's 5.5%, while Rivian still ran an automotive gross loss of $(80)M on 19,248 deliveries and Lucid delivered 3,806 vehicles, down 6.7%.
rows.mechanism: Legacy OEMs carry higher revenue per unit and lower fixed AI spend; sub-scale EV makers carry negative gross margin. Tesla sits between them: a competitive gross margin with an opex load that a 2.6% operating margin barely covers.
rows.benchmark: GM Q3 2026 revenue $50.0B and EBIT-adjusted $4.1B (North America margin 8.7%); Ford revenue $49.5B and adjusted EBIT $2.7B; BYD Q3 2026 gross margin 18% on CNY 195B of revenue.
rows.weakens: GM and Ford margins include high-margin trucks and captive finance, and adjusted EBIT is not GAAP, so the comparison is directional rather than like-for-like.
rows.implication: Compare on operating margin, not gross margin: the gross-margin comparison flatters Tesla, and the operating-margin comparison is what a 12-month holder is paid on.
rows.confidence: high on the reported figures; medium on the comparability
rows.follow_up: How much of GM's and Ford's Q3 2026 margin came from tariffs, pricing and finance arms rather than vehicle gross profit?

plan.decision_question: What are the unit economics of each of Tesla's three reported segments today, and which one actually earns the return?
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla's reported segments show a vehicle business earning an 18.1% gross margin that will not cover group R&D and SG&A, energy storage and services earning the operating profit, and both of those profits helped in Q3 2026 by tariff refunds and warranty true-ups - so the group earns its return on the balance sheet's cash and the storage segment, not on the car.
plan.why_different: The company and market sections describe what Tesla sells and to whom; this section prices one unit of each thing it sells (a vehicle, a GWh, a service transaction, a credit) and shows where the margin actually accrues, which is the input the valuation section needs to separate the auto cash engine from the optionality.
plan.mechanism: Credits are pure profit and are collapsing; energy is project-priced and volatile; services margin rises with network utilisation; group opex is fixed and increasingly aimed at AI and robotics, so the marginal dollar of vehicle gross profit is absorbed before it reaches operating income.
plan.comparison_set: Tesla's own FY2023-FY2025 segment history, plus Q3 2026 GM (8.2% EBIT), Ford (5.5%), BYD (18% gross margin), Rivian (automotive gross loss) and Lucid (deliveries down 6.7%).
plan.counter_evidence: Ex-credit automotive margin rose from 15.4% to 18.1% year on year and services reached a record 15.9%, which is evidence the core is stabilising without credits; Q1 2026 energy at 39.5% and a Megapack backlog sold out through 2027 argue energy can carry the group at a 30%+ margin.
plan.visual: Unit economics waterfall per vehicle for Q3 2026 plus a five-quarter segment gross margin table, with a pricing table (per vehicle, per kWh, per subscription, per credit).
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned, about 5, many customers, recently

rows.finding: Q3 2026 energy gross profit of $954M on $2,881M revenue (33.1%) falls to $428M, 14.8%, once the $526M IEEPA tariff refund credited to energy cost of revenue is removed; the separate $339M customer pass-through remains in revenue.
rows.mechanism: A one-off refund reduces cost without any operating improvement, while the contractual pass-through reduces revenue, so the reported margin overstates the segment's earning power.
rows.benchmark: Q2 2026 20.4% with no refund; nine-month 2026 24.0% ex-refund; Fluence FY2025 13.1% and June 2026 quarter 5.1%.
rows.weakens: The warranty true-up component is not quantified in any filing; Q2 2026's 20.4% shows the underlying margin can exceed 14.8%.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite a 30% storage margin: the base case normalises energy to 14-18%, worth $1.5bn of EBITDA less than the prior 25-30% assumption.
rows.confidence: High on the arithmetic; medium on the normalised level.
rows.follow_up: Does Q4 2026 energy gross margin print above 20% with no tariff refund?

rows.finding: Q1 2026 energy gross margin was 39.5%, Q2 2026 20.4% and Q3 2026 33.1% as reported; on the ex-refund basis Q3 is 14.8% and the nine months 24.0% rather than 30.2%.
rows.mechanism: First-half IEEPA amounts were immaterial, so only Q3 carries the refund; the apparent Q3 improvement over Q2 is entirely the one-off.
rows.benchmark: Prior-quarter and nine-month reported margins.
rows.weakens: Deployment mix and Megapack pricing also move the margin quarter to quarter.
rows.implication: Comparability requires the ex-refund column; the trend is deteriorating, not improving.
rows.confidence: High.
rows.follow_up: What is the Megapack-only margin excluding Powerwall and solar?

rows.finding: Fluence earned 13.1% gross margin in FY2025 (year to 2025-09-30) and 5.1% in the June 2026 quarter on $649.8M of revenue and $33.2M of gross profit.
rows.mechanism: Project integrators absorb liquidated damages and cost overruns; the June 2026 quarter carried both, so it is a trough not a benchmark.
rows.benchmark: Tesla Q3 2026 ex-refund 14.8%.
rows.weakens: Fluence is smaller and less vertically integrated than Tesla.
rows.implication: Tesla at 14.8% is near Fluence's fiscal-year margin, not six times its worst quarter; the 33.1% headline is the outlier.
rows.confidence: High.
rows.follow_up: Does Fluence's FY2026 second half recover toward 13%?

rows.finding: Sungrow's storage business earned 36.49% gross margin in FY2025 on RMB 37.29bn of revenue; CATL's storage battery gross margin was 23.96% in H1 2026.
rows.mechanism: Cell and inverter manufacturers capture component margins; project integrators capture project margins, so the correct comparison set spans both.
rows.benchmark: Tesla energy 14.8% ex-refund; 24.0% nine-month ex-refund.
rows.weakens: Sungrow and CATL margins are as-reported, not adjusted for any tariff refunds, and their product mix differs.
rows.implication: Tesla sits between the integrator and the component maker, consistent with vertical integration but not at a structural premium.
rows.confidence: Medium-high.
rows.follow_up: What share of Tesla's Megapack cost is in-house cell production today?

rows.finding: Robotaxi discloses nearly 2m cumulative unsupervised miles and a 1,051-vehicle authorised Texas fleet, but no revenue, paid trips, insurance cost, remote-supervision cost or cost per paid mile.
rows.mechanism: Contribution per paid mile equals fare less energy, maintenance, depreciation, insurance, remote supervision and platform cost; every cost line is undisclosed.
rows.benchmark: If total cost is 60% of fare, a 2x cost per mile turns a 40% contribution margin into -20%; at 50%, 2x leaves zero.
rows.weakens: Tesla reports rapid mileage growth and a Cybercab launch, which show technical progress even without economics.
rows.implication: The 15% autonomy branch of the bull case cannot be underwritten from filings; disclosure of a positive-contribution revenue line is the proof event.
rows.confidence: High on the disclosure gap; illustrative on the sensitivity.
rows.follow_up: What is Robotaxi revenue per vehicle-week in Austin after insurance and remote supervision?

rows.finding: A Q3 2026 vehicle carried $42,259 of revenue and $34,436 of cost, $7,823 of gross profit ($7,590 ex-credits), against $9,817 of group R&D and SG&A, so automotive alone runs at about -$1,994 a vehicle.
rows.mechanism: Group operating cost is largely fixed and charged to the car; the auto line breaks even only near 611,000 deliveries a quarter including credits (about 629,000 ex-credits) against 486,532.
rows.benchmark: GM 8.2% EBIT-adjusted, Ford 5.5% operating margin, BYD 18% gross margin.
rows.weakens: Ex-credit automotive gross margin rose to 18.1% from 15.4% year on year, level with BYD.
rows.implication: The car does not pay for the group's research budget; storage and services gross profit cover the gap.
rows.confidence: High.
rows.follow_up: Can cost per vehicle fall below $33,000 without a mix shift?

rows.finding: Reported regulatory credit revenue fell to $113M in Q3 2026 after a $475M reversal of previously recognised credits; contracted obligations over one year fell to $384M from $841M at 2025-12-31.
rows.mechanism: The reversal is a clawback of past revenue, so gross credit sales were about $588M; the shrinking backlog caps the line's recovery.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 credit revenue $1,993M; Q4 2025 $542M.
rows.weakens: Gross Q3 sales exceeded Q4 2025, so current demand has not collapsed yet.
rows.implication: The credit line is in structural decline; do not capitalise it.
rows.confidence: High.
rows.follow_up: Who are the remaining credit buyers after Toyota and Stellantis left the EU pool?

plan.decision_question: What are the unit economics of each of Tesla's three reported segments today, and which one actually earns the return?
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla's car earns an 18.1% ex-credit gross margin that does not cover group research and selling cost, and the storage business that appeared to cover the gap at 33.1% in Q3 2026 falls to 14.8% once the $526M IEEPA tariff refund is removed, so the group's operating profit rests on a mixed and partly one-off gross-profit pool and on interest income, not on a structurally superior unit economic model.
plan.why_different: This section works at the segment and per-unit level: who pays, what a car, a MWh and a service transaction earn, and what is missing from robotaxi; the financials section covers the consolidated statements, cash conversion and balance sheet.
plan.mechanism: Gross profit per vehicle, per kWh and per service transaction against allocated group operating cost; one-off tariff refunds and regulatory credits inflate the reported pool.
plan.comparison_set: Fluence FY2025 13.1% and June 2026 quarter 5.1%; Sungrow storage 36.49% FY2025; CATL storage 23.96% H1 2026; GM 8.2% EBIT-adjusted, Ford 5.5%, BYD 18% gross margin.
plan.counter_evidence: Ex-credit automotive margin rose to 18.1% from 15.4% year on year, Q2 2026 energy margin was 20.4% without refunds, Megapack is nearly sold out through 2027 and services set a 15.9% record.
plan.visual: The energy as-reported versus ex-refund table, with the Q1-Q3 series and the storage peer benchmark table.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned; any claim that storage earns the best margin without the ex-refund caveat.

financials.author: Fundamentals Analyst
queries: get_sec_financials TSLA 5 years: income statement, cash flow, balance sheet, ROE/ROA/ROIC, working-capital days, interest coverage, latest quarter and TTM
TSLA 10-Q Q3 2026 item 2: cash flow summary, capex, credit facilities, debt principal, inventory and warranty notes
TSLA 10-Q Q2 2026 item 2: six-month cash flow drivers, capex guidance of more than $25 billion for 2026
TSLA 10-K FY2025 item 7 and item 8: debt and lease obligations, interest income, restructuring, tax rate, warranty critical audit matter, deferred revenue
TSLA 8-K 2026-10-21 exhibit 99.1: five-quarter operating cash flow, capex, free cash flow, GAAP and non-GAAP net income
Tesla Q3 2026 earnings call transcript: capex about $20 billion, $30 billion of new facilities, bitcoin and SpaceX mark-to-market

rows.finding: Operating income fell from $8,891M in FY2023 to $7,076M in FY2024, $4,355M in FY2025 and $3,466M on a trailing-twelve-month basis to 2026-09-30, a 61% decline, while capex over FY2023 to the first nine months of 2026 totalled $41,778M; ROIC fell from 28.3% to 5.5%.
rows.mechanism: Returns fall when invested capital grows faster than profit; capex moved from vehicle capacity into AI compute and robot manufacturing that has no disclosed revenue, so the denominator rises while the numerator falls.
rows.benchmark: FY2023 operating income of $8,891M and ROIC of 28.3%; ten-year Treasury yield 4.93% at 2026-10-30; FY2022 operating income $13,656M.
rows.weakens: Depreciation has also risen ($5,670M trailing twelve months versus $4,120M in FY2024), so part of the operating-income fall is the accounting cost of the capex itself rather than a collapse in gross profit.
rows.implication: Price lower or wait: the incremental capital has produced negative incremental operating income for three years, so the burden of proof sits on management to show a revenue line for the new capex.
rows.confidence: high - all figures from filed statements
rows.follow_up: What is the disclosed return on the Terafab, Cortex and Optimus lines, and when do they have an external revenue line?

rows.finding: Nine-month 2026 free cash flow of $1,883M ($14,897M operating cash flow less $13,014M capex) rests on a $3,868M rise in accounts payable since 2025-12-31; without that payables build, free cash flow would have been about -$1,985M. Management itself attributes $3.51B of the $3.96B operating-cash-flow increase to working capital.
rows.mechanism: Operating cash flow = profit + non-cash charges + working capital; a payables build is a one-period loan from suppliers that reverses when purchases slow or terms normalise.
rows.benchmark: Cash conversion cycle improved to 2.6 days from 13.0 days in FY2025 and 14.4 days in FY2024; accounts payable rose from $13,371M at 2025-12-31 to $17,239M at 2026-09-30.
rows.weakens: Tesla's cash conversion cycle is still positive but short, and days payable of 75.3 remain below FY2022's 91.9, so the current level is not an extreme.
rows.implication: Discount the free cash flow: a company funding capex through supplier credit is borrowing from its supply chain, and that source cannot grow faster than purchases indefinitely.
rows.confidence: high - balances and cash flow lines from the filed 10-Q
rows.follow_up: What are the supplier payment terms and is the payables extension a one-time step-up or an ongoing source of cash?

rows.finding: Interest income was $1,680M in FY2025, $1,301M in the first nine months of 2026 and $445M in Q3 2026, equal to 31.8%, 42.9% and 46.5% of pre-tax income respectively, and to 62% of Q3 2026 operating income.
rows.mechanism: A large cash balance converts into pre-tax income at the short rate; with pre-tax income falling, the same interest becomes a larger share, which flatters earnings quality measures such as the effective tax rate and EPS.
rows.benchmark: FY2024 interest income was 17.5% of pre-tax income ($1,569M of $8,990M); the ten-year Treasury yielded 4.93% at 2026-10-30.
rows.weakens: Interest income is real cash and Tesla earns it without credit risk on Treasury holdings, so it is not an accounting artefact - only a non-operating one.
rows.implication: Strip out financial income: at a 4% yield the $45.4B portfolio contributes roughly $1.8B a year of pre-tax profit that has nothing to do with making or selling anything, and a falling short rate removes it.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; medium on the sustainability, which depends on the cash balance and short rates
rows.follow_up: How much of the $45.4B of cash and short-term investments is required for operations, and how much is available for distribution or buyback?

rows.finding: At 2026-09-30 Tesla held $17,853M of cash, $27,594M of short-term investments and $9,267M of debt ($9.28B principal, $1.32B current), for $36,180M of net cash, plus $30.00B of unused committed facilities under three credit agreements signed in September 2026.
rows.mechanism: Net cash plus undrawn commitments defines the funding gap a capital-intensive programme can absorb before dilution; at $66B of combined liquidity against $20B of annual capex the gap is closed for several years.
rows.benchmark: Total minimum lease payments of $7,955M at 2025-12-31 are excluded from the $9.27B of debt; unused committed credit was $6.43B at 2025-12-31.
rows.weakens: The facilities were signed in the same quarter that capex guidance was cut to about $20B from more than $25B, which suggests the financing and the spending plan are linked to a larger programme than the filings describe.
rows.implication: Balance-sheet risk is not the constraint on a 12-month view: $36.2B of net cash and $30B of undrawn lines cover the $20B capex year without equity, so the decision turns on the return on that capex, not on solvency.
rows.confidence: high - figures from the filed liquidity disclosures
rows.follow_up: What are the covenants and pricing on the three September 2026 facilities, and were they arranged for capex or as a liquidity backstop against a demand shock?

rows.finding: Earnings quality items in the first nine months of 2026: stock-based compensation of $3,346M (4.3% of revenue), up 79% year on year, of which the 2025 CEO Performance Award is the main driver (SG&A stock compensation +$870M); an effective tax rate of 20% versus 27%, helped by a valuation-allowance release on California deferred tax assets in Q2 2026; a warranty reserve of $7,414M, up 20.9% since 2025-12-31, while cost of automotive sales benefited from what management calls warranty adjustments; and GAAP net income of $787M against non-GAAP of $1,697M in Q3 2026.
rows.mechanism: Non-GAAP adds back stock compensation, which is a real transfer to employees; a valuation-allowance release lowers the tax rate without recurring, and warranty true-ups move cost between periods through a judgemental reserve.
rows.benchmark: FY2024 stock-based compensation was $1,999M (2.0% of revenue) and the FY2025 effective tax rate was 27%.
rows.weakens: Diluted shares rose only 0.4% year on year to 3,541M, so the $4.3B trailing stock-based compensation has not yet reached shareholders as dilution - but it will if the performance award vests.
rows.implication: Haircut the run-rate: adjusted profit more than doubles GAAP profit, and two of the margin levers this year (warranty adjustments and the tax rate) are estimates rather than operating gains.
rows.confidence: high on the reported figures; medium on the size of the warranty release, which is not quantified
rows.follow_up: How large was the warranty true-up in cost of automotive sales in Q3 2026, and on what evidence was the California valuation allowance released?

rows.finding: Tesla has paid no dividend and repurchased no shares in any year from FY2021 to the third quarter of 2026, while investing $2.00B of cash in SpaceX common stock during the first nine months of 2026 and disclosing in the FY2025 report an agreement to make a minority equity investment in xAI.
rows.mechanism: Related-party equity purchases convert liquid cash into illiquid minority stakes whose fair value is set by the same controlling shareholder, and the mark-to-market flows through other income rather than through a segment.
rows.benchmark: Rivian and Lucid are the base rate for sub-scale EV makers (automotive gross loss at 19,248 deliveries; Lucid deliveries down 6.7%); GM authorised a $20B buyback in Q3 2026.
rows.weakens: The amount is 5.5% of the $36.2B net cash position, so it is a capital-allocation signal rather than a solvency issue, and the SpaceX stake has a published valuation from its own funding rounds.
rows.implication: Governance discount: capital is being allocated to Musk-controlled private companies at the same time as the core business needs $20B of capex, which is a use of cash the shareholder cannot value.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Were the SpaceX and xAI investments approved by disinterested directors, and how are they marked to market each quarter?

plan.decision_question: What do the reported financials say about earnings quality, free cash flow conversion and balance-sheet capacity to fund capex?
plan.thesis_sentence: The reported financials show Tesla still converting about $1.5 billion of free cash flow a quarter but no longer earning its cost of capital - a 5.5% trailing return on invested capital against a 4.93% ten-year Treasury - because $41.8 billion of capex since 2023 has coincided with a 61% fall in operating income, and the reported profit is propped up by interest on the cash pile and a $3.9 billion payables build rather than by operations.
plan.why_different: The business model section prices a unit and asks which segment earns the margin; this section asks whether the reported numbers can be trusted, whether the cash is real and whether the balance sheet can carry the capex - the three inputs the valuation section discounts.
plan.mechanism: Capex has moved from vehicle capacity, where it earned 28% ROIC in 2023, to AI compute and robot lines that produce no disclosed revenue, so invested capital rises while operating income falls; the profit gap is filled by interest on the cash pile and by stretching payables, both of which have limits, while warranty and tax adjustments soften reported cost.
plan.comparison_set: Tesla's own FY2023-FY2025 statements and returns, the 4.93% ten-year Treasury yield as the risk-free alternative, FY2023 ROIC of 28.3% as the company's own peak, and GM's $20B buyback and Ford's $4.7B quarterly adjusted free cash flow as peer capital-return benchmarks.
plan.counter_evidence: Free cash flow is still positive in three of the last four quarters, net cash of $36.2B plus $30B of undrawn facilities covers the $20B capex programme without raising equity, and the payables extension may reflect deliberate supplier terms on a rising production base rather than stress.
plan.visual: Three-year plus trailing-twelve-month statements table and a returns and working-capital table, with an info warning on the free-cash-flow composition.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned, about 5, many, recently, kitchen-sink

rows.finding: Trailing adjusted EBITDA is $14,995M (Q4 2025 $4,154M + Q1 2026 $3,668M + Q2 2026 $3,273M + Q3 2026 $3,900M); subtracting the $526M Q3 2026 IEEPA energy refund gives $14,469M, held at $14.5bn in the base case.
rows.mechanism: The refund is a non-recurring cost credit, so trailing EBITDA overstates the run-rate by its full amount; no credit recovery, robotaxi line or margin recovery is added back.
rows.benchmark: Prior base case of $16.0bn; the $1.5bn gap is 12 points of energy margin on $12.3bn of trailing energy revenue (27% to 15%).
rows.weakens: Q2 2026 energy margin of 20.4% without refunds and a Megapack backlog sold through 2027 could support more than 15%.
rows.implication: The 40% base case at 70x $14.5bn plus $36.18bn net cash is $266 a share, -33.5% from $399.81.
rows.confidence: High on the arithmetic; medium on the normalised margin.
rows.follow_up: Does Q4 2026 adjusted EBITDA print above $3.5bn without tariff refunds?

rows.finding: The bull case's $506.05 is 3,952.6M shares times price, or $2,000bn, exactly the first market-capitalisation gate of the 2025 CEO Performance Award, and 131 times the $15.3bn of EBITDA the same case assumes.
rows.mechanism: The price is a governance threshold divided by the share count, not a discounted cash flow or an EBITDA multiple.
rows.benchmark: $2,000bn first award gate; $15.3bn bull-case EBITDA; 70x on $14.5bn gives the $266 base.
rows.weakens: A SpaceX combination at a 20-35% premium could independently reach a similar price.
rows.implication: The bull price should be treated as a milestone, not an intrinsic value; it is not evidence about the business.
rows.confidence: High on the arithmetic.
rows.follow_up: What exchange ratio would the SpaceX committees propose?

rows.finding: Nine-month free cash flow of $1,883M is smaller than the $3,868M payables build; without it free cash flow would have been -$1,985M, and Q3 2026 free cash flow of $1,531M rested on a $2,590M working-capital inflow.
rows.mechanism: Payables and accrued liabilities fund the cash conversion; the cash conversion cycle fell to 2.6 days from 13.0, which is a finite source, not a recurring one.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 free cash flow $6,220M; $3,670M of capex sat in liabilities at 2026-09-30.
rows.weakens: Operating cash flow of $14,897M and $30.0bn of undrawn facilities mean liquidity is not at risk.
rows.implication: Reported free cash flow is a ceiling, not a run-rate; the quality of earnings is weaker than the level.
rows.confidence: High.

plan.decision_question: What do the reported financials say about earnings quality, free cash flow conversion and balance-sheet capacity to fund capex?
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla converted $1,531M of free cash flow in Q3 2026, but the statements no longer show it earning its cost of capital: a 5.5% trailing return on invested capital sits 57 basis points above the ten-year Treasury, $41,778M of capex since 2023 has coincided with a 61% fall in operating income, and the profit that remains leans on interest income, a payables build and $526M of one-off energy tariff refunds, so trailing adjusted EBITDA normalises to $14,469M and the 40% base case at 70x plus net cash is $266 a share.
plan.why_different: This section reads the consolidated statements and notes for earnings quality, cash conversion, returns and balance-sheet capacity; the business_model section owns segment and per-unit economics.
plan.mechanism: Normalise adjusted EBITDA for one-offs, bridge EBITDA to free cash flow through working capital and capex, and compare ROIC with the risk-free rate and the cost of the capex programme.
plan.comparison_set: Trailing adjusted EBITDA $14,995M versus $14,469M normalised; 70x plus $36.18bn net cash equals $266; 103x trailing EV/adjusted EBITDA against BYD at 17.3x; ROIC 5.5% against a 4.93% ten-year Treasury.
plan.counter_evidence: Nine-month operating cash flow of $14,897M, $36,180M of net cash and $30.0bn of undrawn facilities fund the plan without equity; nine-month gross margin of 19.0% is the highest since 2023.
plan.visual: The statements table with Q3 2026, the returns and working-capital table, and the adjusted EBITDA bridge from $14,995M to $14,469M.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned; any use of $16.0bn base-case EBITDA or 25-30% energy margin.

plan.prohibited: huge market, well positioned, risks are manageable, clear path, story stock, priced for perfection, about X vehicles, many analysts, leading player

rows.finding: At $399.81 on 2026-10-30 Tesla carried a $1,580.4bn market capitalisation and $1,544.2bn enterprise value on $14,995m of trailing adjusted EBITDA, $3,466m of operating income and $3,303m of free cash flow: 103x EV/adjusted EBITDA, 445x EV/EBIT, 14.9x EV/sales and a 0.2% free-cash-flow yield.
rows.mechanism: Earnings collapsed while the price held: trailing diluted EPS fell from $4.90 in FY2021 to $0.91, so the multiple absorbed the decline rather than the price; a 103x EBITDA multiple means a one-turn move is worth about $15bn, so the price is a multiple, not an earnings, claim.
rows.benchmark: BYD trades at 17.3x EV/EBITDA and 21.2x trailing earnings; GM at 19.1x earnings; the four-legacy-peer median is 19.1x
rows.weakens: Adjusted EBITDA adds back $4.3bn of stock compensation and excludes $863m of unrealised SpaceX gains, so the 103x is flattered; on EBITDA before that add-back the multiple is 144x.
rows.implication: There is no earnings-based defence of the price at any conventional multiple; the buyer at $399.81 is buying a re-rating option, and should size the position accordingly.
rows.confidence: high, both figures dated and registered
rows.follow_up: Does the company intend to keep adding back $4.3bn of stock compensation to EBITDA, and does a buyback or dividend ever enter the capital-allocation policy?

rows.finding: Automotive at 0.6-0.8x sales on $75.0bn, energy at 2.5-3.0x sales on $12.3bn and 30.2% nine-month gross margin, services at 1.5x sales on $16.3bn, plus $36.2bn net cash and a roughly $2.9bn SpaceX stake, value the reported businesses at $139-160bn, or $35-40 a share.
rows.mechanism: The company's filings identify the businesses but not their profit; valuing each on the multiple its closest listed peer earns is the only method that keeps the SOTP tied to disclosed revenue and margin rather than to a narrative.
rows.benchmark: Rivian at 2.6x EV/sales, GM at about 0.4x, Ford about 0.25x, CATL at 19.8x earnings, Fluence at a $0.8bn capitalisation
rows.weakens: If automotive recovers to a 10% operating margin ($7.5bn) and earns 25x, the automotive leg alone is worth $188bn and the SOTP rises to about $285bn, $72 a share; that still leaves 82% of the price unexplained.
rows.implication: Roughly $1.42-1.44tn, 90-91% of the equity value, is paid for robotaxi, FSD and Optimus; a holder is underwriting those, not the car business.
rows.confidence: medium: segment revenue and gross profit are filed, but segment operating income is not disclosed, so the split is an estimate.
rows.follow_up: What energy-segment operating margin does the company earn, and would it disclose it separately as the segment passes $15bn of revenue?

rows.finding: Holding the $1,544.2bn enterprise value requires $89bn of adjusted EBITDA at BYD's 17.3x, $62bn at 25x or $39bn at 40x, against $15.0bn trailing; at a 25% robotaxi operating margin and $100,000 of revenue per vehicle-year, the 20-40x cases need 2.1-4.2m vehicles in commercial service by 2030.
rows.mechanism: Price equals multiple times earnings, so the required earnings can be inverted from the price; comparing that requirement with installed capacity shows whether the requirement is a growth assumption or a step change.
rows.benchmark: Management's own 2025 award pairs a $4.0tn market capitalisation with $50bn of adjusted EBITDA, an 80x multiple; Tesla trades at 103x today
rows.weakens: The $100,000 per vehicle-year assumption drives the fleet number; at Waymo-like revenue per vehicle the required fleet would be a fifth as large, though still thousands of times the 1,051 authorised today.
rows.implication: The market's implied 2030 fleet is 17-34 years of current Cybercab capacity, so the price requires a capacity and regulatory build-out the filings do not describe.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, medium on the milestone detail, which comes from a fan site's reading of the proxy rather than the proxy itself.
rows.follow_up: What revenue per vehicle-week and operating margin has the Austin fleet actually produced, and what does the company expect Cybercab capacity to be beyond the 125,000 units a year installed in Texas?

rows.finding: Energy revenue fell 16% year on year in Q3 2026 to $2,881m and 6% over nine months, with gross margin of 33.1% in the quarter; even at 3x sales the segment is worth about $37bn, 2.3% of the market capitalisation.
rows.mechanism: Energy is a capacity-constrained manufacturing business with a 30% gross margin, so it scales with Megafactory capacity (130 GWh installed) rather than with software economics, and its revenue is currently shrinking as average selling prices fall.
rows.benchmark: Energy storage was 11.8% of trailing revenue and 12.7% of trailing gross profit; CATL, the closest listed peer, earns a 19.8x P/E
rows.weakens: Megafactory Texas added 50 GWh of capacity in Q3 2026 and the order rate is the highest on record, so a revenue reacceleration is plausible even if the multiple case is not.
rows.implication: The strongest counter-argument to the section, that energy growth alone justifies the premium, fails on arithmetic; an investor cannot own Tesla as an energy-storage story at this price.
rows.confidence: high, all four figures filed in the 10-Q or 8-K.
rows.follow_up: Does the highest-ever order rate convert to revenue in the next two quarters, and how much of the backlog is priced at the lower Megapack 3 average selling price?

rows.finding: Consensus is Hold, with 24 buy, 1 strong buy, 20 hold and 3 sell at 48 firms, and an average target of $408.61, 2.2% above the close; the highest observed target is RBC at $480 and the lowest rating is Jefferies at $400.
rows.mechanism: A price target is a multiple times an estimate; with earnings at $0.91 a share the targets are multiple calls on autonomy rather than earnings forecasts, which is why they cluster within 20% of spot despite the 439x P/E.
rows.benchmark: Five aggregators between 2026-10-25 and 2026-10-30 report averages of $408.61 (48 firms) and $442.13 (83 analysts)
rows.weakens: Several targets were raised after Q3 2026 (Mizuho to $460, RBC to $480), so the direction of revisions is upward even if the level implies little upside.
rows.implication: Sell-side consensus offers 2-11% of upside, less than the 12-month realised drawdown of the shares, so an investor is not paid to wait for the analyst community to mark the stock up.
rows.confidence: medium: aggregator pages, not the brokers' notes, and the firm counts differ between providers.
rows.follow_up: What do the notes assume for 2027 deliveries, energy revenue and robotaxi units, and how dispersed are those estimates?

rows.finding: The P/E record is 439.4x against a peer median of 19.1x, but EV/sales at 14.9x is below the 16.5x at the 2025 year end and inside the 2024-2026 range of 14.7-16.5x; the shares are flat over five years (-0.8%) while trailing revenue rose from $53.8bn to $103.6bn.
rows.mechanism: Revenue doubled while the share price went nowhere, so multiple compression, not operating failure, explains the five-year return; the same mechanism can repeat from today's level if autonomy revenue arrives more slowly than the price assumes.
rows.benchmark: Tesla's own fiscal-year multiples: 34.0x in 2022, 57.8x in 2023, 204.6x in 2024, 420.8x in 2025
rows.weakens: EV/sales is at the middle of its recent range, not at a peak, so the de-rating case is weaker on that measure than on earnings.
rows.implication: The multiple has already de-rated once from a higher level and the shares still round-tripped over five years, which is the best evidence that a buyer here is paying for growth to arrive, not for a cheap stock.
rows.confidence: high, all computed from filings and dated prices.
rows.follow_up: Which of the two multiples does the company's own investor communication treat as the reference point, and has the market's chosen multiple changed since the 2024 re-rating?

rows.follow_up: Which of the two multiples does the company's own investor communication treat as the reference point, and has the market's chosen multiple changed since the 2024 re-rating?

rows.finding: The 1.74m active FSD subscriptions are a company definition: the Q3 2026 8-K counts both upfront purchases and monthly subscriptions and excludes free trials; the CFO put half the paid base on monthly plans on 2026-10-21, implying 870,000 one-time buyers and 870,000 monthly payers; FSD-related deferred revenue was $4.08bn at 2026-09-30.

rows.benchmark: The naive 1.74m x $99 x 12 = $2.07bn ceiling; management's 'approaching $1 billion'; $1.03bn at the 50% monthly mix against the $103.6bn top line.
rows.weakens: Tesla does not disclose monthly payers or standalone FSD revenue; the $4.08bn deferred line also includes connectivity, Supercharging and over-the-air updates; the 50% split is call commentary, not a filed number.
rows.implication: Value FSD on the $1bn recurring run-rate, under 1% of revenue, not on 1.74m x $99; the 10m-subscription award milestone is flattered by legacy buyers.
rows.confidence: medium-high: the definition is in the 8-K (primary); the 50% mix is management commentary reported by an independent outlet; the deferred-revenue line mixes several obligations.
rows.follow_up: How many monthly subscribers churn each quarter, and what happens to the count as pre-2026 upfront buyers' cars retire?

rows.finding: China NEV retail fell 16.7% year on year to 1.084m in September 2026, the ninth consecutive decline, with 9M 2026 down 12.8% to 7.758m; penetration nonetheless hit a record 67.0%, BEV retail fell 7.4%, PHEV retail fell 35.6% and EREV 19.3%, while BEV wholesale rose 18.3% and NEV exports rose 163.5%.
rows.mechanism: Tightening the NEV purchase-tax preference and withdrawing local subsidies raised the cash price of the cheapest cars first (CPCA attributes the A00 collapse to subsidy policy), which is why PHEV/EREV demand broke while export volumes absorbed the production.
rows.benchmark: Total Chinese passenger-car retail fell 28.0% in September, so NEV penetration rose while absolute NEV volume fell — a mix effect, not a demand recovery.

rows.confidence: high — CPCA data reproduced with the brand-level retail table.

rows.mechanism: The 2025-2027 CO2 step forces fleet-average emissions down, so BEV volume is regulation-created rather than customer-pulled; the Commission's 2025-12-16 proposal to cut the 2035 target from 100% to 90% shifts the long-dated backstop but not the 2026 compliance year.
rows.benchmark: BEV units rose roughly 49% year on year in 9M 2026 (derived from the 22.7% and 16.1% shares on the 5.7%-larger market) versus PHEV at 10.1% share and hybrids at 36.3%.

rows.confidence: high on the shares and units (ACEA), medium on the derived unit growth rate.
rows.follow_up: Does Tesla's EU unit growth exceed the 49% market growth, i.e. is it holding share in the only growing region?

rows.finding: Global storage installations were 112 GW in 2025 and are forecast at 158 GW / 459 GWh in 2026; Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in 9M 2026 (about 7.8% of the 2026 forecast) but its storage revenue per GWh fell from about $273m in Q3 2025 to $210m in Q3 2026, a 23% decline.
rows.mechanism: Chinese cell and system supply has turned storage into a cost-deflation market: volume compounds at 40%+ while price per GWh falls faster than cost, so revenue growth lags unit growth and value accrues to the lowest-cost cell maker.
rows.benchmark: Tesla storage revenue per GWh of $210m in Q3 2026 against $273m a year earlier; Fluence's gross margin of 5.1% in the June 2026 quarter versus Tesla's 33.1% shows the integration premium.
rows.weakens: Tesla reported its highest-ever storage order rate and backlog in Q3 2026 and its energy gross margin rose to 33.1% (helped by $526m of IEEPA tariff refunds), so demand is not collapsing and Tesla is not the price taker in systems.

rows.confidence: high on Tesla figures (filed statements) and on BNEF GW; medium on the GWh conversion.
rows.follow_up: How much of Tesla's storage backlog is priced at 2026 levels, and what is the contracted price per MWh?

rows.follow_up: What is Tesla's paid Robotaxi ride count and average fare in Austin, and what does the California DMV permit record show about its deployment status?

plan.thesis_sentence: Two of Tesla's three vehicle markets are now shrinking pools — the US after the 2025-09-30 credit repeal and China after its 2026 purchase-tax reset — so the growth it is being paid for sits in European BEVs, in storage where unit prices are falling 23% a year, and in a paid robotaxi market that is still a sub-$1bn business run at Waymo's pace.
plan.why_different: Section 4 measures the pools Tesla can sell into and their direction; section 5 measures who is taking those pools. This section therefore sizes TAM/SAM/SOM in units and revenue per unit, and is the only section that separates policy-created demand from organic demand and that builds a bottom-up paid-robotaxi revenue check against third-party TAMs.

plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla holds the US EV market at 52.9% year to date but is the fourth-largest NEV brand in China at 6.0% of retail, its European recovery is growth off a collapsed 2025 base inside a BEV pool expanding about 49% a year, and the only two positions it clearly owns are the charging standard every major automaker has licensed and a storage gross margin six times Fluence's.
plan.why_different: Section 4 sizes the pools; this section measures who takes them, at what price and with what margin, product by product. It is the only section that compares Tesla's realised gross margins with named competitors' filed margins, and that separates a share gain inside a shrinking market from a share gain inside a growing one.
plan.mechanism: Share is won on price per unit of range and software; a competitor with a 30-40% cost advantage in cells (BYD, Xiaomi through supply scale) can undercut in China and still earn a margin abroad, which is why Tesla's China share falls while its US and storage margins hold.
plan.comparison_set: BYD's 273,143 BEV and 183,570 PHEV sales in September 2026 and 3.08m 9M NEV volume against Tesla's 486,532 quarterly deliveries; Xiaomi's 269,000 9M 2026 units against a 550,000 target; Waymo's ~500k paid rides a week against Tesla's undisclosed Austin ride count; Fluence's 5.1% gross margin and Rivian's 8.2% against Tesla's 33.1% energy and 18.5% automotive margins.
plan.counter_evidence: Tesla's automotive gross margin rose to 18.5% in Q3 2026 from 17.0% a year earlier while its units fell 2%, so it is trading share for margin rather than buying volume; it sets the charging standard (NACS licensed by all major automakers, 8,904 Supercharger stations); and its storage gross margin of 33.1% is 6x Fluence's, the clearest cost advantage in the case.
plan.visual: Per-product competitor table with regulatory status, price, share and gross margin, a positioning table (Product | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat) and a SWOT quad component.
plan.prohibited: fierce competition; competitive moat; best-in-class; clear leader; strong position; many competitors; well positioned

rows.finding: Waymo had 220.6m rider-only miles through 2026-03, about 3,700 vehicles and 500,000 paid rides a week; Tesla reports 2.0m cumulative unsupervised miles, 0.9% of Waymo, with 1,051 vehicles on the Texas authorisation list on 2026-10-27 (544 Cybercab, 507 Model Y), up from 739 on 2026-10-09.
rows.mechanism: Verified driverless miles and permits, not supervised fleet size, set the paid-autonomy lead.
rows.benchmark: Roughly 110x Tesla's 2.0m unsupervised miles; Tesla's 1,051 Texas vehicles are 28% of Waymo's fleet.
rows.weakens: Tesla's unsupervised miles grew 8x quarter on quarter from a small base, and its Texas fleet grew 42% in 18 days.
rows.implication: Waymo, not BYD, is the most dangerous competitor; Tesla is third globally in paid autonomy behind Waymo and Baidu.
rows.confidence: high: operator safety data and state authorisation list.
rows.follow_up: Will Tesla disclose paid trips and revenue, and obtain a California deployment permit?

rows.finding: Tesla's Q3 2026 energy gross margin was 33.1% as reported but 14.8% ex-$526m of IEEPA tariff refunds and warranty true-ups ($428m on $2,881m), below CATL's 23.96% ESS segment and Sungrow's 32.43% storage segment.
rows.mechanism: One-off refunds flattered the reported margin; on a clean basis Tesla is mid-pack among storage manufacturers.
rows.benchmark: CATL ESS 23.96%, Sungrow storage 32.43%, Fluence 13.1% FY2025 and 5.1% June 2026 quarter, LGES 1.5% operating margin.
rows.weakens: Segment definitions differ (cell, system, integrator) and Tesla's 36.0 GWh of 9M 2026 deployments still gives it scale.
rows.implication: Drop the 'unrivaled cost position' claim; Tesla's storage advantage is software and installed base, not cost per kWh.
rows.confidence: high: filed and reported segment figures; Sungrow storage margin from search snippet (page 403).
rows.follow_up: What installed cost per kWh does Tesla achieve on Megapack versus CATL and Sungrow systems in the same tender?

rows.finding: BYD sold 3,078,490 passenger cars in 9M 2026, 2.3x Tesla's 1,324,681, including 273,143 BEVs in September; Geely sold 119,682 retail units, Leapmotor 78,202 and Xiaomi 40,015 in September, with Tesla fourth at 64,837.
rows.mechanism: Local battery cost and vertical integration let BYD price below Tesla and still earn a domestic margin.
rows.benchmark: BYD's domestic 16.66% gross margin in 2025 versus 19.46% overseas.
rows.weakens: Chinese BEV wholesale grew 18.3% while Tesla's China retail fell, so Tesla lost share in a growing BEV sub-pool.
rows.implication: Tesla is the price taker in China; the domestic margin ceiling is set by BYD, not by Tesla.
rows.confidence: medium: volume data high confidence, margin by region from a media calculation.
rows.follow_up: Does Tesla cut China prices again in Q4 2026, and what does that do to automotive gross margin?

rows.finding: Tesla sold 386,194 US EVs in 9M 2026 for 52.9% share (144,094 and 54% in Q3), with automotive gross margin up to 18.5% while regulatory credits fell 73% to $113m.
rows.mechanism: Charging density and brand keep residual buyers after the credit removal, supporting price.
rows.benchmark: The US electric pool fell 30.3% year to date while Tesla's own US volume fell 14.4%.
rows.weakens: Share gains inside a contracting pool can mask absolute decline, and credits were 2.8% of Q3 revenue.
rows.implication: Tesla is the price setter in a shrinking pool; US share gains flatter a smaller revenue base.
rows.confidence: high: Cox/KBB data via trade press and Tesla filings.
rows.follow_up: Can Tesla hold 18%+ automotive margin if US volume falls another 10% in 2027?

rows.finding: Baidu's Apollo Go ran 3.4m trips in Q4 2025 (+200% year on year) and Pony.ai's fleet exceeded 1,400 vehicles on 2026-03-25; Huawei and Momenta together supply more than 80% of China's urban NOA systems.
rows.mechanism: Permit-granting city governments and cheap hardware let Chinese operators add vehicles faster than Tesla adds states.
rows.benchmark: Waymo's 500,000 rides a week; Pony's 3,000 target for end-2026.
rows.weakens: Chinese operations remain geofenced and subsidy-dependent, with no US market access.
rows.implication: Tesla is not the second autonomous operator globally; Chinese fleets scale on geofenced city permits and subsidies.
rows.confidence: medium: operator and trade-press counts, not audited.
rows.follow_up: What are Apollo Go's and Pony's revenue per trip and subsidy per ride?

rows.finding: Super Cruise and BlueCruise are Level 2 hands-free systems on mapped roads, sold on subscription, while Tesla's FSD (Supervised) has 1.74m subscriptions and a broader operational domain.
rows.mechanism: Mapped-road hands-free systems from GM and Ford cap the price Tesla can charge for a supervised product.
rows.benchmark: GM Super Cruise about 750,000 compatible miles; Ford BlueCruise more than 130,000 Blue Zone miles.
rows.weakens: Neither Super Cruise nor BlueCruise operates on city streets, so FSD's domain remains wider.
rows.implication: Hands-free driving is an OEM commodity; Tesla's software premium depends on unsupervised capability, not supervised features.
rows.confidence: medium: document-based comparison of manufacturer claims.
rows.follow_up: What is FSD's monthly churn and revenue per subscriber?

plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla is winning the shrinking US pool, is a price taker in China, a mid-pack storage manufacturer once $526m of refunds are stripped out, and trails Waymo and Baidu in paid autonomy: its wedge protects margin, not volume.
plan.why_different: It names the rival and the price in each product line instead of sizing the pool; the market section supplies the denominators.

rows.finding: No automotive buyer can reach the price: the three closest listing peers together are worth $137.0bn, and the only counterparty with comparable scale that has actually opened a process is SpaceX, whose board and Tesla's formed committees to examine a combination in October 2026.
rows.mechanism: Acquisition maths caps at what a buyer can finance; a $1.58tn equity is four times Saudi Aramco's IPO valuation scale and beyond any automaker's balance sheet, so the acquirer set empties out and the change-of-control route becomes a share exchange.
rows.benchmark: GM $73.7bn, Ford $45.7bn and Rivian $17.6bn are worth $137.0bn together, 8.7% of Tesla's capitalisation
rows.weakens: A SpaceX combination is real enough to change the exit: if it happens on a share-exchange basis, holders receive a faster-growing asset and the premium could be realised inside 12 months.
rows.implication: The exit is a market sale at whatever multiple prevails, or a combination with SpaceX; neither is a cash takeover premium, so a holder cannot count a control premium in the return.
rows.confidence: high on the market data, medium on the inference that no automaker could bid
rows.follow_up: What exchange ratio or valuation framework would each special committee use, and would Tesla holders receive listed or unlisted SpaceX shares?

rows.finding: The shares closed at $356.78 on 2021-12-31, $123.18 on 2022-12-31 and $399.81 on 2026-10-30, a five-year return of -0.8%; the 52-week close range is $297.38-$498.83, a 40.4% peak-to-trough fall and a band 68% as wide as the current price.
rows.mechanism: A 439x earnings multiple has no valuation floor: when the rating falls the price falls by the whole re-rating, which is why one-year losses of 40% recur in a stock whose revenue keeps growing.
rows.benchmark: Tesla fell 65.5% from its 2021 year-end close to its 2022 year-end close and 40.4% from its 52-week high to its 52-week low
rows.weakens: Both drawdowns were followed by recoveries — the 2022 low to today is +225% — so a long horizon has historically been rewarded even from a high multiple.
rows.implication: A 40-65% drawdown has happened twice in five years, so a holder must size for that, not for the 28.5% three-month gain they are buying into.
rows.confidence: high, computed from dated closes
rows.follow_up: What are 12-month realised and options-implied volatility now, and what move does the options market price around the Q4 2026 results?

rows.finding: At $399.81 each 10 turns of EV/adjusted EBITDA is $38 a share, 9.5% of the price; 40x on $15.0bn of adjusted EBITDA plus $36.2bn of net cash gives $636bn, $161 a share and a 60% loss, while the award's $2,000bn gate gives $506.05 and a 27% gain.
rows.mechanism: Return equals the change in the multiple plus the change in earnings; earnings can grow 20% in a year while the multiple halves, and the multiple dominates because it is 103x.
rows.benchmark: Consensus target $408.61; the 2025 award's first gate is a $2,000bn capitalisation; the SOTP floor is $139-160bn
rows.weakens: The bear case assumes a de-rating that no single event forces; if robotaxi revenue is disclosed and scales, 103x on a larger EBITDA can hold and the +27% leg becomes the base case.
rows.implication: The distribution is roughly -60% to +27% around a consensus target 2.2% above spot: an investor is paid about 27% for bearing a 60% drawdown, which is an unfavourable ratio for a 12-month horizon.
rows.confidence: medium: the range follows from stated multiples, but the multiple that prevails is not forecastable.
rows.follow_up: Which multiple has the market actually paid through prior drawdowns, and what disclosure would keep it above 80x?

rows.finding: The downside has no structural cushion: Tesla has never paid a dividend, discloses no repurchase programme, and its $36,180m of net cash covers 2.3% of the equity; the only supports are $13.8bn of daily liquidity and the possibility of a SpaceX combination.
rows.mechanism: A buyback or dividend would create a price-sensitive buyer and a cash floor; without either, the shares clear at whatever rating the marginal buyer applies, and net cash sits on the balance sheet rather than in the return.
rows.benchmark: Net cash is $36.2bn, 2.3% of the $1,580.4bn capitalisation; $13.8bn trades a day
rows.weakens: A company with $36.2bn of net cash and $30.0bn of undrawn facilities is not a forced seller of anything, so the downside from financial distress is effectively zero even if the multiple falls.
rows.implication: Liquidity protects the ability to exit, not the price received; an investor cannot rely on capital return or a strategic bid to truncate the downside.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Would a $36bn net-cash position ever be returned, and does the board have authority for a repurchase it has not used?

rows.finding: Share supply keeps rising: 202m new shares in the nine months to 2026-09-30 (+5.4%), 304.0m shares delivered on option and RSU settlements in the six months to 2026-09-09, and 423,743,904 award shares that begin to vest only above a $2,000bn capitalisation.
rows.mechanism: A fixed award of 423.7m shares transfers value from holders to the CEO in proportion to how far the capitalisation rises, so the bull case is taxed at roughly 11% of the share count above the gate.
rows.benchmark: 423,743,904 award shares against 3,952,648,559 outstanding; 202m shares issued in nine months
rows.weakens: The award's operational conditions — 20m deliveries, 10m FSD subscriptions, 1m robotaxis — mean it is earned only if the equity value rises for holders too, so it is a shared-upside cost rather than a pure transfer.
rows.implication: Dilution caps per-share upside in the bull case — the award is 10.7% of the count — while it does nothing for the holder in the bear case.
rows.confidence: high on the counts, medium on the award's timing
rows.follow_up: How many of the 304.0m shares delivered remain unsold, and what is the insider selling pattern into strength?

plan.decision_question: For an investor entering at $399.81 on 2026-10-30, what are the realistic return paths to an exit in 12 months and what drawdown risk does the entry carry?
plan.thesis_sentence: No buyer can pay $1.58tn and the company returns no cash, so the 12-month exit is a sale into the market at whatever multiple prevails, and with every 10 turns of EV/adjusted EBITDA worth $38 a share the distribution runs from about $161 to about $506 with the consensus target at $408.61.
plan.why_different: This section asks how a holder gets out and at what price, so it prices the drawdown and the liquidity rather than describing the operations or the thesis; the risk section lists what can go wrong, this one converts it into realisation paths and a price range.
plan.mechanism: With no acquirer able to pay $1.58tn and no capital return, the exit is a sale into the market at whatever multiple then prevails; every 10 turns of EV/adjusted EBITDA is $38 a share, 9.5% of the price, so the return is set by the rating, not by the business, and the only genuine change-of-control path is a stock-for-stock combination with SpaceX that would hand holders an unlisted security.
plan.comparison_set: Waymo's $126bn February 2026 mark; SpaceX's Q3 2026 revenue of $14.575bn; GM, Ford and Rivian market capitalisations; Tesla's own 2010 IPO; the 2025 CEO award ladder from $2.0tn to $8.5tn; Tesla's 2021-2022 drawdown of 65.5% and its five-year return of -0.8%.
plan.counter_evidence: The downside-cushion argument: $36.2bn of net cash, $13.8bn a day of liquidity, index membership and a possible SpaceX combination all limit how far the shares can fall; but net cash is 2.3% of the market capitalisation, there is no buyback or dividend, and the SpaceX route is a process without a price, so none of them functions as a floor at today's multiple.
plan.visual: Exit routes table naming each counterparty and venue, and a precedent-exits table with the return-path sensitivity.
plan.prohibited: IPO or M&A, deeply undervalued, asymmetric risk-reward, downside protected, about X%, catalysts abound, long-term story
