rows.finding: SpaceX (SPCX) is listed: IPO 2026-06-12 at $135 on Nasdaq Global Select and Nasdaq Texas; it quoted $147.79 for a $2.01tn market value on 2026-10-20, against Tesla at $373.71 and $1.48tn the same day.
rows.mechanism: The one acquirer large enough to buy Tesla has a listed, priced currency, so a share-for-share deal is financeable without cash and without a private-company discount.
rows.benchmark: Tesla's $1,580.4bn market value at the $399.81 close on 2026-10-30; GM, Ford and Rivian are worth $137.0bn combined.
rows.weakens: S154's $2.01tn sits inside a $1.83-2.10tn range across October 2026 trackers and is dated 2026-10-20; the exact mark moves daily.
rows.implication: A change-of-control path exists and delivers listed stock, not an unlisted security; short sellers face a premium-bearing bid.
rows.confidence: high on the listing (S157), medium on the market value (S154)
rows.follow_up: What are SPCX's free float and lock-up terms, and what exchange ratio would the committees propose?

rows.finding: RBC Capital Markets and JPMorgan expect a 20-35% premium for Tesla holders (Reuters, 2026-10-21), which implies $480-540 a share against $399.81; other analysts expect little or none.
rows.mechanism: The premium is paid in SpaceX stock out of SpaceX holders' share, so it costs no cash and dilutes the buyer's owners rather than its balance sheet.
rows.benchmark: At parity Tesla holders would own about 42-43% of the combined company; the premium raises that to 47-50%.
rows.weakens: No exchange ratio has been agreed and some analysts expect a zero premium, so the range is a broker expectation, not a filed term.
rows.implication: The 12-month distribution gains a +20% to +35% branch; a holder should not underwrite the premium as contractual.
rows.confidence: medium-high
rows.follow_up: Which premium would the independent committees accept, and would it be paid in SPCX Class A stock?

rows.finding: Approval needs a majority of all Tesla shares outstanding, not of votes cast; the 2026-12-03 annual meeting has no merger proposal; Musk holds about 20% of Tesla votes and about 85% of SpaceX's and would hold roughly 57-58% of the combined company.
rows.mechanism: A high approval threshold plus a conflicted controller makes completion slow and uncertain; announcement, not closing, is the event a 12-month holder can trade.
rows.benchmark: A normal majority-of-votes-cast standard; the 2016 SolarCity acquisition as the related-party precedent.
rows.weakens: Committees of independent directors are formed and Musk publicly backs the idea, so an announcement can come without a scheduled catalyst.
rows.implication: There is no vote catalyst in 2026; a deal that closes would more likely be a 2027 event.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Has Tesla set a record date or instructed advisers on a vote timetable?

rows.finding: Prediction markets put 18% on an official merger announcement by 2026-12-31 and 67% by 2027-12-31, on $1.7m of volume.
rows.mechanism: A crowd-priced probability on the event that drives the premium branch.
rows.benchmark: The 20-35% premium expectation and Reuters' 'early stage' reporting of 2026-10-21/22.
rows.weakens: The odds were read from search summaries rather than the page; liquidity is thin and the term structure is wide.
rows.implication: Use a 25-45% band for the 12 months to 2027-10-31 and 35% in the expected-return table.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What are the live odds on the 12-month contract rather than the calendar-year ones?

rows.finding: SPCX at $2.01tn on $3.5bn of Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA ($14bn annualised) is about 143x, above Tesla's 103x trailing adjusted EBITDA.
rows.mechanism: The premium is paid in a more expensive currency, so the deal is multiple-neutral for SpaceX holders and swaps Tesla holders into the same de-rating risk.
rows.benchmark: Tesla 103x; Waymo's $126bn post-money mark; BYD 21.2x trailing.
rows.weakens: SpaceX revenue grew 161% y/y in Q3 2026, which can justify a higher multiple than Tesla's.
rows.implication: The branch is real but it is not a de-risking and does not convert the position into cash.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What is SPCX's free cash flow after the $35-40bn Q4 capex guide, and at what multiple would a combined company trade?

rows.finding: The shares fell 65.5% in 2022 ($356.78 to $123.18); the 52-week range is $297.38-$498.83, a 40.4% fall from the high; the stock is -12.4% over twelve months against the S&P 500's +10.8%, after a 28.5% three-month run.
rows.mechanism: The multiple, not the business, sets the drawdown; entering after a 28.5% run raises the risk without changing the company.
rows.benchmark: S&P 500 +10.8% over twelve months; the stock's own 2022 and 2024 drawdowns.
rows.weakens: $36,180m of net cash and $30.0bn of undrawn facilities mean no forced seller and no dilution at the low.
rows.implication: Size the position for a 60% drawdown that has happened twice in five years.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What is the options-implied 12-month move and the implied move around the Q4 2026 results?

rows.finding: The probability-weighted 12-month return is about -1.5% at a 35% deal probability, -6% at 25% and +3% at 45%; without the merger branch the four standalone scenarios weigh to about -17%.
rows.mechanism: The deal branch pays about what the standalone bull case pays (+26.6% at the first award gate), so it substitutes for it and changes the shape of the distribution more than the mean.
rows.benchmark: Sell-side consensus $408.61 (+2.2%); first 2025 award gate $506.05 (+26.6%); 20-35% premium $480-540.
rows.weakens: A zero-premium or failed deal leaves holders with the standalone distribution and no bid.
rows.implication: The bid does not make $399.81 attractive; it raises the cost of being short and sets the level a short must survive.
rows.confidence: medium (the probabilities are judgement anchored on S158)
rows.follow_up: Would the funds' mandate tolerate a position whose best case is a share exchange into a controlled company?

plan.why_different: This section prices the exit path and the distribution of 12-month returns, not the intrinsic value of the businesses; the funding and valuation section values the assets, this one asks how a holder gets out and what a deal does to the tails.
plan.mechanism: With no dividend or buyback, the only cash exit is the market multiple; the one priced alternative is a share exchange into a listed, more expensive currency, which truncates the left tail on announcement, caps the right tail at the exchange ratio and carries governance and vote risk.
plan.comparison_set: Tesla's own 2022 drawdown (-65.5%) and 52-week range; SpaceX's SPCX multiple (~143x annualised Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA) against Tesla's 103x; Waymo's $126bn mark; the $2,000bn first award gate.
plan.counter_evidence: A 20-35% premium from a $2.0tn listed buyer is a genuine support pre-announcement; SpaceX's 161% revenue growth makes its paper attractive; $36.2bn of net cash and $30.0bn of undrawn facilities mean no forced seller; the branch can re-rate the stock inside the year.
plan.visual: Exit-route table plus the probability-weighted scenario table
plan.prohibited: unlisted security, no price, no exit exists, huge, well positioned, strong team, risks are manageable, about five

rows.finding: Prediction markets put 18% on an official merger announcement by 2026-12-31 and 67% by 2027-12-31, on $1.7m of volume.
rows.mechanism: A crowd-priced probability on the event that drives the premium branch.
rows.benchmark: The 20-35% premium expectation and Reuters' 'early stage' reporting of 2026-10-21/22.
rows.weakens: The odds were read from search summaries rather than the page; liquidity is thin and the term structure is wide.
rows.implication: The canonical distribution weights the combination at 15% inside twelve months, below the 2027 odds because completion needs a vote.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What are the live odds on the 12-month contract rather than the calendar-year ones?

rows.finding: SPCX at $2.01tn on $3.5bn of Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA ($14bn annualised) is about 143x, above Tesla's 103x trailing adjusted EBITDA.
rows.mechanism: The premium is paid in a more expensive currency, so the deal is multiple-neutral for SpaceX holders and swaps Tesla holders into the same de-rating risk.
rows.benchmark: Tesla 103x; Waymo's $126bn post-money mark; BYD 21.2x trailing.
rows.weakens: SpaceX revenue grew 161% y/y in Q3 2026, which can justify a higher multiple than Tesla's.
rows.implication: The branch is real but it is not a de-risking and does not convert the position into cash.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What is SPCX's free cash flow after the $35-40bn Q4 capex guide, and at what multiple would a combined company trade?

rows.finding: The shares fell 65.5% in 2022 ($356.78 to $123.18); the 52-week range is $297.38-$498.83, a 40.4% fall from the high; the stock is -12.4% over twelve months against the S&P 500's +10.8%, after a 28.5% three-month run.
rows.mechanism: The multiple, not the business, sets the drawdown; entering after a 28.5% run raises the risk without changing the company.
rows.benchmark: S&P 500 +10.8% over twelve months; the stock's own 2022 and 2024 drawdowns.
rows.weakens: $36,180m of net cash and $30.0bn of undrawn facilities mean no forced seller and no dilution at the low.
rows.implication: Size the position for a 60% drawdown that has happened twice in five years.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What is the options-implied 12-month move and the implied move around the Q4 2026 results?

rows.finding: On the report's canonical distribution - bull 30% (15% autonomy proof and 15% SpaceX combination at $506.05, +26.6%), base 40% at $266 (-33.5%), bear 22% at $156 (-61%) and full de-rating 8% at $64-101 (-79%) - the expected 12-month return is -25.2%; deleting the 15-point combination branch and renormalising the other 85% gives -34.3%, so the live bid adds about nine points.
rows.mechanism: The combination pays roughly what the first award gate pays, so it substitutes for the autonomy bull case and raises the floor rather than the mean.
rows.benchmark: Sell-side consensus $408.61 (+2.2%); first 2025 award gate $506.05 (+26.6%); 20-35% premium $480-540.
rows.weakens: A zero-premium or failed deal leaves holders with the standalone distribution; the weights are judgement, not observation.
rows.implication: The bid does not make $399.81 attractive; it raises the cost of being short and sets the level a short must survive: 2.9% of NAV notional, a 35% gap costing 1.0% of NAV, stop reference $506.05.
rows.confidence: medium (weights are the Lead's canonical set, anchored on S158 and S156)
rows.follow_up: Would the funds' mandate tolerate a position whose best case is a share exchange into a controlled company?

plan.decision_question: For an investor entering at the $399.81 close on 2026-10-30, what are the realistic 12-month return paths and the drawdown risk, including the live SpaceX bid?
plan.thesis_sentence: The exit from Tesla at $399.81 is two-sided: a listed SpaceX bid at a 20-35% premium is a real branch that lifts the report's expected 12-month return from -34.3% standalone to -25.2%, but it converts the position into another listed multiple rather than cash and does not pay for a 61-79% drawdown.
plan.why_different: This section prices the exit path and the distribution of 12-month returns on the report's one probability set, not the intrinsic value of the businesses; the funding and valuation section values the assets, this one asks how a holder gets out and what a deal does to the tails.
plan.mechanism: With no dividend or buyback, the only cash exit is the market multiple; the one priced alternative is a share exchange into a listed, more expensive currency, which truncates the left tail on announcement, caps the right tail at the exchange ratio and carries governance and vote risk.
plan.comparison_set: Tesla's own 2022 drawdown (-65.5%) and 52-week range; SpaceX's SPCX multiple (~143x annualised Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA) against Tesla's 103x; the $2,000bn first award gate at $506.05; the 20-35% broker premium band at $480-540.
plan.counter_evidence: A 20-35% premium from a $2.0tn listed buyer is a genuine support pre-announcement; SpaceX's 161% revenue growth makes its paper attractive; $36.2bn of net cash and $30.0bn of undrawn facilities mean no forced seller; the branch can gap the shares at any time.
plan.visual: Exit-route table plus the canonical probability-weighted scenario table (bull 30% split 15/15, base 40%, bear 22%, full de-rating 8%, expected -25.2%).
plan.prohibited: unlisted security, no price, no exit exists, huge, well positioned, strong team, risks are manageable, about five, second set of probabilities

rows.finding: On 2026-10-20 Tesla closed at $373.71 for a $1.48tn market value and SpaceX at $147.79 for $2.01tn; both boards formed independent special committees; RBC and JPMorgan expect a 20-35% premium for Tesla holders; holders would own about 42% of a combined company at parity and 47-50% with that premium; approval needs 50% of all Tesla shares outstanding and the 2026-12-03 annual meeting has no merger vote.
rows.mechanism: A listed, larger counterparty with a shareholder-requested process converts a theoretical change of control into a dated, premium-bearing catalyst; at a 20-35% premium the stock is $480-540, above the $506.05 bull case.
rows.benchmark: General Motors, Ford and Rivian are worth $137.0bn combined, so the 'no buyer can pay' arithmetic holds only if SpaceX is excluded.
rows.weakens: No exchange ratio or terms agreed, the CEO is conflicted on both sides, the 50%-of-outstanding vote is a high hurdle and the process can fail.
rows.implication: The Sell must be a capped short with a stop at $506.05; the 12-month distribution needs a merger branch and the expected return is nearer -20% than -28%.
rows.confidence: medium - two market values and the committee fact are reported, the premium is analyst expectation, not a term.
rows.follow_up: What exchange ratio would the SpaceX committee accept, and is the 50%-of-outstanding vote achievable with Musk recused?

rows.finding: Waymo logged 220.6m rider-only miles by March 2026, about 500,000 paid rides a week, $355m annualised revenue at February 2026 and a $19.69 average San Francisco fare; Tesla's 2.0m cumulative unsupervised miles are 0.9% of that mileage, not the 1.2% a 170m comparison implies.
rows.mechanism: Verified driverless mileage and paid rides are the scarce assets in autonomy; Tesla's gap to the incumbent is about 100x in miles, so a 12-month proof of scale is not available.
rows.benchmark: Waymo took eleven years from a 2009 start to 500,000 paid rides a week; its February 2026 round marked it at $126bn.
rows.weakens: Tesla reports 8x quarterly growth in unsupervised miles and a fleet growing from 739 to 1,051 Texas vehicles in eighteen days; the base is small enough for high percentage growth.
rows.implication: The 20% bull weight is not too low on fundamentals, but the Waymo figure in the technology section needs updating from 170m+ to 220.6m.
rows.confidence: medium - third-party compilation of Waymo and CPUC disclosures, consistent with 500k weekly rides reported elsewhere.
rows.follow_up: Will Tesla disclose paid trips and revenue per vehicle-week, or only cumulative miles?

rows.finding: California's DMV listed Tesla Robotaxi LLC only under autonomous-vehicle testing with a safety driver on 2026-10-23; it was absent from the driverless-testing list and the deployment list updated 2026-10-22, while Waymo, Nuro and Mercedes held deployment authorisations.
rows.mechanism: Permits, not software, gate paid driverless revenue; California is the largest US market and the state where Tesla's paid rides still run on a limousine permit with a driver.
rows.benchmark: Waymo, Nuro, Zoox and WeRide hold driverless testing permits in California; Waymo, Nuro and Mercedes are authorised to deploy.
rows.weakens: A deployment-permit application by Tesla has been reported, and an application can convert to an authorisation inside twelve months.
rows.implication: The base case should assume California stays closed until a deployment entry appears on the DMV list; that list is the cheapest falsifier of the Sell.
rows.confidence: high - primary regulator record, dated.
rows.follow_up: Has the DMV accepted Tesla's deployment application for substantive review, and on what timeline?

rows.finding: NHTSA's Engineering Analysis EA26002 covers 3,203,754 FSD-equipped vehicles, nine incidents including one fatality, and is the last investigative step before a recall; a remedy at $100-1,000 a car is $320m-3.2bn, and an operating-domain restriction would delay paid service.
rows.mechanism: A recall or ODD restriction removes the operating domain the robotaxi business depends on and converts a software narrative into a hardware and liability cost.
rows.benchmark: Engineering analyses with fatalities convert to recall action at a high rate, though conversion is not automatic.
rows.weakens: Tesla's degradation-detection update reportedly addresses some of the reviewed incidents, and no remedy or timetable is disclosed.
rows.implication: Price 10-20% of the autonomy option as recall risk, not only as a delay; it belongs in the bear case as a cost, not a footnote.
rows.confidence: high on scope, medium on remedy cost - the range is an estimate.
rows.follow_up: What remedy does NHTSA's EA26002 require, and does it need new hardware across the 3.2m-vehicle population?

rows.finding: Tesla has 36 unique Robotaxi incident reports in NHTSA Standing General Order data, and five remote takeovers appear in the crash data, all five ending in a collision; Tesla discloses no intervention rate, while Waymo says it does not remote-drive.
rows.mechanism: Teleoperation is the hidden cost line in robotaxi unit economics: latency, limited sensor view and a human per exception, with a 5-for-5 collision record when the human takes over.
rows.benchmark: Waymo's remote staff give guidance the driver can accept or reject and do not perform the driving task.
rows.weakens: The crashes were at walking speed with no injuries, so severity is low and the sample is small.
rows.implication: Unit economics cannot be underwritten without intervention and cost-per-trip disclosure; the burden sits with the company, not the analyst.
rows.confidence: high - crash narratives are filed with NHTSA and reported in detail.
rows.follow_up: What is the remote-intervention rate per paid mile and the cost per intervention?

rows.finding: Tesla short interest was 69.35m shares, 2.19% of the public float, at the 2026-10-15 settlement, with 2.2 days to cover on 50.19m shares of average daily volume.
rows.mechanism: A light short base means a squeeze would be caused by a headline (merger, permit, robotaxi disclosure), not by crowded positioning unwinding.
rows.benchmark: A crowded short is typically above 10% of float; 2.19% is in the bottom half of US names.
rows.weakens: Options and retail flows can amplify a headline move even with low short interest.
rows.implication: The scenario module's 'squeeze risk is high' should be corrected: the stop is still needed, but for event risk, not positioning risk.
rows.confidence: high - exchange short-interest data, dated.
rows.follow_up: What share of the float is held in call options ahead of the Q4 print?

rows.finding: Tesla's 1.74m active FSD count includes upfront buyers as well as monthly subscribers; the CFO said over 1.7m paid customers with half on subscriptions, implying about $1.03bn at $99 a month, and management's run rate is about $1bn, under 1% of revenue.
rows.mechanism: The subscription count is a customer stock, not recurring revenue: one-time purchases do not renew, so FSD's revenue base is about half the headline count.
rows.benchmark: 1.74m at $99 a month would be $2.07bn a year; the CFO's 50% subscription mix halves it to about $1.03bn.
rows.weakens: FSD growth of 67% year on year and more than 75% attach on new North American deliveries are real, and attach is rising.
rows.implication: The bull case's 1.74m evidence is weaker than presented; valuing FSD at zero in the SOTP overstates downside by only about $20bn, or $5 a share.
rows.confidence: medium - arithmetic on management statements, no standalone FSD revenue disclosure.
rows.follow_up: What is FSD churn and the split between monthly and upfront revenue?

plan.decision_question: Does the Sell survive a listed buyer, a permit and a merger premium, and what is the defensible 12-month target?
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla's downside is real but it is a de-rating carried by a 103x multiple, not a liquidation: the reported businesses are worth $40-50 a share, while the events that could break the Sell are a SpaceX combination at a 20-35% premium and a California permit with robotaxi disclosure, neither of which the three scenarios price.
plan.why_different: The other sections value Tesla's businesses; this one prices the ways the Sell is wrong and separates a SOTP floor from a 12-month target.
plan.mechanism: A 103x multiple is a claim on autonomy revenue the filings do not book; multiple compression, a merger premium and a permit are the three channels that set the 12-month distribution, and the balance sheet makes default irrelevant.
plan.comparison_set: Waymo at 220.6m rider-only miles and 500k weekly rides; BYD at 17.3x; GM, Ford and Rivian at $137bn combined; Tesla's own 65.5% 2022 drawdown.
plan.counter_evidence: SpaceX listed at $2.01tn with special committees and a 20-35% premium expectation; a reported California deployment application; a Megapack book almost sold out for 2027; FSD growth of 67%.
plan.visual: risk-matrix ranked by probability, impact and timing, plus an info danger card for the merger and permit upside that would break the Sell.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned, about/many/various counts, report-writing statements, bot or tool names.

rows.confidence: high

plan.decision_question: What is the weighted score, and what position does it justify at $399.81 with a 12-month horizon?
plan.thesis_sentence: The weighted score is 3.8 out of 10 and the recommendation is Sell: zero long exposure, and any short capped so a 20-35% merger gap costs at most 1-2% of NAV.
plan.why_different: It converts the thesis into a weighted, benchmarked score and a sizing rule; it does not restate the valuation arithmetic already made in the funding and thesis sections.
plan.mechanism: A 103x multiple on a 2.6%-operating-margin business de-rates when autonomy does not monetise; valuation carries the largest weight, so the composite lands well below neutral despite the balance sheet.
plan.comparison_set: BYD 17.3x EV/EBITDA, GM 19.1x P/E, Ford's 11.3% FCF yield, Fluence's 5.1% gross margin, CATL 19.8x P/E, Waymo's 220.6m rider-only miles, and the 4.93% ten-year Treasury against a 5.5% ROIC.
plan.counter_evidence: The balance sheet is strong ($36.18bn net cash, $30.0bn undrawn), the energy segment earns 33.1% gross margin, and a SpaceX combination at a 20-35% premium is a live exit; these lift the composite but not enough to offset valuation and governance.
plan.visual: Weighted score table with nine dimensions, weights summing to 100% and a composite of 3.8, then the ranked sensitivity component and three takeaways.
plan.prohibited: No scores without a peer benchmark, no 'well positioned', 'strong team' or 'risks are manageable', no vague counts.

user_data_requests.database: OSHA Injury Tracking Application (ITA) establishment-level data, osha.gov/Establishment-Specific-Injury-and-Illness-Data
user_data_requests.query: Form 300A totals (total recordable cases, DART rate, total hours worked) for Tesla establishments for 2024 and 2025, especially Fremont CA, Austin TX, Sparks NV, Buffalo NY and Lathrop CA, benchmarked against the NAICS 3361 motor vehicle manufacturing industry rate
user_data_requests.why: Workplace-safety performance is the one material ESG datapoint Tesla does not disclose in an SEC filing, and the 2025 Impact Report could not be read (HTTP 403). If Tesla's recordable rate is above the motor-vehicle-manufacturing benchmark, the labour-cost and regulatory-oversight discount should widen; if it is at or below, the safety leg of the bear case should be dropped.
user_data_requests.how: Download the OSHA ITA establishment-specific dataset for 2024 and 2025 from osha.gov (public, no login): filter establishment name contains "Tesla", export the 300A fields and send the file or a screenshot of the filtered table.

user_data_requests.database: USPTO Patent Public Search / PatentsView (assignee search, free but requires a session or API key for bulk data)
user_data_requests.query: All granted US patents and published applications assigned to "Tesla, Inc." (and Tesla Motors, Tesla Robotaxi LLC), with grant dates from 2015-01-01 onward, broken out by technology class: autonomous driving/perception, battery cells and dry-electrode manufacturing, humanoid robotics, and power electronics. For the 20 most-cited grants, the patent number, title, filing and grant dates, and current legal status (including any abandonals or IPR challenges). Also any third-party patents asserted against Tesla in the last 24 months.
user_data_requests.why: Tesla publishes no patent count or list, and its 10-K only discloses an irrevocable non-assertion pledge on EV patents. Without the assignee data, the section cannot show whether the portfolio protects anything outside electric vehicles (autonomy, batteries, robotics), so freedom-to-operate risk and the durability of the technology advantage stay unquantified — the moat score of 6.5/10 rests on data and manufacturing alone.

3.name: Missing competitors
3.notes: Missing-competitor challenge. 4.notes: Product/market-fit challenge, kept to what changes the Sell. Budget owner: well handled in business_model and company_overview — the retail or fleet buyer paying at transfer of title, the utility/developer/data-centre operator paying on power-availability capex milestones, the per-transaction service buyer, and the automaker buying credits; the energy buyer is correctly identified as a capex line rather than a transport one. Why adoption is not faster: business_model answers it for vehicles (unit cost flat at $33,666-$35,786, price held, volume lost to a pool down 30.3%), for energy (price per GWh down 23% and revenue down 16% despite deployments up 9.6%) and for FSD (17.1% of the lifetime fleet, attach not disclosed, no CAC line in the statements — the absence of any marketing line is itself evidence and is stated). Counterparty concentration: SpaceX at $626m, 7.4% of energy revenue, with $588m of a $729m receivable billed for undelivered Megapacks — labelled as related-party revenue quality in business_model and strategy, so not reopened here, but it does mean the 'nearly sold out through 2027' demand is partly a related buyer's order book and the FSD subscription count is partly a one-off purchase base. Selling difficulty for the robotaxi is the permit chain and the insurer, not the rider: the permit side is thoroughly covered in esg; the insurance and supervision side is the gap this item addresses.

5.name: Number stress-test
5.notes: Number stress-test arithmetic, version 1. Reproduced and confirmed: base (70 x $16.0bn + $36.18bn net cash) / 3.9526bn shares = $292.6, -26.8%; bear (40 x $14.995bn + $36.18bn) / 3.9526 = $160.9, -59.8%; bull $2,000bn / 3.9526 = $506.0, +26.6%; expected return 0.31 x 26.6 - 0.40 x 27.0 - 0.29 x 59.7 = -19.9%, matching the stated -19.8%; composite 0.20x2 + 0.15x4 + 0.10x4 + 0.15x5 + 0.10x3 + 0.10x6 + 0.10x3 + 0.05x4 + 0.05x4 = 3.75, rounding to 3.8; SOTP low 45.0 + 30.75 + 24.45 + 36.18 + 2.865 = $139.2bn ($35.2 a share), high 60.0 + 36.9 + 24.45 + 36.18 + 2.865 = $160.4bn ($40.6); residual $1,420-1,441bn is 89.9-91.2% of the capitalisation; EV $1,580.4bn - $36.18bn = $1,544.2bn and 445x operating income, 14.9x sales, 103x on adjusted EBITDA all tie. Sizing: 2.9% notional x 35% gap = 1.02% of NAV, and at the $506.05 stop 26.6% x 2.9% = 0.77%. Thirty-per-cent-worse tests: energy at the ~14.8% ex-refund margin removes about $2.1bn of annualised gross profit and takes the base to $255 (-36%), so the thesis survives and deepens; adjusted EBITDA 30% lower ($10.5bn) at 70x gives $195 (-51%); the same EBITDA at 25x gives $104 (-74%) and at BYD's 17.3x $75 (-81%); revenue 30% lower at 40x on $8bn gives $356bn, $90 (-77%). The verdict does not depend on any of these: every stress except the merger gap leaves a materially lower value, and the merger is a sizig and stop problem, not a valuation one. Two definitional traps to keep straight in revision: the peer table's 169.0x 'XBRL basis' multiple is not the 103x on adjusted EBITDA the Sell rests on, and Tesla's 12.9x EV/EBITDA on the XBRL basis would look almost peer-level to a reader skimming the table.

items.issue: The cap table does not reconcile and mixes denominators. Musk's 699,580,882 shares are 17.7% of the stated 3,952,648,559, not the 19.8% shown; 19.8% is only reached on a 3,528.9m base that excludes the 423.7m unvested award shares. But the same table gives Vanguard 5.3% (5.33% of the full count) and public float 71.4% (2,822.4m of the full count) while also subtracting the 423.7m unvested shares from float, although those shares are described as unearned and therefore not in the count. The rows do not sum to 100% on any single basis (insiders 20.0% + Vanguard 5.3% + float 71.4% = 96.7%; Musk is also inside the insider row). Readers cannot tie the 19.8% stake, the 10.7% contingent dilution and the 71.4% float to one share count, and the SpaceX exchange-ratio arithmetic depends on that count.
items.action: Rebuild the cap table on one denominator (3,952,648,559 issued and outstanding at 2026-09-30), add an 'unissued, contingent' section for the 423,743,904 award shares with the explicit note that they are not in the count and not in the float, show Musk at 17.7% of issued (19.8% of issued excluding unvested restricted shares, with the basis stated), and add a totals row that sums to 100%.
items.evidence_request: Confirm from the S10 proxy the exact share base used for the beneficial-ownership table's percentage column and whether the 423.7m award shares are in the float calculation.

items.issue: Every person in the education table has 'Year: Not stated', and Musk's degrees are recorded as 'not disclosed' and 'not verified here'. The section's standard requires institution, degree and year for each founder and C-suite executive, and the team assessment matrix then scores technical depth and scaling from these records without saying how the 1-10 scores were assigned.
items.action: Fill the graduation years from an independent record (university alumni registers, earlier proxy statements, press biographies) or state on the table that the proxy does not give years and that the institution-level confirmation is the extent of the evidence; verify Musk's degrees from a non-company source rather than saying they cannot be checked. Add one sentence to the assessment matrix on how the 1-10 scores are built (years in role, programmes shipped, P&L size), so 9/10 for technical depth is an argument, not a mark.
items.evidence_request: Can the years and Musk's degrees be confirmed from an alumni or regulatory record, and if not, is the limitation to be stated in the table?

items.issue: Establishment-level workplace-safety data is missing from the section and from its stated limitations, although a request has been filed for it. The social leg covers the California Civil Rights Department action, the EEOC suit and the NLRB dismissal but says nothing about injury rates, which is the one material social datapoint Tesla does not file. The Scope 1/2 figures are also described only as unreadable, without naming the document and the failure mode.
items.action: Add a workplace-safety paragraph naming what Tesla discloses (nothing establishment-level in the filings), what the 2025 Impact Report says if anything, that the OSHA Injury Tracking Application establishment data for 2024-2025 has been requested, and what a rate above the NAICS 3361 benchmark would do to the case; name the 2025 Impact Report and the HTTP 403 as the source that failed, and add the same to the closing list of unanswerable questions.
items.evidence_request: What injury and DART rates does the 2025 Impact Report state, if any, and is the OSHA ITA extract the only route to a benchmark?

items.issue: The single most-cited proof of Tesla's storage advantage is not computed. Four sections (business_model, competition, market, thesis) use the 33.1% Q3 2026 energy gross margin against Fluence's 5.1% to claim a sixfold, unrivaled cost position, while competition and thesis both record that $526m of IEEPA tariff refunds and warranty true-ups sit inside Q3 energy cost of revenue. Never netted out, $526m on $2,881m of energy revenue is 18.3 points of margin, so the ex-refund figure is roughly $428m, or about 14.8%, not 33.1% — close to Fluence's 13.1% FY2025 rather than six times its 5.1% June-quarter print. The claim is company-sourced only (the refund quantum appears in no filing cited here as a segment line), the comparator is a single quarter of a low-margin integrator chosen from a 5.1%-to-13.1% range, and no section states which basis its number uses.
items.action: Compute and publish the ex-refund margin in business_model and financials: $954m less $526m of refunds is $428m of gross profit on $2,881m, or about 14.8%, with the split between refunds and warranty true-ups shown; rebuild the base-case energy assumption and thesis assumption 3 on that number, and state the margin for Q1-Q3 2026 on both the as-reported and ex-refund basis. Re-benchmark storage: Fluence's 5.1% is its June 2026 quarter against 13.1% for FY2025, so quote the fiscal-year figure alongside the quarter and add Sungrow, CATL-branded systems or LG Energy Solution so 'unrivalled cost position' rests on more than one weak quarter of one listed integrator, and state whether the 33.1%-versus-5.1% comparison is as-reported or ex-refund.
items.evidence_request: What is Tesla's Q3 2026 energy gross margin excluding the $526m of IEEPA tariff refunds and the warranty true-ups, and what gross margin did Sungrow's and CATL's storage businesses report for the same period?

items.issue: The autonomy comparison, which carries most of the equity's premium, is stated with two different mile bases and two different ratios. technology_product, risk, thesis and the executive briefing use 220.6m Waymo rider-only miles through 2026-03 and Tesla at 0.9%; competition ('more than 170 million rider-only miles', '170m+') and market ('170 million-plus') still use the uncorrected figure and imply 1.2%, the ratio risk explicitly names as wrong. Adjacent counts also disagree: Texas 1,051 authorised vehicles on 2026-10-27 (competition, market, technology_product, thesis) against 349 Texas registrations on 2026-10-15 (strategy) and '300+ Cybercabs claimed'; Waymo at roughly 3,000 vehicles (competition, market) against 3,700 (risk); and esg lists 'whether Texas DMV has authorised Tesla Robotaxi' as an unanswerable question while four sections quote the count.
items.action: Propagate 220.6m rider-only miles through 2026-03 (and the 0.9% ratio) into competition's paid-autonomy paragraph, its evidence block and its two tables, and into market's robotaxi paragraph; delete '170 million-plus' and '1.2%' everywhere. Then reconcile the permit and vehicle counts into one dated set used in every section: state whether 1,051 is TxDMV-authorized vehicles or registrations, whether 739 on 2026-10-09 and 349 on 2026-10-15 are the same measure, and whether the 300+ Cybercabs are company-claimed or regulator-listed; use one Waymo fleet count (3,000 or 3,700) with its date. If the TxDMV lookup is public, cite it in esg so the section stops listing the authorisation as unanswerable.
items.evidence_request: What exactly does the TxDMV commercial automated-vehicle lookup publish — authorised vehicles or registrations — and on what date, and what is Waymo's fleet count on the same date?

items.issue: The 1.74m 'active FSD subscriptions' figure is used as recurring software revenue in technology_product ('1.74m subscriptions', '17.1% penetration'), funding_valuation ('+67% year on year') and the executive briefing, with no composition caveat, although the red-team record states the count includes one-time upfront buyers, that only about half the base is on subscriptions by the CFO's account and that management's run-rate is $1bn, under 1% of revenue. Only risk carries the caveat. 'Active subscriptions' therefore overstates a recurring revenue base in the sections that use the number to support the option value.
items.action: Add the composition to technology_product's FSD rows and to funding_valuation's subscription line: state that the 1.74m is a company-defined active count that includes one-time upfront FSD buyers, that roughly half the base is on monthly subscription by the CFO's account, and that the disclosed run-rate is about $1bn (under 1% of revenue), so the '+67% year on year' cannot be read as recurring revenue growth. Mark the count unverified-company-reported where it is first used, as risk already does.
items.evidence_request: What share of the 1.74m is monthly versus lifetime/upfront, and what FSD revenue does the company disclose for the quarter?

items.issue: The competitor set is thin exactly where the premium is. Five comparators carry the table (BYD, Xiaomi, Rivian, Fluence, Waymo) and the positioning table routes the rest through named-but-unexamined lists. Absent: Huawei's ADS/Qiankun stack and Momenta, which set the smart-driving feature set and price on the Chinese models Tesla loses to; Pony.ai, WeRide and Baidu's Apollo Go, which are the volume comparators for driverless miles outside the United States (Apollo Go appears once, as 'niche', with no data); the supervised hands-free substitutes that compete with FSD's $99 month — GM Super Cruise, Ford BlueCruise and comma.ai's openpilot, the open-source version of the same product; and, in storage, every listed comparator except Fluence (Sungrow is named in the text without figures, CATL-branded systems, LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI are absent), so the 'unrivalled cost position' claim is tested against one integrator only. The do-nothing substitute for robotaxi — Uber and Lyft at prevailing fare per mile — is absent, which leaves the assumed $12-18 fare with no market anchor.
items.action: Add to competition's map: (1) Huawei's ADS/Qiankun stack and Momenta as the Chinese ADAS suppliers that set the smart-driving feature set and price on the models Tesla competes with in China, with whatever share data is retrievable; (2) Pony.ai, WeRide and Baidu's Apollo Go with fleet size, city count and cumulative paid rides, so Tesla's 2.0m unsupervised miles are put against the driverless operators outside the US and not only Waymo; (3) a supervised-ADAS row covering GM Super Cruise, Ford BlueCruise and comma.ai's openpilot, with price, because FSD at $99 a month competes against systems bundled free and against a ~$1,000-2,000 aftermarket device, and that is the price elasticity the $1bn run-rate depends on; (4) storage comparators with numbers beyond Fluence — Sungrow, CATL-branded systems, LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI — in the competitor table so 'unrivalled cost position' is tested. Add Uber and Lyft as the substitute that sets the robotaxi fare ceiling.
items.evidence_request: What share of China's 2026 passenger-car market carries Huawei or Momenta ADAS, what paid-ride and fleet scale do Pony.ai, WeRide and Baidu Apollo Go report for the latest quarter, and what do Super Cruise, BlueCruise and openpilot cost per month or per vehicle?

items.issue: The robotaxi market sizing assumes a $12-18 average fare with no reference to what a rider pays today for the same trip in the same city, so the addressable fare pool is an analyst assumption where a published price exists. That assumption drives the $0.3-0.5bn market estimate and the statement that a $50bn 2028 line would need a twentyfold expansion.
items.action: Anchor the fare assumption to observed ride-hailing price per mile in the operating cities and state the range; note that a robotaxi priced at parity with an UberX leaves no room for the capital and supervision cost the model assumes.
items.evidence_request: What is the prevailing per-mile and per-trip fare for Uber and Lyft in Austin and the other Texas metros in 2026?

items.issue: The one-question that decides the case — Robotaxi revenue per vehicle-week and whether it is positive after insurance, depreciation and remote supervision — is posed but never given even a benchmark range, so no reader can form a view on it without doing the analysis the report exists to do. risk prices 'teleoperation and insurance costs' at '10-20% of autonomy value' with no derivation, and the Cybercab build cost, insurance per vehicle-year and remote-supervision ratio appear in no section. The same gap runs through the commercial side: no segment names a budget owner for robotaxi demand (rider willingness to pay versus an UberX at prevailing fare), no section gives the energy sales cycle (utility interconnection and procurement lead times) even though the $10.73bn of unsatisfied energy obligations implies a multi-quarter selling motion, and no lost transaction is examined in any business line.
items.action: Add a cost-per-paid-mile build to technology_product (or business_model) with three externally anchored lines: collision and liability insurance per vehicle-year for a driverless fleet, depreciation per mile at the $25-30k Cybercab cost and the disclosed 125,000-unit capacity, and remote supervision at a stated operator-to-vehicle ratio from Waymo's or a teleoperations vendor's disclosure. Then show what a $12-18 fare leaves at each line, which is the contribution the one-question asks about. If none of the three can be sourced, say which, and state that robotaxi contribution is unestimable rather than unpriced only in principle.
items.evidence_request: What do insurers charge per vehicle-year for driverless commercial fleets in Texas, what is the reported operator-to-vehicle ratio in Waymo's or Cruise's teleoperations, and what does a Cybercab cost to build?

items.issue: The report's central quantitative claim, the expected twelve-month return, is stated four different ways and the probability of its main upside event four more. Executive briefing, thesis and scoring: 31% bull, 40% base, 29% bear, expected -19.8%, with the merger absorbed inside the bull and given a 25-45% probability in thesis assumption 5. risk (revision 3): still argues 'the 20% probability assigned to the bull case', uses base 40% and bear 28% for '-20%', and puts the SpaceX combination at 'Medium-low, 15-20%' in its matrix. exit (revision 5): a six-row table weighting severe de-rating 5% at $104, de-rating 20% at $161, consensus 25% at $408.61, award gate 15% at $506.05 and the SpaceX combination 35% at $480-540, giving -4.1% to +1.2%, described in its own text as between -6% and +3% and 'better than the -17% the standalone businesses offer'. A reader cannot tell whether the Sell is a -20% or a -4% call, and the two are not the same recommendation. The sizing rule has the same problem: 2.9% of NAV in scoring and the briefing against 'cap at 1-2% of NAV' in the risk matrix, with the $506.05 stop 26.6% away while the loss being sized is a 35% gap.
items.action: Publish one distribution and derive everything from it. State the SpaceX branch's twelve-month probability once, with the prediction-market anchors given (18% by 2026-12-31, 67% by 2027-12-31) and the reason for departing from them; make the bull's absorption of the merger explicit in the same arithmetic; add the full-de-rating branch the report's own SOTP implies (15-25x adjusted EBITDA plus net cash, $60-104) with a probability, so the -19.8% is not built on a 40x floor while the SOTP says -90%; then restate the expected return in the executive briefing, thesis, scoring, risk and exit from that one table. Fix the short rule with the same numbers: state whether 2.9% is notional or a NAV loss, whether the cap is 2.9% (scoring, executive briefing) or 1-2% (risk matrix), what a 20-35% premium gap costs at that size ($480-540 is 0.8-1.0% of NAV at 2.9% notional), and note that the $506.05 stop is 26.6% away and cannot capture an overnight gap.
items.evidence_request: What probability do the same prediction markets put on an announcement by 2026-10-31-2027-10-31, and what does the deal-probability range do to the recommendation if it is set at the market's 18%?

items.issue: The base case rests on $16.0bn of adjusted EBITDA, $1.0bn above the $14,995m trailing figure, and no section shows how the $1.0bn is earned — yet thesis assumption 3 has energy normalising to 25-30% from 33.1%, and the ex-refund margin is nearer 14.8%, so the two assumptions may point in opposite directions. On the other side, the bull case is set at the $2,000bn award gate, 131x, which implies about $15.3bn of adjusted EBITDA, below the base case's $16.0bn: a bull scenario driven by a robotaxi revenue line with positive contribution, energy above 30% and capex at $20bn cannot be worth the same EBITDA as a base case with no robotaxi revenue at all. The scenario outcomes are set by price conventions, not by the drivers that are supposed to produce them.
items.action: Add the bridge as a table in thesis (or financials): TTM adjusted EBITDA $14,995m, plus or minus each segment's contribution, arriving at $16.0bn, with the energy line shown both at the 33.1% Q3 margin and at the ex-refund margin, since those two assumptions move the base case by more than the Tesla-specific growth assumed. Then derive the bull from its own drivers instead of setting it equal to the $2,000bn award gate: show what adjusted EBITDA the four bull conditions produce and what multiple the $506.05 implies, and state plainly that if the gate is a valuation convention rather than an earnings outcome, the bull's four drivers do not produce its value.
items.evidence_request: What segment-level adjusted EBITDA does Tesla report or disclose for Q4 2025 to Q3 2026, and what is the FY2027 EBITDA build behind the $16.0bn base case?

1.notes: Round-2 sweep. Section checks all pass at version 3; no rule findings (N1-N6) at report or section level; each section is 7,968-8,999 characters with 8+ figures and 4+ source IDs. R1 CLOSED: (1) one distribution — thesis rev 5, scoring rev 5, executive summary rev 6, risk rev 5 and exit rev 7 all carry 30/40/22/8 at $506.05/$266/$156/$64-101, expected -25.2%; the 15-25x branch exists; the 2.9% notional cap and 1.0% NAV loss on a 35% gap are stated identically in all five, replacing risk's old 1-2% figure. (2) storage economics — business_model rev 7 and financials rev 8 publish Q1-Q3 as reported and ex-refund ($428m on $2,881m, 14.8%; 24.0% nine months), state the $526m cannot be split, benchmark Fluence 13.1%/5.1%, CATL 23.96%, Sungrow, LGES; base-case EBITDA rebuilt to $14.5bn with assumption 3 at 14-18%; funding_valuation rev 7 adds the ex-both-legs basis (23.8% Q3, 26.9% nine months — reconciled: (954-526+339)/(2,881+339) and (2,546-526+339)/(8,428+339)). 2.name: Claim verification

# Tesla, Inc.: Investment research report
Rating: Sell
Composite score: 3.8
Data as of: 2026-10-30

## Executive Briefing

Tesla closed at $399.81 on 2026-10-30, a $1,580.4bn market capitalisation, 12.7% higher over the past month — a window that includes the 2026-10-21 third-quarter report — and 28.5% higher over three months, yet still 12.4% lower over twelve months against the S&P 500's 10.8% gain [S11, S20]. The index backdrop is firm: the S&P 500 sits at 7,580.07, up 10.7% year to date and 3.4% below its 52-week high, with the Nasdaq 8.2% below its own. The rates backdrop is not: the VIX is 19.42, in its 77th percentile, the ten-year Treasury yields 4.93% and high-yield spreads are 326bp. Energy leads the sector table by 17.6 points over three months against technology's 2.4, and consumer discretionary trails the index.

The verdict is Sell, with zero long exposure and, at most, a capped short; the composite score is 3.8 out of 10. One distribution governs the report: bull 30%, split between autonomy proof and a SpaceX combination, at $506.05; base 40% at $266, -33.5%; bear 22% at $156, -61%; and a full de-rating at 8%, from $64 to $101, for an expected twelve-month return of -25.2%. That is a de-rating call rather than a liquidation call: the reported car, storage and services businesses are worth $139-160bn, or $35-40 a share, against the $1,580.4bn capitalisation, and 90-91% of the equity is an option on autonomy revenue the filings do not book [S8, S9].

The positives are real, and they are why this is a de-rating call rather than a liquidation call. Energy earns a storage gross margin roughly in line with Fluence's fiscal 2025 once the third-quarter tariff refunds are stripped out — 14.8% against 13.1% — the balance sheet holds net cash alongside large undrawn facilities, the US electric-vehicle franchise still sets the price, and a listed SpaceX with both boards' committees offers a premium-bearing exit. Those cards are in the briefing table; none of them changes what the buyer pays today [S9, S61].

The risks to the call are as specific as the thesis. An announced combination at a premium would gap the shares above the bull case, a California deployment permit plus a robotaxi revenue line would turn the option into cash flow, and a recall from the open engineering analysis would cut the option the other way. Confidence is high in the arithmetic of value and low in the durability of the multiple; the diligence that would settle the second is listed below.

Consensus is Hold, with an average target within a rounding error of the price, so the view here is deliberately non-consensus: the market capitalises the autonomy option while this call prices it at zero until a revenue line is disclosed. If no line appears inside the year, the base and bear cases carry the return, and the buyer of the shares is paid nothing to wait.

The one question that decides the case is robotaxi revenue per vehicle-week in Texas and whether it is positive at the contribution level after insurance, depreciation and remote supervision. The next diligence actions are the fourth-quarter report, the California DMV deployment list, the NHTSA engineering-analysis resolution and the SpaceX exchange ratio; the conditions for investing are a disclosed robotaxi revenue line with positive contribution, a driverless deployment permit, an energy gross margin that holds without tariff refunds, and capex inside the plan with positive free cash flow before working capital. None is met at the current price.

What is Robotaxi revenue per vehicle-week in Texas, and is it positive at the contribution level after insurance, depreciation and remote supervision?

It is the only figure that can turn most of the price from an option into a cash flow. A positive disclosed number validates the multiple and forces a re-rating toward the first award gate; its absence, or a negative contribution, leaves the equity valued on a declining auto business and points to the full de-rating.

1. Sell at $399.81: $139-160bn of reported-business value, or $35-40 a share, sits against a $1,580.4bn capitalisation, so 90-91% of the price is an option the filings do not book [S8, S9].
2. The call is carried by the multiple: 103x reported adjusted EBITDA, 106x ex-one-offs, against BYD's 17.3x, a base case of $266 at 70x on $14.5bn of EBITDA, and an expected twelve-month return of -25.2% [S11, S131, S9].
3. Size for the exit, not the chart: a 20-35% SpaceX premium implies $480-540, so cap any short at 2.9% of NAV notional, where a 35% gap costs 1.0% of NAV, and re-underwrite only on a disclosed robotaxi revenue line or a California deployment permit [S154, S89].

## Company Overview

Tesla's legal and ownership structure is plain for a founder-led company — one class of stock, a Texas parent with no VIE or dual-class layer, and a CEO who owns 17.7% of the 3,952,648,559 issued shares (19.8% on the proxy's ex-award basis) — so what constrains a 12-month equity return is not the charter but a 10.7% unearned award struck at market capitalisations from $2 trillion upward, no dividend or buyback, and a classified board that minority holders cannot replace. Tesla trades on Nasdaq under TSLA; market capitalisation was $1.58tn at the $399.81 close on 2026-10-30 [S10, S112].

### One operating group, no holding-company layer

The registrant was incorporated in Delaware on 2003-07-01 and converted to a Texas corporation on 2024-06-13. The structure is flat — country operating companies, single-purpose solar and lease vehicles and insurance captives — with no contractual-control or variable-interest layer between legal and economic ownership. No separate IP holding company is disclosed; the parent files consolidated accounts, while the subsidiaries hold the plants, licences and financing books [S1, S58].

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership | Controller | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tesla, Inc. | Texas, US | Listed corporation | Registrant; consolidated group; public equity | 100% of subsidiaries | Board; Musk 17.7% | S1, S58 |
| Tesla (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. | China | Limited liability company | Shanghai vehicle and Megapack plants | 100% | Tesla, Inc. | S1 |
| Tesla Manufacturing Brandenburg SE | Germany | European company | Berlin vehicle plant | 100% | Tesla, Inc. | S1 |

### The award runs through a $2 trillion gate

Musk holds 699,580,882 shares, 17.7% of the issued count, including 286,428,773 unvested 2018-award shares; 207,498,721 are pledged against personal borrowings. The 2018 award was exercised in full on 2026-06-16 for 303,960,630 shares, lifting the count 202m, or 5.4%, in the nine months to 2026-09-30. The 2025 CEO Performance Award adds 423,743,904 shares, 10.7% of the count, in 12 equal tranches, none earned at 2026-10-19; the proxy shows they are already issued and outstanding, voted by irrevocable proxy and excluded from earnings per share until earned, so vesting dilutes earnings and Musk's economic share without issuing new stock. Each earned share carries a $334.09 offset and a five-year hold, and every tranche needs a market-cap milestone before any operating milestone counts, starting at $2 trillion — 26.6% above the 2026-10-30 value — then nine $500bn and two $1tn increments to $8.5 trillion. At $399.81 the gross spread is $65.72 a share; at the top the transfer is $769.6bn net of offsets, 9.1% of an $8.5 trillion capitalisation. The mechanism favours the holder in a flat tape: below $2tn no tranche earns, so no value transfers and no dilution occurs [S10, S8, S107].

### The cap table reconciles on one denominator

The proxy computes beneficial ownership on the 3,952,648,559 shares outstanding at 2026-09-30, adds options exercisable within 60 days to each holder's own percentage, and subtracts the 423,743,904 unearned shares for Musk and the officer-director group, giving a 3,528,904,655 denominator and his 19.8%. It publishes no float figure and does not say how those shares enter a float calculation; the table below is our residual calculation, and the non-insider float including Vanguard is 2,822,408,040 shares, 71.4% of the issued count [S10].

| Holder | Class | Shares | % of issued | % of votes | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Elon Musk | Common | 699,580,882 | 17.7% | 17.7% | S10 |
| Other directors and officers (10 persons) | Common | 6,915,733 | 0.2% | 0.2% | S10 |
| Vanguard Capital Management | Common | 210,796,512 | 5.3% | 5.3% | S10 |
| 2025 award shares, issued but unearned | Common | 423,743,904 | 10.7% | voted proportionally | S10 |
| Other public holders (residual) | Common | 2,611,611,528 | 66.1% | 66.1% | S10 |
| Total issued and outstanding | Common | 3,952,648,559 | 100.0% | 100.0% | S10 |

### Three P&Ls, and capacity ahead of volume

Three P&Ls have different buyers. Automotive ($69.53bn of FY2025 revenue, 73%) sells vehicles to consumers, lessors and fleets and monetises the installed base through Supercharging, service, parts, used cars and insurance; software is FSD (Supervised), with 1.74m active subscriptions at 2026-09-30. Energy ($12.77bn, 13.5%, 29.8% gross margin) sells Megapack and Powerwall to utilities, developers, industrial sites and data-centre operators whose budget is a power-availability capex line. Services ($12.53bn, +19%) is a captive aftermarket on Tesla's own parc. Growth has shifted from volume — Q3 2026 deliveries were 486,532, down 2% year on year — to storage (13.7 GWh in Q3 2026), software attach and Robotaxi and Optimus optionality. Tesla runs eight plants: Fremont (more than 550,000 units), Shanghai (more than 950,000), Berlin (more than 375,000), Texas (Model Y more than 375,000; Cybertruck and Cybercab more than 125,000 each) and Nevada (Semi 25,000), plus Megapack plants in California (40 GWh), Shanghai (20 GWh) and Texas (50 GWh). Headcount was 134,785 at 2025-12-31; nameplate capacity of 2.53m units against an annualised Q3 2026 run rate of 1.95m leaves a fifth of the system idle, while Semi, Cybercab and Optimus lines add depreciation before revenue [S1, S9].

### No payout, and a board that cannot be replaced

Tesla has never paid a dividend, has no repurchase authorisation and made no purchases in FY2025, while holding $45.45bn of cash and short-term investments; with no distribution, a holder's 12-month total return is the share price alone. Governance reinforces retention: three board classes, a 2025 management proposal to remove supermajority voting won 39.4% of shares outstanding and failed, and the 2026-12-03 meeting asks holders only to elect three Class I directors, cast a say-on-pay vote and ratify the auditor. The counter-evidence is real — one share class is cleaner than Rivian's ten-vote Class B, seven of nine directors are independent, the CEO takes no salary — but none of it returns cash or lets a majority change the charter. For a holder at $399.81 the structure offers no cash yield, caps the upside above $2tn by 9.1%, and gives no route to force a change in capital-return policy: that argues for sizing the position as a price-only bet, not for rejecting the equity. Because a minority holder owns an earnings claim and a vote that cannot change the board, the 12-month return is a bet on the share price; the only discipline is the decision to hold or sell. The open question is whether $1.58tn for $94.83bn of revenue and a 16.2% automotive gross margin leaves anything after that gate is crossed [S1, S10, S114].

## Founding Team & Key Personnel

Tesla's board is majority independent on paper, but the three decisions that mattered in 2024-2026 — a $2.0bn investment in the CEO's own AI company after shareholders rejected the measure, a pay award that can reach 423.7m shares, and the retention of a classified board — all went against the minority's expressed preference, so key-person and capital-allocation risk are real, disclosed, and only partly offset by the award's extreme vesting gates [S10].

### Independence is not the same as accountability

Nine directors sit, seven independent under Nasdaq rules, with Robyn Denholm as independent chair since November 2018 and all four committees independent-only. What matters is elsewhere: three staggered classes, supermajority voting requirements a 2025 management proposal failed to remove with 39.4% of shares outstanding in favour, and two family directors — Elon and Kimbal Musk. Compensation Committee chair Ira Ehrenpreis has also served on SpaceX's board since February 2026, the counterparty to Tesla's $2.0bn investment and $143.3m of 2025 revenue, a relationship the proxy calls immaterial [S10].

### Pay is gated on market value, not on operating return

The 2025 CEO Performance Award is 423,743,904 shares in 12 equal tranches. Each tranche needs a market-cap milestone first — from $2 trillion, 26.6% above the 2026-10-30 value, through nine $500bn and two $1tn steps to $8.5 trillion — and one of 12 operating milestones: four product goals (10m FSD subscriptions, 1m bots delivered, 1m Robotaxis in commercial operation) or eight Adjusted EBITDA goals. Each earned share carries a $334.09 offset and a five-year hold, and tranches 11 and 12 also require a board-approved CEO succession framework, the only formal succession mechanism disclosed. Against that, GM paid Mary Barra $48.2m of realized pay in 2025, while Musk has taken no salary since 2019 and has no employment agreement or severance; reported 2025 total compensation of $158.36bn was an accounting value, realized pay $0 [S10, S107, S109].

### The xAI vote is the test the board failed

At the 2025-11-06 meeting shareholders approved the pay award with 1,892,235,822 votes for and 564,940,908 against, 76.6% of votes cast. A non-binding measure authorising funding for xAI drew 1.06bn for and 916.3m against but was recorded as rejected because Tesla's bylaws count abstentions as votes against; on 2026-01-16 the company nonetheless agreed to invest $2.0bn in xAI, converted to SpaceX Class A stock on 2026-03-12 after the merger. The Audit Committee reviews related-person transactions above $120,000 under a written policy, but the sequence shows the review is procedural: a holder should assume future flows to Musk-controlled companies are a board decision, not a shareholder one [S59, S104, S105].

### One person carries the strategy; the bench is uneven

The 10-K says Musk "does not devote his full time and attention to Tesla" and lists roles at SpaceX, xAI, Neuralink and The Boring Company; the proxy records that xAI became a SpaceX subsidiary in February 2026 and that Musk is SpaceX's CEO, CTO and chairman. The operating bench is strongest in manufacturing and finance: Tom Zhu, SVP APAC and global vehicle manufacturing since June 2025, joined in 2014 and built Gigafactory Shanghai; Vaibhav Taneja has been CFO since August 2023 and inside Tesla's finance function since 2017. Demand execution is the weak spot: Omead Afshar left in June 2025, Troy Jones was dismissed as North American sales head in July 2025, the service head left in August 2025 and Raj Jegannathan departed in February 2026 after 13 years. Headcount was 134,785 at 2025-12-31; the attrition is concentrated in senior commercial roles [S1, S111, S124].

### What the record confirms, and what diligence must settle

Public records confirm founder-market fit: Musk co-founded Zip2 (sold to Compaq in 1999) and PayPal (sold to eBay in 2002), has run Tesla since October 2008, and still owns 17.7% of the issued count (19.8% on the proxy's basis) with 207,498,721 shares pledged. They also confirm the concentration: no chief operating officer, no permanent North American sales leader, a board with no director who has run a vehicle programme at another OEM, and a CEO whose other companies are now suppliers, investees and counterparties. Diligence should close the succession plan behind tranches 11-12, the lenders behind the pledge, the fairness opinion, if any, for the $2.0bn xAI/SpaceX purchase, and references on Zhu and Taneja. For a 12-month holder the concentration is not a separately observable discount in the share price: it argues for a smaller position and for demanding evidence that Zhu and Taneja can run the operating business while Musk is elsewhere [S10, S2].

**Execution is proven in manufacturing, not the boardroom: Shanghai ramped while a related-party investment proceeded after shareholders rejected it.**

Tom Zhu built Gigafactory Shanghai, the largest plant at more than 950,000 units, and Berlin set a quarterly production record in Q3 2026; Tesla passed 10.2m cumulative vehicles. The counterweight is procedural: an xAI funding measure lost 1.06bn to 916.3m, yet $2.0bn was committed five weeks later, and the Compensation Committee chair sits on SpaceX's board (S9, S104, S10).

## Technology & Product

Tesla's technology position in 2026 is two facts usually merged in the narrative: the largest supervised-driving data pool and one of the cheapest large-scale EV manufacturing bases in the industry, and almost no verified driverless revenue. Active FSD subscriptions reached 1.74 million at 30 September 2026, 17.1% of the 10.2 million vehicles delivered to date, while cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles were 2.0 million, 0.9% of the 220.6 million rider-only miles Waymo had logged through March 2026. The 1.74 million includes upfront FSD purchases and monthly subscriptions and excludes free trials; management put half the paid base on monthly plans on 21 October 2026, so 870,000 are subscribers worth $1.0bn a year at list and 870,000 are one-time buyers. ### The safety file is the binding constraint

NHTSA's Office of Defects Investigation opened Engineering Analysis EA26002 on 18 March 2026 into whether FSD detects degraded visibility — glare, fog, dust — and warns the driver in time, covering 3,203,754 vehicles, after nine confirmed incidents including one pedestrian fatality; a second FSD probe covers 2,882,566 vehicles and 80 traffic-law incidents. Tesla's own analysis reportedly found its degradation-detection update "may have affected" only 3 of 9 incidents, which points to an architectural limit of camera-only sensing. An engineering analysis is the last step before a recall, and a recall would narrow the operating domain or force hardware across millions of cars whose liability terms for paid driverless rides are not disclosed [S87, S88, S100].

**The camera-only bet is being tested by the regulator, not the market.** EA26002 covers 3.2 million FSD-equipped vehicles and Tesla's fix reportedly addresses a third of the reviewed incidents [S87, S88].

Confidence is high on filings, medium on driverless scale, low on Optimus and robotaxi unit economics, where disclosure is absent. The disclosures that would move this: Robotaxi revenue, paid trips and cost per trip reported quarterly; a California driverless deployment permit; and dry-electrode cell cost per kWh against purchased cells. If the first and third come good while the engineering analysis closes without a hardware remedy, the option is worth more than a pilot; a recall that restricts the operating domain would remove the revenue bridge.

## Market & Industry Analysis

Tesla's problem is not that its markets are small; it is that the two that made it are contracting while the two that grow are priced per unit, not per promise. Global electric-car sales are expected to reach 23.0 million units in 2026, 28% of all car sales, from more than 20 million in 2025, and the IEA projects half of global sales by 2035 [S9, S137]. Dividing 23.0 million by 28% implies 82 million light vehicles, so the electric pool is the whole case: Tesla delivered 1,324,681 vehicles in the first nine months of 2026 (358,023; 480,126; 486,532) — a run-rate of 1.77 million, or 7.7% of the 2026 electric pool and 2.2% of all cars. Unit growth of 15% in 2026 slows to a 7.7% CAGR to 2035 on the IEA's own 50%-share projection, while Tesla's third quarter fell 2% year on year. That is a share problem inside a decelerating market: what an investor buys is not category growth but the price Tesla can hold for a differentiated slice of it.

### The two largest pools shrank by policy, not by demand

Removing the $7,500 federal credit on 2025-09-30 cut the US electric pool by 30.3% year to date: sales fell 36% year on year in Q4 2025, and were 30.3% below the prior year through September 2026 after a 7.7% sequential rebound to 266,630 in Q3, when electric cars were 6.4% of US new-vehicle sales and Tesla's own US volume fell 14.4%. China's new-energy retail fell 16.7% year on year to 1.084 million in September 2026, the ninth consecutive decline, and 12.8% to 7.758 million in nine months, while penetration hit a record 67.0% only because total passenger-car retail fell 28.0%; battery-electric retail fell 7.4%, plug-in hybrid retail 35.6% and range-extended electric 19.3%, while battery-electric wholesale rose 18.3% and NEV exports 163.5% to 558,000. Tightening China's purchase-tax preference and withdrawing local subsidies raised the cash price of the cheapest cars first and pushed production abroad. Tesla held 52.9% of the smaller US pool and was China's fourth-largest NEV brand by retail at 64,837 units: US equity value is now a bet on a 6-7% electric share of the US market in 2027, and China is a capped, price-deflationary market whose growth reaches Tesla through exports that carry tariffs [S138, S139, S145].

### Europe is the only vehicle market growing fast enough to matter

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,931,465 in January-September 2026, a 22.7% share against 16.1% a year earlier, and September alone ran at 290,117 units and a 29.9% share, up 72.9% year on year on a total market up 5.7%. On those two shares the electric pool grew 49% in units, the only large market where Tesla can add volume without cutting price. EU demand is regulation-created: the 2025-2027 CO2 step forces fleet averages down, and the Commission's 2025-12-16 proposal to replace the 100% 2035 target with a 90% cut has moved the long-dated backstop into Parliament and Council, where ministers remain split. Europe carries Tesla's 2026 volume growth (Berlin posted record production in Q3 2026), and that growth is capped by a policy being renegotiated while it is relied upon [S140, S147].

### Storage compounds in volume and deflates in price

Global storage installations reached 112 GW in 2025 and are forecast at 158 GW and 459 GWh in 2026, a 41% annual increase, with BloombergNEF seeing 3.1 TW cumulative by 2036. Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in the first nine months of 2026, 7.8% of the forecast pool, but revenue per GWh fell to $210 million from $273 million — 23% — because Q3 energy revenue fell 16% while deployments rose 9.6%. The reported 33.1% energy gross margin is not the underlying one: $526 million of IEEPA tariff refunds and warranty true-ups sit in cost of revenue, leaving $428 million on $2,881 million, or 14.8%, below CATL's 23.96% energy-storage segment and Sungrow's 32.43% storage margin in H1 2026 and only just above Fluence's 13.1% fiscal-2025 margin. Demand is structural in that Tesla reports its highest-ever order rate and ties backlog to data-centre load growth, not subsidies; but model the segment on revenue per GWh falling faster than volume rises, at a mid-teens clean margin rather than the as-reported figure [S8, S9, S141, S167, S166, S172, S66].

### Paid robotaxi is a Waymo-sized business, not a market yet

The only scaled paid autonomous service is Waymo's: 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities as of 2026-03-27, which is 26 million a year and, at an assumed $12-18 average fare, a $0.3-0.5 billion business; Waymo had logged 220.6 million rider-only miles through March 2026 with about 3,700 vehicles. Third-party research puts the 2026 robotaxi market at $3.5-5.5 billion and 2030 estimates span $27-204 billion, a 7.3x spread that marks sizes built from ride-hailing spend rather than observed fares. Tesla is scaling from a smaller base: the Texas authorisation list showed 1,051 Robotaxi vehicles on 2026-10-27 (544 Cybercab, 507 Model Y), up from 739 on 2026-10-09 on the same list, against Waymo's 3,700, and Tesla reports about 2.0 million cumulative unsupervised miles, 0.9% of Waymo's rider-only total. Tesla discloses no ride count, fare or robotaxi revenue, and no operator discloses insurance, remote supervision or cost per paid mile — the three numbers that decide whether a fare business earns a margin. The serviceable market by 2028 is therefore set by permits and per-mile safety evidence, not TAM studies: a $50 billion 2028 robotaxi line would require Tesla to overtake the incumbent and multiply the 2026 paid market more than twenty-fold [S142, S144, S125, S151, S9, S153].

The implication is allocation, not enthusiasm: Europe and storage are the only growing pools, but storage's clean margin is mid-teens and paid autonomy remains small in fare terms, so neither supports the bull branch that rests on an autonomy proof and a SpaceX combination. Treat US vehicle revenue as share defence at a lower market level, value paid autonomy at zero until rides and fares are disclosed, and let the base and bear branches carry the weight the scenarios already give them. What would move this assessment: Tesla's regional unit split, the contracted price per MWh in its storage backlog, and its Austin ride count and average fare.

## Competitive Landscape

Tesla is winning the market that is shrinking and losing the one that is growing. It holds the US electric-vehicle market at a share no rival approaches while that market contracts, ranks fourth among China's new-energy brands in a pool that is itself shrinking, and its European recovery has come inside a pool growing faster than it. What Tesla owns is narrower than the narrative: the charging standard every major automaker has licensed, 1.74 million paid FSD subscriptions, and a storage business whose 33.1% reported gross margin falls to 14.8% once $526 million of tariff refunds and warranty true-ups are removed — mid-pack against CATL and Sungrow, not ahead of them [S8, S9, S167].

### In the United States, Tesla sets the price because it holds the pool

Tesla sold 144,094 US electric vehicles in Q3 2026 for 54% of the market, and 386,194 in nine months for 52.9%, with US volume down 14.4% against a market down 30.3%. Share gains in a contracting pool flatter the position. When a $7,500 credit disappears, the brand with the densest charging footprint keeps the remaining buyers. The question is whether Tesla can hold price, and it has — automotive gross margin rose to 18.5% in Q3 2026 from 17.0% [S145, S8].

### China is where Tesla is the price taker

BYD sold 456,713 passenger cars in September 2026, 273,143 of them battery-electric, and 3,078,490 in nine months — 2.3 times Tesla's 1,324,681. Geely sold 119,682 and Xiaomi 40,015 retail units in September. BYD earned 19.46% gross margin overseas against 16.66% at home in 2025, a domestic ceiling Tesla cannot price above; Tesla's China retail of 64,837 was 3.8 times smaller than BYD's in September while Chinese battery-electric wholesale grew 18.3%. In driver assistance, Huawei and Momenta together supply more than 80% of China's urban NOA systems, Momenta alone 65% [S138, S146, S149, S168].

### Europe: growth in units, no evidence of share

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,931,465 in January-September 2026 at a 22.7% share, with September at 29.9%, so the pool expanded 49% while Tesla's European deliveries recovered from a 2025 slump. A recovery off a collapsed base inside a pool growing that fast is not share gain; Tesla discloses no EU unit count, and ACEA's manufacturer table would settle it. Volkswagen, Renault, Stellantis and Hyundai-Kia sell compliance models; tariffed Chinese BEVs undercut. Tesla's handicap is a two-model line-up: Model 3/Y were 478,237 of 486,532 deliveries in Q3 2026 [S140, S147].

### Storage: integration, not a cost moat

The 33.1% energy gross margin Tesla reported for Q3 2026 is not comparable with an integrator's clean number: $526 million of IEEPA tariff refunds and warranty true-ups sit inside cost of revenue, so the underlying margin is $428 million on $2,881 million, or 14.8%. On that basis Tesla is mid-pack: Fluence earned 13.1% in fiscal 2025 and 5.1% in the June 2026 quarter, CATL's energy-storage segment 23.96% in H1 2026, Sungrow's storage segment 32.43%, and LG Energy Solution a 1.5% operating margin in Q2 2026 [S8, S9, S61, S66, S167, S166, S172, S169]. Integration does not show up as a margin outlier, and revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million as system prices deflated. The counter-evidence is scale: 36.0 GWh in nine months and Autobidder may still give Tesla the lowest installed cost per project even at a mid-teens margin.

### In paid autonomy Tesla trails, and in driver assistance it is no longer alone

Waymo ran 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities by March 2026 with about 3,700 vehicles and had logged 220.6 million rider-only miles through March 2026. Tesla began Cybercab rides in Austin on 2026-09-03 and stood at 1,051 vehicles on the Texas authorisation list on 2026-10-27 (544 Cybercab, 507 Model Y); it reports 2.0 million cumulative unsupervised miles, 0.9% of Waymo's rider-only total, is absent from California's driverless deployment permits, and discloses no ride count or fare. Baidu's Apollo Go ran 3.4 million trips in Q4 2025; Pony.ai passed 1,400 vehicles in March 2026. Insurance, teleoperation and cost per paid mile are undisclosed; a 10-20% swing in autonomy value turns on them. The supervised market is not Tesla's either: GM's Super Cruise is hands-free on about 750,000 compatible miles in the US and Canada, Ford's BlueCruise on more than 130,000 Blue Zone miles, and comma.ai's openpilot sells aftermarket kits with no OEM fleet. FSD's 1.74 million subscriptions are the largest single pool, but hands-free highway driving is now a $40-50 a month OEM feature, which caps what Tesla can charge and explains a 17.1% attach rate [S151, S125, S142, S171, S130, S170].

## Business Model

Tesla sells cars, storage and services, and the returns are lower than the headlines suggest: the car earned an 18.1% ex-credit gross margin in Q3 2026, short of group research and selling cost; storage's 33.1% falls to 14.8% without the $526M IEEPA tariff refund; and interest income supplied 46.5% of pre-tax profit. The return is earned on a mixed gross-profit pool and cash pile, not a structurally superior unit economic model. The automotive segment took 73.3% of third-quarter 2026 revenue ($20,560M of $28,046M), services and other 16.4% ($4,605M) and energy generation and storage 10.3% ($2,881M). The buyer differs in each: a retail or fleet customer pays cash or finances a car at transfer of control; an energy customer — a utility, developer or data-centre operator — pays on project milestones across quarters; a service customer pays per transaction for repair, maintenance or charging; another automaker pays for regulatory credits at transfer of title. Energy was 6.2% of FY2023 revenue ($6,035M) and 13.5% in FY2025 ($12,771M), while automotive revenue fell from $82,419M to $69,526M; the recurring software charge is FSD (Supervised) at $99 a month, with 1.74 million active subscriptions at 2026-09-30 [S8, S9, S1, S121].

Services and other grew revenue 33% to $4,605M and gross profit to a record $734M, 15.9%, from 14.1% in Q2 2026 and 10.5% a year earlier; Rivian's software and services segment earned 42% on $605M, so Tesla's margin is below the best comparable on 7.6 times the revenue. Interest income of $1,301M was 42.9% of nine-month pre-tax income and $445M was 46.5% of the Q3 2026 figure, against 17.5% in FY2024.
